cards.question: Jailed by Italy's Fascist regime, a Marxist wrote that the old is dying and the new cannot be born, and that in this _____ a great variety of morbid symptoms appear.
cards.abstract:
The interregnum began as a legal term for the gap between one ruler and the next, a notion traced back to Roman law and later adopted in Europe. Its best-known political use comes from the Italian Marxist Antonio Gramsci, whom Italy's Fascist regime imprisoned in 1926 and who died in 1937. He used the word in only one entry of his prison notebooks, the 34th of the third notebook, written in 1930. There he ties it to a 'crisis of authority', in which a ruling class that has lost the consent of the masses is no longer 'leading' but only 'dominant', exercising coercive force alone. The crisis, he wrote, consists precisely in the fact that the old is dying and the new cannot be born, and in this interregnum a great variety of morbid symptoms appear.

International relations scholars used the word in a neutral sense for the decade after 1989, but Gramsci's line became common only after the financial crisis of 2008, when Zygmunt Bauman and Slavoj Žižek invoked it around 2011 and 2012. Rune Møller Stahl argues that the periods between one stable hegemony and the next are undertheorised, and he applies the concept to a neoliberal hegemony shaken in 2008 with no clear successor. For world order, Milan Babic argues that the liberal international order is in crisis, that most writers study either what is dying or what comes next, and that the interregnum between them could last years or even decades. In his account the crisis of authority arises because states withdraw their support, leaving a void that the old actors cannot fill, and the morbid symptoms include leaders who undermine institutions and open hostility to multilateral cooperation. The phrase has costs, since one critic says it has been reduced to an analytical meme, and one close reading holds that Gramsci meant the ultra-left turn of his own party rather than the rise of fascism.

Writers on world order say the US-led liberal order is in crisis, stuck in an _____ between a dying order and a successor that could take decades to emerge.

cards.question: A state that sits in the Quad with the United States and also in BRICS, choosing partners issue by issue rather than joining one bloc, is practising _____ in its foreign policy.
cards.answerDate: Bandung1955NAM founded1961À la carteAugust 2023
cards.abstract:
Multi-alignment is a foreign-policy approach in which a state builds partnerships with several rival powers at once instead of committing to one bloc, choosing partners on different issues. A 2023 article in the Financial Times called the wider pattern the 'à la carte world', in which a fixed menu of alliances gives way to a more fluid order. The article's example was Kenya, which in one summer received American, Russian, European Union and Chinese officials, because, as one analyst put it, it is 'a question of picking everyone'. Non-alignment is older and collective: the Bandung conference of 1955 brought together 29 Asian and African governments and laid the foundation for a movement that tried to avoid taking sides in the Cold War. That movement was formally established in 1961, yet non-alignment should not be confused with neutralism, because India kept out of both blocs but was neither neutral nor indifferent on every question.

India shows the pattern, since it belongs to the Quad with Australia, Japan and the United States and also to BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, described in one policy paper as led by China and Russia. India's foreign minister has called this a time to 'engage America, manage China, cultivate Europe, reassure Russia' and bring Japan into play. South Africa professes non-alignment and belongs to no military alliance, yet it hosted naval exercises with China and Russia in February 2023 and has also exercised with the United States, France, Germany, India and Brazil. For middle powers such as India, Turkey and Brazil, open lines to ideologically diverse partners create chances to broker deals, and the stand-off between Washington and Beijing lets many play one off against the other. Whether this is a new strategy is debated: one analysis calls non-alignment and multi-alignment 'two sides of the same coin', and others find non-alignment living on in India's strategic autonomy and in the stances of India, Brazil and South Africa over Ukraine.

cards.question: A leader who must reach a bargain abroad and then win ratification from legislators, unions or other supporters at home is said to be playing a _____, with both bargains interlocked.
cards.answerDate: Versailles vote19 March 1920Bonn summit1978Theory set out1988
cards.abstract:
A two-level game is a model of diplomacy in which a leader bargains at two tables at once, with foreign counterparts and with the domestic constituents who must approve the result. The political scientist Robert Putnam set the model out in 1988 as a theory of ratification, arguing that state-centred theories could not explain the links between domestic and international politics. He divided the process into Level I, the bargaining between negotiators that produces a provisional agreement, and Level II, the separate discussions among domestic supporters about whether to ratify it. Ratification means any Level II decision needed to endorse or implement a deal, from a formal vote to the cooperation of trade unions in a debtor country that has agreed austerity with the International Monetary Fund. It need not be democratic, since in 1930 the Meiji Constitution was read as giving the Japanese military a special role in ratifying the London Naval Treaty.

The central idea is the win-set, the set of all Level I agreements that would win the necessary support at Level II, and a deal is possible only if the two sides' win-sets overlap. Larger win-sets make agreement likelier, but a small win-set can be a bargaining weapon, because a negotiator can say he would accept a proposal but could never get it accepted at home. Pressure from abroad can also help a negotiator at home, as at the Bonn summit of 1978, which Putnam argues succeeded because a powerful minority in each government favoured the policy demanded internationally. The danger is rejection at home, as when the Treaty of Versailles fell seven votes short in the United States Senate on 19 March 1920, although President Woodrow Wilson had championed the League of Nations. Later work explains a win-set's boundaries by an issue's salience and the credibility of domestic sanctions and finds evidence of two-level games in the Oslo accord talks, though one comparison finds its assumptions clash with policy-process frameworks.

cards.question: As rivalry spreads from armies into trade, chips, finance and navigation, analysts speak of the _____, in which ordinary economic links between states are turned into tools of pressure.
cards.abstract:
The weaponisation of everything is a phrase for the spread of coercion from armies into the ordinary links between states, such as trade, finance, technology and energy. The EU's 2023 economic security strategy lists the weaponisation of economic dependencies or economic coercion as one of four broad categories of risk. It defines the danger as third countries using measures on trade or investment to bring about a change of policy that lies within legitimate policymaking space. In one influential account, the networks of globalisation became so centralised that governments able to control a few key firms could gather information about rivals or shut them out of vital points in the economy. After 2001 the United States used dollar clearing, correspondent banks and the SWIFT messaging network, first against terrorist finance and later to cut whole countries such as Iran out of the global financial system.

Technology is another arena, because American firms control chip design software and China controls about 90 per cent of rare earth processing, and each has built export controls that exploit the chokepoint it holds. Central bank economists note that China's rare earth controls of April 2025 showed how such dominance can serve as leverage in trade talks, although they were too brief to affect output. Trade offers a further case, since in 2021 China blocked all goods of Lithuanian origin, direct or indirect, over a Taiwanese office in Vilnius, and Lithuania's direct exports to China fell by nearly 70 per cent without changing its course. Navigation is a fourth arena, as eight EU states told the Council in June 2025 that jamming and spoofing of satellite signals was a systematic, deliberate action that could serve as a hybrid attack, one in which causing damage had been simple and cheap. Rules are lagging, and two analysts judge that the EU's anti-coercion instrument is encumbered by legal safeguards that lead China and the United States to doubt it will ever be used against them.
questions: When China blocked all goods of Lithuanian origin in 2021 after Taiwan opened an office in Vilnius, it was cited as an example of the _____ in the arena of trade.

The EU's 2023 economic security strategy treats the risk that dependencies become weapons as one of four categories of risk, a danger that some summarise as the _____ across trade, technology and finance.

cards.question: When two economies can each cripple the other's industry, the prospect of equal damage may deter escalation, a logic of _____ that analysts compare with nuclear deterrence.
cards.answerDate: Peak tariffsApril 2025Geneva truce12 May 2025
cards.abstract:
Mutually assured economic pain is the idea that two economies able to hurt each other badly are deterred from escalating, much as nuclear rivals were deterred by the prospect of mutual destruction. One policy note calls this economic mutually assured destruction and argues that deterrence does not need equal strength, only a weaker side able to impose costs high enough to matter. Its raw material is dependence on chokepoints, since American firms control the chip design software that China needs while China controls about 90 per cent of rare earth processing. Two US-based scholars describe the wider age of weaponised interdependence as one in which Washington finds that others can do to it what it has long done to them through chokepoints in finance, information and technology. They compare the spread of such economic weapons with the spread of nuclear weapons, which also created new dilemmas for the major powers.

In April 2025 the escalation ran quickly, as Washington raised its additional duty on Chinese goods to 125 per cent from 10 April and Beijing matched it at 125 per cent two days later. China had already imposed licensing controls on seven rare earth elements on 4 April, which central bank economists judge effectively pressed the United States to return to the negotiating table. The United States gets about 75 per cent of its rare earth imports from China, so supply cuts threaten carmakers and electronics firms most. On 12 May a joint statement issued in Geneva cut both sides' April increases to 10 per cent for an initial 90 days from 14 May and set up a mechanism for further talks. The statement mentioned neither chips nor rare earths, chip software concessions came in later talks, and the policy note calls the standoff 'unstable stability' that could end if either side escaped the other's chokepoint.
questions: In April 2025 tit-for-tat tariffs between Washington and Beijing climbed to 125 per cent before a truce in Geneva, an episode that some analysts read as _____ restraining both sides.
Chinese control of rare earth processing, set against American control of chip design software, gave each side a chokepoint, a standoff of _____ that paused the escalation in May 2025.

cards.question: Unlike jamming, which merely drowns out satellite signals with noise, _____ broadcasts counterfeit signals so that a receiver computes a false position while appearing to work normally.
cards.abstract:
GPS spoofing is the broadcasting of counterfeit satellite navigation signals so that a receiver calculates a false position, speed or time while appearing to work normally. It differs from jamming, which only drowns out the genuine signals with noise so that receivers cannot lock on to them. Military GPS waveforms are designed to be unpredictable and so resist spoofing, whereas civil waveforms are unencrypted, unauthenticated and openly published, which makes them an easy target. In 2013 a university team used a briefcase-sized device costing about 2,000 US dollars to push a superyacht worth 80 million US dollars off course by several degrees without tripping a single alarm. Because satellite signals reach the ground very weakly, a low-power transmitter near a vessel can overpower them, and a gradual drift of this kind can pass for the effect of currents or wind.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency reports a notable rise in jamming and spoofing since February 2022, particularly around conflict zones and sensitive areas that include the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea. A 2019 study counted 9,883 suspected spoofing episodes at ten locations in Russia, Crimea and Syria that affected 1,311 civilian vessels, and linked some of them to the protection of leaders and facilities against drones. In 2017 at least 20 ships near the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk reported positions at an airport about 32 kilometres (20 miles) inland, and in 2021 trackers showed two NATO warships heading for Sevastopol although satellite imagery put them still at Odessa. In June 2025 eight EU states told the Council that jamming and spoofing in Baltic airspace, which they traced mainly to Russia and Belarus, had risen sharply since August 2024 and was a systematic, deliberate action. No international agreement clearly forbids jamming or spoofing, partly because states also use jamming defensively against drones and remotely triggered bombs, so one legal study finds the rules fragmented and the practice's status uncertain.

cards.question: In September 2022 an army captain, _____, deposed Burkina Faso's junta leader Damiba, accusing him of failing to contain jihadist violence, and went on to rule the country.
cards.abstract:
Ibrahim Traoré is the army captain who has led Burkina Faso since September 2022, when he overthrew Lieutenant Colonel Paul-Henri Damiba in the country's second coup of that year. He was then a relatively unknown officer who had at first backed the January coup, and he justified the takeover by pointing to Damiba's failure to contain jihadist violence and his reluctance to broaden security partnerships. One study reads the September coup as a revolt of junior officers against senior ones that reflected grievances among front-line soldiers. The first coup had followed an attack on military police at Inata in November 2021, and soldiers' anguish over battlefield losses was a key grievance against elected politicians. A briefing on that January coup noted that its leaders justified it by the fight against armed groups and that, unlike in 2015, unions and mass organisations did not mobilise active resistance.

Citing nationalist appeals to sovereignty, the Sahelian juntas halted military cooperation with France, and in 2023 the military governments of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger formed the Alliance of Sahel States. A study of the coups' digital narratives finds that Traoré's supporters present him as a young, disciplined and patriotic leader in the mould of Thomas Sankara, through murals, T-shirts and viral videos. The same study says the junta's claim to legitimacy is built mainly on security restoration, patriotic sacrifice and national survival. The Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland, a civilian force created in 2020 to arm villagers against extremists, were expanded in size and mandate by the junta, a step that one analysis says has further worsened the crisis. Assessments divide, since some see in him a figure of decolonisation, national sovereignty and Pan-Africanism while others accuse him of authoritarianism and of repressing civil society and the media, and the election planned for July 2024 was postponed indefinitely.

cards.question: Around the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, Spain's prime minister _____ argued that a 5 per cent defence target was incompatible with the welfare state and that 2.1 per cent would suffice.
cards.abstract:
Pedro Sánchez is the Socialist prime minister of Spain, whose government says it raised defence spending from 0.9 per cent of GDP in 2018 to 2 per cent in 2025. At The Hague on 25 June 2025 NATO leaders committed to invest 5 per cent of GDP a year on core defence and on defence- and security-related spending by 2035. That total comprises at least 3.5 per cent of GDP for core defence requirements and up to 1.5 per cent for areas such as infrastructure, cybersecurity and resilience, with the plan to be reviewed in 2029. In 2024 Spain spent the lowest share of GDP in the alliance, 1.28 per cent on preliminary NATO figures that its government disputed, and it announced a rise of 10.4 billion euros for 2025. At home his minority coalition is divided, since its junior partner Sumar voted for a March 2025 motion that rejected more defence spending and called for Spain to leave NATO.

On 22 June 2025 Sánchez announced an agreement under which, he said, Spain would not raise spending to 5 per cent, a level he called incompatible with the welfare state and with Spain's view of the world. He argued that Spain's armed forces had calculated that 2.1 per cent of GDP would meet NATO's capability targets, and that 5 per cent would force tax rises or severe social cuts. After the summit he told reporters that NATO, Spain, security and the welfare state had all won, and Spain signed the declaration all the same. Mark Rutte, NATO's Secretary General, called it an agreement to disagree, since Spain thought it could meet its capability targets at 2.1 per cent while NATO held that it had to be 3.5 per cent, as for all allies. Analysts note that GDP percentages are a useful political benchmark but cannot settle what a fair share is, because decisions on defence spending are in the end political.

NATO's Mark Rutte called it an agreement to disagree when the Spanish prime minister _____ insisted on meeting capability targets with 2.1 per cent of GDP rather than 3.5 per cent.

cards.question: Jailed under Mussolini, a Marxist described a _____ as the condition in which a ruling class has lost the consent of the masses and can govern only by coercive force.
cards.abstract:
A crisis of authority is a condition in which a ruling class has lost the consent of the people it governs and holds power by coercion alone. The Italian Marxist Antonio Gramsci framed it as a loss of leadership, since a ruling class that is no longer 'leading' is only 'dominant'. In his account the great masses have become detached from their traditional ideologies and no longer believe what they used to believe. He identified it with the crisis of the ruling class's hegemony, which he also called the general crisis of the State. It counts as an organic crisis rather than a conjunctural one, because it concerns wider social groupings and not only top leaders, and it can last for decades.

Gramsci traced it to a failure in some major undertaking, such as a war, for which the masses had been asked or forced to consent, or to huge masses passing suddenly from passivity to political activity. The 'represented' then drift from their 'representatives', and the situation becomes dangerous because the field lies open to violent solutions and to charismatic 'men of destiny'. One recent reading adds that where hegemony and legitimacy are gone only force remains, which is defensive, reactive and ever more naked in its exercise. Later writers have applied the idea to domestic politics, finding a crisis of authority for political elites in Britain around the Brexit vote and a breakdown in the authority of established parties in the United States and across Europe. At the level of world order, one account says the crisis arises when states withdraw support for the liberal order, while another doubts that a United States increasingly reliant on political and military means can sustain its hegemony.
questions: In one Marxist analysis, a ruling class that fails in a war it demanded consent for, or faces masses suddenly entering politics, suffers a _____, equated with a general crisis of the State.
Observers of the liberal international order argue that a _____ arises when states withdraw their support for it, leaving a void that its old defenders cannot fill.

cards.question: After a system containing one state in a class by itself comes to an end, scholars speak of a _____ and study how the former hegemon and rising powers adapt.
cards.abstract:
A post-unipolar world is one that has left unipolarity, a system containing one state whose share of capabilities places it in a class by itself. The idea of unipolarity entered the debate when the Cold War ended, as a columnist argued that the new world was not multipolar but unipolar, with the United States as the unchallenged superpower. He expected multipolarity to come in time, perhaps in another generation or so, and called the present the unipolar moment. Scholars define unipolarity differently, so that one definition requires a single state able to run sustained military operations far from home unaided, and another that one state holds over half of all capabilities. Scholars now also write of a post-unipolar era and study how leaving unipolarity changes the strategies of the former hegemon and of rising powers, above all China.

After the financial crisis of 2008 and China's economic rise, claims that unipolarity is ending or has ended became common, including a 2012 assessment by the United States National Intelligence Council that the 'unipolar moment' was over. One scholar argued in 2012 that the Great Recession showed the distribution of power was no longer unipolar and that the era of American ascendancy that began in 1945 was winding down. A realist account takes the world to have become multipolar in or close to 2016, because the rise of China and the revival of Russian power ended the unipolar era on which the liberal international order depended. Others reject that verdict, since one study holds that the United States will long remain the only state with the capability to be a superpower, with China in a class by itself but nowhere near a peer. A third view says the emerging order is multiplex rather than multipolar, with no single hegemon, and a 2023 poll found multipolarity the most popular expectation in China and Russia, while Europeans and Americans mostly expected bipolarity.
questions: The 2008 financial crisis and China's economic ascent led many to say that America's post-Cold War dominance had ended, ushering in what some call a _____ without a single dominant state.
Whether a _____ has truly arrived is disputed, since one realist dates multipolarity to about 2016 while another study holds that only the United States can still be a superpower.

cards.question: A lecture course names the United States, China, India, Russia and the European Union as the world's _____, a word that scholars define by broad capabilities exercised globally and acknowledged by other states.
cards.abstract:
Any claim of five superpowers has to meet a demanding test, since one standard definition requires a broad spectrum of capabilities, military and economic, exercised across the whole system and acknowledged by other states. A second definition adds that a superpower must dominate its own region and extend its reach and influence beyond it. On the first definition, great powers differ from superpowers in that they need not be strong in every field and may rest on economic or nuclear strength alone. Economic size alone separates the United States, the European Union and China, with gross domestic products in 2024 of about 29.3, 19.5 and 18.7 trillion dollars, from India at 3.8 and Russia at 2.2. In nuclear weapons Russia and the United States together possess around 90 per cent of the world's total, while China is estimated to have at least 600 warheads.

Scholars therefore count superpowers very differently, and one study holds that the United States will long remain the only state with the capability to be a superpower, with China in a class by itself but nowhere near a peer. Another study argues that Europe is the only superpower besides the United States, because only these two can project the full range from hard to soft power, and that China and India must wait several generations. A realist account counts three great powers, the United States, China and Russia, calls Russia by far the weakest of them, and expects most European states to join a US-led bounded order. On India, one 2017 assessment judged it still a rising middle power that would probably not be among the Great Powers within a decade. For the European Union, a long-standing gap between expectations and capability means that becoming a new pole in place of the Soviet Union proved the least accurate of the roles once expected of it.
questions: With a 2024 economy of about 2.2 trillion dollars against America's 29.3 trillion, Russia is the smallest of the so-called _____ yet holds, with America, around 90 per cent of nuclear weapons.
Scholars cannot agree how many superpowers exist, with answers ranging from one to two, so the claim of _____ is contested.

cards.question: States dissatisfied with the existing rules of order or the distribution of power, unlike satisfied status-quo states, are called _____, a label central to power transition theory.
cards.abstract:
Revisionist powers are states dissatisfied with the international order or the distribution of power, while status-quo powers are satisfied with both. In power transition thinking a rising state that accepts the rules lets the order endure, but one that wants more status or new rules forces the leader to accommodate it or face a challenge. One proposal splits revisionism into two wishes, to change the rules of order and to change the balance of military power, giving status-quo actors, reformists who want only new rules, positionalists who want only a different balance of power, and revolutionaries who want both. In its 2017 National Security Strategy the United States officially named China and Russia as revisionist powers threatening its interests. Politics at home can drive revisionism too, since one study argues that representational crises raise the appeal of sovereigntist frames that push leaders towards revisionist foreign policy.

On Russia, a study of its legal arguments from 2014 to 2019 found little sign of a sustained effort to change international law, yet concluded that Moscow still seems to aspire to revise regional power relations. Some scholars find Moscow far more aggressively revisionist than Beijing, and one explanation is that Russia faces a closing window of opportunity while China prospers under the present order. China is harder to place, since a study of its leaders' travel from 1998 to 2008 found behaviour more consistent with a status-quo state, with exceptions such as visits to rogue states. One 2025 study sets a pro-Western Middle Eastern camp led by Saudi Arabia against an anti-Western camp led by Iran and argues that Turkey, joining neither, has increasingly taken a revisionist orientation. Critics add that the label is political, since China and the United States each present their positions as defending established norms while casting the other as the threat, and a declining hegemon can itself turn revisionist.
questions: The 2017 United States National Security Strategy officially labelled China and Russia as _____ threatening American interests, a label that critics call political.
Moscow is sometimes judged more aggressive than Beijing among _____, one explanation being that Russia faces a closing window of opportunity while China prospers under the present order.

cards.question: Born in the demand that empires end, _____ now also criticises neo-colonial control, in which a formally independent state has its economic system and policy directed from outside.
cards.abstract:
Anti-colonialism began as the demand to end foreign rule, and in 1960 the UN General Assembly proclaimed the necessity of ending colonialism speedily and unconditionally in all its forms and manifestations. That declaration called subjugation, domination and exploitation of peoples a denial of fundamental human rights and affirmed that all peoples have the right to self-determination. In 1955, 29 Asian and African governments met at Bandung to discuss decolonisation, economic development and the Third World's role in the Cold War. Independence did not end the argument, as Kwame Nkrumah wrote in 1965 that a neo-colonial state has all the outward trappings of sovereignty while its economic system and policy are directed from outside. Two scholars argue that anticolonial thinkers did more than criticise the West, since they also had a constructive theoretical agenda that postcolonial political thought has taken up.

In 2019 the International Court of Justice advised that the decolonisation of Mauritius was not lawfully completed at independence in 1968 and that the United Kingdom must end its administration of the Chagos Archipelago as rapidly as possible. The Court called resolution 1514 a defining moment in state practice on decolonisation and found that a non-self-governing territory's right to territorial integrity has customary law character. The language of redress also reaches diplomacy, since the 2024 Pact for the Future lists redressing the historical injustice against Africa as a priority in its parameters for reforming the Security Council. Over Ukraine, one analysis found Global South leaders exasperated at Western hypocrisy about sovereignty, over 40 UN members abstaining or voting against condemnations of Russia, and many states looking beyond the liberal system to address what they see as its structural deficiencies. The same analysis notes that these states share a history of Western colonialism and imperialism yet are divided along national and ideological lines.
questions: A 2019 International Court of Justice opinion on the Chagos Archipelago shows how _____, whose principles the General Assembly proclaimed in 1960, still shapes arguments over sovereignty in international law.

Many Global South states with a shared history of Western colonialism abstained or voted against Ukraine resolutions, citing Western hypocrisy over sovereignty, a stance that echoes _____ in contemporary politics.

cards.question: Grown out of the Shanghai Five, a border confidence-building group formed in 1996, the _____ was founded in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian republics to combat terrorism, separatism and extremism.
cards.answerDate: Founded15 June 2001Charter signed7 June 2002First enlarged2017Latest memberBelarus, 2024
cards.abstract:
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation is a regional security body founded in June 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. It grew out of the Shanghai Five, a looser group formed in 1996 by all of them except Uzbekistan, whose members signed agreements in 1996 and 1997 on military confidence-building and on mutual reduction of forces along their borders. Its charter, signed at Saint Petersburg on 7 June 2002, names as goals the strengthening of mutual trust, joint action against terrorism, separatism and extremism, and cooperation in fields such as trade, defence, energy and transport. The charter places the secretariat in Beijing and the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure in Tashkent, and it requires bodies to decide by consensus, so that a decision stands only if no member objects. A study of its focus on the 'three evils' of terrorism, extremism and separatism concludes that it is best seen as a regional organisation concerned with non-traditional security, not as a hostile new Warsaw Pact.

For sixteen years it did not enlarge, and the Astana summit of June 2017 brought its first expansion, when India and Pakistan became full members. One analyst argues that Beijing dropped a decade of opposition to India's entry partly because of its Belt and Road Initiative, Pakistan's simultaneous entry and a growing choice of other regional institutions. Iran became a full member in 2023 and Belarus in 2024, the first exclusively European member and the tenth overall. Its members now account for roughly a quarter of world economic output and half of its population, and a second analyst reads enlargement as an effort to assemble a coalition behind a global order not dominated by the West. Critics add that it helps authoritarian governments defend themselves against democratic trends, and another analysis finds that it has failed to build the structures to counterbalance Western formats, while Russia has used the unanimity rule to withhold support for Chinese plans for a free-trade zone.
questions: After admitting India and Pakistan in 2017, its first enlargement since 2001, the _____ added Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024, growing from six members to ten.
With a secretariat in Beijing and a Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure in Tashkent, the _____ decides by consensus, a rule that has let Russia withhold support for Chinese free-trade proposals.

cards.question: Chinese diplomats urge states to abandon the _____, a way of thinking that ties security to rival military blocs, alliances and power politics, and which Beijing says cannot bring lasting peace.
cards.answerDate: Defence paperJuly 1998Position paper2002Joint statement4 February 2022Keynote speech21 February 2023
cards.abstract:
Cold War mentality is a phrase of Chinese diplomatic rhetoric for security thinking, tied to the Cold War, that rests on military alliances, arms build-ups and power politics. A Chinese defence white paper of July 1998 listed cold war mentality, which it said still had a certain currency, among factors of instability alongside hegemonism, power politics and the enlargement of military blocs. It argued that lasting peace required abandoning that mentality for a new concept of security based on mutual trust, since arms and military alliances could not guarantee security. A 2002 position paper asked states to 'discard the mentality of cold war and power politics' and recalled that China had proposed a new security concept for the Asia-Pacific in 1996. One study of Chinese security discourse argues that the phrase connects to views of polarity in world politics and is a crucial aspect of the People's Republic's identity politics.

In February 2022 China and Russia called jointly on NATO to abandon its 'ideologized cold war approaches' and said that all nuclear-weapon states should abandon the cold war mentality and zero-sum games. The same statement opposed closed bloc structures in the Asia-Pacific and expressed vigilance about the Indo-Pacific strategy of the United States, extending the criticism of blocs from Europe to Asia. In February 2023 China's foreign minister, releasing the Global Security Initiative Concept Paper, said that China stood against the Cold War mentality and bloc confrontation and favoured partnership over alliance. One study argues that Beijing has used the phrase since the Cold War ended to keep China off other major powers' security agendas, and another finds that Beijing kept urging the United States and NATO to drop it after the Ukraine war began. Whether a new Cold War is under way is disputed: most Chinese observers see competition with the United States as inevitable and some fear a new Cold War, while one study finds that China differs in important ways from the Soviet Union.
questions: A Chinese defence white paper of July 1998, listing hegemonism and military blocs among threats to stability, said that _____ still had a certain currency and had to be abandoned for lasting peace.

cards.question: Europe was the first region through the _____, in which falling death rates were followed by falling birth rates from about 1800, before other regions followed.
cards.abstract:
The demographic transition is the shift of a society from high death and birth rates to low ones, made up of declines in mortality and fertility that are not synchronised. It began around 1800 in Europe, with declining mortality followed by declining fertility, and has since spread around the world. Because fertility starts to fall some time after mortality has dropped, the lag between the two produces a burst of population growth. Economists have proposed several triggers for the fall in fertility, and one survey concludes that rising demand for human capital in industrialising economies was the main one, as families shifted from the quantity of children to their quality. Where the transition came later it has tended to be faster, with longer gaps between falling mortality and falling fertility, which has meant decades of higher population growth and a quicker passage to population ageing.

One estimate holds that about a fifth of the world's people lived in Europe, Russia included, at the start of the 18th century, and that Europe's population then boomed with the Industrial Revolution. The trend reversed after the First World War, as basic health care and sanitation spread to poorer countries, where people began to live longer while birth rates stayed high or fell only slowly. Using UN data and counting Russia separately, the Dutch government's foreign-policy advisers put Europe's share of world population at 17.9 per cent in 1950 and 7.4 per cent in 2023, while Africa's doubled from 9 to 18 per cent. The UN estimates that Europe and Northern America have grown by less than 1 per cent a year since the mid-1960s and projects that their 1.12 billion people in 2022 will be about the same in 2050, while sub-Saharan Africa grows from 1.15 to 2.09 billion. The shift is not over, since fertility in Europe has been below replacement level since the late 1970s and the countries whose populations have already peaked are predominantly in Europe.
questions: Because fertility starts to fall some time after mortality, the lag in the _____ drives a burst of growth, and its later arrival elsewhere cut Europe's share of world population.
Fertility in Europe has been below replacement level since the late 1970s, a late stage of the _____ that leaves the continent with a shrinking share of the world's people.

cards.question: Where economies converge only with others that begin in a similar position, rather than with the whole world, economists speak of _____, a rival to the claim that all countries eventually catch up.
cards.abstract:
Convergence clubs are sub-groups of economies whose members converge towards one another while diverging away from the members of other clubs. The club hypothesis says that countries with similar structural characteristics converge in the long run if their initial conditions are also similar, unlike absolute convergence, in which every country converges whatever its starting point. Studies of the world distribution of income found it polarising into twin peaks of rich and poor, with the middle-income group eventually vanishing, rather than collapsing to a single point. A 1995 study of cross-country growth, later cited as evidence for clubs, rejected a single linear model in favour of one in which economies obey different models when grouped by their initial conditions. Later work built statistical methods for sorting panel data into club convergence groups, and a survey notes that finding between two and five clubs is common.

The gap is wide: between 1870 and 1990 the ratio of the richest to the poorest country's income rose from roughly 9 to 1 to 45 to 1. A survey of fifty years of growth concluded that developing countries as a group had not closed the income gap, though a few, mostly in South and East Asia, including China and South Korea, did. In data to 2010 it found no movement in closing the gap for most poorer countries, mostly in Africa but elsewhere too, as more advanced economies grew faster. The Dutch government's foreign-policy advisers show the same split, with price-adjusted GDP per head between 1990 and 2023 rising from 5 to 32 per cent of the Dutch level in China, but falling from 9 to 7 per cent in sub-Saharan Africa and from 29 to 22 per cent in the Middle East and Central Asia. Whether the clubs will persist is debated, since a later study found a trend towards unconditional convergence since 1990 and convergence since 2000, driven by both faster catch-up growth and slower growth at the frontier.

Because China and South Korea closed much of the income gap while most poorer economies, mostly in Africa, did not, some economists read the world as split into separate _____ rather than moving together.

cards.question: Trade among developing economies, about 8 per cent of the world total in 1990 and around a quarter by 2014, goes by the name _____, and China and India have led its growth.
cards.abstract:
South–South trade is trade among developing economies, as distinct from North–North trade among rich countries and North–South trade between the two groups. The World Trade Organization reported in 2014 that it had grown from 8 per cent of world trade in 1990 to around 25 per cent and was projected to reach 30 per cent by 2030, with trade corridors between Africa and Asia gaining importance. An analysis of UN trade data found that low- and middle-income countries more than doubled their share of world exports between 1992 and 2008, from 21 to 43 per cent, led by China and India. Its author attributed this partly to demand in China and India for raw materials to build cities and factories, and partly to production networks across the South. Supply-chain trade shifted heavily towards Factory Asia between 1995 and 2009, and the world's economic centre of gravity moved from the mid-Atlantic in 1980 to east of Helsinki and Bucharest by 2008.

The Dutch government's foreign-policy advisers report that in 1995 Europe was still the largest supplier for many Global South countries, including Brazil, India and South Africa, and that only three African countries imported mainly from Asia. By 2022, they find, most countries worldwide imported mainly from Asia, which had also become the main export destination for most Global South countries. Africa shows the change: Europe's share of its exports fell from 55 per cent in 1995 to 37.5 per cent in the council's latest figures, and Asia overtook Europe as its main export market around 2013. A UN economist adds that China's trade with Africa rose from $2.7 billion in 1990 to over $209 billion in 2022, making China Africa's largest single trading partner, though African exports to China are almost all commodities. Definitions matter: UNCTAD figures put South–South trade at 25 per cent of world trade and North–North at 37.1, but fixing the rich-country group at its 1980 membership gives 35 and 25 per cent respectively.

cards.question: Strategy documents from Washington, Brussels, Tokyo and Berlin set out what foreign policy is for with a recurring trio of aims, namely _____, though each government words and ranks them differently.
cards.abstract:
Security, prosperity and values are three aims that governments keep returning to when they set out what their foreign policy is for. The 2010 United States National Security Strategy named four enduring national interests, namely security, prosperity, values and an international order, and said that none can be pursued in isolation. The European Union's global strategy of 2016 listed peace and security, prosperity, democracy and a rules-based global order as its vital interests, adding that its interests and values go hand in hand. Japan's strategy of 2013 named its survival and security, its prosperity through economic development, and an international order based on rules and on universal values such as freedom, democracy and human rights. Germany's first national security strategy, issued in June 2023, calls German foreign and security policy values-based and interest-driven.

A former Australian foreign minister, Gareth Evans, warned in 2016 that policymakers think of national interests far too often only as the familiar duo of security and prosperity. He proposed a third national interest, being and being seen to be a good international citizen, and argued that it earns reputational and reciprocal returns rather than being a charitable extra. He also accepted that traditionally defined national interests are often in tension with more broadly defined international values. Rex Tillerson showed the tension in 2017 when he told State Department staff that conditioning national security efforts on another country adopting American values would probably prevent the United States reaching its security goals. He did not want values left on the sidelines, however, and held that values stay constant while policies change; the 2010 American strategy had said that positive action in one area helps advance all four interests.

cards.question: Realist scholars count the states with enough economic, military and demographic strength to rank as great powers, and this count gives the international system its _____, whether one, two or several.
cards.abstract:
Polarity is the number of especially powerful states, or poles, at the top of the international system, a number that shapes how international politics works. Three or more especially powerful states make a multipolar system, two states substantially more powerful than all others make a bipolar one, and one state too strong to be counterbalanced makes a unipolar one. To count as a pole a state must score well on every component of power, listed by Waltz as population and territory, resources, economic capability, military strength and competence. Researchers also measure capability directly: the Correlates of War project averages a state's shares of world military spending, military personnel, iron and steel output, energy use, total population and urban population, weighted equally. Waltz noted that changes of polarity alter how states provide for their security, because with more than two great powers they need alliances as well as their own efforts and uncertainty about capabilities multiplies.

The Soviet collapse left one pole, which Wohlforth argued in 1999 was both peaceful and durable, since no state was likely for many decades to be able to challenge the United States in any underlying element of power. Waltz and Layne predicted in the 1990s that multipolarity would soon return, and Layne later conceded that the prediction was wrong while suggesting that China's rise may gradually fulfil it. Monteiro argued that unipolarity breeds conflict likely to involve the sole great power, noting that the United States was at war for 13 of the 22 years after the Cold War ended. Brooks and Wohlforth later called polarity too blunt to track change and judged that the United States would long remain the only state able to be a superpower, with China in a class by itself. Beckley warned that GDP, population and energy use conflate size with power and overstate large but underdeveloped countries, while Germany's strategy of 2023 simply declares the world multipolar, so the count of poles stays contested.

cards.question: The power to shape the frameworks within which states, firms and others have to operate is called _____, which one scholar traced to control over security, production, credit and knowledge.
cards.abstract:
Structural power is, in Susan Strange's definition, the power to shape and determine the structures of the global political economy within which other states, firms and professionals have to operate. She set it against relational power and argued that a structural approach gives a more realistic assessment of power in the international economy. Its four sources, she wrote, are control over security, production, credit, and knowledge, beliefs and ideas. Control of credit matters because purchasing power can be acquired through it without working or trading for it, and control of knowledge rests on limiting the terms of access to it. In 1988 she challenged the view that the United States had lost hegemonic power, concluding that it and its corporations had not lost their structural power, though they might have changed their minds about how to use it.

Drezner uses the term for modern networks, arguing that the structural power of the United States over financial and cyber networks enhanced its coercive tools, through the dollar's centrality for sanctions and control over internet protocols for surveillance. He cautions that claims of weaponisation need testing, since Russian pipeline coercion yielded uneven results, Chinese debt-trap diplomacy is contested and fears about medical supply chains proved exaggerated. Posen argued in 2003 that the United States commanded the sea, space and air, the key military enabler of its global power position, while adversaries could still contest other arenas of military action. Chen and Evers call global supply chains crucial battle lines in power transitions, where states use trade, finance, manufacturing and investment policies as economic weapons and a firm at odds with its home state undermines the state's agenda. Brooks and Wohlforth treat technology as a dimension of power, observing in 2016 that China was at a much lower technological level than the leader, while the European Union's 2023 economic security strategy lists supply chains, infrastructure, technology leakage and economic coercion as four broad categories of risk.

cards.question: Studies of the Bolsheviks begun after the Second World War gave rise to the _____, a profile of a leader's beliefs about the political universe and about which strategies and tactics work.
cards.abstract:
The operational code is a construct for studying how a political actor sees the political universe and the actor's own place within it. It began with Nathan Leites's studies of Bolshevik negotiating behaviour, made after the Second World War at the request of the United States government, and Alexander George later recast it as a framework of questions. George saw the code as a prism that influences the actor's perceptions of political events and the choice of strategy and tactics. It has two clusters of beliefs: philosophical beliefs about the nature of political life, such as whether the political universe is friendly or hostile, and instrumental beliefs about which strategy and tactics to use. Because leaders rarely submit to questioning, analysts code the verbs in a corpus of speeches with software to score five beliefs of each kind, assuming that what leaders say reflects how they think.

Applied to over a million words by Vladimir Putin, the method found broadly mainstream beliefs, qualified by hyper-aggressiveness towards terrorism and a preoccupation with political control, and suggested an opportunist rather than a strategist. A study of seven European populist radical right leaders, among them Marine Le Pen and Viktor Orbán, found no common pattern in their beliefs, though on average they were more conflictual in their world views and resembled other leaders in their instrumental approaches. Another study found Donald Trump's beliefs and traits, scored from his 2016 campaign speeches, consistent with his foreign policy in 2017 to 2020, and its authors concluded that such analysis can help to predict foreign policy. Beliefs matter for diplomacy because decisionmakers read an adversary's signals through their own theories and expectations, as when Reagan, Shultz and Weinberger disagreed over which Soviet actions revealed real intentions. The method has limits, since George warned that the code is only one variable cluster in a complex causal framework, and the reference groups used to judge a leader against the norm are predominantly male.
questions: Analysts code the verbs in a leader's prepared speeches to score five philosophical and five instrumental beliefs, which together make up the leader's _____, a profile built from a distance.

A study of over a million words spoken by Vladimir Putin used the _____ to conclude that his beliefs about international politics are broadly mainstream and that he is more opportunist than strategist.

cards.question: Political scientists long preferred impersonal forces, but critics argued that the goals, abilities and foibles of individuals shape state behaviour, a claim now studied as _____ in foreign policy analysis.
cards.abstract:
Leader personality is the idea that the goals, abilities and foibles of those at the top of a state shape its intentions, capabilities and strategies, not only its power or institutions. Waltz rejected the first image, in which the behaviour of nations springs from that of individuals, and even his critics have mostly argued from the state level. Byman and Pollack replied that human nature varies, and that personalities matter more when power is concentrated in a leader's hands, when institutions conflict, or in times of great change. Henry Kissinger said in 1975 that as a professor he had thought history run by impersonal forces, but that in practice you see the difference personalities make. Researchers profile leaders at a distance, and Margaret Hermann's leadership trait analysis scores seven traits, among them need for power, conceptual complexity, self-confidence and distrust of others.

A study of 298 assassination attempts on national leaders since 1875 treated success or failure as plausibly chance, and found that killing an autocrat changed a country's institutions while killing a democrat did not. At the negotiating table, personal experience of a counterpart colours later judgment: Carter, who felt he had built frank rapport with Brezhnev in Vienna in June 1979, read the invasion of Afghanistan as a sign that the Soviet leader could not be trusted. A study of crisis bargaining argued that variation in the experience of American decision-makers in 2002 to 2006 plausibly explains a large shift in United States signalling towards North Korea. A study of Donald Trump's 2016 campaign speeches found his scored traits and beliefs consistent with his foreign policy in 2017 to 2020, and its authors concluded that profiling can help to predict policy. One article scored Vladimir Putin's conceptual complexity from interviews against a reference group of 214 world leaders and argued that his lower score appears to have influenced his choices over Ukraine in 2022.

cards.question: A first-lecture slide promises that diplomacy in times of _____ will be a theme throughout the course, exploring defining moments such as 9/11, the 2008 financial crisis and the ISIS caliphate.
cards.abstract:
Radical uncertainty is the phrase with which the first lecture frames the course, saying that diplomacy in times of radical uncertainty will be a theme throughout. The same slide says the course will explore the uncertain and unexpected in world politics, with defining moments such as 9/11, the 2008 financial crisis, the ISIS caliphate, the Ukraine war, Sudan and South Sudan, and the China–US contrast between strategic autonomy and interdependence. The lecture's third part is headed 'Unpredictability and the importance of domestic politics', and it goes on to present the two-level game. A slide in the Ukraine lecture lists unpredictability, and geopolitical and geoeconomic rivalry after 9/11, 2008 and COVID-19, among the features of post-Cold War security order and disorder. A 2022 leader in The Economist reports that, as firms grappled with the aftershocks of a financial crisis, a populist revolt and a trade war, many bosses postponed big investment decisions abroad and no one knew whether globalisation faced a blip or extinction.

A 2026 article in Foreign Affairs speaks of uncertainty rather than radical uncertainty, saying that the central feature of the author's conversations with world leaders is a sense that the world defies conventions and understanding. The leaders, it reports, agree only that they do not know what will come next, struggle to use history or theory to find their bearings, and no longer get certainty from intelligence and diplomatic briefings. Its examples include a Gulf leader with no idea what would settle the Hormuz dispute and an Indo-Pacific adviser unsure whether the United States would defend his country. The article adds that the uncertainty pervading this orderless age is driven by three forces upending the international system, fragmentation, contagion and strangulation. A 2025 article on economic coercion says that American policymakers in the first decades of the nuclear age faced enormous uncertainty about how to achieve stability and peace, which led them to make major investments in institutions and strategic doctrines.

The three forces of fragmentation, contagion and strangulation drive the _____ that an article says pervades this orderless age and leaves leaders unable to say what comes next.

cards.question: A state’s own duty, the world’s duty to help it and collective action when it manifestly fails are the three pillars of the _____ as the Secretary-General set them out in 2009.
cards.answerDate: CoinedDecember 2001Adopted16 September 2005Pillars set out12 January 2009
cards.abstract:
The Responsibility to Protect is a principle, agreed by world leaders in September 2005, that every state must protect its own population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. Its name comes from a commission convened by Canada in 2000, which reported in December 2001 that sovereignty implies responsibility and that the state itself bears the primary duty. It divided the idea into responsibilities to prevent, to react and to rebuild, and called prevention the most important. The 2005 text kept the scope narrow, naming only four crimes, and left any collective use of force to the Security Council acting case by case. In 2009 the Secretary-General read the text as resting on three pillars, which are the protection responsibilities of the state, international assistance and capacity-building, and a timely and decisive response.

Pillar one is the enduring duty of the state, the bedrock of the idea, while pillar two commits the international community to assist states in meeting it. Pillar three is a collective response to a state manifestly failing, drawing on a broad range of tools in which measures under Chapter VII need Security Council authorisation, and the report sets no sequence between the pillars. In March 2011 the Council authorised all necessary measures to protect civilians in Libya, which one study called the first authorisation of the invasion of a functioning state for such a purpose. Russia and other states later argued that the operation had exceeded its mandate, and that distrust was one reason the Council deadlocked over Syria, where Russia and China vetoed draft resolutions in October 2011 and February 2012. One scholar argued in 2010 that the duties of states to their own people are well defined while the international duties are indeterminate, which limits how far the doctrine can generate the political will to act.

cards.question: Convened by Kofi Annan in March 2000 and chaired by a former Algerian foreign minister, the _____ demanded robust rules of engagement and mandates backed by firm troop commitments.
cards.answerDate: Panel convened7 March 2000Report dated17 August 2000
cards.abstract:
The Brahimi Report is the August 2000 review of United Nations peace operations by a panel that Kofi Annan convened in March 2000 under the former Algerian foreign minister Lakhdar Brahimi. The panel had four months and began by saying that the organisation had repeatedly failed in the previous decade to save succeeding generations from war. It argued that missions of the 1990s often deployed where fighting had stopped without a victory and some parties were not seriously committed to peace, so the United Nations tried to create post-conflict situations. The panel kept consent, impartiality and force only in self-defence as the bedrock of peacekeeping but defined impartiality as adherence to the Charter, saying no failure had damaged peacekeeping more in the 1990s than reluctance to distinguish victim from aggressor. United Nations doctrine of 2008 called the report a landmark, and the review panel of 2015 said it had galvanised political, institutional and financial support for reform.

Its central demand was that deployed peacekeepers must be able to defend themselves and their mandate, with rules of engagement robust enough not to cede the initiative to attackers. It urged the Secretariat to tell the Council what it needs to know rather than what it wants to hear, and asked the Council to leave resolutions for large missions in draft until troop commitments were firm. For speed, it proposed full deployment of a traditional operation within 30 days of a Council resolution and a complex one within 90, backed by an on-call list of about 100 military officers. In 2015 the review panel found that the United Nations had been unable to come close to those targets, taking six months on average to deploy a contingent. Analysts noted that some of its political insights were sidelined during implementation and its more ambitious recommendations still awaited action in 2015, though one found its advice to tell the Council what it needs to know still relevant.

Defining impartiality as adherence to the Charter, the _____ said that no failure had damaged peacekeeping more in the 1990s than reluctance to distinguish victim from aggressor.

cards.question: Chaired by the former head of state of Timor-Leste and convened in October 2014, the _____ reported in June 2015 under the title Uniting Our Strengths for Peace: Politics, Partnership and People.
cards.answer: High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations
cards.answerDate: Convened31 October 2014Report issued17 June 2015
cards.abstract:
The High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations, known as HIPPO, was convened by Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon on 31 October 2014 to review United Nations peace operations. It was chaired by José Ramos-Horta, the former head of state of Timor-Leste, and held regional consultations in Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America. Its report, titled Uniting Our Strengths for Peace: Politics, Partnership and People, reached the General Assembly and the Security Council on 17 June 2015 after six months of work. It was the first comprehensive review of the field since the Brahimi Report of 2000, with over 100 pages and more than 100 recommendations. It used a broad definition of peace operations, covering a spectrum from special envoys and mediators to large multidimensional missions that draw on civilian, military and police personnel.

Its diagnosis was that changes in conflict might be outpacing the ability of peace operations to respond, with some missions deployed in environments where there was little or no peace to keep. In response it called for four essential shifts, namely the primacy of politics, a flexible use of the whole spectrum of operations, a stronger partnership with regional bodies, and a more field-focused and people-centred organisation. It advised that United Nations troops should not undertake military counter-terrorism and that enforcement mandates be exceptional, a caution that fits one study’s warning that mandates targeting particular groups have long-term implications for the organisation’s role as an impartial arbitrator. Critics called it technocratic and short of a compelling narrative, and one assessment found that it kept the principles of peacekeeping valid except when they should not be, so that little would change in practice. The Secretary-General’s response in September 2015 adopted its broad definition, member states received the report well, and a later study noted that neither document said how missions should operate where they confront violent extremism.

cards.question: In 2015 a review panel urged that politics drive missions, the full spectrum of operations be used flexibly, partnerships deepen and headquarters serve the field, naming these the _____ the organisation must embrace.
cards.abstract:
The four essential shifts are the changes that the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations said in 2015 the United Nations must embrace in how it designs and delivers its peace operations. The first is that politics must have primacy, because lasting peace is achieved through political solutions and not through military and technical engagements. The second is that the full spectrum of peace operations must be used flexibly, so that the United Nations delivers tailored missions rather than template ones. The third is a stronger and more inclusive partnership for peace and security, in which the United Nations works with regional organisations and also acts as an enabler of others. The fourth is that the Secretariat must become more field-focused and peace operations more people-centred, so that the legacy of the ‘white-SUV culture’ gives way to closer interaction with local people.

The first shift answers a gap in practice, because operations such as those in Darfur and the Central African Republic often seem to have been deployed without being embedded in a political strategy. The panel added that, whenever the United Nations has a peace operation on the ground, it should lead or play a leading role in political efforts, while accepting that political primacy ultimately rests with national actors. A meeting of experts in 2015 called this shift a key one but stressed that the pursuit of political settlement is a broad topic, so it matters to identify what needs to be done by whom. A study of terrorism and peace operations credited the report with a strong case for people-centric missions, in contrast with traditionally state-centric peacekeeping. Analysts also noted that the language sounded more revolutionary than it was, since calls for prevention and a field focus went back to earlier reports, and that the report lacked a compelling narrative to win member states over.

cards.question: Missions in Mali, the Congo and South Sudan were struggling, the 2015 review panel said, because they were deployed amid continuing fighting with _____ and tools built for implementing agreements.
cards.abstract:
No peace to keep is the 2015 review panel’s phrase for settings where a United Nations mission is deployed although no political agreement exists or efforts to reach one have faltered. Peacekeeping was built for the opposite case, supporting a political commitment to a ceasefire or peace agreement, where the panel called it an effective and highly cost-effective tool. As early as 2000 the Brahimi Report noted that missions had deployed where some parties were not seriously committed to ending the confrontation, so the United Nations tried to create post-conflict situations. By 2015 missions in Mali, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and South Sudan were among a growing number working without a political agreement. The panel said that the difficulties of implementing a mandate increase exponentially when there is little or no peace to keep, and that political solutions, not military force, are the true force multipliers.

It called these situations conflict management, in which missions try to deter escalation, contain conflict, protect civilians and revive a peace process, and warned that concepts built for peace implementation may not suit them. It advised limited, focused mandates tied to a political strategy, fewer civilian tasks that assume a peace to keep, and ad hoc coalitions or regional actors as first responders where the United Nations lacked the capability for sustained combat. One review observed that recent missions had generally been deployed to ongoing conflicts, making stabilisation more the rule than the exception for the Council. One study argued that enforcement mandates in the Central African Republic, the Congo and Mali have long-term implications for the organisation’s role as an impartial arbitrator, another that stabilisation is a distinct form of intervention by invitation. Terrorism sharpens the problem, since seven of the eleven countries most affected by it host United Nations peace operations, and deploying missions where there is little or no peace to keep and violent extremism is present poses complex challenges.

cards.question: In the Security Council, the _____ initiates and chairs the informal drafting of resolutions on a situation, a role the Council's 2017 working-methods note supports and says any member may take.
cards.abstract:
A penholder is a member of the Security Council that initiates and chairs the informal drafting of the Council's resolutions and statements on a particular situation or subject, under an informal arrangement. The Council's 2017 working-methods note supports the practice as a way to take timely initiatives while keeping an element of continuity, and it says that any member may be a penholder. In practice France, the United Kingdom and the United States, known as the P3, each hold the pen without a partner on most country files, 22 of 33 in one 2023 count, including 11 of 12 peacekeeping contexts. The three are self-designated rather than appointed by the Council, which publishes no official list of who holds which pen. A penholder usually prepares a full first draft, circulates it among the P3 and close allies, then shows it to Russia and China, and only then to the full Council.

Accounts differ on when this settled pattern began, offering dates from around 2003 to around 2008. It is said to have grown out of a race among the P3, each trying to be first to circulate a draft that would gain traction. Critics say it limits other members' chances to draft, gives the penholder control over negotiations, and can leave the Council seeming paralysed when the penholder is unwilling or unable to act. Defenders point to efficiency and continuity as texts grow longer and more technical, and one study argues that the system also gives elected members a way to strengthen their influence in support of the rule of law. In March 2023 Mali wrote to the Council's president rejecting France as penholder on all issues concerning Mali, a demand that found no support among Council members.

cards.question: In United Nations jargon, mission mandates overburdened with disparate tasks that reflect the agendas of many negotiating actors are derided as _____, unlike the one-paragraph mandate of the Cold War force in Cyprus.
cards.abstract:
Christmas tree mandates are a pejorative term in United Nations jargon for peacekeeping missions overburdened with tasks that reflect the agendas of the many actors involved in the mandate negotiations. A Cold War mission such as the force in Cyprus had two main tasks, set out in one paragraph of a Security Council resolution. The mission in the Central African Republic, by contrast, must protect civilians, coordinate electoral assistance, support state authority, monitor human rights, assist security sector reform and support reconciliation, and its mandate runs to 14 pages. A 2015 high-level panel found that mandates had become lengthier and more specific, and at times less realistic or manageable. It said that the Secretariat and the Council had been unable to overcome the so-called Christmas tree mandate dilemma, in which template language for many tasks routinely appears in mission mandates.

The panel traced the problem to early planning, where expansive technical assessments produce comprehensive reports by the Secretary-General that in turn drive large mandates with often formulaic tasks. Who drove the growth is disputed, and a study of 19 missions from 1998 to 2014 found that the Council dropped tasks the Secretariat recommended as often as it added tasks on its own initiative. An earlier review of peacekeeping had already warned that the compromises needed for consensus can cost specificity, and that a mandate to protect civilians must come with the specific resources to carry it out. The 2015 panel's remedy was a two-stage process, with an initial mandate that sets an overall political goal and a few priority tasks, and the Secretary-General returning within six months with a proposal for sequenced activities. Since then the Council has marked priority tasks in some mandates, but a 2020 study found that this did not mean fewer tasks, and a 2024 meeting heard that Christmas tree mandates can create unreasonable expectations of what a mission can do.

cards.question: Three high-profile United Nations operations in the former Yugoslavia, Somalia and Rwanda, namely _____, came under such criticism in the mid-1990s that the Security Council limited the number of new peacekeeping missions.
cards.answerDate: UNPROFOR set up21 February 1992UNAMIR set upOctober 1993UNOSOM II left2 March 1995UNAMIR leftMarch 1996
cards.abstract:
UNPROFOR, UNOSOM and UNAMIR were the United Nations missions in the former Yugoslavia, Somalia and Rwanda, which the United Nations singles out as three high-profile operations criticised in the mid-1990s. They followed a rapid expansion in which the Security Council authorised 20 operations between 1989 and 1994 and the number of peacekeepers rose from 11,000 to 75,000. UNPROFOR was established on 21 February 1992, and in June 1993 a Chapter VII resolution gave it the task of deterring attacks on the safe areas in Bosnia. UNOSOM II was created under Chapter VII in March 1993, and when a raid on 3 October 1993 by American forces outside United Nations command left 18 Americans dead, Washington announced its withdrawal. UNAMIR was set up in October 1993 to help implement the Arusha peace agreement, and on 21 April 1994 the Council cut it from 2,548 to 270 troops, a decision the later inquiry found difficult to justify.

In 1995 the Secretary-General argued from Somalia and Bosnia that peacekeeping rests on consent, impartiality and the non-use of force, and that nothing is more dangerous than asking an operation to use force without the capacity. The 1999 report on the fall of Srebrenica judged that the safe areas were set up without the parties' consent or any credible military deterrent, and that errors rested on a philosophy of impartiality and non-violence wholly unsuited to the conflict. The 1999 Rwanda inquiry named a lack of resources and will as the overriding failure and said the Council bore responsibility for its hesitance to support new operations after Somalia. The result was a retreat: the Council limited new missions, and an American directive of May 1994 said large American forces in major peace enforcement should ordinarily serve under American command, through NATO or in a coalition. By 2000 the permanent members were sending far fewer troops to UN-led operations, and the Brahimi panel linked that reluctance to memories of peacekeepers murdered in Mogadishu and Kigali.

cards.question: Appointed by the Secretary-General in May 1999 and counting a former Swedish prime minister among its three members, the _____ concluded that the overriding failure was a lack of resources and of will.
cards.answer: Independent Inquiry into the Rwanda genocide
cards.answerDate: GenocideApril – July 1994Inquiry began17 June 1999Report dated15 December 1999
cards.abstract:
The Independent Inquiry into the Rwanda genocide was a panel of three appointed by the Secretary-General in May 1999 to establish the facts of the United Nations response between October 1993 and July 1994. Its members were Ingvar Carlsson, a former Swedish prime minister, Han Sung-Joo, a former South Korean foreign minister, and Rufus Kupolati, a retired Nigerian lieutenant-general. It reported on 15 December 1999 that approximately 800,000 people were killed in the genocide, which the international community neither prevented nor stopped once it had begun. It judged that the failure was one of the United Nations system as a whole, shared by the Secretary-General, the Secretariat, the Security Council, the mission and the wider membership, and said an apology was warranted. It named the overriding failure as a lack of resources and of will, since the mission was not planned, dimensioned, deployed or instructed in a way that allowed a proactive and assertive role.

Planning assumed that the peace process would succeed and made no contingency for failure, and the force was set at 2,548 troops, not the 4,500 a reconnaissance mission had estimated, because the Secretariat doubted the Council would back more. Drawing on the Srebrenica report published weeks earlier, it concluded that there can be no neutrality in the face of genocide, whereas headquarters had kept applying UNAMIR's mandate as a traditional neutral role. It found the mission starved of equipment, with Belgian troops using recycled materiel, and in May 1994 not one of 19 governments with troops on stand-by agreed to contribute to its expansion. On 21 April 1994 the Council cut UNAMIR to 270 troops while the killings were known to all, a decision the inquiry found difficult to justify and blamed on a lack of political will. Its finding that a mission's presence raises an expectation of protection was quoted in the Brahimi report, though one study argues that peacekeeping remains based on consent, impartiality and minimal use of force.
