cards.question: Five questions put in Chicago in April 1999, from whether we are sure of our case to whether national interests are involved, are the core of the _____, named after a British prime minister.
cards.abstract:
The Blair Doctrine is the shorthand commentators gave to a speech by Prime Minister Tony Blair in Chicago on 22 April 1999, in which he described a new doctrine of international community. He spoke on the 29th day of the NATO air campaign over Kosovo, fought without United Nations authorisation, and called it a just war based not on territorial ambition but on values. He argued that isolationism had no reason to exist and that non-interference must be qualified, because acts of genocide can never be a purely internal matter. His best-remembered passage lists five considerations for intervening: whether the case is sure, diplomacy exhausted, sensible military operations possible, the long term accepted and national interests involved. He did not present them as absolute tests, and he said there had been too much talk of exit strategies, preferring to stay on with moderate numbers of troops than to return later with large numbers.

One analysis likens the criteria to the American Weinberger and Powell doctrines, but argues that those were meant to restrict the use of force while Blair sought a justification for using it. The five considerations do not mention Security Council approval, and the speech called for the Council's workings to be reconsidered, a task for its five permanent members once the Kosovo conflict was over. In September 1999 the Secretary-General told the General Assembly that Kosovo set the legitimacy of acting without a United Nations mandate against the imperative of halting gross violations, while declining to propose criteria. In 2001 an international commission set out six tests for intervention, from right authority to reasonable prospects, and in 2005 world leaders accepted a responsibility to protect that acts through the Security Council case by case. One study argues that the Iraq war exposed the doctrine's flaw, which was to assume that individual states could speak for international society even when a majority on the Security Council opposed them.

cards.question: Adopted on 20 December 2012 under Chapter VII, _____ authorised an African-led international support mission to help Mali's army recover the north from armed groups and terrorist networks.
cards.answerDate: Adopted20 December 2012Succeeded25 April 2013
cards.abstract:
Resolution 2085 was adopted by the United Nations Security Council on 20 December 2012, acting under Chapter VII after finding that the situation in Mali threatened international peace and security. Its central decision, in paragraph 9, was to authorise an African-led International Support Mission in Mali, known as AFISMA, for an initial period of one year. AFISMA was to take all necessary measures to help rebuild the Malian armed forces, to support the authorities in recovering the north from terrorist, extremist and armed groups, and then to move to stabilisation tasks. The resolution also urged the transitional authorities to restore constitutional order through elections, demanded that rebel groups cut all ties to terrorist organisations, and called for talks with northern groups that had done so. It asked the African Union to report every 60 days and, before any offensive in the north, on political progress, human-rights training, operational readiness and the chain of command.

A study published in June 2013 noted that no West African state had stepped forward to lead the mission, and that Nigeria, which had played that role in the past, was consumed by its own Boko Haram insurgency. The resolution fitted a French preference for collective African and European mechanisms, since President Hollande took office in 2012 with a non-interventionist agenda that promised to draw down French troops in Africa. In 2013, however, he deployed about 4,000 combat troops to Mali, at first without any multilateral participation, because swift and robust action seemed to be required. One critical reading holds that, because paragraph 9 provided only for an African mission, the French ground operation lacked a basis in the resolution. On 25 April 2013 the Council established MINUSMA, to which authority would pass from AFISMA on 1 July 2013, with suitable AFISMA military and police personnel absorbed into the new United Nations force.

cards.question: Established in April 2013 to stabilise northern Mali and support the political transition, _____ took over from an African-led force and could field up to 11,200 military personnel.
cards.answerDate: Established25 April 2013Took over1 July 2013Mandate ended30 June 2023Withdrawn by31 December 2023
cards.abstract:
MINUSMA was the United Nations Multidimensional Integrated Stabilisation Mission in Mali, established by Security Council Resolution 2100 on 25 April 2013. Authority passed to it from the African-led force AFISMA on 1 July 2013, and it was authorised to field up to 11,200 military personnel and 1,440 police. Its mandate had several strands, among them stabilising key population centres in the north, supporting the transitional road map and elections, protecting civilians and United Nations staff, and monitoring human rights. It could use all necessary means for tasks such as stabilising population centres and protecting civilians, and French troops were separately authorised to use force to support it if it came under imminent and serious threat. After the 2015 peace agreement it also gained a role in implementation, supporting the cantonment of combatants and leading the secretariat of the committee that monitored the accord.

Peacekeepers were regularly targeted, and by 30 April 2017 the mission had suffered 117 fatalities, which made it the United Nations' most dangerous mission. By the time it closed, the United Nations counted 311 personnel killed and more than 700 injured, among more than 15,000 troops and personnel who served in Mali over the decade. One study argued that robust mandates, collaboration with counterterrorist operations and the return of NATO troop contributors reinforced militarisation within the mission and among its peacekeepers. Another study of Mali found that the overlap between peacekeeping and counterterrorism undercut efforts to protect civilians, one of the mission's central priorities. After Mali's transitional government asked for it to leave without delay, the Council ended its mandate on 30 June 2023, since missions cannot operate without host cooperation, and set 31 December as the date for completing withdrawal.

cards.question: Signed in Bamako in two stages in May and June 2015, the _____ promised the north elected regional assemblies, a development zone and a share of state revenue under Algerian mediation.
cards.answerDate: Signed15 May and 20 June 2015Declared ended25 January 2024
cards.abstract:
The Algiers Agreement is the common name of the 2015 Agreement on Peace and Reconciliation in Mali, negotiated in Algiers under Algerian leadership between the government and two coalitions of northern armed movements, the Coordination and the Platform. It was signed in Bamako in two stages, on 15 May 2015 by the government, the Platform and the mediators, and on 20 June 2015 by the Coordination of Azawad Movements, which had refused to join the first ceremony. Its text promised elected regional assemblies with wide powers, a Northern Development Zone and, by 2018, a mechanism to transfer 30 per cent of state revenues to local authorities. It also provided for the cantonment of combatants, their integration into reconstituted state forces or return to civilian life, and a phased redeployment of those forces across the north. Algeria was to chair the committee monitoring implementation, which would meet at least monthly in Bamako, and an independent observer was to report every four months on progress and responsibility.

The Carter Center, serving as that observer, found in January 2020 that only 18 of 78 commitments were complete, so that almost 80 per cent remained unfulfilled more than four years after signing. An analysis from 2017 called it a framework agreement that left much to be settled during implementation, requiring intensive mediation, and warned that the legacy of earlier accords had fed mistrust. A study of 2021 argued that the foreign military umbrella over Mali let the elites who signed the accord pursue their own agendas rather than face the consequences of their inaction. By 2023 a United Nations panel of experts reported that implementation was at a substantial impasse, with crucial mechanisms non-operational and the monitoring committee not convened. On 25 January 2024 Mali's military government declared the agreement over, citing other signatories' change of posture and hostile acts by Algeria, after fighting between the army and northern rebels had resumed in August 2023.

cards.question: Created in 2023 after the Wagner rebellion and placed under Russia's Ministry of Defence, the _____ took over Wagner's military operations in Africa, including in Mali.
cards.answerDate: Createdsummer 2023Wagner left MaliJune 2025
cards.abstract:
The Africa Corps is a Russian entity that, according to reports, was created in summer 2023 after the failed Wagner rebellion and has taken over Wagner's military operations in Africa. Wagner was treated as semi-autonomous, giving Moscow deniability, whereas the Africa Corps is supervised by the Defence Ministry and its intelligence arm, the GRU, and takes orders from Moscow, which undermines that deniability. It required many Wagner mercenaries to sign new contracts with the Russian government, and on the ground it appears to be a mix of state personnel, private military companies and former Wagner fighters. One analysis argued that the change lets Moscow pursue its African strategy through direct state means, and that a unit reporting to the Defence Ministry could in theory be held to account for violations. As of late 2024 the largest Russian deployments in Africa were in the Central African Republic, Libya and Mali, with smaller contingents in Burkina Faso and Niger.

In Mali the Wagner Group appeared in 2021, reportedly after the junta contracted it, and in November 2023 it helped the Malian army retake the northern town of Kidal from Tuareg separatists. Russian officials told a United Nations panel in March 2023 that Wagner elements were in Mali as private contractors, alongside a small number of Russian military instructors based at Bamako airport. There the Africa Corps kept using the Wagner brand while moving fighters onto government contracts, which let it build on Wagner's local ties and gave Moscow some shielding if the mercenaries took heavy casualties. The handover had difficulties, with a Wagner push at Tinzaouaten in July 2024 ending in an ambush, and on 6 June 2025 Wagner announced the end of its Mali operations, confirming that the takeover was complete. One analyst judged the exit a rebranding rather than a military setback, with Moscow keeping Wagner's core functions under state control, and expected a shift from frontline combat towards training, intelligence support and regime protection.
questions: Wagner announced the end of its Mali operations on 6 June 2025, confirming that the _____, a Defence Ministry force, had completed its takeover from the mercenary group.

cards.sub: Lecture 2 · The military–political nexus

cards.question: A colonel who headed the army officers behind the August 2020 coup, _____ moved again in May 2021 against the civilian transitional president and prime minister, clearing his way to the presidency.
cards.answerDate: First coup18 August 2020Second coup24 May 2021Confirmed28 May 2021
cards.abstract:
Assimi Goïta is the Malian colonel who led the army officers behind the coups of August 2020 and May 2021 and became president of the transition in 2021. The first coup, on 18 August 2020, removed President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta, and Goïta then took a vice-presidency created for him in a transition meant to last 18 months. His junta, the Committee for the Salvation of the People, was officially dissolved, yet it stayed active behind the scenes and its officers took key posts in the transitional government. On 24 May 2021 soldiers arrested the transitional president Bah N'Daw and prime minister Moctar Ouane, accusing them of preparing, without informing Goïta, a reshuffle that removed two former junta members from the defence and security ministries. The Constitutional Court confirmed Goïta as transitional president on 28 May 2021, and a civilian prime minister from the opposition M5-RFP movement headed a new civilian-military government.

One assessment concluded that the second coup restored military control and raised more fears than hopes, because the officers who plotted it controlled the executive. Regional pressure had limits, since ECOWAS suspended Mali's membership yet did not question Goïta's self-promotion, and analysts noted that the military could not be sidelined merely by international pressure. The coups also accelerated Mali's turn away from Western partners, France above all, towards Russia, as the junta sought partners more aligned with its priorities and less critical of its undemocratic rise to power. A study of his rule argues that Goïta built a new social contract on a strongman narrative of national defender, drawing on dissatisfaction with international interventions, and that his support substantially exceeds that of the elected president he replaced. Analysis of Afrobarometer survey data finds that concern about Western influence and national sovereignty, rather than economic hardship, is the main driver of support for the junta.

Despite the country's security and economic troubles, the strongman narrative of national defender built by _____ has won him more public support than the elected president he helped to remove.

cards.question: To assist the armed forces of the G5 Sahel states and strike jihadist groups before they built sanctuaries, France began _____ on 1 August 2014 as the successor to Operation Serval.
cards.answerDate: Launched1 August 2014Left Mali15 August 2022Ended9 November 2022
cards.abstract:
Operation Barkhane was the French military operation against armed terrorist groups in the Sahel, which ran from 2014 to 2022 and followed the shorter Operation Serval of 2013 to 2014. It began on 1 August 2014, with the mission of assisting the armed forces of the five G5 Sahel countries, Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania and Niger, and of striking jihadist forces before they could establish new sanctuaries. Its main target was al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, and with partner countries it was also designed to prevent a link-up between Boko Haram and the other terrorist groups of the Sahel. After Serval, the international effort in Mali was divided between United Nations peacekeeping and French-led counterterrorism, and Barkhane was the French half, which President Macron described in 2017 as complementary to the UN mission. A surge of 600 soldiers in 2020 lifted it to about 5,100 troops, and its notable successes included the neutralisation of the AQIM leader Abdelmalek Droukdel.

Yet analysts noted that tactical successes did not translate into overall progress, since its political objectives stayed vague and its claim to be apolitical never had credibility among Malians. It was also costly, at 695 million euros in 2019 and close to 1 billion euros in 2020, and scrutiny grew in France as the number of French casualties rose. On 17 February 2022 France and the European states operating alongside it announced a coordinated withdrawal from Mali, judging that the political, operational and legal conditions for their military engagement were no longer met. The last French soldier left Mali on 15 August 2022, and the presidency said that 59 soldiers had died fighting armed terrorist groups there over nine years. President Macron formally ended Barkhane in a speech on 9 November 2022, and when the last troops left Mali the presidency had said that France remained engaged in the Sahel, the Gulf of Guinea and the Lake Chad region.

cards.sub: Lecture 2 · The military–political nexus

cards.question: Armed force blended with sabotage, cyberattacks and information operations, often kept below the threshold of open war, is widely called _____, a term European governments use for such campaigns.
cards.answerDate: First public use8 September 2005Crimea annexed2014
cards.abstract:
The hybrid warfare label describes conflict in which one side blends conventional force with irregular tactics, terrorism and criminal behaviour, rather than choosing a single way of fighting. American military thinkers took the idea into public debate in 2005 and found their clearest example in the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah, whose decentralised cells fielded state-like rockets. In their account the regular and irregular parts of a force, once kept in separate theatres or formations, become blurred into the same force in the same battlespace. The idea was never limited to armed groups, since states can also shift conventional units into irregular formations, as the Iraqi fedayeen did in 2003. The label gained a new political life after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, an operation that combined special forces, an information campaign and loyal proxies before a conventional takeover.

European governments call actions below the threshold of conventional war hybrid warfare or hybrid threats, and a CSIS database found that Russian-linked sabotage and subversion in Europe, from incendiary devices to electronic attack, nearly tripled between 2023 and 2024. The toolkit ranges across information operations, cyber tools, proxies and economic pressure, and the Hybrid CoE model holds that no single action is hybrid, since it is the combination that counts. Critics reply that combining force, subversion and propaganda is as old as warfare itself, so that the word 'hybrid' merely names a combination of previously defined types of warfare. They add that Western observers attached the label to Russian actions rather than Russian planners devising it, and that it can skew understanding of Russian military modernisation. Scholars agree that such conflict is conducted in the grey zone between war and peace but define it differently, so the EU-linked model treats hybrid warfare as one part of a wider family of hybrid threats.
questions: After Hezbollah fought Israel in 2006 with decentralised cells and state-like rockets, American defence analysts pointed to it as the clearest example of _____, a blend of regular and irregular methods.

cards.question: Phones, satellite terminals and apps now sit inside Ukraine's military operations, one result of the _____ that lets shooters, sensors and targets operate far apart.
cards.answerDate: iPhone, Android2007 – 2008Makiivka strike31 December 2022
cards.abstract:
The explosion of connectivity is the spread of the internet, mobile phones, satellite services and smartphones, which began in the 1980s and by one account is the most significant trend of recent decades for resistance warfare. By 2017 more than 5 billion satellite navigation devices were in use worldwide, which made it possible to weaponise consumer technologies such as drones and smartphones. Shooters, sensors and targets no longer have to be in the same place, so fighters can plan, gather intelligence and publicise their operations from handheld devices while others support them from far away. Because commercial technology is easy to buy, it spreads fast between enemies, and Russian forces copied Ukraine's use of commercial drones and later adopted Starlink terminals of their own. The same study says this environment rewards fighters who can quickly repurpose consumer systems and use civilian devices in combat.

A RUSI study credits Ukraine's Kropyva mapping software with cutting artillery deployment time by 80 per cent and the time to open counter-battery fire by 90 per cent. Civilians are drawn in as well, since Ukraine adapted its Diia government app so that users can send geolocated reports of troop movements and missile trajectories, while soldiers use the Delta app for a shared real-time picture. Satellite internet matters as much, because Starlink terminals kept Ukrainian society connected after its telecommunications network was disrupted, although one study argues that a private company's mix of commercial and political motives shaped how the service was offered. The same devices are also targets, as when a Ukrainian rocket strike on a Russian barracks at Makiivka on 31 December 2022 was later blamed by Moscow on its soldiers' use of mobile phones. Such reporting by civilians challenges the legal distinction between civilians and combatants, and one study argues that some real-time operational reporting may amount to direct participation in hostilities in limited circumstances.
questions: A Ukrainian rocket strike on a Russian barracks at Makiivka on 31 December 2022, later blamed on soldiers' mobile phones, showed one hazard of the _____ in modern war.
Ukraine's Diia government app, adapted so civilians can report troop movements, illustrates how the _____ pulls ordinary smartphone users into the fighting.

cards.question: Russia's use of biker clubs, criminal networks and private military companies to deny its hand in operations is an instance of _____, while the Islamic State's bureaucracy and courts show the reverse.
cards.answerDate: Iraqi fedayeen2003Hezbollah warSummer 2006
cards.abstract:
States acting like nonstate actors describes governments that pursue their aims through irregular tactics, deniable proxies and other cut-outs, while its mirror image has armed groups acquiring the weapons and institutions of a state. Analysts of hybrid conflict argue that the old assumption that states are conventional and nonstate actors irregular may be increasingly irrelevant, since states can shift conventional units into irregular formations, as the Iraqi fedayeen did in 2003. The usual route is indirect, because a state such as Russia can act through armed groups, private military companies, biker clubs or criminal networks, which makes harm harder to detect and to attribute and so impedes the target's response. Scholars of surrogate warfare note that states use local armed nonstate actors to externalise the burden of fighting, which echoes pre-modern war, although the relation between the state and its military agent is new. A CSIS study of Russian-linked attacks in Europe found that intelligence agencies frequently recruited local assets and used criminal groups, companies and commercial ships as cut-outs that let governments deny responsibility.

The reverse movement is clearest in the Islamic State, which a 2015 survey of jihadi proto-states found ruling some 8 million people over a territory larger than the United Kingdom, with a bureaucracy, police and courts. The same author prefers the term proto-states, since few of the 'emirates' that jihadi groups have announced over 25 years lasted for more than a year. Armed groups can hold state-like weapons too, as Hezbollah showed in 2006 with thousands of short and intermediate-range rockets, and an American study of that war treated it as the prototype of the hybrid threat. The EU-linked Hybrid CoE report adds that the concept began with weaker nonstate actors using smart tactics against stronger parties, even though analysis today concentrates on states. The tactic has costs, because outsourcing to nonstate or quasi-state actors creates a principal–agent problem in which recruits whose goals differ from their patron's may go rogue.

cards.question: Researchers argue that parties tend to start bargaining in earnest when they reach a deadlock they cannot escalate out of and which hurts both, a _____ that makes a negotiated way out attractive.
cards.answerDate: FMLN offensiveNovember 1989Intense combatApril 1993 – February 1994
cards.abstract:
A mutually hurting stalemate is a deadlock in which the parties to a conflict cannot escalate to victory and find the impasse painful, so that each begins to look for a way out. The pain need not be equal on both sides or have the same cause, but the parties must also sense that a negotiated exit exists and that the other side shares that sense. The reasoning is a cost-benefit one, since parties on a painful path look for a better alternative, so the stalemate acts as a push that impels them to start and keep negotiating. Because the stalemate is perceptual, it exists once the parties believe they are trapped, however flimsy the evidence looks to outsiders, and it does not exist while they believe otherwise, however clear the evidence. With a perceived way out it is a necessary but not sufficient condition for negotiations to begin, since it must be seized by the parties or by a mediator who helps them see their predicament.

In El Salvador a United Nations mediator judged that the guerrillas' November 1989 offensive, which reached the capital without dislodging the government, had codified a mutually hurting stalemate. A study of six mediation attempts over Nagorno-Karabakh found that violence changed significantly only after the intense combat of April 1993 to February 1994, not after any mediation, which supports the stalemate hypothesis. The idea needs care, since a stalemate can feel comfortable rather than painful, as in Cyprus, where the parties have judged the status quo preferable to the costs of a negotiated settlement. In the American-led Israeli–Palestinian talks of 2013 one study found no such deadlock, since Israel preferred the status quo and the Palestinians a unilateral track. Outside backers can keep a stalemate from hurting, since external states bear lower costs of fighting than local combatants, and rebels who receive money and guns are less likely to see conflict end.
questions: Because it rests on perception, a _____ exists once both sides believe they are trapped, however flimsy the evidence looks to outsiders, and not before, however clear the evidence.

cards.question: Cheap uncrewed aircraft that direct artillery, strike armour and force defenders to spend costly interceptors have made _____ a defining feature of the war in Ukraine.
cards.abstract:
Drone warfare is the use of uncrewed aircraft to watch, target and strike, and in Ukraine it runs from cheap commercial quadcopters to long-range one-way attack drones. Before 2022 many security scholars overlooked small drones, although a 2019 study already noted the weaponising of consumer drones, and in Ukraine they are changing battlefield dynamics from the lower airspace. Their most consequential job has been gathering intelligence and directing artillery, and dense overlapping drone networks have made the battlefield close to the front largely transparent to both armies. Strike drones add cheap precision, because first-person-view craft are in effect very cheap anti-tank weapons with roughly six times the range of the most advanced alternative. RUSI interviews in 2024 and 2025 credited tactical drones with 60 to 70 per cent of Russian systems damaged or destroyed, although 60 to 80 per cent of Ukrainian first-person-view drones never reached their targets.

The cost balance favours the expendable, because a drone that is cheap to replace need not survive: about 90 per cent of the drones Ukraine used in the war's early phases were destroyed, and a quadcopter lasted about three flights. Air defence faces the same arithmetic, since RAND estimates a Shahed-type drone at 20,000 to 30,000 US dollars against 450,000 US dollars to 3.7 million for the Western interceptors that would normally stop it. Russia exploits this by flying such drones high to make interception as expensive as possible, gaining less from the damage than from mapping defences and forcing Ukraine to spend its stocks. Drones have not made artillery obsolete, for Ukrainian officers said drones alone were inadequate, and one think-tank study found that even large numbers of small drones cannot match the firepower of artillery. Scholars therefore dispute whether this is a revolution, since one study of earlier wars finds drones too vulnerable to air defences and electronic warfare to be decisive alone, while another concludes that Ukraine shows evolution rather than revolution.

cards.question: In 1999 the Security Council set up a mission in Sierra Leone and, for the first time, gave peacekeepers a mandate for the _____, limited to their capabilities and areas of deployment.
cards.answerDate: PoC resolution17 September 1999First mandate22 October 1999
cards.abstract:
The protection of civilians is a mandate to prevent, deter or respond to threats of physical violence against civilians, within a mission's capabilities and areas of deployment and without prejudice to the host state's primary responsibility. It began with resolution 1265 of 17 September 1999, the Council's first on the subject, which said it was willing to consider how peacekeeping mandates might better address the effect of war on civilians. Five weeks later resolution 1270 created a mission in Sierra Leone and, acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, let it protect civilians under imminent threat of physical violence, within its capabilities and areas of deployment and taking account of the responsibilities of the government and a regional force. United Nations policy records resolution 1270 as the first time a peacekeeping operation was given such a mandate. By 2008 the organisation's own doctrine said that most multidimensional peacekeeping operations were mandated to protect civilians, a task needing concerted action from military, police and civilian components.

The promise was never unqualified, for the panel behind the 2000 report on peace operations doubted that a blanket mandate was credible, warning that forces then deployed could protect only a small fraction of the hundreds of thousands of civilians at risk. A mission given the task, it added, must also be given the specific resources to carry it out. An internal oversight evaluation of 2014 found that, of 507 incidents involving civilians reported between 2010 and 2013, only 101 drew a reported immediate mission response. It found that force, though authorised, appeared to be routinely avoided, and pointed to divided views among Council members and troop contributors, a de facto dual line of command and contingents' fear of being penalised. One analyst traces such limits to the state-based nature of the United Nations, in which host-state consent and sovereignty tend to win out in the end.

cards.question: In the 1990s the successful holding of national elections seemed to offer a ready _____ for United Nations peace operations, but later missions deployed into conflicts that were still unfinished.
cards.abstract:
An exit strategy is a plan for how an international operation will hand over its tasks and withdraw, and in United Nations peacekeeping the final decision belongs to the Security Council. United Nations doctrine of 2008 says a traditional operation has completed its mandate once the states concerned reach an agreed settlement, which is why some have stayed for decades when none came. For a mission deployed after a civil war success is harder to judge, since a domestic peace is sustainable when the warring parties move their struggle into institutions, and there is no standard checklist of benchmarks. It offers examples such as completed disarmament, national forces able to keep order, an effective judiciary and elections producing legitimate institutions, and says the transition should be planned from the outset. A panel convened by the Secretary-General noted in 2000 that in the 1990s missions implementing peace accords were time-limited and elections seemed to offer a ready exit strategy, but that later missions went into unfinished conflicts, where peacekeepers had no exit without the work of peacebuilders.

The Secretary-General's report of April 2001, titled No Exit Without Strategy, addressed the Council's decisions on closing or transitioning missions, and a 2012 roundtable referring back to it saw transitions as gradual reconfigurations, not single events. Research finds that exit strategies shifted from the election-based approach of the 1990s to peacebuilding, a shift the Peacebuilding Commission institutionalised. Studies of transitional administrations add that first elections can be extremely unstable for a country emerging from conflict, and that voting's technical side has drawn more attention than its political purpose. Peacebuilding of the liberal kind has itself drawn considerable criticism, though one scholar finds many of the critiques exaggerated or misdirected. Evidence on what follows an exit is thin: a descriptive study of countries after UN missions left finds a seemingly positive but uncertain trajectory, in a sample of at most 20 missions, from only 44 completed since the Cold War.
questions: United Nations doctrine asks that transition be planned from the outset against benchmarks such as completed disarmament and capable security forces, leaving the final decision on a mission's _____ to the Security Council.

cards.question: Heading United Nations peacekeeping from 2000 to 2008, longer than anyone before him, the French diplomat _____ had earlier directed policy planning at the French foreign ministry from 1989 to 1993.
cards.answerDate: Led peacekeeping2000 – 2008Crisis Group CEO2014 – 2017
cards.abstract:
Jean-Marie Guéhenno is a French diplomat who ran United Nations peacekeeping from 2000 to 2008, becoming its longest-serving head and leading an unprecedented expansion of it. He had directed policy planning at the French foreign ministry from 1989 to 1993 and later served as ambassador to the Western European Union. He recalls joining in 2000 after writing a book doubting the relevance of nation states, and wondering how he could serve an organisation composed of them with the Security Council as his boss. The doctrine he approved in January 2008 records that during the Cold War peacekeeping was necessarily limited to maintaining ceasefires and stabilising situations on the ground. Later he led the International Crisis Group as president and chief executive from 2014 to 2017, and in 2015 he published the memoir The Fog of Peace.

In it he writes that the interaction of the international community, the Security Council and the Secretariat puts a unique responsibility on the Secretary-General and the head of peacekeeping. Interviewed in 2015 he said peacekeeping cannot work without the agreement of the five permanent members of the Council, since no resolution, the legal foundation of any operation, is possible without it. He added that the Council was paralysed over Ukraine and Syria yet found some agreement on the protection of civilians and counterterrorism, which he saw as examples of a non-political approach to peace. His 2018 essay on the United Nations and civil wars names growing divisions in the Council as a challenge and urges the organisation to recalibrate its ambitions and keep its focus on politics. These views support reading him as holding that an organisation of states mirrors power relations among its members, a summary rather than his phrase, and a study of civilian protection traces similar limits to its state-based nature.

While leading the International Crisis Group from 2014 to 2017, _____ said that peacekeeping cannot work without agreement among the five permanent members of the Security Council.

cards.question: Cutting spending, paring back overseas commitments and cementing new friendships are the tools of _____, which a study of eighteen cases of decline since 1870 found to be common and often effective.
cards.abstract:
Strategic retrenchment is the strategy by which a great power facing relative decline adjusts, whether by cutting spending or reviving its economy at home, or by paring back commitments or cementing new friendships abroad. A comparison of eighteen cases of acute relative decline since 1870 found that great powers frequently retrench and that retrenchment is often effective, contrary to the view that it demoralises allies and invites predation. A related case for restraint, made in 2013, urged the United States to abandon liberal hegemony, give up on global reform, build a smaller force and remove large numbers of troops from forward bases. Critics reply that advocates of retrenchment radically overestimate the costs of deep engagement and underestimate its benefits, and that keeping a grand strategy of deep engagement is what a rational leading power would do. A review of a 2018 book on the subject stresses that retrenchment is not necessarily a retreat and that historical cases show complex, multifaceted strategies rather than either camp's caricature.

A 1990 essay titled The Unipolar Moment declared the post-Cold War world unipolar, with the United States as the unchallenged superpower, and expected multipolarity only in perhaps another generation. Its author allowed that the moment might last only a decade rather than three or four if the United States ran its economy into the ground, but denied that overreach abroad would be the cause. By 2013 a proponent of restraint argued that over a decade of costly, indecisive warfare the country's relative power had deteriorated, and that its strategy provoked pushback from rivals and free riding by allies. A recent study argues that the American decision to sign the 2020 agreement with the Taliban and withdraw from Afghanistan was driven by the need to reallocate resources as part of a retrenchment policy. A former head of United Nations peacekeeping argues that nothing is more damaging than excessive ambition followed by precipitous retrenchment, and urges calibrated ambitions.

cards.question: One commentary on the rise of _____ argues that mediation, once the preserve of diplomats and statesmen, has become an arena for entrepreneurs seeking influence and profit.
cards.abstract:
Commodified peace is the claim, made in a 2025 commentary for the International Peace Institute, that peace is increasingly commodified, so that mediation, once the preserve of diplomats and statesmen, has become an arena for entrepreneurs seeking influence and profit. The commentary contrasts the dealmaker, whose bargaining it calls transactional, zero-sum and contractual, with the peacemaker, who aims to build trust, transform relationships and address the injustices behind a conflict. Business interests in mediation are not new: a 2010 Swiss guidance note, which the commentary cites, found that business actors are driven mainly by profit, security concerns and reputation, and that a mediator need not mind whether business interest or altruism moves them. The same note warned that links to business actors can tarnish a mediator's impartiality, and that businesspeople acting as individuals may present themselves as new political leaders. Work on private peace entrepreneurs shows that citizens without official authority have initiated diplomatic correspondence with the other side and used unofficial resources to influence official processes.

An older line of work describes fragile African states as political marketplaces, where elites seek the highest reward for their loyalty, and argues that outside peace efforts can distort those markets. Another study treats peacekeeping as enterprise, a political-economic exchange rather than primarily a project of beneficence or extraction. A 2025 study of Libya, Syria and Yemen, drawing on over 70 interviews, argues that geopolitical competition has made transactionalism more pronounced, turning peace processes into political marketplaces of bilateral, interest-based, short-term deals. A 2026 article agrees that rival interventions turn peace processes into a political marketplace where actors compete for influence, and notes that guarantors of a settlement can win preferential arrangements for reconstruction contracts and resource extraction. The break may be less sharp than the phrase suggests, for a 2026 analysis finds core practices such as the number of mediators per round stable and locates the change in competing liberal, coercive and transactional logics.

cards.question: During the Cold War, the unarmed observers and lightly armed troops of _____ monitored ceasefires between states, stood as a buffer between their forces and left the politics to diplomats.
cards.answerDate: Began1948UNEF I deployed1956
cards.abstract:
Traditional peacekeeping is the Cold War model of United Nations operations, deployed as an interim measure to help manage a conflict and create conditions in which a lasting settlement can be negotiated. Its tasks were essentially military: observing, monitoring and reporting, supervising a ceasefire, and standing as a buffer between forces that had been separated after a war between states. It grew up in the Cold War, when the goals of peacekeeping were necessarily limited to maintaining ceasefires and stabilising situations on the ground, and the early missions were small teams of unarmed observers and lightly armed troops. The armed model took shape in 1956, when Secretary-General Dag Hammarskjöld designed a force for Egypt after the Suez crisis, and it became the template for later missions. The force was drawn from states other than the permanent members of the Security Council, entered Egypt with its government's consent, and was not meant to influence the military balance in the conflict.

Such operations were developed for conflicts between states and were deployed mainly between two previously warring governments, after a negotiated peace agreement. A later UN panel described the style as a symbolic and non-threatening presence working alongside the conventional armies of the parties. Because the missions did not normally play a direct role in political efforts to resolve the conflict, some stayed for decades before a lasting settlement was reached. Dependence on consent was also a weakness: in 1967 Egypt demanded that the force leave, the Secretary-General complied, and war broke out within weeks. Critics add that the passive style could freeze a conflict, and a study of the longest-running mission, UNTSO, finds it restricted throughout the Cold War to managing a deliberately created impasse.

cards.question: Consent of the parties, impartiality and non-use of force except in self-defence together form the _____, which the UN calls a compass for those planning and running its operations.
cards.answerDate: UNEF I deployed1956Summary study1958Brahimi Report2000HIPPO report2015
cards.abstract:
The holy trinity of peacekeeping is the nickname scholars give to three principles that the UN says set its operations apart: consent of the parties, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate. The UN calls the three inter-related and mutually reinforcing, a compass for those planning and running operations. Two of them can be traced to the first armed force, sent to Egypt in 1956, and the Secretary-General's study of it in 1958 said such an operation needs the consent of the government on whose territory it takes place. That study added that the troops may answer an armed attack with force but must never take the initiative in using it, a rule the UN today traces back to 1956. Without consent a mission risks becoming a party to the conflict, while impartiality, the UN stresses, is not neutrality, since a good referee is impartial but still penalises infractions.

Consent is the principle a host can withdraw: in 1967 Egypt demanded the emergency force's removal and the Secretary-General complied, because such operations rest on consent. The 1990s tested all three, as consent proved fragile in Somalia and was manipulated in Bosnia, while in Rwanda the force was not allowed to use force against obvious mass killing. The Brahimi Report of 2000 kept all three as bedrock principles, but warned that a party can consent merely to gain time and then withdraw, and that impartiality means adherence to the Charter, not equal treatment of aggressors and victims. A 2015 high-level panel heard that many leading troop contributors wanted the principles upheld while other states called them outmoded, and it urged a flexible and progressive reading that never excuses a failure to protect civilians. Today the argument centres on missions mandated to fight armed groups: one analysis says such mandates have taken the UN far beyond the principles, yet an interviewee at headquarters insisted they are not open for debate.

cards.question: Created by a Security Council resolution of 29 May 1948 to supervise a truce in Palestine, the _____ was the first peacekeeping operation established by the United Nations.
cards.answerDate: Authorised29 May 1948In operation1948 – present
cards.abstract:
The United Nations Truce Supervision Organization, known as UNTSO, grew out of the first group of military observers that the Security Council called for in May 1948, and it was the first peacekeeping mission established by the United Nations. Its basis was Security Council Resolution 50 of 29 May 1948, which called for a four-week cessation of hostilities in Palestine and told the UN Mediator, working with the Truce Commission, to supervise it with a sufficient number of military observers. The Mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, needed observers quickly from states with forces nearby, and on 31 May 1948 Washington suggested that Belgium, France and the United States, the states on the Truce Commission, each send 21 officers. Washington pointed to the precedents of observers already provided to the Balkan Commission and to the Good Offices Committee in Indonesia. The observers were unarmed, and UNTSO and the Kashmir observer group both had authorised strengths in the low hundreds.

UNTSO and the observer group in India and Pakistan, active in Kashmir since 1949, were the first two UN peacekeeping operations, and both are still operating. Its observers today monitor ceasefires, supervise armistice agreements, prevent isolated incidents from escalating and help other UN operations in the region. The mission website's background page places the establishment of UNTSO in 1949, to supervise the armistice agreements, whereas the resolution that provided for observers is dated 29 May 1948. After the wars of 1956, 1967 and 1973 its functions changed, yet the observers stayed as go-betweens who stopped isolated incidents growing into larger conflicts, and they have formed the nucleus of other operations at short notice. One study of its first quarter-century finds that the longest-running mission begun by the UN often fell short in the 1950s and 1960s in staying neutral and credible, a bare observer corps whose value was mainly tactical.

cards.question: Created by a 1981 protocol after the United Nations proved unable to supply a peacekeeping force, the _____ supervises the security provisions of the Egypt–Israel peace treaty in the Sinai.
cards.answerDate: Treaty signed26 March 1979Protocol signed3 August 1981Mission began25 April 1982
cards.abstract:
The Multinational Force and Observers, or MFO, is an independent international organisation that supervises the security provisions of the 1979 Treaty of Peace between Egypt and Israel, mainly in the Sinai Peninsula. The treaty's first annex committed both countries to ask the United Nations to provide forces and observers, to be drawn from nations other than the permanent members of the Security Council. The parties foresaw trouble, so on the day the treaty was signed the United States assured both that it would take the steps needed to ensure an acceptable alternative multinational force if the Security Council failed. No UN force came: the mandate of the second emergency force expired in July 1979, and on 18 May 1981 the President of the Security Council announced that the United Nations could not provide a peacekeeping force. Egypt and Israel then negotiated with American help and signed a Protocol on 3 August 1981 that created the MFO with the same functions as the planned UN force.

Those functions are operating checkpoints, reconnaissance patrols and observation posts, verifying that the troop limits in the treaty are respected, and ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Tiran. The mission began on 25 April 1982, the day Israel returned the Sinai to Egyptian sovereignty. Egypt, Israel and the United States were to fund it in equal parts, an arrangement meant to give each government an active interest in the organisation, and a 1995 audit found that the United States also supplied the largest military contingent. Its own history stresses that it does not stand between combatants, since the two states were already bound by a permanent peace, and a US audit judged it closest to a traditional UN operation that observes and reports. One study calls it the first modern multinational peacekeeping force independent of any organisation, another says it succeeded mostly because it fitted the parties' needs, and American defence officials noted that it began under almost optimum conditions.

cards.question: Cold War observer missions, civilian-task missions, peace enforcement, peacebuilding and hybrid operations are the five stages of one scheme of _____, though scholars dispute the count and the dates.
cards.answerDate: Began1948Rapid growth1989 – 1994Administrations1999
cards.abstract:
The generations of peacekeeping are a way of dividing the history of UN peace operations into numbered stages, each adding a feature that sets it apart from the one before. One published scheme counts five: traditional peacekeeping, missions with civilian tasks, peace enforcement, peacebuilding and, only just emerging, hybrid missions run jointly with regional organisations. In that scheme the first generation begins in 1948, and its first two missions, in the Middle East and in Kashmir, are still active. The UN's own history marks different turning points, with a rapid rise in operations from 1989 to 1994, a reassessment in the mid-1990s after setbacks in Rwanda, Srebrenica and Somalia, and in 1999 its administration of Kosovo and East Timor. The five-stage scheme lines up with several of those breaks, since its second generation added civilian tasks such as elections after the Cold War, its third allowed more force after Rwanda, Somalia and Bosnia, and its fourth, peacebuilding, included the transitional administrations of 1999.

The scheme's author admits there is no consensus on exactly where the lines fall or whether the taxonomy is useful, and notes that generations build on one another, sometimes inside a single mission. The count itself varies, as one lecturer sorts missions into observer, interposition, multidimensional and transitional-administration types, and asks whether there are two, three or four generations. A 2022 study argues that the generational approach is ambiguous, reductionist, linear in its connotations and limited in its application, and proposes sorting missions by objective as minimalist, moderate or maximalist. The newest generation is the most disputed, since the scheme above ends in hybrid missions while another analysis says since 2010 the Security Council has created a new generation of stabilisation missions to support host governments. A related argument holds that liberal peacebuilding, the guiding concept of many interventions since the Cold War, especially the UN's, is waning, with Western states shifting their strategy to stabilisation and counter-terrorism.

cards.question: Mandated to help a government extend or restore its authority, sometimes while fighting continued, UN _____ were sent to Mali in 2013 under a resolution authorising all necessary means.
cards.answerDate: Resolution 209828 March 2013Resolution 210025 April 2013HIPPO report2015
cards.abstract:
Stabilisation missions are UN operations that the Security Council and Secretariat have described as supporting the extension or restoration of state authority, in at least one case during ongoing armed conflict. By 2019 the word was in the titles of four missions, yet there was no UN-wide interpretation of it, and mandates listed different activities under the heading. A leading case is the mission in Mali, MINUSMA, created in April 2013 after Mali's transitional authorities asked for a UN operation to stabilise the country and restore the authority of the Malian state. Its mandate began with stabilising key population centres and supporting the re-establishment of state administration across the country, and the Council authorised it to use all necessary means within the limits of its capacities. A month earlier the Council had given the mission in the Congo an Intervention Brigade to neutralise armed groups, 'on an exceptional basis and without creating a precedent or any prejudice to the agreed principles of peacekeeping'.

Peace operations deploy where state authority is contested, and the UN has no formal definition of what extending it involves, so mission and host government must keep negotiating the meaning. In Mali the president accused the mission of partiality after the Secretary-General warned the government against branding non-signatories of the peace deal as spoilers to justify using force against them. One legal analysis argues that stabilisation is not just the next step in a drift from traditional to robust peacekeeping but a more radical departure from conventional doctrine on force, a distinct form of intervention by invitation. The 2015 high-level panel judged that UN peacekeeping missions are not suited to military counter-terrorism, lacking the equipment, intelligence and logistics, and advised that missions not be mandated to conduct it. One scholar argues that the shift from peacekeeping towards stabilisation and counter-terrorism undermines impartiality by making the UN a party to the conflict, and earlier warned it was likely to prove counterproductive.

cards.question: A Lecture 3 slide sets 'Interdependence' and 'Peace' beside the German phrase _____, in a list that also names comparative advantage and a gas pipeline between the EU and Russia.
cards.abstract:
The Wandel durch Annäherung idea appears on a Lecture 3 slide about the weaponisation of interdependence, where the German phrase sits beside the words 'Interdependence' and 'Peace'. The same slide, which continues an earlier discussion, goes on to list 'Comparative advantage' and two quoted labels, 'Gas pipeline EU – RF' and 'Choking off Ukraine'. A slide in the Ukraine lecture returns to the phrase under Nord Stream 2, where it is set against 'Business Interests' and against 'Interdependence as conflict avoider or conflict enhancer'. The same slide also asks whether war is normalcy and peace the exception, and whether Europe was naive, and it puts 'Peace projects' among its questions. An Economist leader of June 2022 describes the hope that economic integration would lead to reform as what the Germans call 'change through trade'.

The leader says those hopes have been dashed, because autocracies account for a third of world GDP, and that Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine has painfully exposed Europe's reliance on Russian energy. A conclusion slide in Lecture 4 says interdependence is increasingly seen not only as a stabilising factor in the international system but also as an element of insecurity and vulnerability, depending on relative power position. Lecture 3 likewise ends its slide with limits to interdependence and limits to the use of chokepoints, naming alternatives and pipelines. An earlier slide gives the other side, noting that while co-dependency on critical supply chains exists, mutually assured economic pain appears to work as a deterrent against escalation. The reading on the weaponised world economy takes the darker view, saying that as economic power and national security merge, economic and technological integration have turned from a promise to a threat.

cards.question: A Lecture 3 slide lists the _____, reactions to it and sanctions on Iran and Afghanistan among the state instruments, in a list that also names SWIFT and rare earths.
cards.abstract:
The dollar clearing system heads the list of 'State instruments' on a Lecture 3 slide about the weaponisation of interdependence, followed by 'reactions to it and sanctions' and the names Iran and Afghanistan. The same list continues with a line pairing a centralising state with markets, a string of names running AI, Big 5, SWIFT and Huawei, and rare materials and rare earths. A Lecture 4 slide describes the wider setting, saying that after the Cold War ended businesses built an independent global economy on top of US-centred infrastructure, which in finance meant the US dollar as the global currency and SWIFT messaging. It adds that for over two decades the United States has unilaterally weaponised chokepoints in these infrastructure systems for strategic advantage. It also says that economic and technological integration have turned from a promise to a threat, and that US adversaries, and even allies, are disconnecting, hiding or retaliating.

Another Lecture 4 slide lists the extraterritorial use of sanctions against Iran among its examples of economic diplomacy used to advance national strategic advantage. Lecture 1 included a poll question asking students to rate the risk of a secondary US–China trade war triggered by Washington enforcing sanctions over Iranian oil. The Financial Times reported on 25 August 2026 that Beijing had warned Washington it would retaliate if Chinese companies were included in any significant expansion of the new US secondary sanctions relating to Iran. The article adds that the United States had sanctioned some private Chinese refiners earlier that year, and that China ordered domestic companies not to comply. Leonard argues that cutting Russian banks out of SWIFT and freezing $300 billion of Russian central bank reserves in 2022 weaponised the dollar, and that China, learning from this, is rapidly expanding its own authority over chokepoints.

cards.question: A lecture slide listing state instruments runs AI, Big 5, _____, Huawei, and the payments system it names is the one from which a Western coalition cut Russian banks in 2022.
cards.abstract:
SWIFT appears on a Lecture 3 slide about the weaponisation of interdependence, in a string of names running AI, Big 5, SWIFT and Huawei under the heading 'State instruments'. The same list opens with the dollar clearing system, reactions to it and sanctions, and goes on to a line pairing a centralising state with markets and to rare materials. A Lecture 4 slide says that after the Cold War ended businesses built an independent global economy on US-centred infrastructure, and in finance that meant the US dollar as the global currency and SWIFT messaging. The slide names three areas of that infrastructure, information flows, finance and technology, and says the United States has for over two decades unilaterally weaponised chokepoints in them. The Lecture 3 slide ends by noting limits to interdependence and to the use of chokepoints, and it names unchecked crypto as a risk.

Leonard writes that states are increasingly turning the systems that once connected them, among them energy routes, financial infrastructure and shipping lanes, into weapons, and that control over chokepoints is becoming a key marker of a country's power. He says that in 2022 a coalition of European and North American countries took the remarkable step of weaponising the dollar when it cut Russian banks out of the SWIFT payments system and froze $300 billion of Russian central bank reserves. He adds that China, learning from this, is rapidly expanding its own authority over chokepoints. He also observes that identical barrels of oil now trade at vastly different prices depending on where they are sold, through which payment system, to which buyer and under which sanctions regime. Farrell and Newman add that American enthusiasm for stablecoins, a kind of cryptocurrency, is pushing China and Europe to accelerate their efforts to develop alternative payment systems.

cards.question: A Lecture 4 slide says _____, in the Netherlands, has a monopoly over ultra-violet lithographic machines that pattern the ultra-fine circuit features which make chips so powerful.
cards.abstract:
ASML appears on a Lecture 3 slide about the weaponisation of interdependence, in a line reading 'The Netherlands, ASML, China + US'. The next line speaks of 'Ecosystems', with the US and Taiwan as co-producers, and the one after names geographic chokepoints, the Strait of Hormuz and the Taiwan Strait. The Lecture 4 deck also has a slide titled 'Chips Supply Chain: ASML', which in the text supplied carries only a link to a video. Another Lecture 4 slide, on the technological stack, says ASML in the Netherlands has a monopoly over ultra-violet lithographic machines, which use light to pattern the ultra-fine circuit features that make chips so powerful. The same slide sets this beside China's 90 per cent of global refining capacity for rare earths, around 60 per cent of all chips made by Taiwan's TSMC, and 84 per cent of the GPU market held by Nvidia.

A conclusion slide in Lecture 4 says geostrategic rivalries are overlaid by an effort to obtain key technologies such as AI and quantum computing, with a risk of a two-tier world. The same slide names the balance between dependence and autarky on issues like semiconductors, and calls market power and the power to set standards key. Lecture 1 recalls that by 10 May the US had been forced to accept a mutual 10 per cent tariff, after conceding on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals. Leonard does not name ASML, but writes that the Biden administration widened export controls, taking advantage of the fact that US and allied firms dominate the production of chip manufacturing equipment and the software required for advanced chips. Farrell and Newman say the concession lets US chip design software firms such as Synopsys and Cadence sell in China again, which will help the Chinese semiconductor industry escape the bind that the Biden administration's limits created.

cards.sub: Lecture 3 · Economic diplomacy, humanitarian aid and development

cards.question: A slide on economic diplomacy says governments can only choose two of hyper-globalisation, national sovereignty and democracy, a heuristic idealtype known as _____ after the economist who framed it.
cards.abstract:
Rodrik's trilemma is presented on Lecture 3's two trilemma slides as a choice between hyper-globalisation, national sovereignty and democracy, of which governments can only choose two. The first slide introduces it as one of the differences of opinion that economic diplomacy does not exclude, since economic diplomacy can also strengthen international economic governance and multilateral agreements on trade, investment, aid and climate. It adds that markets are nationally supported by rules such as contract law, private property arrangements, anti-monopoly legislation, social support systems and ecological rules, in some cases leading to a social contract. In times of deepening globalisation, it says, the quest is for rules at the global level, for example to avoid tax evasion and a race to the bottom and to increase monetary and trade predictability. The next slide calls the trilemma a heuristic idealtype and pairs each choice with what is given up: sovereignty with democracy limits globalisation, sovereignty with globalisation limits democracy, and globalisation with democracy limits national sovereignty.

Each pairing gets an example on that slide: 'America First', the Washington consensus policies together with current-day Singapore, and an 'ever closer' European Union. The reading by Rodrik says today's woes have their roots in the 1990s, when policymakers set the world on a hyperglobalist path, requiring domestic economies to be put in the service of the world economy instead of the other way around. The pages supplied do not use the word trilemma, but they say politicians downplayed the problems of the new global economy, denying that its terms entailed sacrificing sovereignty. The article calls hyperglobalisation more a state of mind than a genuine, immutable constraint on domestic policy, and it points to the more flexible principles of Bretton Woods as a model. Lecture 3's second slide also poses its key question, how to combine the need to reinforce the domestic social contract with international economic traffic rules and policy space.
questions: Pairing sovereignty with democracy limits globalisation, sovereignty with globalisation limits democracy, and globalisation with democracy limits sovereignty, runs the heuristic idealtype of the two slides titled _____ in Lecture 3.

The lecture's key question asks how to combine the domestic social contract with global traffic rules and policy space after setting out _____, a choice of two among sovereignty, democracy and hyper-globalisation.

cards.question: On a slide about the trilemma, pairing national sovereignty with democracy means limits on globalisation, and the example given is '_____' in the lecture's three-way scheme.
cards.abstract:
'America First' is the example that Lecture 3's second trilemma slide gives for pairing national sovereignty with democracy, a pairing it says means limits on globalisation. The slide calls the trilemma a heuristic idealtype and sets two other examples beside this one, the Washington consensus policies and an 'ever closer' European Union. None of the readings uses the phrase, but the Rodrik article describes a populist backlash, personified by President Donald Trump, that was in full swing when it appeared in 2019. Lecture 3's slide on reform of the World Trade Organization carries a line about the impact on global trade of Trump's 'liberation day' in April. Lecture 1 adds that tit-for-tat tariffs between the US and China peaked at 125 per cent on 1 April 2025, and that by 10 May the US had been forced to agree to a return to a mutual 10 per cent tariff.

Leonard writes that Trump launched a rebellion from within against the US-led order, bullying American allies, ditching the World Health Organization, scrapping the US Agency for International Development and imposing widespread punitive tariffs. He adds that Americans had already lost interest in being the world's primary provider of public goods, its police officer and its free-trade champion. Farrell and Newman say a framework deal with China, announced in June, was not the beginning of Trump's imagined epoch of liberation under unilateral American greatness. The administration's rush to make a deal, they argue, demonstrates the limits of going it alone, and the United States is ratcheting back its own threats to persuade adversaries not to cripple vital parts of its economy. Lecture 3's second trilemma slide poses its key question, how to combine the need to reinforce the domestic social contract with international economic traffic rules and policy space.

A 2025 article says the Trump administration's rush to make a deal with China shows the limits of going it alone, a check on the corner of the trilemma labelled _____ on the slide.

cards.question: On the trilemma slide, pairing national sovereignty with globalisation means limits on democracy, and the examples given are the _____ policies and current-day Singapore.
cards.abstract:
The Washington Consensus policies appear on Lecture 3's second trilemma slide as an example of pairing national sovereignty with globalisation, a pairing the slide says means limits on democracy. The slide pairs them with current-day Singapore, and sets 'America First' and an 'ever closer' European Union as its other two examples of the trilemma. Without using the phrase, Rodrik's article traces today's woes to the hyperglobalist path that policymakers set in the 1990s, and says that in finance the change was a shift in governments' attitudes away from managing capital flows and toward liberalisation. It says the United States and organisations such as the International Monetary Fund and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development pushed countries to free vast quantities of short-term finance to move across borders for higher returns. At the time, it says, these changes seemed to rest on sound economics, since openness to trade would put resources where they were most productive and capital would flow where it was needed.

The article lists downsides the hyperglobalists did not foresee, among them falling manufacturing employment in the developed world, the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression and austerity after the crash. More and more of what happened to ordinary people, it says, seemed the result of anonymous market forces or of distant decision-makers in foreign countries. It adds that politicians downplayed these problems, and that the centre-right and centre-left disagreed not over the rules of the new world economy but over how to accommodate national economies to them. Oks and Williams, likewise without the phrase, write that structural adjustment programmes, required by the IMF for debt relief or advocated by enthusiastic liberalisers, further diminished state capacity through privatisations, deregulation and government layoffs. They add that many poor-world governments liberalised their capital accounts, increasing volatility and ending in financial crises in Mexico in 1994, in Asia in 1997 and in Russia in 1998, and that the reforms did little to improve growth fundamentals.
questions: A 2019 article describes the 1990s hyperglobalist turn towards liberalised finance and open trade, which the lecture's sovereignty-and-globalisation corner illustrates with the _____ policies and Singapore.
Liberalised capital accounts led to crises in Mexico in 1994, Asia in 1997 and Russia in 1998, a 2022 article says, among reforms of the kind the lecture's slide calls the _____ policies.

cards.question: A trilemma slide pairs globalisation with democracy at the cost of national sovereignty and gives as its example an _____, which sovereigntists criticise for its political integration.
cards.abstract:
The ever closer European Union is the example Lecture 3's second trilemma slide gives for pairing globalisation with democracy, a pairing it says means limits on national sovereignty. The slide says that in the EU, Rodrik depicts the dilemma in essence as one between more political integration, which is criticised by sovereigntists, and less economic integration, which is criticised by business and mainstream politicians. It adds that populism thrives on what it calls this di/trilemma. A Lecture 4 slide defining economic diplomacy lists, for the Dutch Foreign Ministry, a directorate for European cooperation, with trade agreements as an EU competence and Brexit. Rodrik's article says politicians and policymakers downplayed the problems of the new global economy, denying that its terms entailed sacrificing sovereignty, yet seemed immobilised by the same forces.

The lecture's key question is how to combine the need to reinforce the domestic social contract with international economic traffic rules and policy space. A Lecture 4 slide on institutional adaptation says short-term dependence on US security guarantees limits the EU's strategic autonomy, and that the EU lacks capacity to coordinate national capitals and empower the European Commission. Farrell and Newman say China and the United States can usually bet on the principle that 'Europe Always Chickens Out' in geoeconomic confrontations, because Europe lacks the information, institutional clout and internal agreement to do much else. Leonard argues that groupings such as the EU should turn their efforts to creating rules-based orders in their own neighbourhoods rather than striving for an unattainable global order. Lecture 3's second trilemma slide closes by asking what must be organised nationally and what should be organised as multilateral traffic rules on ecology, security, tax, and fragility and development.
questions: Populism thrives on the choice between more political integration, criticised by sovereigntists, and less economic integration, criticised by business, a slide says of the _____ in the trilemma.
Trade agreements are an EU competence, a Lecture 4 slide notes, and the same deck's trilemma slide pictures the Union's integration as an _____ that costs national sovereignty.

cards.question: A slide on economic diplomacy cites the _____ of African countries, with EPA agreements as its example, as a difference of opinion that economic diplomacy does not exclude.
cards.abstract:
Policy space appears on Lecture 3's first trilemma slide, which says economic diplomacy can strengthen international economic governance and multilateral agreements but does not exclude differences of opinion, citing the 'policy space' of African countries, with EPA agreements as an example. The slide adds that markets are nationally supported by rules such as contract law, private property arrangements, anti-monopoly legislation, social support systems and ecological rules. It says that in times of deepening globalisation the quest is for rules at the global level, for example to avoid tax evasion and a race to the bottom. The next slide poses the key question as how to combine the need to reinforce the domestic social contract with international economic traffic rules and policy space. It also asks what must be organised nationally and what should be organised as multilateral traffic rules on ecology, security, tax, and fragility and development.

Rodrik's article says the World Trade Organization, created in 1995, made it harder for countries to shield themselves from international competition and reached into policy areas such as agriculture, services, intellectual property, industrial policy, and health and sanitary regulations. The article adds that hyperglobalisation was more a state of mind than a genuine, immutable constraint on domestic policy. Oks and Williams write that the infrastructure of global free trade has limited the scope of national industrial policies, through WTO agreements from TRIPS to TRIMS that ban or limit strategies used by successful industrialisers of the past. They add that reshaping the IMF's global reserve system and forming a Bretton Woods style framework are also necessary, to prevent boom-bust cycles and to return some measure of autonomy over economic policy to poor-world policymakers. A Lecture 4 slide credited to the WTO director-general lists, among the reasons the WTO needs reform, that it does not deliver sufficient benefits for the most vulnerable and that it is difficult to industrialise, for emerging and advanced economies alike.

One reading says WTO rules from TRIPS to TRIMS limit national industrial policies and wants autonomy over economic policy returned to poor-world policymakers, a concern close to the lecture's _____ in its trilemma slides.

cards.question: A Western Balkans slide says over 8,000 Muslim men and boys went missing from the 1995 genocide at _____, and that 90 per cent of those missing are accounted for.
cards.abstract:
Srebrenica appears on a lecture slide about the Western Balkans as the 1995 'Srebrenica Genocide', from which the slide says over 8,000 Muslim men and boys went missing. The slide sets that figure beside a larger one, more than 40,000 missing persons at the end of the conflict, which it gives first. The Western Balkans is the first of three case studies that the guest speaker announces, the others being Syria and Gaza, grouped on the slide under MENA, and Ukraine. Her biography slide lists the Western Balkans first, ahead of Cyprus, Armenia, Iraq and others, among the places where her work in conflict and post-conflict zones has taken her. The same slide says she is director-general of the International Commission on Missing Persons, or ICMP, appointed in 2004 after helping to lead the organisation's development from 1998.

On the Western Balkans slide, ICMP is said to have facilitated institutional and legislative capacities, including a regional Missing Persons Group and a Regional Group of Families of Missing. The slide adds that ICMP pioneered the application of state-of-the-art DNA and advanced database informatics to locate and identify large numbers of missing persons. It calls the results unprecedented, with 70 per cent of the missing accounted for, including 90 per cent of those missing from the Srebrenica genocide, and these are the last figures on the slide. Two slides later a photograph is captioned 'Courtroom Evidence' and shows Thomas Parsons, a former ICMP Director of Science and Technology, testifying at the ICTY, though the caption names no case. A later slide records that in October 2025 a delegation, labelled NCMP, met the Mothers of Srebrenica and discussed their efforts to deliver justice and answers to families.
questions: A Western Balkans slide credits ICMP with facilitating a regional Missing Persons Group and pioneering DNA identification, and reports 90 per cent of those missing from _____ in 1995 accounted for.
A lecture slide records that in October 2025 a delegation labelled NCMP met the Mothers of _____ to discuss their efforts to deliver justice and answers to families.
