cards.question: ICMP's Western Balkans slide says it pioneered state-of-the-art _____ and advanced database informatics to locate large numbers of missing persons, with 70 per cent of the missing accounted for.
cards.abstract:
DNA identification is the method that the Western Balkans slide of the guest lecture says ICMP pioneered, in the form of state-of-the-art DNA and advanced database informatics applied to locating and identifying large numbers of missing persons. The slide reports unprecedented results, with 70 per cent of the missing accounted for, including 90 per cent of those missing from the Srebrenica genocide. It opens with more than 40,000 missing persons at the end of the conflict, and it adds that ICMP facilitated institutional and legislative capacities in the region. A slide on building state capacities lists a centralised missing persons mechanism, central records and proper investigations that harness state-of-the-art technologies. A principles slide says that establishing cause and manner of death is fundamental in upholding the right to the truth.

In the Syria case study, a slide on data collection reports that ICMP has collected missing persons reports from more than 80,000 relatives and documented more than 30,000 missing persons in its Integrated Data Management System, or iDMS. The next slide, which shares the heading 'Laying the foundations' with the data collection slide, says that more than 800 family members have provided DNA reference samples for reported missing persons. The slide on current support for Syria lists high-throughput DNA laboratories, an interoperable data system and transfer of data, and out-of-country data collection that includes Syrian refugees. The Ukraine strategy slide lists developing a shared missing persons data system and extensive training in all aspects of the process, from data collection to data protection and processing, DNA testing and excavations. The first objective on the Ukraine slide is to help locate and investigate missing persons cases to judicial standards, in order to hold perpetrators of atrocities to account.

In the Syria case study, ICMP lists data collected from more than 80,000 relatives and reference samples from more than 800 family members, steps beside the _____ it pioneered in the Western Balkans.

cards.question: A regional _____ and a Regional Group of Families of Missing are the bodies that a Western Balkans slide lists among the institutional and legislative capacities ICMP helped to develop.
cards.abstract:
The Missing Persons Group is named once in the lecture, on the Western Balkans slide, as a regional body whose development ICMP facilitated. The slide lists it among the institutional and legislative capacities that ICMP helped to develop, beside a Regional Group of Families of Missing. The slide gives no membership, founding date or mandate for the group, so the rest of this card rests on what the lecture says about cooperation. The group is placed in a case study that opens with more than 40,000 missing persons at the end of the conflict and over 8,000 Muslim men and boys missing from the 1995 Srebrenica genocide. The Western Balkans also appears, as Western Balkans including Albania Communist Era, on the lecture's list of current country and regional programmes, a slide that says ICMP has worked in over 40 countries.

The speaker's biography says she has helped governments, courts, prosecutors, NGOs, scientists and academics build capacity, draft effective legislation and establish institutions to handle missing persons issues. A principles slide says that effective responses require cooperation between states and with international institutions, while the slide on building state capacities lists cooperation, a centralised missing persons mechanism, purpose-specific legislation and central records. The slide on current support for Syria lists cross-border cases, conferences and regional meetings, and cooperation among families, civil society and relevant ministries. The Ukraine strategy slide includes securing cooperation between regional states and developing a shared missing persons data system. The slide on international and regional organisations names INTERPOL and the regional European bodies EUROPOL, EUROJUST and the OSCE, and the next names five international NGOs, from the ICRC to Impunity Watch, though neither slide links them to the Missing Persons Group.

cards.question: A lecture slide puts the number of _____ at almost 300,000 over many decades, listing atrocity crimes, incommunicado detention, conflict, earthquakes and migration beneath the figure.
cards.abstract:
Syria's missing are put by the lecture's Syria slide at almost 300,000 people missing over many decades. Beneath the figure the slide lists atrocity crimes, incommunicado detention, conflict, earthquakes and migration, without saying how many of the missing fall under each. It also lists 'Syrian and non-Syrian', orphaned children and the point that the majority of survivors are women. It ends with under-reporting, linked on the slide to stigma and fear, and an earlier slide likewise says that women are often disappeared but that these cases are underreported, naming Syria, Iraq, Mexico, Nigeria and Canada among its examples. Under the heading 'Laying the foundations', one slide reports that ICMP has collected missing persons reports from more than 80,000 relatives and documented more than 30,000 missing persons, with data collected from persons inside and outside Syria.

A second slide under that heading says that more than 800 family members have provided DNA reference samples for reported missing persons. A third says that more than 70 sites of forensic interest, including mass graves, have been reported anonymously through ICMP's Online Inquiry Center, with verification ongoing. A slide titled 'The Liberation of Damascus, 8 December 2024' carries the phrase 'Emerging State Responsibility', and a later slide shows mass grave sites in the towns of Qutayfah and Najha near Damascus. A slide caption records that ICMP and the Syrian National Commission for Missing Persons signed a memorandum of understanding at Leiden University, and the slide on current support lists a legislative framework, an interoperable data system and cross-border cases. A slide headed 'Challenges' lists a non-discrimination guarantee, reparations, access to justice, transparency, data protection standards and a national plan, and it also lists scale, timeframe and complexity.
questions: The slide that lists under-reporting, linked to stigma and fear, and notes that the majority of survivors are women concerns _____, put at almost 300,000 over many decades.
ICMP's case study of _____ includes data from more than 80,000 relatives, DNA samples from more than 800 family members and a memorandum signed at Leiden University with a Syrian commission.

cards.question: ICMP's _____ has received anonymous reports of more than 70 sites of forensic interest in Syria, including mass graves, which are being verified with open source intelligence technologies.
cards.abstract:
The Online Inquiry Center, or OIC, is named on a Syria slide as the route by which more than 70 sites of forensic interest, including mass graves, have been reported anonymously to ICMP. The slide's heading gives the same figure as more than 70 sites of forensic interest reported to ICMP, under the title 'Laying the foundations'. It adds that verification is ongoing, using Open Source Intelligence technologies, known as OSINT, and partnering with others. The same heading covers two other slides, one on data collection, with reports from more than 80,000 relatives, and one on DNA reference samples, from more than 800 family members. The data slide adds that more than 30,000 missing persons are documented in the Integrated Data Management System and that data has been collected from persons inside and outside Syria.

A slide on the missing in Syria lists under-reporting, linked on the slide to stigma and fear, and says that the majority of survivors are women. A later slide shows mass grave sites in the towns of Qutayfah and Najha near Damascus, without saying whether they are among the sites reported, and the slide before it is titled with the Liberation of Damascus on 8 December 2024 and the phrase 'Emerging State Responsibility'. The principles slides say that crimes are at the source of persons going missing and must be fully investigated, and that establishing cause and manner of death is fundamental in upholding the right to the truth. The slide on building state capacities lists active public engagement and good governance, which it glosses as the provision of credible and honest information and trust in public institutions. The Ukraine objectives slide includes ensuring that the public is provided with factual and credible information regarding disappeared persons and related crimes.

cards.question: On the lecture's Way Forward slide, _____ comes first, ahead of truth, justice and reparations, strengthening justice mechanisms, and empowering survivors, families and civil society.
cards.abstract:
State responsibility to investigate is the first of four items on the missing persons lecture's slide called The Way Forward. The other three are truth, justice and reparations, strengthening justice mechanisms, and empowering survivors, families and civil society. An earlier slide asks who is responsible for finding the missing and securing rights, and answers that states are responsible for securing rights. The same slide lists the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, the ICMP Paris Principles, the ICMP treaty, the Universal Declaration on Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. A principles slide states that states have a responsibility to resolve the fate of missing persons and that fundamental human rights are invoked when a person goes missing.

It adds that investigations must be capable of establishing the facts, that meaningful investigations ensure individuals protection under the law, and that effective responses require cooperation between states and with international institutions. The next slide says that crimes are at the source of persons going missing and must be fully investigated, and that addressing the issue must uphold and advance the rule of law. In the Syria case study, the slide on the Liberation of Damascus carries the phrase 'Emerging State Responsibility'. The Gaza slide lists ongoing conflict, no ICMP presence, war crimes, atrocity crimes and human rights violations, and ends with the words 'No political will'. A slide in the rule of law lecture gives the UN system's definition, under which the State itself is accountable to laws that are publicly promulgated, equally enforced and independently adjudicated, and another says strengthening the rule of law involves recognising the primary responsibility of States to protect their populations from genocide, crimes against humanity, ethnic cleansing and war crimes.

In a rule of law slide's definition, even the State itself is accountable to laws, and a missing persons slide lists _____ first among its ways forward.

cards.question: A missing persons lecture gives a slide to _____ alone and then lists it first among the ways of building state capacities, ahead of a rule of law and human rights approach.
cards.abstract:
Political will is the title of a slide in the missing persons lecture and the first item on its list of ways of building state capacities. The title slide has no other text and comes after a slide on war and peace, so what the lecture means by it has to be read from the slides around it. The slide after it says that states have a responsibility to resolve the fate of missing persons and that fundamental human rights are invoked when a person goes missing. It adds that investigations must be capable of establishing the facts and that effective responses require cooperation between states and with international institutions. The next slide says that crimes are at the source of persons going missing and must be fully investigated, and that addressing the issue must uphold and advance the rule of law.

The capacity slide lists 'Ensure Political Will' first, followed by a rule of law and human rights approach, a centralised missing persons mechanism, central records and purpose-specific legislation. It goes on to proper investigations that harness state-of-the-art technologies, active public engagement, good governance, glossed as credible and honest information and trust in public institutions, and cooperation. On the Gaza slide the lecture lists thousands of missing, including hostages, ongoing conflict with no ICMP presence, and war crimes, atrocity crimes and human rights violations, and it closes with the words 'No political will'. Lecture 2 uses the word will in other settings, and a slide on the independent inquiry into Rwanda lists the inadequacy of the mandate, due to lack of will, resources and intel. Another Lecture 2 slide, on the Blair Doctrine, includes among its questions whether there is a will to hold out for the long term.

Following the war and peace slide and the single-heading slide _____, the principles slides say that states must resolve the fate of missing persons and that crimes behind disappearances must be fully investigated.

cards.question: A slide on Ukraine headlines roughly 100,000 and growing as the number of _____, with ICMP objectives running from judicial standards to the rights of families to justice, truth and reparations.
cards.abstract:
Ukraine's missing persons are headlined on the lecture's Ukraine slide as roughly 100,000 and growing. The slide is the last of three case studies that an earlier slide announces, after the Western Balkans and Syria and Gaza. Ukraine is also on the slide of current country and regional programmes, and on the speaker's biography slide among the places where her work has taken her. Beneath the figure the slide lists objectives of ICMP support, and the first is to help locate and investigate missing persons cases to judicial standards to hold perpetrators of atrocities to account. The second is to ensure that the public is provided with factual and credible information regarding disappeared persons and related crimes.

The third is to help counter false narratives that seek to undermine public trust, social cohesion and peace and stability, and the fourth is to secure the rights of all families of the missing to justice, truth and reparations. The Ukraine Strategy slide lists developing institutional and technical capacities and a legislative framework, and providing international technical expertise to conduct largescale investigations. It also lists supporting the meaningful participation of Ukraine's civil society and families of the missing, especially those that are women-led, and ensuring cooperation between Ukrainian authorities, civil society and families. It adds securing cooperation between regional states, developing a shared missing persons data system, and working with thousands of families of the missing to collect data and to enhance their understanding of the process and their rights. The last item is extensive training in all aspects of the process, from data collection to data protection and processing, DNA testing and excavations, for Ukrainian institutions, CSOs, families of the missing and others.

Ukraine is the last of three case studies, after the Western Balkans, Syria and Gaza, and its slide aims to secure justice, truth and reparations for the families of _____, the slide says.

cards.question: Among the aims the lecture lists for rules at the global level are avoiding tax evasion, avoiding a _____, and increasing monetary and trade predictability.
cards.abstract:
Race to the bottom is a phrase on Lecture 3's first trilemma slide, where it is one of the things that rules at the global level are meant to avoid. The slide starts from the point that markets are nationally supported by rules, among them contract law, private property arrangements, anti-monopoly legislation, social support systems and ecological rules, in some cases leading to a social contract. It says that in times of deepening globalisation, when the intensity and scope of economic transactions across borders increase, the quest is for rules at the global level. The aims it gives include avoiding tax evasion, avoiding a race to the bottom and increasing monetary and trade predictability, which it sums up as a quest for international economic traffic rules. On the same slide, the trilemma is the choice between hyper-globalisation, national sovereignty and democracy, of which governments can only choose two.

The next slide poses the key question as how to combine the need to reinforce the domestic social contract with international economic traffic rules and policy space. It also raises what must be organised nationally and what should be organised as multilateral traffic rules on ecology, security, tax, and fragility and development. The climate slide does not use the phrase, but it describes governments that fear losing competitiveness or capital flight if they impose stricter rules, which it says erodes the space for democratic choice on climate. The Rodrik pages in the course material do not use the phrase either, but they say the centre-right and the centre-left agreed that economies needed to be refashioned in the name of global competitiveness, the right wanting to cut taxes and slash regulations. Leonard writes that architects believe there can be a single rule book for everyone while artisans accept that multiple sets of guidelines will coexist, and that groupings such as the EU should build rules-based orders in their own neighbourhoods rather than strive for an unattainable global order.

cards.question: The lecture's climate-and-trilemma slide gives the 2015 _____ as its example of a compromise in which countries set their own Nationally Determined Contributions and keep their sovereignty.
cards.abstract:
The Paris Agreement of 2015 is the example that Lecture 3's slide headed 'Climate and Rodrik's Trilemma' gives of a compromise. The slide says countries keep sovereignty under it because each sets its own Nationally Determined Contribution, which preserves democracy at home. It adds that this means Paris lacks enforceability, because it relies on peer pressure, not supranational authority. Before the example, the slide pairs democracy with national sovereignty and says climate policy will then likely be weak, because voters may prefer growth or cheap energy and governments face incentives to free-ride on others' reductions, which it labels insufficient action to address a global problem. It pairs democracy with hyperglobalisation and says ambitious climate action then needs sovereignty to be shared in international institutions, for example through binding treaties with enforcement and carbon pricing across borders.

That route, it adds, requires supranational governance that many states and publics resist. Its third pairing, sovereignty with hyperglobalisation, constrains climate action because governments fear losing competitiveness or capital flight if they impose stricter rules. Lecture 3's first trilemma slide says economic diplomacy can strengthen international economic governance and multilateral agreements on trade, investment, aid and climate. The next slide poses as its key question how to combine the need to reinforce the domestic social contract with international economic traffic rules and policy space, and it raises what should be organised as multilateral traffic rules on ecology, security, tax, and fragility and development. Leonard does not name the Paris Agreement, but he writes that UN climate change conferences convene to chart an increasingly hopeless path to net-zero emissions, and that the competition to dominate renewable technologies has probably done more to combat rising emissions than all the Conference of the Parties meetings combined.

cards.question: The assignment question asks what multilateral interventions can mitigate the _____ by which a maritime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz delivers a severe socio-economic and political shock to the Sahel.
cards.abstract:
Hormuz–Sahel transmission is the name used here for the question that slide 16 of Lecture 3 poses under the heading 'Assignment Question', and no text uses the phrase itself. The question asks how a maritime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz transmits a severe socio-economic and political shock for the Sahel, and what multilateral interventions can be deployed to mitigate this. The next slide, headed 'Potential Answers', says the Sahel is not directly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz, unlike the Gulf states, but remains integrated into the global economy affected by disruptions there. It argues that international cooperation should prioritise supporting the Sahel in managing such shocks, rather than leaving individual countries to address them independently. Slide 23 names the Strait of Hormuz among its geographic chokepoints, and Leonard writes that Iran's closure brought 20 per cent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipping to a near halt.

On the slide's account, rising oil prices raise the costs of transportation, agriculture and food, disproportionately affecting populations already facing poverty and food insecurity. It adds that these pressures can erode public trust in government institutions, potentially bringing protests and more opportunities for recruitment by armed groups. Winer writes that war-time disruption of shipping through the strait is spreading through the fertiliser market, and that more than 40 million people in the Sahel already face acute food insecurity, with projections above 50 million in the June to August 2026 lean season. He says the stress predates the conflict, pointing to local conflicts that had constrained access to farmland in the Lake Chad Basin and the Liptako-Gourma region as of February 2026. He also reports that benchmark urea prices rose by roughly 46 per cent month-on-month between February and March 2026, according to the World Bank, and that the difference between mitigation and crisis in much of the Sahel will be determined over the next four to eight weeks, as planting decisions are made and input use is fixed.

cards.question: A lecture slide warns of a potential _____ in which economic insecurity exacerbates political instability, impeding efforts to contain existing conflicts, after listing higher fuel and food prices and reduced government revenues.
cards.abstract:
Fiscal feedback loop is the name used here for the dynamic that slide 17 of Lecture 3 describes as a potential feedback loop, and the slide itself does not use the label. The slide starts from the global effects of a disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, which it lists as increased fuel and food prices, reduced government revenues and the diversion of already limited resources toward crisis management. It adds that governments may be required to allocate additional funds to security at a time when fiscal space is diminishing. The slide says this dynamic generates a potential feedback loop in which economic insecurity exacerbates political instability, thereby impeding efforts to contain existing conflicts. The slide's other paragraph says economic pressures can erode public trust in government institutions, potentially bringing protests, diminished confidence in state structures and more opportunities for recruitment by armed groups.

Winer's article, which does not use the loop language, says governments across the Sahel, already under fiscal strain, face increasing difficulty sustaining subsidy programmes or extending seasonal credit to smallholders. He adds that several Sahelian importers, already facing currency weakness and tighter access to trade finance, are meeting higher financing costs and delayed procurement just when fertiliser purchases are normally finalised. He also says humanitarian agencies, facing funding constraints, had been cutting rations or narrowing coverage, so people in the Sahel were already getting less food before the war in the Gulf. Oks and Williams write that in the two decades that followed the Volcker shock, deep recessions across the poor world led to fiscal insolvency, social and political collapse and massive bloodletting. They also write that the link between youth bulges, high youth unemployment and social unrest has been studied for decades, and that instability, violence and the loss of state capacity can poison even the most hopeful attempts at development.

cards.question: A slide on the Sahel says an effective _____ could integrate emergency financial assistance from the IMF and the World Bank, humanitarian support, African Union coordination and conflict-prevention mechanisms.
cards.abstract:
Multilateral shock response is the label used here for the package that slide 17 of Lecture 3 proposes for the Sahel, and the slide itself does not use the label. It says an effective multilateral response could integrate emergency financial assistance from institutions such as the International Monetary Fund, or IMF, and the World Bank, humanitarian support, regional coordination through the African Union, and conflict-prevention mechanisms. The slide gives the purpose as preventing financial grievances from growing into further instability. Its first paragraph argues that international cooperation should prioritise supporting the Sahel in managing such shocks, rather than leaving individual countries to address them independently. The preceding slide asks what multilateral interventions can be deployed to mitigate the shock that a disruption in the Strait of Hormuz transmits to the Sahel.

Slide 12 sets out the recommendation of the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations for a strong push on prevention, including earlier engagement by the Security Council and reinforced prevention and mediation capabilities in the UN secretariat. Slide 13 adds that the panel wants a stronger network of national and regional standby capabilities, and a Lecture 2 slide says the African Union often prefers stronger military mandates and that the UN needs to work closely with regional organisations. Lindborg and Hewitt write that US administrations become hostage to the latest crisis and focus on responding rather than preventing, at a cost they call increasingly untenable, with attention coming only after crisis hits, when action is more urgent and expensive. Winer writes that redirecting fertiliser cargoes, securing trade finance and moving inputs inland through fragile logistics networks takes time the region does not have. Oks and Williams are more critical of the IMF, writing that the structural adjustment programmes it required for debt relief further diminished state capacity, and that reshaping its global reserve system and its allocation of special drawing rights to poor economies will be necessary.

cards.question: Described on a slide as a treaty-based body in The Hague, the only international organisation mandated exclusively to help governments locate missing persons, the _____ has worked in over 40 countries.
cards.abstract:
The International Commission on Missing Persons, or ICMP, is described on slide 44 of Lecture 3 as a treaty-based intergovernmental organisation based in The Hague. The slide calls it the only international organisation mandated exclusively to secure the cooperation of governments and to assist them in their efforts to locate missing persons from conflict, human rights abuses, disasters, migration and other involuntary causes. Slide 36 includes the ICMP Paris Principles and the ICMP Agreement on Status and Functions, also called the ICMP Treaty, in its list of instruments, and slide 45 is headed 'Agreement on the Status and Functions of the ICMP'. Slide 29 introduces Kathryne Bomberger as ICMP's director-general, appointed in 2004 after helping lead the organisation's development from 1998. Slide 47 says ICMP has worked in over 40 countries, with current programmes including the Western Balkans, Syria and the wider Middle East and North Africa, Ukraine, Iraq, Libya and Mexico.

For the Western Balkans, slide 50 reports more than 40,000 missing persons at the end of the conflict, among them over 8,000 Muslim men and boys missing from the 1995 Srebrenica genocide. It says ICMP facilitated institutional and legislative capacities there, including a regional Missing Persons Group, and pioneered state-of-the-art DNA and advanced database informatics to locate and identify large numbers of missing persons. The slide reports that 70 per cent of the missing have been accounted for, including 90 per cent of those missing from Srebrenica, and calls these results unprecedented. For Syria, slides 54 and 55 report that ICMP has collected missing persons reports from more than 80,000 relatives, documented more than 30,000 missing persons in its Integrated Data Management System, and received DNA reference samples from more than 800 family members. A closing slide, headed 'The Opportunity', lists a standing capacity, rapid and scalable response, intergovernmental cooperation, strong national institutions and upholding the rule of law, under the call to be ready for the next conflict or mass calamity.

cards.question: The first legal instrument on a guest lecture's slide about who must find the missing and secure rights is the convention for protecting all persons from _____, abbreviated ICPPED.
cards.abstract:
Enforced disappearance appears in the course texts only inside the title of the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, abbreviated ICPPED, which slide 36 of Lecture 3 puts first among its instruments, and no text defines it. The slide asks who is responsible for finding the missing and securing rights, and answers that states are responsible for securing rights. Slide 32, which carries the heading 'Missing & Disappeared Persons', says hundreds of thousands are missing worldwide from wars, human rights abuses, organised crime including human trafficking and slavery, disasters and migration. Slide 33 lists men as the majority of the missing, along with civilians, the poor, minorities and migrants. Slide 34 says women are often disappeared but that these cases are underreported, and it gives examples from Syria, Iraq, Mexico, Nigeria and Canada.

For Syria, slide 53 reports almost 300,000 missing over many decades, lists atrocity crimes, incommunicado detention, conflict, earthquakes and migration beneath that figure, and notes under-reporting through stigma and fear. Slide 39 says fundamental human rights are invoked when a person goes missing, and that states have a responsibility to resolve the fate of missing persons. Slide 40 says crimes are at the source of persons going missing and must be fully investigated, and that addressing the issue of missing and disappeared persons must uphold and advance the rule of law. Lecture 6 gives the UN definition of the rule of law as a principle in which all persons, institutions and entities, including the State itself, are accountable to laws that are publicly promulgated, equally enforced and independently adjudicated, and consistent with international human rights norms and standards. For Ukraine, slide 64 lists as objectives to investigate missing persons cases to judicial standards so as to hold perpetrators of atrocities to account, and to give the public factual and credible information about disappeared persons and related crimes.

cards.question: A slide asking who must find the missing and secure rights lists the _____, abbreviated ICPPED, first, ahead of the ICMP Paris Principles and the Universal Declaration on Human Rights.
cards.answer: International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance
cards.abstract:
The International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, abbreviated ICPPED on the slide, is the first of the legal instruments listed on slide 36 of Lecture 3, and the course texts do not describe its provisions. The same list names the ICMP Paris Principles, the ICMP Agreement on Status and Functions, also called the ICMP Treaty, the Universal Declaration on Human Rights and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Beside the Declaration the slide cites Article 3 on the right to life and Article 12 on the right to privacy, and beside the Covenant Articles 6, 7 and 17, on life, the prohibition against torture and privacy. The slide poses the question of who is responsible for finding the missing and securing rights, and it answers that states are responsible for securing rights. Slide 39, headed 'Addressing the Missing: Underlying Principles', says states have a responsibility to resolve the fate of missing persons and that fundamental human rights are invoked when a person goes missing.

It adds that investigations must be capable of establishing the facts and that effective responses require cooperation between states and with international institutions. Slide 40 continues that addressing the issue of missing and disappeared persons must uphold and advance the rule of law. Lecture 6 gives the UN definition of the rule of law as a principle in which all persons, institutions and entities, including the State itself, are accountable to laws that are publicly promulgated, equally enforced and independently adjudicated, and consistent with international human rights norms and standards. Slide 41 lists what building state capacities involves, among it a rule of law and human rights approach, a centralised missing persons mechanism, central records and purpose-specific legislation. Slide 44 describes ICMP as a treaty-based intergovernmental organisation, and slide 67, headed 'The Way Forward', lists state responsibility to investigate and truth, justice and reparations, with a closing call to protect rights and enforce responsibility.

cards.question: Establishing cause and manner of death is called fundamental in upholding the _____ on a slide about the underlying principles of addressing the missing, which also says crimes must be fully investigated.
cards.abstract:
Right to the truth appears on slide 40 of Lecture 3, which says that establishing cause and manner of death is fundamental in upholding it, and no text in the course defines it. The same slide says crimes are at the source of persons going missing and must be fully investigated. It adds that addressing the issue of missing and disappeared persons must uphold and advance the rule of law. The slide before it says investigations must be capable of establishing the facts and that meaningful investigations ensure individuals protection under the law. Slide 37, headed 'War & Peace', lists the dignity of the dead, investigations to find the missing, accountability and the rights of the living among its concerns.

Slide 41 includes, among the ways of building state capacities, proper investigations that harness state of the art technologies and good governance, glossed as the provision of credible and honest information and trust in public institutions, on a list that also names active public engagement and cooperation. Slide 52 shows a photograph captioned 'Courtroom Evidence', of ICMP's former director of science and technology testifying at the ICTY. Among the objectives of ICMP's support in Ukraine, slide 64 lists providing the public with factual and credible information about disappeared persons and related crimes, countering false narratives, and securing the rights of all families of the missing to justice, truth and reparations. Slide 67, headed 'The Way Forward', lists state responsibility to investigate and truth, justice and reparations, and ends with a call to protect rights and enforce responsibility. For Gaza, slide 63 lists thousands missing, including hostages, ongoing conflict with no ICMP presence, war crimes, atrocity crimes, human rights violations and no political will.

cards.question: The first group of recommendations from the panel on peace operations, shown on a Lecture 3 slide, urges a strong push on _____, including an international forum and earlier Security Council engagement.
cards.abstract:
Conflict prevention is the first subject in the recommendations that a Lecture 3 slide attributes to the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations. The slide says that existing conflicts are proving harder to resolve and yet new ones are emerging, and that the panel calls for a strong push on prevention. Its proposals include an international forum on prevention that draws on external resources and knowledge, and a reinforcement of the UN secretariat's prevention and mediation capabilities. They also include earlier engagement by the Security Council to address emerging threats, and earlier use of UN expert resources to support national and regional prevention and mediation efforts. One potential answer on slide 17, to a question about a Hormuz disruption and the Sahel, says an effective response could include conflict-prevention mechanisms to prevent financial grievances from growing into further instability, beside emergency financial assistance, humanitarian support and African Union coordination.

The slide's first answer warns that economic pressures can erode public trust in government institutions, with protests, diminished confidence in state structures and more opportunities for recruitment by armed groups as possible results. A 2018 essay in Dædalus says administrations in the United States tend to become hostage to the latest terrible crisis, responding to it rather than preventing it, with reactive tools such as military action, peacekeeping missions and humanitarian assistance. The essay adds that attention comes only after a crisis hits, when action is more urgent and expensive, options are more limited and problems are harder to solve. It also says that the United Nations and the World Bank have adopted conflict prevention as core priorities, and that efforts inside the United States government have sought to link early warning with early action. Its closing pages say that more comprehensive evidence on the cost-effectiveness of long-term peace-building remains elusive, and that the case for prevention would be stronger with evidence of its modest costs against the immense costs of crisis response.

cards.question: A lecture slide defines _____ as the collective, coordinated rule-making among countries in conference settings to formulate trade policies and agreements, used as a tool of foreign policy and including sanctions enforcement.
cards.abstract:
Economic diplomacy is defined on Lecture 4's definition slide, after Barston, as the collective and coordinated rule-making among countries in conference settings to formulate collective trade policies and trade agreements, as a tool of foreign policy. Its list covers support for trade, investment opportunities abroad through economic and agricultural attachés, regional and bilateral trade agreements, and sanctions enforcement, with sanctions against Russia as the example. The slide adds that international economic relations become more important in foreign ministries, and takes the Dutch ministry as its case, with directorates-general for foreign economic relations, development cooperation and European cooperation. It calls this a traditional definition, complemented by weaponised interdependence, which it credits to the political scientists Farrell and Newman as leveraging global networks of informational and financial exchange for strategic advantage. Those authors' Foreign Affairs article says the new era will be shaped by sanctions, supply chain attacks and export measures that repurpose points of control in the infrastructure underpinning the interdependent global economy.

The next slide says economic diplomacy is increasingly used to advance national strategic advantage through sanctions, tariffs and export controls, including on technology, and by defining a framework of security, technology and international economic cooperation. Its examples include tariffs to stop Mexican migration, extraterritorial sanctions against Iran, a potential EU framework on Chinese investments and security, and the Taiwan embassy in Lithuania. The slide adds that this is not new but becomes more important in times of geo-economic and geostrategic rivalry and reluctance to use military means. Lecture 4 also says economic diplomacy can enhance and strengthen international economic governance and multilateral agreements on trade, investment, aid and climate. An earlier lecture shows its sharper edge, with US-China tariffs peaking at 125 per cent on 1 April 2025 and the US conceding on semiconductor export controls in return for eased rare-earth restrictions.

cards.question: The Dutch Foreign Ministry's Directorate-General for Development Cooperation, which runs bilateral and multilateral aid programmes, has a budget goal of _____ of GDP, according to a slide in Lecture 4 on economic diplomacy.
cards.abstract:
On Lecture 4's slide on economic diplomacy, the Dutch Foreign Ministry's Directorate-General for Development Cooperation is given a budget goal, stated as a share of GDP, of 0.7 per cent. The slide describes that directorate's work as bilateral and multilateral aid programmes, and lists it among three directorates-general, under the point that international economic relations become more important in foreign ministries. The other two, it says, handle foreign economic relations, including trade facilitation instruments and preparation of high-level visits, and European cooperation, including trade agreements as an EU competence. The slide gives no source, year or outcome for the figure, so the course material does not say who set the goal or whether it has been met. Lecture 4's next slide lists the use of development cooperation to sanction certain behaviour, such as on migration and governance, among the uses of economic diplomacy.

The lecturer says he was Foreign Minister and Development Cooperation Minister in an earlier Dutch cabinet, and invites students to raise questions about that professional experience. A CMI brief on humanitarian diplomacy says that humanitarian efforts, foreign policy and strategic interests increasingly overlap, and it lists development assistance among the forms of support whose relation to humanitarian action is evolving. An article on global development says that after the crises of the 1980s and 1990s, what little remained of government in the worst-hit places, such as Somalia, could be termed government by means of the aid industry. Leonard lists scrapping the US Agency for International Development among the steps by which Trump rebelled against the US-led order, beside ditching the World Health Organization and imposing punitive tariffs. A reading on the Sahel says that humanitarian agencies, facing funding constraints, had been cutting rations or narrowing coverage even before the war in the Gulf began.
questions: Among the three directorates-general the slide lists for the Dutch Foreign Ministry, only the one for aid is given a budget goal, set at _____ of GDP, rather than just a list of tasks.

The lecturer, a former Dutch Foreign Minister and Development Cooperation Minister, shows a slide giving the aid directorate's budget goal as _____ of GDP, beside directorates for trade and European cooperation.

cards.question: Using development cooperation to sanction behaviour on migration or governance is, in effect, _____, which a reading on EU funding of the African Union says can lower a recipient's agency.
cards.abstract:
Aid conditionality is the label used here for what Lecture 4's slide on the uses of economic diplomacy describes as development cooperation used to sanction certain behaviour, with migration and governance as its examples. The slide does not use the label, but a reading in the course uses the word conditionality for conditions that funders attach to the money they give. The slide places this among uses of economic diplomacy to advance national strategic advantage through sanctions, tariffs and export controls, in what it calls an increasingly competitive geostrategic environment. It adds that this is not new but becomes more important in times of geo-economic and geostrategic rivalry and reluctance to use military means. Lecture 4's definition slide shows where aid sits, since the Dutch Foreign Ministry's directorate for development cooperation runs bilateral and multilateral aid programmes beside directorates for trade and for European cooperation.

An article on EU funding for the African Union says coercive relationships lower a recipient's capacity to act intentionally, because funders may apply sanctions or conditionality to achieve particular policy agendas. It links this to the Europeanization literature, in which the EU offers cash payments or promises of progress in accession for policy reforms. Its case is EU security funding for the African Union, not a development budget, though it says that in both organisational funding and development cooperation principals stipulate the resources and the terms of transfer. In that case the EU interrupted disbursements for several months after the African Union Commission failed a 2014 assessment of its financial management, and later cushioned its conditions with short-term fixes. A reading on fragile states describes a compact between fragile-state governments, donors and civil society as a possible model for a carrot-and-stick approach to states trapped in fragility and conflict.

cards.question: Record trade and near-universal internet access beside geopolitical division make up what a lecture slide calls a paradox, a world that is _____, facing threats no state can manage alone.
cards.abstract:
The interconnected but fragmented world is the paradox on Lecture 4's slide on renewed multilateralism, which says the world is economically more interconnected than ever, with record trade and near-universal internet access, yet geopolitically more fragmented. The slide gives the paradox no short name, and its screenshot of an opinion page carries a caption saying that economies remain deeply intertwined while geopolitics moves the other way. It follows the paradox with the most armed conflicts since 1946 in 2025 and record military spending, and calls climate change, AI, pandemics and conflict-driven displacement threats that no state can manage alone. The first lecture's summary of a Foreign Affairs article calls the present an orderless age defined by fragmentation, stagnation and strangulation, with blocs and alliances splintering. Its slide on arenas of power names weaponising interdependence and the weaponisation of everything as increasingly common terms for what it calls the axis of fragmentation.

That article says trade restrictions are breaking up world markets, but not into tidy blocs, and that global problems no longer attract global solutions but a patchwork of short-term fixes. It calls the deepest fragmentation epistemic, since inhabitants of a digitally connected world no longer agree on facts, which erases the shared reality that underpins diplomacy itself. Farrell and Newman say that as countries insulate themselves from American coercion, global markets are experiencing deep fragmentation and fracturing, and they quote Larry Summers on a growing acceptance of fragmentation. A slide in Lecture 6 quotes a European Commission report as saying that it is witnessing the erosion of the rules-based international order and the fracturing of the global landscape. The same slide goes on to say that authors it identifies as leaders of Brazil, the EU Council, Kenya and Canada argue that multilateralism is not obsolete but needs reform.
questions: A newspaper caption on the slide says that while the world's economies remain deeply intertwined, geopolitics is moving the other way, which is the _____ world that the lecture describes.

cards.question: According to a slide on the case for renewed multilateralism, 2025 had the _____, and military spending hit a record high, even as the world was more economically interconnected than ever.
cards.answerDate: Record year2025Compared since1946
cards.abstract:
A record count, the most armed conflicts since 1946, is what Lecture 4's slide 12 says 2025 had, alongside record military spending. The slide gives no source or count for the figure, so the course material does not say how conflicts were counted. It sets the figure against a paradox, a world economically more interconnected than ever, with record trade and near-universal internet access, yet geopolitically more fragmented. From there the slide moves to climate change, AI, pandemics and conflict-driven displacement, which it calls threats no state can manage alone, and to an argument that multilateralism needs reform, not abandonment. Lecture 3 describes the shape of recent conflict as a return of interstate wars, naming Ukraine-Russia, Azerbaijan-Armenia and Cambodia-Thailand, beside proxy wars, internal conflict and rising defence expenditures.

The same slide says the lines between types of war have become more fluid, and puts the NATO goal of 5 per cent in the next ten years under rising defence expenditures. Leonard warns that the most worrying prospect is a proliferation of small wars for territory, with Taiwan, Essequibo, Eritrea's Red Sea ports and the border town of Narva named as possible catalysts. An earlier reading, from 2018, says positive trends of more democracies, less poverty and fewer violent conflicts had abruptly reversed in the last decade, with a new wave of civil wars. That reading adds that internationalised internal conflicts, a rarity 25 years earlier at about 3 per cent of conflicts, had become one-third of all global conflicts, and that conflict deaths had reached a 25-year high. Lecture 6 opens by asking whether the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are the final nails in the coffin of the rule-based international order.

cards.question: Leaders of Brazil, the EU Council, Kenya and Canada argue multilateralism needs reform, and a slide describes _____ as a flexible, cross-regional coalition, not a new bloc, to reform the UN.
cards.abstract:
Partners for Multilateralism is described on Lecture 4's slide 12 as a flexible, cross-regional coalition, not a new bloc, that aims to reform the UN around core Charter principles. The slide names Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, António Costa, William Ruto and Mark Carney, leaders of Brazil, the EU Council, Kenya and Canada, as authors arguing that multilateralism is not obsolete and needs reform, not abandonment. It says the coalition bets that competition does not have to mean confrontation, and it counts climate change, AI, pandemics and displacement among threats no state can manage alone. A screenshot on the slide shows an opinion page headed 'Multilateralism is not idealism, it is a necessity', with the subheading that we need to strengthen our system of co-operation, not replace it. Lecture 4's economic diplomacy slides add that it can strengthen international economic governance and multilateral agreements on trade, investment, aid and climate.

Lecture 1 describes paralysis in multilateral institutions and a WTO crisis, and says the EU and the Netherlands should invest in reforming institutions, pursue de-risking and build coalitions. Lecture 1 also says medium-sized powers shop freely with superpowers, and that new alliances and partnerships emerge constantly, with major implications for the cohesion and strength of existing international institutions. A Foreign Affairs essay in the readings argues that architects who try to reform the UN Security Council or restore the WTO's appellate body would be wasting their time. The slide argues for reform, while the essay says projects to shore up formal multilateral commitments are primarily legalistic, aiming for change by adhering to increasingly obsolete frameworks. Farrell and Newman quote Mark Carney, one of the four authors on the slide, as warning that the United States is beginning to monetise its hegemony.

cards.question: A slide says a flexible coalition wants to reform the UN around _____: sovereignty, territorial integrity and human rights, betting that competition does not have to mean confrontation.
cards.abstract:
The core Charter principles named on Lecture 4's slide 12 are sovereignty, territorial integrity and human rights, around which the slide says a coalition wants to reform the United Nations. The slide lists the three principles without defining them, and other lectures in the course touch on each of them. The Charter itself appears elsewhere, in a Lecture 2 appendix slide titled UN Charter Chapter VII, enforcement operational problems, and in a Lecture 6 slide showing a 2022 address that invokes its Article 51. Lecture 6's slide on sovereignty lists the principle of legal equality between states and the principles of territorial integrity and non-interference of one state in the internal affairs of another. The same slide quotes a 1928 edition of a work called International Law as saying that perhaps no conception is more controversial in meaning than sovereignty.

Lecture 3 lists sovereignty and non-interference in domestic affairs as the golden rules of international relations, among the characteristics of traditional peacekeeping. Lecture 5 says that expansionism became a primary objective and that rules based on territorial integrity and sovereignty were broken, in its account of how European security failed to prevent war. A Lecture 5 slide, summarising a 2025 analysis, calls Ukraine's external sovereignty a non-negotiable red line, since Russia seeks to block its NATO and EU ambitions, which infringes its right to set its own foreign policy. Lecture 3 describes Malians' idea of sovereignty as regaining control of their own destiny, and quotes the question that many will ask if authorities make no progress, what have we gained from sovereignty. On human rights, Lecture 6 gives the UN system's definition of the rule of law, which requires laws consistent with international human rights norms and standards, and calls the rule of law a core element of the humanitarian and human rights agendas.

cards.question: On the first lecture's perspective slide, international politics is about power and hierarchies, and multilateralism remains _____, the lecturer says, in a course told from a practitioner's point of view.
cards.abstract:
The claim that multilateralism remains power politics by other means comes from Lecture 1's slide 11, which says international politics is about power and hierarchies. The slide is headed Perspective, and the lecturer says there that he will tell the story from a practitioner's point of view, including his role as Foreign Minister. Lecture 1's slide on The Abandoned Order says that multilateral institutions continue to function but in a state of decay and stagnation, with major projects stalling out. Lecture 1's framework slide on power centres describes five superpowers pursuing different versions of world order with different instruments, while medium-sized powers have their own positions and agendas. A Lecture 2 slide headed Guéhenno on modern diplomacy says peacekeeping illustrates power politics and that international organisations always reflect the power dynamics driving relations between their member states.

It cites paralysis in the Security Council after the Cold War, with Syria as the example, and says the advantage goes to actors with the most at stake. Lecture 2 adds that one of France, the US or the UK is mostly the penholder of a resolution authorising a peacekeeping operation, a role it calls more complex amid major divisions in the Council. Lecture 1's Gramsci slide lists paralysis in multilateral institutions and a WTO crisis among the results of an old order that can no longer lead through consent while a new one is not yet consolidated. A Foreign Affairs essay argues that the old rules-based order was never just about rules, since it offered rules backed by a specific power willing to bear disproportionate costs to maintain them. Farrell and Newman say the United States enjoyed the advantages of an international economy built on multilateral institutions while acting in unilateral and sometimes illiberal ways to secure its interests.

cards.question: Founded in 1995 as successor to the GATT of 1947, the _____ is described on a slide as the only international organisation dealing with the rules of trade between nations.
cards.answerDate: GATT1947WTO founded1995Appeals stalledsince 2019
cards.abstract:
The World Trade Organization was founded in 1995 as the successor to the GATT of 1947, according to a slide that appears in both Lecture 3 and Lecture 4. The slide calls it the only international organisation dealing with the rules of trade between nations, founded for a stronger institutional framework meant to improve living standards, create better jobs and promote sustainable development. Its listed functions include a forum for negotiations, administering agreements on goods, services and intellectual property, and settling disputes between members through a binding legal process. A Foreign Affairs article says the creation of the WTO in 1995 signalled the transformation in trade towards a hyperglobalist path, and that the WTO made it harder for countries to shield themselves from international competition. It adds that the WTO reached into policy areas that trade rules had not touched before, namely agriculture, services, intellectual property, industrial policy, and health and sanitary regulations.

Slide 14 lists criticisms: rigid negotiation progress, with the Doha Round deadlock as an example, a perceived bias favouring developed nations, and rising challenges from regional trade agreements and trade disputes. Slide 13, credited to Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, says the WTO was built for interdependence, not over-dependence, and that its appellate body has been paralysed since 2019 by a US veto. The slide's screenshot shows her opinion piece headed 'A stress test for global trade', with the line that the WTO core still holds but members must use this crisis to push reform. A Foreign Affairs essay says the WTO carries on adjudicating trade disputes despite a surge in protectionism, but that complaining about US tariffs at the WTO is the equivalent of shouting into the void. A reading on development argues that WTO agreements from TRIPS to TRIMS, which ban or limit strategies of past industrialisers, will need to be adjusted.

cards.question: Under the _____, a slide says, a country that lowers a trade barrier must do so for the same goods or services from all its trading partners, rich or poor.
cards.abstract:
On Lecture 4's slide 14, the most-favoured-nation principle means that a country lowering a trade barrier or opening up a market must do so for the same goods or services from all its trading partners. The slide adds that this holds whether partners are rich or poor, weak or strong, and it sets the principle directly beneath its paragraph on the founding of the WTO in 1995. The same slide lists what the WTO does, beginning with a forum for trade negotiations such as tariff reductions and rules, and administering agreements on goods, services and intellectual property. It also lists settling disputes between members through a binding legal process, monitoring trade policies and technical assistance for developing countries, and its text appears unchanged in Lecture 3. Its criticisms are rigid negotiation progress, with the Doha Round deadlock as an example, a perceived bias favouring developed nations, and rising challenges from regional trade agreements and trade disputes.

A box on the slide headed the impact of Trump's 'liberation day' in April on global trade shows three pairs of figures joined by arrows. One pair is labelled global trade under MFN tariff and runs from 80 per cent to 72 per cent, which the slide does not explain further. The other pairs are labelled global trade growth forecast for 2025, from 2.7 per cent to 0.9 per cent, and average tariff level, from 2.4 per cent to 18.4 per cent. Slide 14 also quotes the WTO's director-general as saying that the global trading system looks increasingly like a stable core within an unstable equilibrium. A Foreign Affairs essay does not name the principle, but says gone is the notion that consistent rules ought to govern the global economy, citing Trump's tariffs among other measures.

cards.question: A lecture slide listing criticisms of the World Trade Organization cites the deadlock of the _____ as its example of rigid negotiation progress.
cards.abstract:
The Doha Round is named on a Lecture 4 slide as the example of 'rigid negotiation progress', the first of three criticisms the slide lists of the World Trade Organization. The slide's wording is 'Doha Round deadlock', and it gives no date, subject or cause for the deadlock, so the lecture presents the Round only as a negotiation in deadlock. The same slide says that the WTO, founded in 1995 as the successor to the GATT of 1947, provides a forum for trade negotiations, for example on tariff reductions and rules. A reading adds that the WTO of 1995 reached into policy areas that trade rules had not touched before, among them agriculture, services and intellectual property. The slide's other two criticisms are a perceived bias favouring developed nations and rising challenges from regional trade agreements and trade disputes.

The slide before it lists, as reasons the WTO needs reform, that it does not deliver sufficient benefits for the most vulnerable and allows too many subsidy-related market distortions. Among the reforms that slide lists are plurilateral agreements, which loosen the areas of consensus decision-making so that coalitions can negotiate in areas of importance to them. The slides do not link this reform to the Doha deadlock, so the two points stand side by side. A Lecture 1 slide lists a 'WTO crisis' among the results of paralysis in multilateral institutions, at a time when the old order is dying and a new one is not yet consolidated. Mark Leonard's article says that the WTO still carries on adjudicating trade disputes, but also that no coalition can keep it relevant, whereas the lecture proposes reform.

cards.question: A Lecture 4 slide says the veto of the United States has paralysed the WTO's _____, part of its dispute settlement mechanism, since 2019.
cards.abstract:
The Appellate Body is named on a Lecture 4 slide as part of the dispute settlement mechanism of the World Trade Organization, in a list of reforms the WTO is said to need. The lecture says that the WTO settles disputes between its members through a binding legal process, one of five functions its slide lists for the organisation. According to the slide, the Appellate Body has been paralysed since 2019 by the veto of the United States. The slide lists reform of this dispute settlement mechanism as one of two reforms the WTO needs, the other being plurilateral agreements that loosen consensus decision-making. The same slide also lists the potential over-reach of the appellate body among the reasons it gives for why the WTO needs reform, next to a lack of transparency and unfair trading practices.

A Lecture 1 slide lists a 'WTO crisis' among the results of paralysis in multilateral institutions, as an old order is dying and a new one is not yet consolidated. Mark Leonard's article says that the WTO carries on adjudicating trade disputes, despite a surge in protectionism. It says that leaders in many middle powers in Europe, the Indo-Pacific and North America are attempting to build a carbon copy of the WTO's deadlocked appeals mechanism and keep lodging complaints against American tariffs at the WTO, the equivalent of shouting into the void. The article adds that the old rules-based order was never just about rules but about rules backed by a specific power willing to bear disproportionate costs to maintain them. It says that architects who might restore the WTO's appellate body would be wasting their time, whereas the slide lists reform of the mechanism as a need.

cards.question: A Lecture 4 slide lists _____, which loosen consensus decision-making so that coalitions can negotiate in areas of importance to them, as one of two WTO reforms needed.
cards.abstract:
Plurilateral agreements are listed on a Lecture 4 slide titled Multilateral Trading System: WTO Reform as one of two reforms that the World Trade Organization needs, the other being reform of its dispute settlement mechanism. The slide's gloss is 'loosening the areas of consensus decision-making to allow for coalitions to negotiate in areas of importance to them'. That one line is the slide's only description of the term, and it gives no further detail on how such agreements would work. The lecture describes the WTO as providing a forum for trade negotiations, for example on tariff reductions and rules, and as administering trade agreements on goods, services and intellectual property. The same slide lists rigid negotiation progress among its criticisms of the WTO, with the Doha Round deadlock as the example, and a perceived bias favouring developed nations.

The slide on Partners for Multilateralism likewise describes a flexible, cross-regional coalition, not a new bloc, whose aim is to reform the UN around core Charter principles, sovereignty, territorial integrity and human rights. A Foreign Affairs article describes a world in which many organising systems coexist and compete, with some frameworks organised around regions and others seeking to govern arenas such as technology, trade and security. The same article says that, rather than constructing a grand strategy, states will need to develop far more flexible and artisanal responses. It says that investing in new infrastructure nodes around corridors and ports promises greater rewards than sweeping trade deals, such as those the EU has sought with India or Mercosur, which can take decades to negotiate. The lecture also counts regional and bilateral trade agreements as part of economic diplomacy, and lists rising challenges from regional trade agreements among criticisms of the WTO.

cards.question: A Lecture 4 slide reproduces a 4 September 2025 piece headlined 'A stress test for global trade' by the WTO's Director-General, _____, who says its core still holds.
cards.abstract:
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala appears on a Lecture 4 slide as the Director-General of the World Trade Organization and the author of a piece dated 4 September 2025. The slide reproduces the headline 'A stress test for global trade' and the subheading 'The WTO core still holds, but members must use this crisis to push reform'. The organisation she leads was founded in 1995 as the successor to the GATT of 1947, and the lecture calls it the only international organisation dealing with the rules of trade between nations. A reading adds that the WTO of 1995 reached into policy areas that trade rules had not touched before, among them agriculture, services and intellectual property. Another reading says that the WTO carries on adjudicating trade disputes, despite a surge in protectionism.

As the slide lists her case for reform, the WTO was built for interdependence, not over-dependence, yet too many members rely on the US for market demand and on China for critical supplies. It adds complaints of a lack of transparency, level playing field issues, unfair trading practices, insufficient benefits for the most vulnerable and too many subsidy-related market distortions, and says it is difficult to industrialise for both emerging and advanced economies. The reforms it names are plurilateral agreements, loosening consensus decision-making so that coalitions can negotiate, and a dispute settlement mechanism whose appellate body the US veto has paralysed since 2019. The next slide credits the WTO director general with the view that the global trading system has a stable core within an unstable equilibrium. Mark Leonard's article takes a different line, saying that no coalition can keep the WTO relevant and that restoring its appellate body would be a waste of time.

cards.question: The WTO director general, a slide says, sees the current global trading system as increasingly a _____, a phrase the lecture does not define.
cards.answer: Stable core within an unstable equilibrium
cards.abstract:
The phrase stable core within an unstable equilibrium is how, according to a Lecture 4 slide, the WTO director general describes the current global trading system. The slide says it looks increasingly as if the system were so characterised, and it does not define either the core or the equilibrium. A subheading on the preceding slide says that the WTO core still holds but that members must use this crisis to push reform. The slide sits under the title Multilateral Trading System: WTO Reform and describes the WTO as the only international organisation dealing with the rules of trade between nations. It adds that the WTO was founded in 1995 as the successor to the GATT of 1947, and lists what it does, from providing a forum for negotiations to settling disputes.

Beside the quotation, a box on the impact of Trump's 'liberation day' in April gives three pairs of figures joined by arrows. They are 2.7 and 0.9 per cent for the 2025 global trade growth forecast, 2.4 and 18.4 per cent for the average tariff level, and 80 and 72 per cent for global trade under MFN tariff. The slide does not say what the two ends of each arrow represent or how the figures relate to the quotation. A Lecture 1 slide records tit-for-tat tariffs between the US and China peaking at 125 per cent on 1 April 2025, then returning to a mutual 10 per cent tariff by 10 May. Mark Leonard's article says that the WTO carries on adjudicating trade disputes despite a surge in protectionism, but also that the notion that consistent rules ought to govern the global economy is gone.
cards.answerText: Stable core within an unstable equilibrium

cards.question: A lecture slide gauges the impact on global trade of Trump's _____ in April with three pairs of figures joined by arrows, among them 2.7 per cent and 0.9 per cent.
cards.abstract:
Liberation Day is the day named in a box on a Lecture 4 slide headed 'Impact of Trump's liberation day on global trade', which adds only the month, April. The slide never says what happened that day or what the two ends of each arrow represent; it gives only three pairs of figures joined by arrows. The pairs are 2.7 and 0.9 per cent for the 2025 global trade growth forecast, 2.4 and 18.4 per cent for the average tariff level, and 80 and 72 per cent for global trade under MFN tariff. The lecture lists tariffs among the instruments that economic diplomacy increasingly uses for strategic advantage, with tariffs to stop Mexican migration as one example. The preceding slide reproduces a headline, 'A stress test for global trade', but the slides do not tie it to the box.

A Lecture 1 slide, which does not mention the day, says that tit-for-tat tariffs between the US and China peaked at 125 per cent on 1 April 2025. By 10 May, it says, the US was forced to agree to a return to a mutual 10 per cent tariff on all imports. It explains the reversal by US concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals on which the American car industry depends. A Foreign Affairs article says that a June framework deal with China was not the start of Trump's imagined epoch of 'liberation' under unilateral American greatness, but the true opening of the age of weaponised interdependence. Another Foreign Affairs article says that Trump's tariffs, with the EU's carbon border mechanism and China's export controls, are all accelerating the breakup of the global economy.

cards.question: A Lecture 4 slide says the WTO was built for interdependence rather than _____, while too many members rely on the US for market demand and on China for critical supplies.
cards.abstract:
Over-dependence is the word a Lecture 4 slide uses for members of the World Trade Organization that rely too heavily on the US for market demand and on China for critical supplies. The slide sets it against interdependence, saying that the WTO was built for interdependence, not over-dependence. A 2022 article in The Economist says that the single-minded pursuit of cost advantage led to a dependency on autocracies that abuse human rights and use trade as a means of coercion. It cites Europe's reliance on Russian energy, and says China's trade footprint is seven times as big as Russia's, with the world relying on it for goods from active pharmaceutical ingredients to processed lithium. It adds that the choke-points autocracies control amount to only about a tenth of global trade.

The stack slide, which does not use the word, lists concentrations: China controls 90 per cent of global refining capacity of resources for high-tech industry, and one Taiwanese firm makes over 90 per cent of the most advanced chips. A Foreign Affairs article quotes the US Secretary of State saying that 'our industrial capability is deeply dependent' on potential adversary nation-states, including China, 'who can hold it over our head'. It says that the administration made concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals that were crippling the US car industry. A Financial Times report says that China showed last year that it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals. The Economist article's remedy is diversification rather than concentration at home, requiring firms to diversify their suppliers in the areas autocracies control and letting the market adapt.

cards.question: Warning of a race to obtain key technologies such as AI and quantum computing, a lecture's closing slide names the risk of a _____ without saying who would be in each tier.
cards.abstract:
Two-tier world is a risk named on the closing slide of Lecture 4, where geostrategic rivalries are said to be superimposed by a race to obtain 'key technologies' such as AI and quantum computing. The slide does not say what the two tiers are or who would belong to each, and it names no consequence of the split. Under the risk it lists three points: China against the US, including on internet governance, the importance of market power and the power to set standards, and the balance between dependence and autarky on semiconductors. The lecture's slide on the technological stack says that the US company Nvidia dominates 84 per cent of the market for graphics processing units. It adds that since 2017 70 per cent of foundational AI models have been developed in the US and 15 per cent in China.

A Lecture 1 slide on the 2025 Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit says that an important focus was AI governance, and that Xi urged regional leaders to oppose 'Cold War mentality', blaming the US for geopolitical 'bullying'. An Economist piece published in September 2026 says that America will struggle to make the technology safe while staying ahead of China. A headline linked from the same piece says that real co-operation on AI is likely to elude China and America. A Foreign Affairs article says that other countries are building technological stacks that may be more appealing than the American one, and that if China leaps ahead on energy technology, others will be pulled into its orbit. Mark Leonard's article describes trade restrictions that are breaking up world markets but not into tidy blocs, and many organising systems that coexist and compete.

cards.question: Among the three points a Lecture 4 slide lists under the risk of a two-tier world is that market power and _____ are key.
cards.abstract:
Standard-setting power is the power to set 'standards', which the closing slide of Lecture 4 lists beside market power as key. The line sits under the risk of a two-tier world, beside China against the US including on internet governance, and the slide does not define it. A Lecture 1 slide says that international regulation and standards are being set to keep a grip on the weaponisation of arenas such as chip production, ports and research, but that the question is how successful this is. A Foreign Affairs article says that China already behaves like an artisan state, for instance when it used the International Telecommunication Union to build surveillance-friendly controls into global internet standards. The same article says that the institutions China creates, such as BRICS+ and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, are flexible in membership and purpose and not intended to set global rules.

A reading on the EU's security partnership with the African Union says that the EU still has strong indirect influence in Africa-EU relations, such as through standard-setting, ideational leadership and blueprints for regional integration. It adds that the diffuse nature of these indirect forms of power makes them harder to pinpoint and criticise. A reading on EU external governance, which does not use the slide's phrase, says EU rules may gain prescriptive qualities towards third countries by default, most spectacularly through competition policy, which also applies to firms such as Boeing or Microsoft based outside Europe. It says more generally that firms interested in participating in the EU market need to follow the EU's rules, because ignoring or violating them would create costs. Its power-based explanation says that the EU's ability to impose its rules on third countries in a hierarchical way depends on high and asymmetric interdependence in its favour.
