cards.question: Whether the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are the final nails on the coffin of the _____ is the question that opens a Lecture 6 slide, followed by charts.
cards.abstract:
The rules-based international order is the subject of the question on the second slide of Lecture 6, which asks whether the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are the final nails on the coffin of the rule based international order. The next six slides show charts without commentary, among them child mortality rates, the number of people living on less than $2.15 a day, estimated nuclear warhead stockpiles, battle-related deaths in 2022 and 2023, and armed conflicts by type since 1946. Later slides list opinion articles whose titles ask whether there is such a thing as a rules-based international order, and call it a myth, quietly disintegrating or cracking. A slide headed Challenges to the Rules-Based International Order lists problems of legitimacy, questions of equity and issues of self-confidence. A slide quoting the European Commission's 2025 Strategic Foresight Report has it say 'we are witnessing' the erosion of the rules-based international order and the fracturing of the global landscape, with key pillars from the United Nations to the World Trade Organisation under stress.

A Lecture 1 slide headed The Abandoned Order says the liberal rules-based order is eroding, abandoned by its former champion, the United States. The set article of the same title says the order was never fully accepted by China and Russia and was resented by newly assertive middle powers, and that its main financial backers, the American people, have lost interest in underwriting its development. It adds that the old rules-based order was never just about rules, because it proffered rules backed by a specific power willing to bear disproportionate costs to maintain them. A Lecture 5 slide on the period after the Minsk agreements says that expansionism became a primary objective and that rules based on territorial integrity and sovereignty were broken. The article also separates a disordered world, where actors violate rules they still recognise, from a world of 'un-order', where they act without reference to any common framework at all.

cards.question: The three challenges to the rules-based international order listed on a Lecture 6 slide, as problems, questions and issues, are _____, and the slide explains none of them.
cards.abstract:
Legitimacy, equity and self-confidence are the three bullet points on a Lecture 6 slide headed Challenges to the Rules-Based International Order, which lists problems of legitimacy, questions of equity and issues of self-confidence. The slide gives only those three lines, and neither equity nor self-confidence appears on any other slide of the lecture. The lecture's reading list names a 2015 Chatham House conference paper with the same title as the slide, but the slides give nothing of its content. A Lecture 1 slide on Gramsci says that the old order can no longer lead through consent, and that the liberal international order led by the United States loses legitimacy and coherence. A Lecture 5 slide on ending wars says that the legitimacy of governments and political leaders becomes a real factor, and that the legitimacy of actors also plays a role, asking whether there are equal positions.

An article set for the course says that the strategies of many middle powers grieving the rules-based order too often propose maintaining its form without its substance, the legitimacy and enforcement capacity conferred on it by the United States. The same article says the order was never fully accepted by China and Russia and was resented by newly assertive middle powers. A reading on EU external governance states a hypothesis that the effectiveness of external governance increases with the legalisation of rules, the legitimacy of rules, or both, though its subject is EU rules rather than the global order. A Lecture 4 slide lists a perceived bias favouring developed nations among the criticisms of the World Trade Organization, without using the word equity. The article also says many former allies of the United States are better equipped for the shift than they realise, though it never uses the word self-confidence.

cards.question: In the address of 24 February 2022 quoted on a Lecture 6 slide, the decision to begin a special military operation is justified by _____, set beside treaties with the Donetsk and Lugansk republics.
cards.abstract:
Putin's Article 51 claim is the label for the passage of the address of 24 February 2022, quoted on a Lecture 6 slide, in which the Russian president says he decided on a special military operation in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter, placed in Chapter VII by the quotation. The quoted line adds the permission of Russia's Federation Council, and ratification in execution of the treaties of friendship and mutual assistance with the Donetsk and Lugansk People's Republics by the Federal Assembly on 22 February. Before it, the people's republics of Donbass are said to have asked Russia for help, and the slide puts asked and for help in bold. Earlier lines recall that in 2015 Russian armed forces created a reliable shield against terrorists from Syria, a matter of defending ourselves, and say Russia was left no other option for defending its people. The last lines give the purpose as protecting people who for eight years have faced humiliation and genocide perpetrated by the Kiev regime, and say Russia will seek to demilitarise and denazify Ukraine.

The slide names the speaker only as the President of the Russian Federation, while the lecture's lists of opinion articles carry titles such as Putin's war on the liberal order. A Lecture 5 slide lists the 2022 Ukraine invasion after 2014 Crimea and MH17 among the milestones of post-Cold War security disorder. A Lecture 5 slide on the period after the Minsk agreements says expansionism became a primary objective and rules based on territorial integrity and sovereignty were broken, without mentioning this address. The lecture's slides on the rule of law say that strengthening it involves respect for the norms of international law, including on the use of force. Summary slides say that states behave as if they are bound by international law and assert if they do not want to be bound by it, and that international law is politics but not just politics.

cards.question: The first chart slide after the lecture's opening question plots the _____, the estimated share of newborns who die before reaching the age of five, from 1816 to 2023.
cards.abstract:
The child mortality rate is the measure on the first chart slide of Lecture 6, an Our World in Data chart whose subtitle describes it as the estimated share of newborns who die before reaching the age of five. The chart is drawn as lines from 1816 to 2023 on a vertical axis that runs from 0 to 50 per cent. It follows ten countries, which its key lists as Niger, Mali, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ghana, India, Indonesia, Brazil, the United Kingdom, France and the Netherlands. A source note names Gapminder for 2015 and the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation for 2025. The slide adds no words of its own, and it follows the lecture's second slide, which asks whether the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are the final nails in the coffin of the rule-based international order.

On the chart every line ends well below where it begins, and in 2023 the lines for Niger, Mali and the Democratic Republic of the Congo still sit above those of the other seven countries. An article in the readings describes the optimism of the 2000s and 2010s as a view in which health outcomes were improving and mortality was declining among both children and adults. It says the implication was clear, that whatever one said against the structure of the global economy, something was working, because the right lines were going up. The same article says that mortality has fallen sharply in nearly every African nation over recent decades, though it is still quite high, and that many African economies, despite improvements in health, cannot be said to be meaningfully richer than in 1980. A reading on fragile states lists reducing child mortality among the eight Millennium Development Goals, and separately names high infant mortality rates among the variables that track with fragility in terms of poor effectiveness.

cards.question: A chart of _____ counts warheads assigned to military forces, leaves retired ones queued for dismantlement out of the country lines, and takes its estimates from the Federation of American Scientists for 2023.
cards.abstract:
Nuclear warhead stockpiles are what the fifth slide of Lecture 6 charts, in an Our World in Data chart titled 'Estimated nuclear warhead stockpiles'. Its subtitle says that stockpiles include warheads assigned to military forces but exclude retired warheads queued for dismantlement, which are counted only in the global total. The key names the world and ten countries, from Russia and the United States to North Korea and South Africa, and the lines run from 1945 to 2023 on an axis that rises to 70,000. The data source is the Federation of American Scientists for 2023, and a note says the exact number of each country's warheads is secret, so the estimates rest on publicly available information, historical records and occasional leaks. The slide adds no commentary and comes after the lecture's second slide, which asks whether the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are the final nails in the coffin of the rule-based international order.

On the chart the line for the world peaks in the 1980s at about 70,000 and has fallen to well under 20,000 by 2023. Lecture 5 places the Helsinki Accords of 1975 in the context of the need for détente in the nuclear age. An article on the post-American world says that in a world of unreliable allies countries will hedge, that the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty could cease to function as a meaningful constraint, and that Germany, Iran, Poland, Saudi Arabia and South Korea could move to acquire nuclear weapons within two decades. The same article adds that countries beyond the United States may be tempted to blackmail their allies, and that the threat of nuclear attacks could become normalised. An article on economic coercion recalls that in the first decades of the nuclear age American policymakers invested in institutions and strategic doctrines to prevent nightmare scenarios, and says that, as during the nuclear era, the United States needs to turn towards détente and arms control.

cards.question: A Lecture 6 chart captioned 'trends between 1990 and 2021' plots the _____ for the world, the OECD countries and six developing regions, with Sub-Saharan Africa lowest throughout.
cards.abstract:
The Human Development Index, shortened to HDI, is the measure on the vertical axis of the chart on slide 33 of Lecture 6, which is captioned 'HDI trends between 1990 and 2021'. The chart has a line for the world and one for the OECD countries, with six more for developing countries, listed as the Arab States, East Asia and the Pacific, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. Its axis runs from 0.2 to 1.0, and the slide adds no commentary and no definition of the index. On the chart the OECD line stays highest and the Sub-Saharan Africa line lowest throughout, and every line ends higher than it begins. A working paper in the readings uses the index of the United Nations Development Programme to place one country, Sierra Leone.

That paper says Sierra Leone had sunk to the bottom of the index by the end of its civil war, which ran from 1991 to 2002, and that in 2008, the latest year with data, it remained there. It adds that GDP per capita was halved between 1980 and 2000, from a mere $300 to $150, and that in 2006 70 per cent of the population still lived under the national poverty line. An article in the readings says that the average age of death in Sierra Leone rose from 32 years in 1960 to 55 years in 2020, and that mortality has fallen sharply in nearly every African nation. The same article says that many African economies, despite improvements in health, cannot be said to be meaningfully richer or more economically developed than in 1980. A Lecture 1 slide says, on a different measure, GDP per capita as a percentage of the Netherlands, that countries in the Middle East and Africa are falling further behind, whereas every line on the HDI chart ends higher than it begins.

cards.abstract:
Famine is one of three words in the headline of the article shown on slide 32 of Lecture 6, dated 16 November 2023, which says that the world is ignoring war, genocide and famine in Sudan. The slide gives the subtitle 'America is distracted, the UN is not interested' and the label 'Dying in plain sight', but it adds no words of its own and no publisher's name. A reading on fragile states says that in late 2017 four of the most fragile states on any index, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen and Northeastern Nigeria, were still teetering on the edge of famine. It says this put twenty million people at risk of severe malnutrition or starvation. It treats this as part of the moral challenge of fragility, saying that the human suffering engendered by dysfunctional interactions between governments and their people places a responsibility on the international community to respond.

The same reading says that whether fragility compounds the spread of a pandemic, contributes to famine or enables the conditions for armed violence, the devastating toll on human life demands a remedy. It also recalls that in the late 1990s the Clinton administration recognised that states unable to provide basic governance, safety and security could potentially generate internal conflict, mass migration, famine and epidemic diseases. A 2026 analysis of the Sahel says that more than 40 million people there were already experiencing acute food insecurity, with projections rising above 50 million for the June to August 2026 lean season. It adds that in parts of northeastern Nigeria some people were at risk of catastrophic hunger, a potential precursor to famine if conditions worsen, a region that the reading on fragile states also names. An article on development recalls a historical case, saying that China's attempt at rapid rural industrialisation produced a famine that killed tens of millions, perhaps the single most calamitous man-made catastrophe of the postwar era.

A 2026 analysis says that in parts of northeastern Nigeria catastrophic hunger is a potential precursor to _____ if conditions worsen, in a Sahel where over 40 million face acute food insecurity.

cards.question: A slide shows an article saying the world is ignoring war, genocide and famine in _____, with the subtitle that America is distracted and the UN is not interested.
cards.abstract:
Sudan is the country named in the headline of the article shown on slide 32 of Lecture 6, dated 16 November 2023, which says that the world is ignoring war, genocide and famine there. The slide gives the subtitle 'America is distracted, the UN is not interested', and it adds no words of its own and no publisher's name. On slide 8, in the panel of 2024 deaths in armed conflicts per 100,000 people, Sudan comes fifth at 13.9, after Palestine, Ukraine, Lebanon and Syria. Slide 6 names Sudan in the key to its chart of battle-related deaths in 2022 and 2023. A slide on the military political nexus, which appears in both Lecture 2 and Lecture 3, lists Sudan among proxy wars, beside Syria, Rwanda-DRC and Libya, and again among cases of internal war or conflict, beside Ivory Coast and Liberia.

That slide adds that the demarcation lines between different types of war have become more fluid. Lecture 1 names Sudan and South Sudan among the defining moments, with 9/11 and the 2008 financial crisis, that it says the course will explore as uncertain and unexpected in world politics. A reading on fragile states says that the top seven states responsible for refugees and migrants rank at the top of nearly every index on fragility, and an endnote lists them in order as Syria, Afghanistan, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic. An article on development gives the fertility rate of Sudan as falling from 6.8 children per woman in 1980 to 4.3, in a list with Niger, Nigeria, Mali, Angola and Uganda, and says that fertility has followed the fall in mortality more slowly. A brief on humanitarian diplomacy says that Qatar's involvement in regional mediation since 2005 has included countries such as Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq.

cards.question: Borrowing the Chinese word for unfinished apartment blocks that people moved into, an essay says a _____ is emerging, in which states must adapt cunningly and improvise new uses for the old order.
cards.abstract:
A rotten-tail world is the essay's name for the world now emerging as the US-led rules-based order is abandoned, in which states must adapt cunningly and improvise new uses for what remains valuable in the old order. The image comes from the Chinese word lanwei lou, which literally means 'rotten-tail buildings' and signifies a project gone awry, a plan in suspension. The essay opens with a Chinese housing crash, placed five years ago, that left thousands of apartment buildings unfinished, after which some intrepid people moved into the ruins and improvised a way of surviving an economic storm. A Lecture 1 slide titled 'The Abandoned Order' says that multilateral institutions continue to function in a state of decay and stagnation. The essay calls the housing market a good metaphor for the US-led rules-based order, which after decades of expansion is also being abandoned.

It says China and Russia never fully accepted the order, newly assertive middle powers resent it, its main financial backers, the American people, have lost interest in underwriting it, and no alternative provider is stepping in. Too many leaders, it says, still act as if the old order can be salvaged, while the General Assembly still meets every year despite being sidelined and the World Trade Organization still adjudicates disputes despite a surge in protectionism. It denies that this moment is a short interregnum between a US-led order and a Chinese-led one, saying that for some time the world will be without any order at all. A Lecture 1 slide on Gramsci quotes a line about the interregnum, in which the old is dying and the new cannot be born, and calls the new order of China, BRICS and multipolarity not yet consolidated. The essay ends by saying that the most successful leaders will, like the inhabitants of the rotten-tail buildings, take their fate into their own hands instead of waiting for new rules to rescue them.
questions: Because the order's American backers have lost interest and no alternative provider is stepping in, as with China's failed housing projects, the essay says a _____ is emerging.

The most successful leaders in a _____, the essay concludes, will be like the resourceful inhabitants of unfinished Chinese buildings, taking their fate into their own hands instead of waiting for new rules.

cards.question: An essay distinguishes a disordered world, where actors break rules they still recognise, from one it calls _____, where they act without reference to any common framework at all.
cards.abstract:
Un-order is the term that the essay suggests for a world in which actors act without reference to any common framework at all. It sets this against a disordered world, in which actors violate rules they still recognise. Episodes of rule breaking, the essay adds, always characterised the rules-based order, but they took place within an overall framework that still held. Its introduction says that for some time the world will be without any order at all, rather than passing through a short interregnum between a US-led order and a Chinese-led one. Lecture 1's slide on the abandoned order says that what defines the new 'orderless age' is fragmentation, stagnation and strangulation.

The essay says that in dozens of private conversations over the past year with leaders worldwide, the only thing they agree on is that they do not know what will come next. It reports that these leaders struggle to use history or theory to find their bearings and that the briefings from their intelligence agencies and diplomatic services no longer give them any certainty. One Gulf leader admitted he had no idea what arrangement would settle the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, and an Indo-Pacific national security adviser said his government no longer knew whether the United States would defend his country in a crisis. The central feature of these conversations, it says, is uncertainty, a sense that the world defies conventions and understanding, and Lecture 1 likewise says that diplomacy in times of radical uncertainty will be a theme throughout the course. Later the essay adds that in this era of disinhibition many of the world's most powerful actors no longer even seem aware that they are breaking rules.
questions: When leaders say history, theory and intelligence briefings give them no bearings and they cannot guess what comes next, an essay suggests calling the resulting world _____ rather than merely disordered.
A lecture slide says the liberal order is eroding into an orderless age, and the essay of the same title separates rule breaking inside a framework from _____, which ignores any common framework.

cards.question: An essay says a former US Secretary of State held that world order rests on _____, a reasonably stable balance of power and commonly agreed rules, and that today both are crumbling.
cards.abstract:
Kissinger's two pillars are the supports on which, the essay says, Secretary of State Henry Kissinger once asserted that world order rests: a reasonably stable balance of power and a set of commonly agreed rules about what states may or may not do. The essay says that today both pillars are crumbling and that it is unlikely they can be fortified or rebuilt any time soon. On the power pillar, it grants that the United States remains the world's preeminent military, economic and technological power but says Washington can no longer prevent conflicts or ensure the free flow of commerce worldwide. As evidence it says the United States could not even open the Strait of Hormuz after a militarily hobbled Iran shuttered the waterway. It adds that cheap missiles and drones are rapidly undermining the American military's command of the seas and skies.

On the rules pillar, it says that even before Trump the alliance system that helped enforce the rules was weakening, as China, Russia and rising powers that did not make the rules pushed against them. Trump then launched a rebellion from within, bullying allies, ditching the World Health Organization, scrapping the United States Agency for International Development and imposing widespread punitive tariffs. Even after his presidency ends in 2029, the essay says, the United States is highly unlikely to resume its old role, and Americans had already lost interest in being the world's primary provider of public goods, its police officer and its free-trade champion. The old order, it adds later, was never just about rules but offered rules backed by a specific power willing to bear disproportionate costs, and the United States and its European allies, its architects, no longer have the resources to maintain it. Lecture 1 likewise says the liberal rules-based order is eroding, abandoned by its former champion, and that the US-led liberal international order loses legitimacy and coherence.

The essay says that _____ are unlikely to be rebuilt any time soon, adding that even after 2029 the United States is highly unlikely to resume its old role.

cards.question: Three forces said to be upending the international system in an orderless age are _____, the last of them tied to the temptation to weaponise geographic, economic and technological chokepoints.
cards.abstract:
Fragmentation, contagion and strangulation are the three forces that the essay says are upending the international system and driving the uncertainty of an orderless age. Its introduction says that for some time the world will be without any order at all, and that states will need flexible and artisanal responses rather than a grand strategy. Fragmentation, it says, means that Trump's predatory approach to partners is fragmenting the West as a political community, alliances are splintering, and trade restrictions are breaking up world markets, but not into tidy blocs. It adds that global problems no longer attract global solutions but rather a patchwork of short-term fixes. Lecture 1's slide on the abandoned order says that what defines the orderless age is fragmentation, stagnation and strangulation, naming stagnation where the essay names contagion.

Contagion, the essay says, means that in this era of disinhibition crises no longer stay in their original domain and actors no longer feel constrained by norms governing proper conduct. France and Germany strongly opposed the 2003 Iraq war yet kept sharing intelligence and trade with the United States, whereas Trump's tariff threats over Greenland showed that even among allies economic and security relations are no longer separate. During the recent Iran war, it adds, Trump threatened to halt trade with European countries that expressed reservations and to withdraw troops stationed in their countries. The introduction pairs strangulation with the temptation to weaponise chokepoints, and a later section says states are increasingly turning the systems that once connected them, such as energy routes and shipping lanes, into weapons. The closure of any single chokepoint might be manageable, the essay warns, but numerous lockdowns would not be.

States turning energy routes, chip supply chains, financial infrastructure and shipping lanes into weapons illustrate the last of three forces that an essay lists as _____ and a lecture slide lists differently.

cards.question: A digitally connected world that no longer agrees on facts, erasing the shared reality that underpins diplomacy, suffers from _____, which an essay calls the deepest fragmentation of all.
cards.abstract:
Epistemic fragmentation is what the essay calls the deepest of the fragmentations it describes, in which a digitally connected world divides over facts and not only over interpretations. Its inhabitants, the essay says, no longer agree on facts, which erases the sense of shared reality that underpins diplomacy itself. The essay's example is the war that the United States and Israel launched against Iran in February, in which the parties have been unable even to agree on whether a cease-fire exists, what leverage they have, or who won or lost. Lecture 1's slide on the abandoned order makes a similar point without the term, saying that blocs and alliances are splintering while shared truth dissolves in a post-truth world. Lecture 1 treats worldviews, the frames through which people and institutions view, interpret and communicate what is going on around them, as the third axis of its framework for the course.

The essay says in the same section that the idea of the United Nations or the United States overseeing comprehensive peace deals is gone, and that limited cease-fires and truces now aim to freeze conflicts rather than resolve them. Earlier it reports that the leaders the author speaks to say the briefings from their intelligence agencies and diplomatic services no longer give them any certainty. Lecture 1 lists the media arena, with disinformation and media capture, among the arenas where power is exercised. Lecture 2 lists disinformation campaigns, beside sabotage, arson and cyberattacks, among the tools of subversion that hybrid warfare fuses with conventional instruments of power. A Lecture 4 slide notes the paradox of a world more economically interconnected than ever, with record trade and near-universal internet access, yet geopolitically more fragmented.

cards.question: Listed beside AUKUS and a trans-Pacific trade agreement as frameworks seeking to govern arenas such as technology, trade and security, the _____ is described as a new initiative to secure tech supply chains.
cards.abstract:
Pax Silica is named once in the essay, which describes it in a short gloss as a new initiative to secure tech supply chains. The essay lists it with the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership and AUKUS as frameworks that seek to govern arenas such as technology, trade and security. Some frameworks, it says, are organised around regions, while others, including these three, seek to govern arenas. It sets them in a reality in which the aspiration to establish a single global order is giving way to many organising systems that coexist and compete. A 2022 leader in The Economist already described a new kind of globalisation that is about security, not efficiency, and prioritises doing business with people you can rely on, in countries your government is friendly with.

A Lecture 4 slide argues that in a world of weaponised interdependence power comes from controlling technological stacks, systems of interconnected layers from foundational technologies to advanced applications. Its layers include rare earths, where China controls 90 per cent of the global refining capacity of resources used in high-tech industry, and manufacturing equipment, where ASML has a monopoly over ultra-violet lithographic machines. The slide adds that the Taiwanese company TSMC produces around 60 per cent of all chips and more than 90 per cent of the most advanced ones, while Nvidia's graphics processors dominate 84 per cent of the market. Another Lecture 4 slide says Europe should build its own comprehensive suite of institutions and an independent stack of technologies, but that short-term dependence on American security guarantees limits its strategic autonomy. The essay's section on technological sovereignty says states should neither accept dependence on American technology nor bet the bank on building autonomous tech stacks, but use the leverage they already have.

cards.question: An essay says that in this era of _____ actors no longer feel constrained by norms of proper conduct and many of the most powerful no longer seem aware that they are breaking rules.
cards.abstract:
Disinhibition is the word the essay uses for an era in which actors no longer feel constrained by norms governing proper conduct. International law and norms, it says, formerly put limits on states' actions, and great powers did not always keep to the rules but imposed them on smaller powers and set expectations for how business would be conducted. In this era crises no longer stay in their original domain, and many of the world's most powerful actors no longer even seem aware that they are breaking rules. Disputes are also less likely to stay compartmentalised, and where France and Germany opposed the 2003 Iraq war yet kept sharing intelligence and trade, Trump's tariff threats over Greenland showed that even among allies economic and security relations are no longer separate. Lecture 2 lists disregard for international law among the points under its heading that peacemaking has grown ever more complex, while Lecture 6 says states do not always adhere to international law but do so most of the time.

The essay says this same disinhibition increasingly governs how war itself is waged, and that the taboos against assassination, targeting civilians and wars of territorial conquest are vanishing. It cites reporting in The New York Times that Israel planned to assassinate the Iranian foreign minister and the speaker of parliament while the two were negotiating with the United States. It says that throughout its war in Gaza Israel attacked people and facilities previously not considered legitimate targets, such as journalists, hospitals and cultural sites, claiming that Hamas used them as covers, and that Russia regularly targets civilian infrastructure in Ukraine. It adds that this uncontrolled escalation will almost certainly lead to more wars and that the threat of nuclear attacks could become normalised. Its greatest worry is a proliferation of small wars for territory, with China possibly targeting Taiwan outright and Russia possibly seizing the Estonian border town of Narva.

cards.question: The idea of _____ holds that control over energy routes, chip supply chains, financial infrastructure and shipping lanes now counts towards a state's power alongside its GDP and the size of its military.
cards.answer: Chokepoints as a marker of power
cards.abstract:
Chokepoints as a marker of power is the essay's claim that a country's control over chokepoints is becoming a key marker of its power, just like its GDP and the size of its military. It draws an analogy with a marriage that has gone wrong, in which the house, the children and the dog become weapons the couple use to hurt each other. Likewise, it says, states are increasingly turning the systems that once connected them, namely energy routes, semiconductor supply chains, financial infrastructure and shipping lanes, into weapons. Lecture 1 puts the claim in similar terms, saying that control over strategic chokeholds and the ability to weaponise global interdependence are now just as vital markers of national power as GDP or the size of the military. The same lecture lists the nature and size of the economy, the military and demographic sources as markers of power, and says that not all superpowers share the same markers.

The essay says the potential bottlenecks are innumerable, existing not only in physical waterways but also in supply chains for weapons, food, health care and basic technology. It adds that over 55 per cent of globally traded maize, wheat, rice and soybeans pass through at least one maritime chokepoint, and that energy disruptions can become food-price crises within weeks. Blocking one chokepoint, it notes, diverts traffic to others and congests the alternatives, and while the closure of any single one might be manageable, numerous lockdowns would not be. A Lecture 3 slide on weaponised interdependence names geographic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Taiwan Strait, and notes limits to interdependence but also limits to the use of chokepoints. The Economist argued in 2022 that the chokepoints autocracies control amount to only about a tenth of global trade, counting exports where they hold a leading market share of over 10 per cent and substitutes are hard to find.
cards.answerText: Chokepoints as a marker of power

cards.sub: Reading 1 · The Abandoned Order (Leonard)

cards.question: In late 2025 China adopted its own version of the _____, asserting a right to decide whether companies anywhere can access magnets containing trace amounts of Chinese materials or made with Chinese technology.
cards.abstract:
The foreign direct product rule is, in the essay's account, an American extraterritorial tactic that Washington invented to control chips and of which China adopted its own version in late 2025. In late 2025, it says, China adopted its own version, asserting a right to decide whether companies can access magnets anywhere in the world if they contain even trace amounts of Chinese materials or were made using Chinese technology. On the American side, it says, the first Trump administration restricted Chinese companies' access to high-level microchips and the Biden administration widened export controls, exploiting the dominance of American and allied firms in chip-making equipment and software. China, learning from the 2022 freezing of $300 billion of Russian central bank reserves, is rapidly expanding its own authority over chokepoints. In 2010, the essay adds, Beijing briefly experimented with cutting off rare-earth exports to Japan but lacked the bureaucracy to target such controls precisely, whereas it has since built an export control system explicitly modelled on Washington's.

It says China has also extended the resource chokepoints it commands from raw materials to processing. It warns that China could further restrict the rare earths used in American and European weapons systems and high-end technologies, or leverage its control over the global electric vehicle, solar and wind industries. Lecture 1 recounts that after tit-for-tat tariffs peaked at 125 per cent on 1 April 2025, the United States made concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals that its auto industry depends on. Lecture 4 says China controls 90 per cent of global refining capacity of resources used in high-tech industry, and describes its approach as leveraging interdependencies through export controls applied with precision. In August 2026 the Financial Times wrote that Beijing the year before had shown it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals essential to high-tech production.

cards.abstract:
The 2010 rare-earth cut-off to Japan was a brief Chinese experiment in which, a 2026 article says, Beijing tried cutting off rare-earth exports to Japan amid a territorial dispute. The article adds that Beijing had not yet established the bureaucracy needed to target such controls precisely at that time. Since then, it says, Beijing has built its own export control system explicitly modelled on Washington's and has extended the resource chokepoints it commands from raw materials to processing. In late 2025, the article says, China adopted its own version of the foreign direct product rule, asserting a right to decide whether companies anywhere can access magnets containing even trace amounts of Chinese materials. A lecture slide listing the technological stack puts China's share of global refining capacity at 90 per cent for resources used in high-tech industry, under the heading 'Rare Earths'.

A 2026 Financial Times article says that last year Beijing showed it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals essential to high-tech production. Farrell and Newman, writing in 2025, say administration officials acknowledge making concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals that were crippling the American car industry. They quote Secretary of State Marco Rubio as saying that China had 'cornered the market' for rare earths and that American industrial capability was deeply dependent on potential adversaries, China among them, who could 'hold it over our head'. A lecture slide on the tariff war asks why tit-for-tat tariffs that peaked at 125 per cent in April 2025 fell to a mutual 10 per cent by 10 May, and answers with a bargain over chip export controls and rare-earth restrictions. Leonard warns that China could further restrict the rare earths used in American and European weapons and high-end technologies, while a lecture slide credits it with a 'whole of nation' approach to rare earths extraction and processing.

cards.question: After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, European and North American countries weaponised the dollar by cutting Russian banks out of SWIFT and carrying out the _____ of 300 billion dollars.
cards.abstract:
The Russian reserves freeze was the 2022 step, after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in which a coalition of European and North American countries froze 300 billion dollars of Russian central bank reserves. A 2026 article calls it a remarkable step, the weaponising of the dollar to punish a G-20 country, and says the same coalition cut Russian banks out of the SWIFT payments system. It sets the step within a pattern, saying Western countries have been particularly active in identifying and weaponising chokepoints, above all through control of the global financial system and essential technologies. A lecture slide says that after the Cold War businesses built an independent global economy on US-centred infrastructure, including the US dollar as the global currency and SWIFT messaging. The same slide says that for over two decades the United States has unilaterally weaponised chokepoints in these systems for strategic advantage, and that adversaries and even allies are now disconnecting, hiding or retaliating.

Farrell and Newman describe the new era as one shaped by sanctions, supply chain attacks and export measures that repurpose points of control in the infrastructure underpinning the interdependent global economy. A second lecture slide lists the dollar clearing system, reactions to it and sanctions among the state instruments of weaponised interdependence, naming Iran and Afghanistan as examples rather than Russia. Leonard says China, learning from this, is rapidly expanding its own authority over chokepoints, and predicts the dollar's dominance will erode, perhaps with its share of global foreign exchange reserves falling below 50 per cent. He adds that global transaction costs will balloon as incompatible systems multiply, and Farrell and Newman say American enthusiasm for stablecoins is pushing China and Europe to accelerate their efforts to develop alternative payment systems. Another lecture slide gives sanctions against Russia as an example of sanctions enforcement within economic diplomacy, and a further slide says economic diplomacy increasingly uses sanctions, tariffs and export controls for strategic advantage.

cards.question: A 2026 article says a militarily hobbled Iran shuttered the _____, bringing 20 per cent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipping to a near halt.
cards.abstract:
The Strait of Hormuz is a maritime chokepoint that Leonard's 2026 article says Iran shuttered, bringing 20 per cent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipping to a near halt. The article says the closure forced oil shipments around the Cape of Good Hope, and that both Iran and the United States have suggested they intend to extract tolls from ships transiting the strait. It uses the episode to show that Washington can no longer ensure the free flow of commerce worldwide, since it could not even open the strait after a militarily hobbled Iran shuttered it. A lecture slide names the strait and the Taiwan Strait as geographic chokepoints among the state instruments of weaponised interdependence, and adds that there are limits to interdependence but also to the use of chokepoints. The Financial Times article puts the situation as continued restrictions on shipping through the strait, which Zhu Feng of Nanjing University is quoted as saying strain the entire global economy.

Zhu adds that if the strait dilemma continues it will also be more dangerous for China, whose main oil imports come from Saudi Arabia and Iraq rather than from Iran. Leonard reports that one Gulf leader admitted he had no idea what arrangement would settle the dispute over the strait, an example of the uncertainty he finds among leaders. Winer, writing in May 2026, says war-time disruptions of shipping through the strait are spreading through the fertiliser market into regions with no margins to absorb the impact, the Sahel among them. He reports that benchmark urea prices rose by roughly 46 per cent month on month between February and March 2026, according to the World Bank, reflecting the tightening of fertiliser flows linked to the conflict. A lecture assignment slide asks how a disruption in the strait transmits a severe shock to the Sahel, and a slide of possible answers points to higher fuel and food prices and reduced government revenues.

cards.sub: Reading 1 · The Abandoned Order (Leonard)

cards.question: In a 2026 article's contrast between _____, one side draws blueprints for order and anchors security in multilateral institutions while the other improvises in a world that resists sweeping plans.
cards.abstract:
Architects and artisans are the two broad ways of dealing with the new world that Leonard's 2026 article says are emerging. Architects, it says, develop blueprints for order and try to mould the world to their designs, developing universal norms and anchoring security in multilateral institutions. Artisans, by contrast, do not assume they have the power or resources to build grand structures from scratch, and use improvisation and flexibility to cope with a world that does not lend itself to sweeping plans. The article's opening says states will need far more flexible and artisanal responses rather than a grand strategy, and a lecture slide summarising it describes an order abandoned by its former champion. It calls the emerging condition a 'rotten-tail world', after Chinese 'rotten-tail buildings', in which states must adapt cunningly and improvise new uses for what remains valuable in the old order.

Architects seek stability whereas artisans prepare for chaos and change, the article says, and architects who try to reform the UN Security Council or restore the WTO's appellate body would be wasting their time. Whereas architects believe there can be a single rule book for everyone, artisans accept that multiple sets of guidelines will coexist, and groups such as the EU should create rules-based orders in their own neighbourhoods. Whereas architects see globalisation as a means to transform others, artisans worry about the vulnerabilities interconnectedness creates, and where architects think about security from the outside in, artisans defend a country from the inside out. It says many middle powers in Europe, the Indo-Pacific and North America show an architectural instinct, proposing to maintain the form of the old order without its substance, for primarily legalistic purposes. A lecture slide lists plurilateral agreements and reform of the WTO dispute settlement mechanism, whose appellate body the US veto has paralysed since 2019, as needed reforms, whereas the article says restoring that body is a waste of time.

cards.question: A 2026 article says China already behaves like an _____, advancing its interests by repurposing existing institutions and by creating flexible new ones that are not intended to set global rules.
cards.abstract:
The artisan state is a term in Leonard's 2026 article, which says China already behaves like one, in the sense of the artisan who relies on improvisation and flexibility rather than blueprints for order. The article says China advances its interests by repurposing existing institutions, as when it used the International Telecommunication Union to build surveillance-friendly controls into global Internet standards. It also says China creates new institutions, such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and BRICS+, the bloc that marshals Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and four other new members. These institutions, it says, are flexible in their membership and purpose and are not intended to set global rules. A lecture slide says the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation was co-established by China in 2001 and was initially intended to settle border disputes after the collapse of the Soviet Union, before India, Pakistan, Iran and Belarus joined.

The article says other middle powers such as Brazil, India, Iran and Turkey are creating and joining a plethora of similar groupings, balancing and hedging between the great powers. A lecture slide on power centres says medium-sized powers shop freely with superpowers according to their needs and wishes, which it calls multi-alignment or the a-la-carte world. Leonard says Beijing has built its own export control system explicitly modelled on Washington's and extended its resource chokepoints from raw materials to processing. A lecture slide on institutional adaptation says China introduced information security and data sovereignty into its national security strategy in 2013 and developed a 'whole of nation' approach to technological independence. The article also says China is an observer on the Arctic Council and urges the EU to apply to the SCO, BRICS+ or ASEAN as an observer, since artisans follow the course diplomacy is already taking.

cards.question: A 2026 article cites the _____, a logistics route connecting mineral-rich central Africa to the Atlantic, as a node of the kind that an artisanal approach to trade would invest in.
cards.abstract:
The Lobito Corridor is named in Leonard's 2026 article as an example of the new infrastructure nodes, built around corridors and ports, in which an artisanal approach to trade would invest. The article describes it as a logistics route connecting mineral-rich central Africa to the Atlantic and gives it no further description. It argues that such nodes promise greater rewards than sweeping trade deals, naming those the EU has sought with India and with the South American bloc Mercosur as deals that can take decades to negotiate. The passage sits in the section called 'Get Real', which says that two broad ways of dealing with the new world are emerging, the method of the architect and the approach of the artisan. Artisans, it says, do not assume they have the power or resources to build grand structures from scratch, and rely instead on improvisation and flexibility.

In the same paragraph the article says China is an observer on the Arctic Council and urges the EU to apply as an observer to BRICS+, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation or ASEAN. A lecture slide on the multilateral trading system lists plurilateral agreements, which let coalitions negotiate in areas of importance to them, as one reform that the WTO's director-general says is needed. Elsewhere the article says potential bottlenecks are innumerable, existing in waterways and in supply chains for weapons, food, health care and basic technology, and that blocking one chokepoint diverts traffic to others and congests the alternatives. A lecture slide on arenas of power says rivalry between superpowers now reaches beyond geopolitics into chip production, international ports and the research sector. The Economist argued in 2022 that resilience comes from diversification, not concentration at home, and that the answer to dependence on chokepoints held by autocracies is to require firms to diversify their suppliers.

cards.question: A 2026 article says states must not simply replicate American capital-intensive methods but develop _____ suited to their own situations, citing how Ukraine and Iran adapted cheaper technologies against costlier opponents.
cards.abstract:
Frugal ways of war is the phrase Leonard's 2026 article uses for military methods that European and Indo-Pacific states should develop instead of simply replicating the capital-intensive military methods of the United States. The article says these methods must be relevant to each country's individual situation, and that the states concerned must become far less reliant on the United States as an eternal security provider. Ukraine and Iran, it says, have both shown how to adapt cheaper technologies for offensive and defensive purposes, neutralising their opponents' advantage in vastly more expensive high-tech systems. It expects many countries to benefit from similar 'hedgehog' strategies that draw on the technological revolution favouring defence and insulate their territories against contagion. For European countries it says this means building military capacity, fighting to prevent Russia and the United States from making deals over their heads, and taking a more detached approach to distant conflicts.

The article's 'Reality Check' section says that swift technological change, especially the proliferation of cheap missiles and drones, is rapidly undermining the U.S. military's command of the seas and skies. It adds that even before Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthi militia in Yemen was using cheap drones and missiles to block transit through the Red Sea. It says allies do not yet understand that Washington has withdrawn its support, calling NATO's July 2026 summit one of the most surreal examples of cognitive dissonance, as European leaders pledged arbitrary defence spending increases unrelated to their own analysts' assessments. A lecture slide on the military political nexus lists emerging technologies such as drones and a NATO goal of 5 per cent defence spending in the next ten years among the things always in flux. Another slide, setting out a scholar's account of current conflict, cites iPad firing tables using consumer electronics in the Ukraine war and says both non-state actors and states take advantage of low-tech capabilities.

cards.question: A 2026 article treats pursuing _____ as a core part of thriving, urging countries to use existing leverage instead of depending on American technology or betting the bank on autonomous tech stacks.
cards.abstract:
Technological sovereignty is described in Leonard's 2026 article as a core part of how countries can thrive, alongside boosting their security, industrial competitiveness, clean energy leadership and global influence. The article says that instead of accepting dependence on American technology or betting the bank on building autonomous tech stacks, countries should use the leverage they already have to minimise the risk of aggressive actions against them. Its example is the United Kingdom, whose National Health Service awarded the U.S. technology company Palantir a major contract in 2023 and whose new police AI programme expressed interest in working with the firm this year. The article says Britain should instead use the power of its purse to incentivise domestic providers, using open-source technology, to develop specialised tools. It would also mandate open standards and portable data formats as a condition of public contracts, so that no single vendor's platform becomes a permanent chokepoint.

The passage belongs to an argument that artisans worry about the vulnerabilities interconnectedness creates, and that Europe and its allies have more means to develop self-reliance than they give themselves credit for. Its examples of such leverage are that Europe could withhold software updates for China's Airbus fleet, which it says would ground more than half the country's commercial planes, and that Taiwan could restrict its critical semiconductor industry. A lecture slide says that in a world of weaponised interdependence power comes from controlling technological stacks, systems of interconnected layers from foundational technologies to advanced applications. Under the EU, another slide says Europe is to build its own comprehensive suite of institutions and an independent stack of technologies, citing the EuroStack project, which differs in emphasis from the article's warning about autonomous stacks. Farrell and Newman add that other countries are building technological stacks that may be more appealing to the world than the American one, and that if China leaps ahead on energy technology others will be pulled into its orbit.

cards.question: Alongside Trump's tariffs and China's export controls, the EU's introduction of the _____ is listed in a 2026 article as accelerating the breakup of the global economy.
cards.abstract:
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism is the EU measure that Leonard's 2026 article lists with Trump's tariffs and China's export controls as accelerating the breakup of the global economy, without saying how it works. The article places the three in a passage saying that economic nationalism and protectionism are on the rise. That passage opens by declaring gone the notion that consistent rules ought to govern the global economy. As evidence of fragmentation, the article says identical barrels of oil now trade at vastly different prices depending on where they are sold, through which payment system, to which buyer and under which sanctions regime. In early April, it says, Brent futures traded at around 113 dollars per barrel while physical cargoes sold for as much as 144 dollars, a spread it calls extremely unusual.

The article predicts that the dollar's dominance will erode more rapidly and that global transaction costs will balloon as incompatible systems multiply. On climate it says global frameworks to solve problems such as climate change are losing efficacy, and that the competition to dominate renewable technologies has probably done more to combat rising emissions than all the Conference of the Parties meetings combined. In its opening it says UN climate change conferences still convene to chart an increasingly hopeless path to net-zero emissions. A lecture slide on climate and the trade-off between hyper-globalisation, sovereignty and democracy says ambitious global climate action with democratic accountability needs sovereignty shared in international institutions, for example binding treaties with enforcement and carbon pricing across borders. The slide adds that such supranational governance is something many states and publics resist, and describes the 2015 Paris Agreement as a compromise that lacks enforceability; it does not mention the EU measure.

cards.question: Beijing warned that it would retaliate if Chinese companies were included in any significant expansion of the Trump administration's new _____ relating to Iran.
cards.abstract:
The secondary sanctions in a 2026 Financial Times article are new United States measures relating to Iran, unveiled by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, that targeted companies based in Hong Kong and mainland China. They stopped short of listing large Chinese financial institutions, and the article's standfirst calls them a crackdown on business with Tehran. The article also speaks of a secondary sanctions regime on Iran, and says any attempt by the US to expand it aggressively to Chinese companies would risk retaliation from Beijing. A lecture slide lists the extraterritorial use of sanctions against Iran among the examples of economic diplomacy used to advance national strategic advantage through sanctions, tariffs and export controls. Another slide places the dollar clearing system, reactions to it and sanctions, with Iran and Afghanistan as examples, among the state instruments of weaponised interdependence.

The article says any serious increase in US sanctions on China, which buys 90 per cent of Iran's oil, would risk exploding the relationship. The article notes the timing, since presidents Trump and Xi Jinping were scheduled to meet in Washington only a month later, at a summit it says is seen as crucial to the world economy. Asked about the secondary sanctions, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said that China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its rights and interests. Wang Dong of Peking University is quoted saying that it remains to be seen whether Washington is bluffing or seriously thinking about putting secondary sanctions on China. A lecture poll asked students to rate the risk of a secondary US–China trade war being triggered by Washington enforcing sanctions over Iranian oil.

cards.question: China's large state-owned refiners largely comply with sanctions on Iranian crude, but Beijing allows private sector _____ to import and process oil from Iran.
cards.abstract:
The teapot refiners are the private sector refiners, known as 'teapots', that Beijing allows to import and process oil from Iran, according to a 2026 Financial Times article. The article sets them against China's large state-owned refiners, which it says largely comply with sanctions on Iranian crude. It reports that the United States imposed sanctions on some of these refiners earlier this year, but that China ordered domestic companies not to comply. The article goes on to describe an increasingly strident Chinese anti-sanctions regime, which includes countermeasures against foreign individuals and organisations that assist with foreign restrictions on Chinese companies and supply chains. It also says China buys 90 per cent of Iran's oil, though it does not say what share of that the teapots take.

Zhu Feng of Nanjing University, quoted in the article, notes that China's main oil imports come from the Middle East, not from Iran but from Saudi Arabia and Iraq. He adds that China does not want to get involved in a US-Iranian fight, but is very aware that a continuing dilemma in the Strait of Hormuz would be more dangerous for China. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, quoted in the same article, says China has made clear its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council. A lecture slide lists the dollar clearing system, reactions to it and sanctions, with Iran and Afghanistan as examples, among the state instruments of weaponised interdependence. A lecture poll put a related question to students, asking them to rate the risk of a secondary US–China trade war being triggered by Washington enforcing sanctions over Iranian oil.

cards.question: A month before presidents Trump and Xi were due to meet in Washington, they were expected to discuss extending a _____ in their trade war that they had agreed in October.
cards.abstract:
The one-year trade truce is, in a 2026 Financial Times article, the pause in the trade war between the United States and China that presidents Trump and Xi Jinping agreed in October and that a cordial visit to Beijing by Trump in May cemented. When the article appeared, the leaders were expected to discuss extending the truce at a Washington summit that it says is seen as crucial to the world economy. The article warns that any serious increase in US sanctions on China, which buys 90 per cent of Iran's oil, would risk exploding the relationship only a month before that meeting. A lecture slide describes an earlier episode: tit-for-tat tariffs between the US and China peaked at 125 per cent on 1 April 2025, and by 10 May the US was forced to agree to a return to a mutual 10 per cent tariff. The slide says the US made concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals on which the US auto industry depends.

An essay in Foreign Affairs reads a June framework deal with China as the true opening of the age of weaponised interdependence, in which the United States is discovering what it is like to have others do unto it as it has eagerly done unto others. The lecture slide concludes that, so long as there is co-dependency on critical supply chains, mutually assured economic pain appears to function as a deterrent against escalation. The Financial Times says Beijing last year showed that it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals essential to high-tech production. Wang Dong of Peking University is quoted saying that China will absolutely defend its national interest if secondary sanctions come, as it already did during round one last year. A slide on weaponised interdependence notes limits to the use of chokepoints and adds 'TACO', glossed on the slide as Trump trade plus Chinese rare earth.

The same slide says states do not always adhere to international law but do so most of the time, and that international law is politics although it is not just politics. A slide on the three pillars of R2P lists sanctions among the steps the international community must take if protection and assistance both fail, and says only the UN Security Council can decide whether military intervention is the last resort. A slide on economic diplomacy lists the extraterritorial use of sanctions against Iran among its examples of states using sanctions, tariffs and export controls for strategic advantage.

cards.question: Emerging as a concept in the early 2000s, _____ is defined as persuading decision makers and leaders to act in the interest of vulnerable people with full respect for fundamental humanitarian principles.
cards.abstract:
Humanitarian diplomacy emerged as a concept in the early 2000s, according to a 2018 brief, which defines it as persuading decision makers and leaders to act, at all times and in all circumstances, in the interest of vulnerable people and with full respect for fundamental humanitarian principles. According to the brief, it traditionally ranges from negotiating the presence of humanitarian organisations to negotiating access to civilian populations in need of protection. It also involves monitoring assistance programmes, promoting respect for international law and advocating for broader humanitarian goals, a description for which the brief cites a 2007 work by Minear and Smith. Historically, it says, humanitarianism has been conducted in situations of extreme insecurity and unstable political conditions to secure access, assistance and protection for civilians. Improving access to humanitarian aid in conflict and complex emergencies, the brief adds, has always been a major concern for policy makers and humanitarian actors.

The brief says it discusses how the concept is key to understanding critical changes in the humanitarian field and how humanitarian efforts, foreign policy and strategic interests increasingly overlap in the contemporary scenario. It notes that the definitions and content of humanitarian diplomacy vary as widely as the number of organisations or states using the term. It also says there is a significant difference between the idea of humanitarian diplomacy, the use of the term and international recognition for an agreement on how it should be conducted. Although the practice is increasingly framed as a crucial aspect of providing access to aid in conflict areas, the brief says few agencies and political actors reflect on their humanitarian diplomatic practices. To assess the role of the traditional humanitarian actors, it adds, humanitarian diplomacy has to be observed in a historical perspective, and the course timetable gives the third lecture the title 'Economic Diplomacy, Humanitarian Aid and Development'.

cards.question: Because diplomacy works through pragmatic dealings and humanitarian action serves universal ideals, the brief sees _____ as a significant tension embedded in the phrase humanitarian diplomacy.
cards.abstract:
Compromise against principle is a summary of the tension that the brief says is embedded in humanitarian diplomacy, though the brief does not use that phrase itself. Diplomacy, the brief says, is essentially about the representation of one polity in relation to another, whereas humanitarianism is about advocating for and helping people in need. Diplomacy is characterised by compromise and pragmatic dealings, it continues, whereas the public image of humanitarian action is the opposite, since it is about working for ideals and universal principles regardless of the interests of specific political actors. The section is headed with the question whether humanitarian diplomacy is an oxymoron, and its text then speaks of a significant tension embedded in the concept. The opening of the brief defines the concept as persuading decision makers and leaders to act in the interest of vulnerable people and with full respect for fundamental humanitarian principles.

The brief says that unravelling this tension and exposing the complex diplomatic architecture of humanitarian aid, with its variety of actors and intentions, makes the study of the subject crucial, timely and important. It adds that humanitarian neutrality has always been questioned by scholars and, more rarely, by practitioners, because of hidden political interests, the politics of humanitarian negotiation and the wider sphere of humanitarian diplomacy. Humanitarian organisations, it says, often depend on a network of formal or informal relations with the parties to armed conflicts to guarantee access to aid, and the tension between negotiations and neutrality has traditionally been a challenge for them. A research question at the end of the brief asks about the relationship between means, such as working with unsavoury actors and compromising neutrality, and ends, which it gives as leaving no one behind. The first lecture says, in general terms and not about aid, that to pursue ideals we need strategy and an understanding of the means, the risks and opportunities.

cards.question: Humanity, neutrality, impartiality and independence are called 'the foundations for humanitarian action', the fundamental _____ that, by the brief's definition, humanitarian diplomacy must respect in full.
cards.abstract:
The humanitarian principles are never set out as a list in the brief, which says that neutrality, along with humanity, impartiality and independence, constitutes 'the foundations for humanitarian action' and gives the website unocha.org as its source. The brief explains only neutrality, which, it says, is seen as necessary to prevent humanitarian actors from taking sides or engaging in controversies of a political, racial, religious or ideological nature. Its opening defines humanitarian diplomacy as persuading decision makers and leaders to act in the interest of vulnerable people and with full respect for fundamental humanitarian principles. Humanitarian neutrality, the brief says, has always been questioned by scholars and, more rarely, by practitioners, because of hidden political interests, the politics of humanitarian negotiation and the wider sphere of humanitarian diplomacy. The tension between negotiations and the principle of neutrality, it adds, has traditionally represented a challenge for humanitarian organisations.

Neutrality, the brief says, proves difficult to keep, and it points out that humanitarian organisations often depend on a network of formal or informal relations with the parties involved in armed conflicts to guarantee access to aid. It says humanitarian efforts are challenged by regional competition between traditional and new donors and by the ability of international humanitarian organisations to remain relevant and faithful to humanitarian principles. It says humanitarian actors now work with increased uncertainty about the support for key norms and principles, and with new actors who hold very different views of how those norms should be interpreted and advanced. One of its research questions asks about the relationship between means, such as working with unsavoury actors and compromising neutrality, and the end of leaving no one behind. A different reading, on fragile states, says real change in the United States government has been hampered by chronic underfunding and a lack of full acceptance among many humanitarian and development professionals, especially those skittish of becoming too engaged with politics.

cards.question: As the character of violent conflicts changes, with civilians the intended victims of protracted crises, the _____ has become an integral element of conflict itself, the brief says.
cards.abstract:
The politicisation of access to aid has, according to the brief, become an integral element of conflict itself, as the character of violent conflicts changes. It says that access to humanitarian aid is increasingly challenged in ways that also redefine the role of humanitarian actors, though it gives no formal definition of the term. It traces the dangers humanitarians now face to protracted conflicts and prolonged crises in which civilians are the intended victims, access to remote areas is difficult and aid workers risk being perceived as a threat. Access has long been a concern, since the opening says that improving access to humanitarian aid in conflict and complex emergencies has always been a major concern for policy makers and humanitarian actors. Humanitarian organisations, the brief adds, often depend on developing a network of formal or informal relations with parties involved in armed conflicts to guarantee access to aid.

The trend has come to the fore in the Middle East, especially in Syria, where the involvement of both new and traditional donors has created new processes of negotiation and definition of the humanitarian space. Aid delivery there merges with regional competition animated by different stabilisation efforts, as well as with unilateral, bilateral and multilateral humanitarian flows. The brief says humanitarian actors now operate in political environments where there is less agreement between the parties involved, the cast of actors is more diverse and the challenges in providing access to victims are more politicised. Its closing call is for research on the long term implications that changes in humanitarian action have on the main imperative to provide access to aid in contexts of conflict and regional political tension. On Qatar, it says new knowledge is needed on what its humanitarian diplomacy can do in facilitating negotiations between political parties and humanitarian organisations to improve access to aid for civilians affected by conflicts.

cards.question: Bosnia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen and Syria are named in the brief as crises showing that the _____ that humanitarian action was meant to provide have become targets of political violence.
cards.abstract:
The safe havens that humanitarian action was originally meant to provide have, the brief says, become targets of political violence. The brief names the massive humanitarian crises in Bosnia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen and Syria as having shown this. This leaves many people, it says, either trapped within the conflict itself or forced to flee along routes with high risk of exploitation from traffickers, and where humanitarians have little or no access. Historically, the brief says, humanitarianism has been conducted in situations of extreme insecurity and unstable political conditions to secure access, assistance and protection for civilians. It traces the dangers humanitarians now face to protracted conflicts and prolonged crises where civilians are the intended victims, access to remote areas is difficult and aid workers risk being perceived as a threat.

The brief adds that access to humanitarian aid is increasingly challenged in ways that also redefine the role of humanitarian actors. A lecture slide on the nature of modern conflicts says present conflicts differ from those of 15 years ago, with less emphasis on the protection of civilians and the Geneva Conventions, and points to Syria. The same lecture calls the protection of civilians a very difficult challenge for peacekeeping operations whose credibility is at stake. Another slide in that lecture lists 'Protection / safe areas' among items that also include humanitarian aid, truce supervision, demining and the supervision of elections. A different reading says that, as the refugee and migrant crisis of 2015 began, protracted conflicts in Africa and Afghanistan were overlaid with new wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen and a renewed conflict in Iraq, and that the global humanitarian system strained to address these crises at once.

A lecture slide on modern conflict cites Syria for less emphasis on protecting civilians, and the brief cites Syria among the crises in which _____ have become targets of political violence.

cards.question: When foreign policy could no longer meet the requirements of regional and global development, _____ became a useful term for engagement with new foreign policy actors and entry into Somalia, then Syria.
cards.abstract:
Turkey's humanitarian diplomacy is one of the brief's three case studies, alongside Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The brief says that when Turkey's foreign policy was no longer able to meet the requirements of regional and global development, humanitarian diplomacy became a useful term to explain Turkey's engagement with new foreign policy actors, including non-state actors. The term provided, it says, legitimate entry into unstable zones such as Somalia before and Syria later on. Turkey has recently extended its humanitarian and development aid in Africa and Asia, the brief adds, and increasingly characterises its foreign policy as humanitarian diplomacy. Over the past few years, it says, Turkey has become one of the world's biggest donor countries, and the growing humanitarianism of its foreign affairs has produced both new challenges and opportunities for its development plans and security cooperation in Asia and Africa.

What is not known, the brief says, is to what extent Turkey's humanitarian diplomacy has been able to prioritise and facilitate more protection and more access to humanitarian aid, and in what specific ways Turkey's political agenda guides it. To advance knowledge, it calls for an empirical review of its political status, the ways in which it is produced and consumed, and its concrete effects. The brief groups Turkey with Qatar and the United Arab Emirates as new major humanitarian actors whose merging of foreign policy and humanitarian efforts shows that the redefinition of the humanitarian agenda must be understood in light of new politics of negotiation. Among its research questions it asks about the key characteristics of humanitarian diplomacy conducted by new state donors. Elsewhere in the course, a reading says the first-ever Global Humanitarian Summit was held in Turkey, and a lecture slide lists Turkey among middle players competing for regional hegemony.

Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are the other two case studies beside _____ in the brief, whose merging of foreign policy and humanitarian efforts it links to a redefinition of the humanitarian agenda.
