cards.question: Because of its extensive involvement since 2005 in mediation in Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq, analysts dubbed Qatar the _____, according to the brief.
cards.answerDate: Mediating since2005Two projectslate 2011 – early 2012
cards.abstract:
The non-stop mediator is the label that analysts have given Qatar, the brief says, because since 2005 the country has been extensively involved in regional mediation in places such as Sudan, Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq. In late 2011 and early 2012, it says, Qatar pushed ahead with two of its most ambitious mediation projects: facilitating unity negotiations between the rival Palestinian factions Fateh and Hamas, and hosting talks between the United States and the Taliban. These efforts made full use of the country's tradition of providing both refuge to controversial Islamist figures and a safe space for negotiations. The brief calls Qatar a new donor that combines support for peace negotiations with a more active use of humanitarian and development assistance, and says it is today one of the main donors in Palestine. Qatar prioritises its humanitarian aid to Arab recipients, it adds, but over the past decade its programme has reached more than 25 countries, many of them non-Arab.

Qatar's mediation strategies, the brief says, have paralleled its growing role as an international humanitarian donor and have paved the way to its current humanitarian diplomacy in the region. Since 2013, under Sheikh Tamim, Qatar has shifted from an active to a passive role in foreign affairs, but it still wields influence and its humanitarian diplomacy is rapidly developing. New knowledge is needed, it says, on the role that this new humanitarian diplomacy can play in stabilisation processes in the Middle East and in facilitating negotiations between political parties and humanitarian organisations. The brief groups Qatar with Turkey and the United Arab Emirates as new major humanitarian actors, and asks how regional competition and contingent governments' priorities influence states' humanitarian diplomacy. A lecture slide says peace is increasingly commodified and that mediation, once the preserve of diplomats and statesmen, has become an arena for entrepreneurs in search of influence and profit.

cards.question: Based in Dubai, the _____ is described as the largest logistics centre for the storage and distribution of humanitarian aid in the Middle East.
cards.abstract:
The International Humanitarian City is, according to the brief, based in Dubai and is the largest logistics centre for the storage and distribution of humanitarian aid in the Middle East. The brief mentions it in a passage saying that the special interest of the United Arab Emirates in humanitarian aid lies in the current trend of humanitarianism as business. Humanitarianism, it adds, is part of the country's ambition to diversify its national economy. Since 2004 Dubai has also hosted the annual DIHAD, the Dubai International Humanitarian Aid and Development Conference and Exhibition, which brings together hundreds of private corporations and profit-oriented organisations operating in the sector of humanitarianism. Since 2004, the brief says, the country has been the second largest Arab donor of development assistance and humanitarian aid, and since 2013 the world's largest donor of foreign assistance per capita.

The country was once, it says, a gulf state with a humble and neutral foreign policy defined by trade and business interests, and since 2001 it has become an emerging military actor in foreign interventions in places such as Afghanistan, Bahrain and Yemen. Over the last two decades, the brief adds, it has emerged as a regional power with an increasingly assertive foreign policy and has become a player in the humanitarian sector. Today its humanitarian diplomacy is to be understood, the brief says, within the broader shift in its foreign policy towards vigorous engagement with the rest of the world as an ambitious political and economic actor. The brief groups the country with Qatar and Turkey as new major humanitarian actors and asks, among its research questions, what the key characteristics are of humanitarian diplomacy conducted by new state donors. A lecture slide makes a parallel point about mediation, saying that peace is increasingly commodified and that mediation has become an arena for entrepreneurs in search of influence and profit.

cards.question: Launched in September 2017 during the Government's Annual Meetings, the _____ has six main pillars that together form the framework for the country's public diplomacy.
cards.abstract:
The UAE Soft Power Strategy was launched in September 2017 by the UAE Soft Power Council during the Government's Annual Meetings, according to the brief. The strategy includes six main pillars that together form the framework for the country's public diplomacy, according to the brief. Its first pillar is humanitarian diplomacy, which the brief says represents the principal way for the country to establish its Middle Eastern regional relevance and expand its role more broadly in international relations. The brief does not name the other five pillars, so the course material cannot say what they are. The brief describes the country as once a gulf state with a humble and neutral foreign policy defined by trade and business interests, and says that since 2001 it has become an emerging military actor in foreign interventions.

Over the last two decades, the brief says, the country has emerged as a regional power with an increasingly assertive foreign policy in regional conflicts. It has also become a player in the humanitarian sector, with parallel visibility in the foreign aid and strategic investment sectors, the brief adds. Today the country's humanitarian diplomacy is to be understood, the brief says, within the broader shift in its foreign policy towards vigorous engagement with the rest of the world as an ambitious political and economic actor. The brief adds that humanitarianism is part of the country's ambition to diversify its national economy, within the current trend of humanitarianism as business, and in the same passage it names the International Humanitarian City based in Dubai. Elsewhere in the course, a Ukraine lecture slide notes the possibility of technical peace talks in the United Arab Emirates, and a reading reports a deal on data centres using advanced American semiconductors.

cards.question: The brief reports a growing political consensus and commitment to '_____' in the 2030 Agenda, and says humanitarian diplomacy is seen as an instrument for reaching the most vulnerable people.
cards.abstract:
The pledge to leave no one behind is, in the brief, the subject of a growing political consensus and commitment in the 2030 Agenda. The brief adds that humanitarian diplomacy is seen as an instrument through which to reach the most vulnerable people. It defines humanitarian diplomacy as persuading decision makers and leaders to act, at all times and in all circumstances, in the interest of vulnerable people and with full respect for fundamental humanitarian principles. A different reading says the Millennium Development Goals, announced by the United Nations in 2000, were a fifteen-year plan for realising eight global goals to end extreme poverty, and that at their conclusion in 2015 poverty was increasingly concentrated in the most fragile countries. It says the Sustainable Development Goals adopted in 2015 recognise that development investments cannot be sustained unless states and societies are inclusive, accountable and just.

That essay does not use the phrase 'leave no one behind' or the name 2030 Agenda, so the course texts do not themselves say how the goals it describes relate to the commitment the brief names. A page on investing in fragile and conflict-affected states says the World Bank expects around 80 per cent of the global extreme poor to be living in such states by 2030. The same essay adds that the elimination of extreme poverty could not advance without tackling the messy dynamics of exclusion, conflict and fragility. In one of its research questions, the brief sets the end of leaving no one behind against the means of humanitarian diplomacy, such as working with unsavoury actors and compromising neutrality. It lists the relationship between these means and that end in the practice of humanitarian diplomacy as a question that deserves further exploration.

cards.question: Working with unsavoury actors and compromising neutrality are set against leaving no one behind in a research question about the relationship between _____ in the practice of humanitarian diplomacy.
cards.abstract:
Means and ends is the pairing at the centre of one of the six research questions that the brief says deserve further exploration, alongside questions on the history of the field, traditional actors, international organisations, new state donors and regional competition. That question asks about the relationship between means, such as working with unsavoury actors and compromising 'neutrality', and ends, which it gives as leaving no one behind, in the practice of humanitarian diplomacy. The question writes neutrality in quotation marks, and the brief elsewhere names neutrality with humanity, impartiality and independence as the foundations for humanitarian action. Its definition of humanitarian diplomacy is persuading decision makers and leaders to act in the interest of vulnerable people and with full respect for fundamental humanitarian principles. Humanitarian diplomacy traditionally ranges from negotiating the presence of humanitarian organisations to negotiating access to civilian populations in need of protection, the brief says.

In practice, it says, humanitarian organisations often depend on a network of formal or informal relations with parties involved in armed conflicts to guarantee access to aid. It says the tension between negotiations and the principle of neutrality has traditionally represented a challenge for humanitarian organisations. It adds that humanitarian negotiations conducted by countries such as Sweden, Norway, Switzerland and the United Kingdom are motivated by a multitude of factors, including geopolitics, economic interests, international law and underlying humanitarian principles and values. A lecture slide on what has changed in modern warfare lists the legitimacy of actors, asking whether there are equal 'positions' and giving peace partners and 'terrorists' as an example. The first lecture says, in general terms and not about aid, that to pursue ideals we need strategy and an understanding of the means, the risks and opportunities.

cards.question: A retrospective study found a decade of coalition work split into _____: intelligence efforts seeking information on Al Qaeda, military units fighting the Taliban and development actors helping the state rebuild.
cards.answer: Three lines of effort in Afghanistan
cards.abstract:
The three lines of effort in Afghanistan were, according to a retrospective study that the essay cites, essentially three separate and simultaneous strands of coalition work over the decade the study examined. The essay says the study came from Stanford University, Chatham House and the United States Institute of Peace and underlined the absence of a 'shared consciousness' among executive branch agencies, which leaves each branch essentially operating with blinders on. The first strand was made up of intelligence efforts, which sought information on Al Qaeda. The second was made up of military units, which fought the Taliban. The third was made up of development actors, who helped the Afghan state and society to rebuild.

The essay says the methods used by the intelligence and military actors served to exacerbate corruption and undermine the trust that people had in their state. That, it adds, undercut the significant investments into rebuilding the state, which were meant to strengthen the confidence of the Afghan people in it in the first place. The authors call this a stark illustration of efforts pursued with a different definition of the problem, differing timelines and frameworks for action, and fundamentally different goals. Earlier they note that the Department of Defense is organised regionally, the Department of State works government to government and the US Agency for International Development has a hybrid approach, which can lead diplomacy, development and defence to analyse fragile contexts within different frameworks. The opening pages call for a move from deeply stovepiped bureaucracies to what General Stanley McChrystal has called a 'shared consciousness', and the closing pages say that policymakers across the US interagency have yet to arrive at one.

cards.question: Announced by the United Nations in 2000 as a fifteen-year plan to end extreme poverty, the _____ conspicuously avoided the challenges of conflict, inequity and lack of human rights and justice.
cards.abstract:
The Millennium Development Goals were announced by the United Nations in 2000 as a fifteen-year plan for realising eight global goals to end extreme poverty. The essay names among them universal primary education, gender equality, lower child mortality, better maternal and child health, and a global partnership for development. It says they mirrored traditional development efforts, which long focused on investing in productive economic growth and on key objectives in health, agriculture or education, with a steady determination to steer clear of politics. The programme ran to 2015, and as it approached its conclusion United Nations member states began negotiating the Global Goals for the next fifteen years. The essay sets three recent changes in the development sector against this older approach, saying that together they signal a paradigm shift towards a more integrated way of working in fragile states.

Despite these ambitious objectives, the authors say, the goals conspicuously avoided any of the challenges posed by conflict, inequity, or lack of human rights and justice. At their conclusion in 2015, poverty was increasingly concentrated in the most fragile countries. The essay adds that this result did not come as a surprise to many, and notes that as early as the late 1990s the US Agency for International Development had sought to address the need to understand the political dynamics of development. It says the track record of the goals demonstrated that the elimination of extreme poverty could not advance without tackling the messy dynamics of exclusion, conflict and fragility, which opened the door for change. Another course reading, a web page from FMO, says the World Bank expects around 80 per cent of the global extreme poor to be living in fragile and conflict-affected states by 2030.
questions: By the conclusion of the _____ in 2015, poverty was increasingly concentrated in the most fragile countries, a result the essay says did not come as a surprise to many.

Negotiations on the Global Goals began as the _____ neared their end in 2015, and their track record showed that eliminating extreme poverty could not advance without tackling exclusion, conflict and fragility.

cards.question: Announced at the Busan forum in 2011, the _____ rested on an agreement between self-identified fragile-state governments called the g7+, international donors and civil society organisations.
cards.answer: New Deal for Engagement in Fragile States
cards.abstract:
The New Deal for Engagement in Fragile States was announced in 2011 by the International Dialogue on Peacebuilding and Statebuilding at the Fourth High-Level Forum on Aid Effectiveness, held in Busan, South Korea. The essay describes that forum as the quadrennial gathering of international development actors to forge key agreements and chart global development progress. It says the New Deal rested on an agreement between self-identified fragile-state governments, known as the g7+, international donors and civil society organisations, under a heading that says fragile states self-identify for the first time. It was designed explicitly to create more inclusive, accountable systems of governance and called for new ways to invest financially and politically in fragile states. An endnote adds that the New Deal outlined new modes of operation for donors, including committing to locally owned and led development priorities.

Its five peacebuilding and statebuilding goals were to foster inclusive political settlements and conflict resolution, establish and strengthen people's security, address injustices and increase access to justice, generate employment and improve livelihoods, and manage revenue and build capacity for accountable and fair service delivery. Although it was not officially incorporated into the main platform of the forum, it was included as one of eight streams of activity, a significant shift in the mainstream development world. Support among the G7 countries, which the essay lists as Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States, has been limited to development agencies. The authors say its potential is further limited by the inability of most g7+ countries so far to demonstrate proof of concept, with many member states having instead continued to descend into further conflict. They still say it retains promise as a model for the kind of compact that could create greater coherence and effectiveness in a carrot-and-stick approach to states trapped in fragility and conflict.
cards.answerText: New Deal for Engagement in Fragile States

cards.question: Seeking peaceful and inclusive societies, access to justice for all and effective, accountable institutions at all levels, _____ was a 2015 goal that the g7+ countries were among the most active in advocating.
cards.abstract:
Sustainable Development Goal 16 is the goal that, in the essay's account, seeks to promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development. It also seeks to provide access to justice for all and to build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels. It belongs to the Sustainable Development Goals adopted in 2015, the Global Goals for the next fifteen years that United Nations member states began negotiating as the Millennium Development Goals approached their conclusion. A separate reading, on the European Union's partnership with the African Union, says the Sustainable Development Goals strongly overlap with the African Union's Agenda 2063, citing a 2016 mapping exercise that found 93 per cent correspondence between their indicators and targets. The essay says the Millennium Development Goals before them conspicuously avoided any of the challenges posed by conflict, inequity, or lack of human rights and justice.

Their track record, it argues, demonstrated that the elimination of extreme poverty could not advance without tackling the messy dynamics of exclusion, conflict and fragility. Some member states were at first reluctant to introduce politics into the development agenda, but the new goals recognise that development investments cannot be sustained unless states and societies are inclusive, accountable and just. The g7+ countries, the self-identified fragile-state governments that were party to the New Deal, were among those most active in advocating for Goal 16. The authors say the goals represent a deep shift in the collective mindset of development practitioners and have already ignited a new approach. They also list Goal 16 among the values-based institutions that the US government under the Obama administration established and actively supported, alongside the Community of Democracies, the Open Government Partnership and the Inter-American Democratic Charter.

cards.question: Released in October 2017 by the United Nations and the World Bank, _____ was an unprecedented joint report presenting a comprehensive overview of global evidence on conflict prevention.
cards.abstract:
Pathways for Peace is the unprecedented joint report of the United Nations and the World Bank released in October 2017, which the essay says presents a comprehensive overview of global evidence pertaining to conflict prevention. The essay's endnote gives the full title as Pathways for Peace: Inclusive Approaches to Preventing Violent Conflict, although its main text calls the report Pathways to Peace. The essay says both bodies have recently adopted conflict prevention as core priorities, a commitment highlighted by the release of the report. The essay presents the report as the last in a run that includes the World Bank's 2011 World Development Report: Conflict, Security and Development, which called for a different approach emphasising citizen security, access to justice and job creation. The essay says these reports were key in articulating the evidence base and developing the frameworks for addressing fragility.

Yet the authors add that in the US government real change has remained hampered by chronic underfunding and a lack of full acceptance among many humanitarian and development professionals, especially those skittish of becoming too engaged with 'politics'. They describe a crisis-driven focus in which administrations become hostage to the latest terrible crisis and rely on reactive tools, including military action, peacekeeping missions and higher levels of humanitarian assistance. In their closing pages they say the policy case for long-term conflict prevention would be strengthened considerably by compelling evidence about the relatively modest costs of prevention versus the immense costs of crisis response. They add that the debate is not about whether peace-building investments cost less than humanitarian responses, which of course they do, but about a more complicated case that combines evidence about results with informed speculation about a counterfactual. A lecture slide on a different body, the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations, says existing conflicts are proving harder to resolve and yet new ones are emerging, and that the panel calls for a strong push on prevention.

cards.question: A bipartisan study group convened in 2016 based its recommendations on the _____, whose four words are strategic, selective, systemic and sustained, drawing on the lessons of the last three administrations.
cards.abstract:
The four S approach is a policy framework whose four words, in the essay, are strategic, selective, systemic and sustained. It comes from recommendations that, the essay says, take the lessons of the last three administrations and build on the collective wisdom of what to do. Those recommendations were made by a bipartisan study group convened in 2016 by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, the Center for a New American Security and the United States Institute of Peace. The group was composed of former US government officials and private-sector and NGO leaders and was convened specifically to capture key lessons and make recommendations to the next administration. The essay's biographical notes say that one author is president of the United States Institute of Peace and the other its vice president for policy, learning and strategy, so one of the three conveners is the authors' own institute.

The recommendations are organised into three compacts, one domestic, within the administration and within Congress, one within the international community and one within fragile states. The essay says the study acknowledges that the United States cannot tackle fragility everywhere, but can apply strategic and selective criteria to determine priority areas for action, where it is most likely to have a positive impact. It can also take specific efforts to enable more systemic action that uses all the capabilities of the US government over a sustained period. Elsewhere the essay lists at least five principles for fragile states, the last being to sustain efforts over time, since change can take a generation or more to reveal itself. The authors give Colombia as an example of how this approach can result in success, saying Plan Colombia combined security, diplomatic and development investments over a sustained period spanning three administrations.

cards.question: Offered as an example of how a strategic, selective, systemic and sustained approach can succeed, _____ combined security, diplomatic and development investments over a sustained period spanning three administrations.
cards.abstract:
Plan Colombia is the example that the essay gives of how its four S approach, which is strategic, selective, systemic and sustained, can result in success. The essay says it combined security, diplomatic and development investments over a sustained period that spanned three administrations. The essay calls the country's starting point a failed narcostate that threatened US security. Elsewhere it says that fragile states often lack the capacity to extend the reach of government over their whole territory, and that as a result illicit transnational forces such as terrorist and organised criminal groups often hold territory in them. A different reading, on the decline of global development, lists the escalating internal conflict in Colombia between drug cartels, leftist insurgents and the Colombian state among the events of what it calls two lost decades for development.

The authors say the approach helped transform the country into a partner with a rising economy and a new peace agreement ending fifty years of conflict. Their account of the case is brief, two sentences that give no start date, budget or programme detail. Elsewhere they say that the US government is organised to divide security, development and political action, each with its own frameworks, theories of change and time horizons, which precludes more effective joint approaches. They argue that diplomacy and development cannot be separated from security and stability, and that the government needs a shared consciousness about how best to deploy the tools of US foreign policy. Their closing pages say that more comprehensive evidence on the cost-effectiveness of long-term peace-building investments remains elusive, and ask what evidence exists that investments in a fragile state reduced the likelihood of a future outbreak of major armed conflict.

cards.question: Policy-makers often call the absence or breakdown of the social contract between people and their government _____, a condition to which many of them trace nearly all outbreaks of violent intrastate conflict.
cards.abstract:
State fragility is the name policy-makers often give to the absence or breakdown of the social contract between people and their government. The essay says that many policy-makers, especially in development, agree that nearly all outbreaks of violent intrastate conflict can be traced back to that condition. Its abstract puts the point more briefly, that fragility creates the conditions for violent intrastate conflict and that its consequences contribute to global disorder and mounting threats to United States national security. Several decades of scholarship and experience, the authors write, have identified a strong correlation between state fragility and higher levels of violent conflict, extreme poverty, violent extremism and vulnerability to the predations of regional and international powers. They also call fragility the common denominator running through some of the steepest security challenges the United States faces.

The authors note that while policy-makers use fragility as a helpful concept for framing a complicated set of problems, conflict researchers do not test hypotheses about its singular influence on the risks of conflict. Fragility refers to multiple dimensions of the state-society relationship, they write, which a regression-based model of violent conflict would typically represent as separate independent variables. Even so, the authors think conflict researchers have successfully made the case that fragility enables the conditions for violent conflict, on the accumulated evidence of many studies of structural attributes of the state-society relationship. A web page by FMO says there is no widely agreed-upon definition of fragility and that actors in the international community generically refer to it as a continuum rather than a binary concept. Lecture 3 uses the phrase in another setting, asking how to reinforce the domestic social contract alongside international economic traffic rules, and it lists fragility and development among the fields where it asks what should be organised as multilateral rules.

cards.question: Fragility can come from an absence of _____, the first weakened where institutions are not inclusive or accountable and the second diminished when a state fails to supply adequate public goods.
cards.abstract:
Legitimacy and effectiveness are the two qualities the essay examines, saying that the source of state fragility can be an absence of state legitimacy in the eyes of its citizens, of effectiveness, or of both. Legitimacy is weakened, it says, wherever societal and governing institutions are not inclusive or responsive to all identity groups, including minority and marginalised populations. Legitimacy may also be undermined, it adds, when populations have only weak mechanisms for holding governing institutions accountable for their performance. Effectiveness is diminished when interactions between state and society fail to produce adequate public goods for citizens' needs in security, health, economic well-being and social welfare. High levels of fragility, whether caused by illegitimacy, ineffectiveness or both, create conditions for armed conflict and political instability.

The essay says that variables aligning with fragility in terms of low legitimacy include factionalised zero-sum political competition, past ethnic conflict, ethnic discrimination and weak justice systems. Variables that track fragility in terms of poor effectiveness, it adds, include high infant mortality rates, high youth unemployment rates, low growth in gross domestic product per capita and high poverty rates. In 2011, it says, the World Bank's World Development Report: Conflict, Security and Development called for an integrated set of activities on citizen security, access to justice and job creation and proposed an evidence-based framework that emphasised institutional legitimacy as fundamental to stability. Sustainable Development Goal 16 seeks to build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels, and the essay says the goals recognise that development investments cannot be sustained unless states and societies are inclusive, accountable and just. Among the principles it lists for fragile states are supporting legitimate governments, characterised by inclusive politics, accountable institutions and reconciliation, and creating conditions for inclusive, equitable economic growth.

According to the essay, fragility that arises from a shortfall in either or both of _____ creates the conditions for armed conflict and political instability in a state.

cards.question: The essay reports that the _____ on earth are home to 43 per cent of the world's most impoverished people, a finding it draws from composite indices of state-society dysfunction.
cards.abstract:
The fifty most fragile states on earth, the essay says, are home to 43 per cent of the world's most impoverished people. The figure appears among the combined insights of a growing number of composite indices that directly measure state-society dysfunction and rank key elements of fragility at national and subnational levels. An endnote credits the finding to the Development Assistance Committee of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and its report States of Fragility 2015. The same passage says that five of the top seven most fragile states are also the top five sources of terrorist attacks. It adds that the top seven states responsible for refugees and migrants rank at the top of nearly every index on fragility, and says these combined insights have clarified the nexus between fragility and challenges to national and international security.

A majority of the unprecedented 65 million people displaced by violent conflict, it says, are fleeing the forty ongoing internal conflicts worldwide. At the end of the Millennium Development Goals in 2015, it says, poverty was increasingly concentrated in the most fragile countries. A web page by FMO says the World Bank expects around 80 per cent of the global extreme poor to be living in fragile and conflict-affected states by 2030, a different measure from the essay's count of fifty states. In late 2017, the essay adds, four of the most fragile states on any index, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen and Northeastern Nigeria, were still teetering on the edge of famine, putting 20 million people at risk of severe malnutrition or starvation. It argues that the human suffering engendered by dysfunctional interactions between governments and their people places a responsibility on the international community to respond.

One page cites a World Bank expectation that 80 per cent of the extreme poor will live in fragile states by 2030; the essay's figure is 43 per cent for the _____ on earth.

cards.question: Conflicts such as those in Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Ukraine, labelled _____ by the essay, accounted for about 3 per cent of the world's conflicts 25 years earlier and one-third of them today.
cards.abstract:
Internationalised internal conflicts are the essay's term for internal conflicts that have become increasingly internationalised, as fragile states in turmoil are more vulnerable to the predations of regional and international powers. It gives those unfolding in Syria, Iraq, Yemen and Ukraine as examples. In its figures they were a rarity 25 years ago, accounting for approximately 3 per cent of the world's conflicts, and today they account for one-third of all global conflicts. It says they have contributed to a 500 per cent increase in global battle deaths over the past 10 years and have pushed conflict deaths to a 25-year high. An endnote to the sentence giving the one-third share and the battle-death figures credits the Institute for Economics and Peace and its Global Peace Index 2016.

The essay opens by saying that earlier progress on democracy, poverty and violent conflict has abruptly reversed in the last decade, and that a new wave of civil wars, among other developments, is fuelling a sense of global disorder. Civil war in Syria alone, it says, has taken a staggering toll, with estimates of 250,000 to 470,000 lives lost since 2011. It adds that these conflicts have become much harder to solve, providing proxy ground for external powers to manipulate fragile institutions and exercise their own interests, and raising concerns about renewed great-power conflict in vulnerable fragile states. Lecture 2 says present conflicts differ from those of 15 years ago and lists, among the situations that make peacekeeping harder, increased proxy war fighting by competing regional or global powers, and elsewhere it names proxy wars in Sudan, Syria, Rwanda-DRC and Libya. The essay counts Ukraine among internationalised internal conflicts, while Lecture 2 lists Ukraine-Russia under the return of interstate wars, so the two texts frame it differently.
questions: Because fragile states in turmoil are vulnerable to the predations of regional and international powers, the essay says, _____ provide proxy ground for external powers and raise concerns about renewed great-power conflict.
The essay counts Ukraine among its _____, whereas a Lecture 2 slide files Ukraine and Russia under the return of interstate wars and lists proxy wars as separate entries.

cards.question: The essay's first reason why fragility rarely becomes the focused area of effort is a _____, in which administrations become hostage to the latest terrible crisis and respond rather than prevent.
cards.abstract:
A crisis-driven focus is the first reason the essay gives for why fragility rarely becomes the focused area of effort in United States policy, despite significant attention in foundational strategic documents. On paper, it says, Republican and Democratic administrations alike have made 'weak', 'failed' and 'fragile' states a priority in their national security strategies, yet the United States has not become measurably better at achieving its desired outcomes there. Administrations, it says, inevitably become hostage to the latest terrible crisis and focus energy and resources on responding to crisis rather than preventing it. The cost of this approach, it says, has become increasingly untenable, with an ever greater reliance on reactive tools, including military action, peacekeeping missions and higher levels of humanitarian assistance. The result is a persistent focus on fragile states, but only after crisis hits, when action is more urgent and expensive, options are more limited and problems are harder to solve.

Its example is the Ebola outbreak, which quickly spread from West Africa to the United States and led Congress to pass a significant package of postcrisis assistance meant to build longer-term global health security in the region. Such investments, it says, rarely occur until after an attention-grabbing threat has landed. Its broader prescription is a concerted effort to transform the business model of government, making it more proactive, adaptive and integrated. Near its end the essay says the case for long-term conflict prevention would be strengthened considerably by compelling evidence on the relatively modest costs of prevention against the immense costs of crisis response. Lecture 3 lists recommendations by the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations that call for a strong push on prevention and warn that ad hoc approaches to crisis responses will not be sufficient for the future.

cards.question: Moving away from deeply _____ that work without a shared framework, the essay says, means shifting from vertical structures to horizontal approaches that can prevent crises more nimbly.
cards.abstract:
The essay describes United States defence, diplomatic and development capabilities as organised in deeply stovepiped bureaucracies that work without a shared framework. It says the shift means moving from vertical structures that inhibit effective action on complex, interrelated challenges to horizontal approaches that can more nimbly work to prevent crises. Vertical government structures are the second obstacle it names to effective policy in fragile states, and it calls them a significant impediment. The United States government, it says, is organised to divide security, development and political action, each with its own frameworks, theories of change and time horizons, which precludes more effective joint approaches. A confusing web of authorities and areas of responsibility, it adds, ignites turf battles and creates incentives for competition rather than collaboration.

Agencies are also organised geographically in inconsistent ways, with the Department of Defense organised regionally, the Department of State around government-to-government interaction and the United States Agency for International Development, or USAID, in a hybrid of state-based and regional operations. Those differences, together with the different capabilities each brings, can lead the three D's of diplomacy, development and defence to analyse fragile contexts within different frameworks, with results often cast in terms of the analysing agency's own capabilities, which can undermine the potential for coordinated action. Congressional constraints add budget inflexibility through earmarks and competing committee jurisdictions, and in 2010 a joint plan for Iraq from the State Department, the Department of Defense and USAID went to two different appropriations committees. The Armed Services Committee fully funded the defence plan, while the State Department and USAID were allotted only a fraction of the necessary funding by their committee, invalidating the plan's core assumptions and effectiveness. It adds that, under the Obama administration, many efforts within the government focused on breaking down internal stovepipes and linking early warning with early action, such as the Atrocities Prevention Board and a new Center for Resilience within USAID.

cards.question: The absence of a _____, a term the essay credits to a general, leaves each branch operating with blinders on, unable to see the larger ecosystem of the challenge.
cards.abstract:
A shared consciousness, a term the essay credits to General Stanley McChrystal, is the aim it sets for United States defence, diplomatic and development capabilities, to enable more cohesive joint action. The essay calls the absence of a shared consciousness among executive branch agencies about exactly why, what, how and when to engage collectively in fragile states the most important challenge of those it lists. The result, it says, is that each branch essentially operates with blinders on, limiting its ability to see the larger ecosystem of the challenge. It quotes Jean-Marie Guéhenno that, in preventing and ending civil wars, intelligent orchestration is the most important strategic variable and isolated policies, even well-executed ones, are unlikely to produce lasting results unless part of an overall coherent and consistent strategy. Its abstract says that policy-makers across the United States interagency have yet to arrive at a shared consciousness about the challenge of fragility.

As an illustration it uses a study of coalition efforts in Afghanistan, which found three separate, simultaneous lines of effort, and it calls this a stark illustration of efforts pursued with different definitions of the problem, timelines, frameworks and goals. Development typically looks at longer-term change, it adds, while defence and diplomatic efforts address more immediate security and political problems, and without more closely aligned goals progress on fragility will remain limited. A new approach, it says, requires a shared consciousness among the United States government interagency about how best to deploy the tools of foreign policy, and the horizontal effectiveness to work with one another. It points to the 2003 report Play to Win of the Commission on Post-Conflict Reconstruction as a cohesive framework for putting states back together after a major conflict, though attention had already shifted to the 9/11 attacks by its release. The essay ends by calling a shared consciousness a steep ambition that can be supported and accelerated with better evidence about what works in fragile contexts.
questions: Among executive branch agencies, the essay says, there is no common understanding of why, what, how and when to engage collectively in fragile states, and it calls this missing _____ the most important challenge.
Three separate lines of effort in Afghanistan, each with a different definition of the problem, are the essay's stark illustration of a missing _____ among the agencies of government.

cards.question: A June framework deal with China was the true opening of the age of _____, the article says, when the United States finds others doing unto it as it has done unto them.
cards.abstract:
Weaponised interdependence is defined on a Lecture 4 slide as leveraging global networks of informational and financial exchange for strategic advantage. The slide says the term complements the traditional definition of economic diplomacy, and it credits the term to the political scientists Farrell and Newman. Their Foreign Affairs article says the new era will be shaped by sanctions, supply chain attacks and export measures that repurpose the many points of control in the infrastructure underpinning the interdependent global economy. It says that for over two decades the United States has unilaterally weaponised these chokepoints in finance, information flows and technology for strategic advantage. A Lecture 4 slide lists that infrastructure as the internet, e-commerce and social media, the US dollar and SWIFT messaging, and the software design of the most advanced chips, built after the Cold War on US-centred foundations.

The article argues that the June framework deal with China was the true opening of the age of weaponised interdependence, in which the United States is discovering what it is like to have others do unto it as it has done unto others. It adds that market exchange has become hopelessly entangled with national security, so the United States must now defend its interests in a world in which other powers can leverage chokepoints of their own. The Lecture 4 slide draws the consequence that economic and technological integration have turned from a promise to a threat, with US adversaries and even allies disconnecting, hiding or retaliating. Lecture 1 says that control over strategic chokeholds and the ability to weaponise global interdependence have become as vital as GDP or the size of its military as markers of national power. A Lecture 1 slide adds that, so long as critical supply chains are co-dependent, mutually assured economic pain appears to deter escalation, while a Lecture 3 slide notes limits to interdependence but also limits to the use of chokepoints.
questions: A lecture slide defines _____ as leveraging global networks of informational and financial exchange for strategic advantage, and sets the idea beside the traditional rule-making definition of economic diplomacy.
Sanctions, supply chain attacks and export measures that repurpose points of control in finance, information flows and technology are the weapons of _____, which the United States long wielded alone.

cards.question: Washington relaxed export controls on chip design software and chips, and China eased rare-earth limits that were crippling carmakers, in the _____ that an article calls the true opening of a new age.
cards.answerDate: Tariffs peak1 April 2025Back to 10%by 10 May 2025Framework dealJune 2025
cards.abstract:
The June 2025 framework deal is the agreement with China that, in the words of Farrell and Newman, marked a silent shifting of gears in the global political economy when Washington announced it. They write that it was neither the start of Trump's imagined epoch of 'liberation' under unilateral American greatness nor a return to Biden's dream of managed great-power rivalry. The article says administration officials now acknowledge concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals that were crippling the US auto industry. US companies that provide chip design software, such as Synopsys and Cadence, can once again sell in China, a concession the article says will help the Chinese semiconductor industry escape the bind of the Biden administration's limits on advanced semiconductors. The article adds that Nvidia can again sell H20 chips for training artificial intelligence to Chinese customers.

In a little-noticed June speech, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said China had 'cornered the market' for rare earths and put the United States and the world in a 'crunch'. Rubio added that US industrial capability is deeply dependent on potential adversaries, including China, who can 'hold it over our head'. Although Rubio stressed self-reliance, the authors argue that the rush to make a deal shows the limits of going it alone, since the United States is ratcheting back its own threats to persuade adversaries not to cripple vital parts of its economy. A Lecture 1 slide says tariffs peaked at 125 per cent on 1 April 2025 and fell to a mutual 10 per cent by 10 May, while the article dates its framework deal to June, and the texts do not say whether these were one agreement or two. The slide concludes that mutually assured economic pain appears to deter escalation, and a 2026 Financial Times article says Beijing showed last year that it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals.

cards.question: The article says the use of weaponised interdependence always exploited the advantages of the _____, a mutually reinforcing suite of institutional and technological relationships that drew others into the United States' orbit.
cards.abstract:
The American stack is the article's term for the mutually reinforcing suite of institutional and technological relationships that drew others into the United States' orbit. The article says the use of weaponised interdependence always exploited the advantages of this stack, and that, when used wisely, weaponisation advanced slowly and within boundaries that others could tolerate. A Lecture 4 slide describes the foundations, saying that after the Cold War ended businesses built an independent global economy on US-centred infrastructure in information flows, finance and technology. Its examples are the internet, e-commerce and social media, the US dollar as the global currency together with SWIFT messaging, and the software design of the most advanced chips. The article says other countries relied on US technological and financial infrastructure despite the risks because they saw a government whose self-interest was constrained, at least to some extent, by the rule of law and a willingness to consider allies' interests.

It argues that this calculus has shifted, likely irreversibly, because the second Trump administration has made clear that it views the countries closest to the United States less as allies than as vassal states. It says the United States is now spiralling into a rapid and uncontrollable drawdown of its assets, pursuing short-term goals at the expense of long-term objectives and using its tools in a haphazard way that invites miscalculations. In finance, it says, the administration pushes cryptocurrencies that are more opaque and less accountable than the dollar, while American enthusiasm for stablecoins is pushing China and Europe to accelerate their work on alternative payment systems. In energy, it argues, a spending bill effectively cedes control of next-generation energy technology to China, and if China leaps ahead, as seems likely, other countries will be pulled into its orbit. A Lecture 4 slide sums up the argument by saying that across finance, technology and energy the administration is making the United States less central than it used to be.

cards.question: A slide describes a _____ as a system of interconnected layers from foundational technologies to advanced applications, each building on the one below, and says that power now comes from controlling it.
cards.abstract:
A technological stack is defined on a Lecture 4 slide as a system of interconnected layers, ranging from foundational technologies to advanced applications. The slide says each layer builds upon the capabilities of the one below it while dynamically interacting with all the others. It states that, in a world of weaponised interdependence, power comes from controlling such stacks. It adds that simply identifying key supply-chain chokepoints is not enough, because the state must also build the apparatus that can gather enough information to grasp the immediate benefits and risks and then put that information to use. The slide's four layers are rare earths, manufacturing equipment, high-precision manufacturing, and chip design and AI.

It names China as controlling 90 per cent of global refining capacity for rare earths, ASML of the Netherlands as holding a monopoly over ultraviolet lithographic machines, and the Taiwanese firm TSMC as producing around 60 per cent of all chips. It adds that Nvidia graphics processing units dominate 84 per cent of the market, and that since 2017 70 per cent of foundational AI models have been developed in the US and 15 per cent in China. The article uses the same word for the American position, describing the American stack as the mutually reinforcing suite of institutional and technological relationships that drew others into the United States' orbit. It warns that other countries are not only developing their own capacities to punish the United States but also building technological stacks that may be more appealing to the world than the United States'. The next Lecture 4 slide records the aim for Europe to build an independent stack of technologies, while a 2026 Foreign Affairs essay advises countries that, instead of accepting dependence on American technology or betting the bank on building autonomous tech stacks, they should use the leverage they already have.

cards.question: A lecture slide says China controls 90 per cent of global _____ capacity for resources used in a variety of high-tech industrial purposes, the first layer in its account of the technological stack.
cards.abstract:
Rare-earth refining is the stage at which a Lecture 4 slide says China controls 90 per cent of global capacity, for resources used for a variety of high-tech industrial purposes. The slide lists it first, under the heading 'Rare Earths', among the layers of its technological stack, ahead of manufacturing equipment, high-precision manufacturing, and chip design and AI. A 2026 essay in Foreign Affairs says China has extended the resource chokepoints it commands from raw materials to processing. The same essay recalls that in 2010 Beijing briefly experimented with cutting off rare-earth exports to Japan amid a territorial dispute, but had not yet established the bureaucracy to target such controls precisely. A slide on China's institutional adaptation says it developed a 'whole of nation' approach to secure technological independence, focusing on rare earths extraction and processing.

Farrell and Newman write that administration officials now acknowledge making concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals that were crippling the US auto industry. They report a June speech in which the US Secretary of State said China had 'cornered the market' for rare earths, putting the United States and the world in a 'crunch'. A 2026 Financial Times article says Beijing showed last year that it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals essential to high-tech production. The Foreign Affairs essay adds that in late 2025 China adopted its own version of the US foreign direct product rule, asserting a right to decide whether companies anywhere can access magnets containing even trace amounts of Chinese materials. It warns that China could further restrict the rare earths used in US and European weapons systems and high-end technologies.

cards.question: Under 'High-Precision Manufacturing', a lecture slide says the Taiwanese company _____ produces around 60 per cent of all chips and more than 90 per cent of the most advanced ones.
cards.abstract:
TSMC is named on a Lecture 4 slide as the Taiwanese company that produces around 60 per cent of all chips globally. The same slide says it produces more than 90 per cent of the most advanced chips, as against around 60 per cent for chips of all kinds. The slide files it under 'High-Precision Manufacturing', the third of four layers in its account of the technological stack. The other layers are rare earths, manufacturing equipment, where ASML of the Netherlands has a monopoly over ultraviolet lithographic machines, and chip design and AI, where the slide names Nvidia. The slide defines a stack as a system of interconnected layers, each building on the one below it, and says that in a world of weaponised interdependence power comes from controlling stacks.

A Lecture 3 slide on the weaponisation of interdependence lists 'ecosystems' with the US and Taiwan as coproducers and names the Taiwan Strait among geographic chokepoints, while noting limits to interdependence but also limits to the use of chokepoints. Farrell and Newman say the Biden administration started limiting China's ability to build advanced semiconductors, and that concessions in the June deal will help the Chinese industry wriggle out of that bind. None of the readings names TSMC, but a 2026 Foreign Affairs essay argues that Taiwan could restrict its critical semiconductor industry to deter China from threatening its sovereignty. The essay adds that the Biden administration imposed wider export controls, taking advantage of the fact that US and allied firms dominate the production of chip manufacturing equipment and the software required to make advanced chips. The conclusions of Lecture 4 list among their points a balance between dependence and autarky on issues like semiconductors.

cards.question: A lecture slide says the American firm _____ has graphics processing units that dominate 84 per cent of the market, at the chip design and AI layer of the technological stack.
cards.abstract:
Nvidia is named on a Lecture 4 slide as the US company whose graphics processing units dominate 84 per cent of the market. The slide places it in the last layer of its technological stack, headed 'Chip Design and AI', after rare earths, manufacturing equipment and high-precision manufacturing. It adds that since 2017, 70 per cent of foundational AI models have been developed in the US and 15 per cent in China. The slide introduces the stack by saying that, in a world of weaponised interdependence, power comes from controlling such layered systems. It also says each layer builds upon the capabilities of the one below it while dynamically interacting with all the others.

Farrell and Newman say the June deal with China let Nvidia sell H20 chips for training artificial intelligence to Chinese customers again. In the same deal, they write, US makers of chip design software such as Synopsys and Cadence can again sell in China, which will help the Chinese semiconductor industry escape the bind created when the Biden administration began limiting its ability to build advanced semiconductors. They add that in some instances the Trump administration has reversed Biden's policies and promoted the diffusion of previously controlled technology, as in a deal to expand data centres in the United Arab Emirates using advanced US semiconductors. A 2026 Foreign Affairs essay says the first Trump administration restricted Chinese companies' access to high-level microchips and that the Biden administration's wider export controls exploited US and allied dominance of chip manufacturing equipment and software. Lecture 4's conclusion cites a drive to obtain key technologies like AI and quantum computing, with a risk of a two-tier world, and a September 2026 Economist leader asks whether the AI arms race can be stopped.

cards.question: A slide on China's institutional adaptation says it developed a '_____' to secure technological independence, focusing on rare earths extraction and processing, after writing data sovereignty into its security strategy in 2013.
cards.abstract:
China's whole-of-nation approach is described on a Lecture 4 slide as a way to secure technological independence, focusing on rare earths extraction and processing. The slide puts it under the heading 'Institutional adaptation', beside parallel assessments of the EU and the US. It says China introduced the concepts of 'information security' and data sovereignty into its national security strategy in 2013, a date the slide gives without further explanation. It adds that China has adapted institutionally to leverage interdependencies strategically through export controls with precision. The slide also warns that excessive state intervention in the domestic economy for purely political purposes risks hampering investment and potentially strangling innovation.

The preceding slide supplies the substance, listing rare earths first among the layers of the technological stack and saying that China controls 90 per cent of global refining capacity of resources used for a variety of high-tech industrial purposes. A 2026 Foreign Affairs essay says Beijing's brief experiment with cutting off rare-earth exports to Japan in 2010 came before it had established the bureaucracy to target such controls precisely. The essay says China has since built its own export control system explicitly modelled on Washington's, and in late 2025 adopted its own version of the US foreign direct product rule. A line set apart in the Farrell and Newman article says that China built a bureaucratic apparatus to turn chokepoints into practical leverage. A 2026 Financial Times article describes an increasingly strident Chinese anti-sanctions regime that includes countermeasures against foreign individuals and organisations that assist with foreign restrictions on Chinese companies and supply chains, and says Beijing showed last year that it could bring American manufacturing to a standstill through its control of critical minerals.
questions: China's export controls, applied with precision, are paired with a state-led push for technological independence that a slide calls a '_____', though it warns that excessive intervention may strangle innovation.
Beijing's 2010 rare-earth cut-off to Japan lacked precision, but since then, a 2026 essay says, it has built an export control system, while a lecture slide credits it with a '_____'.

cards.question: A slide urges Europe to build its own suite of institutions and an independent technology stack, and points to the _____ project as the place to look.
cards.abstract:
EuroStack is the name of a project to which a Lecture 4 slide points when it says Europe should build its own comprehensive suite of institutions and an independent stack of technologies. The slide gives no further description of the project, and none of the readings uses the name, so the course texts say little more about it than this. It appears in the EU part of a slide on institutional adaptation that also assesses China and the United States. The idea of a stack is defined on the previous slide, as a system of interconnected layers, ranging from foundational technologies to advanced applications. That slide says that in a world of weaponised interdependence power comes from controlling such stacks, and that identifying chokepoints is not enough without a state apparatus able to gather and use information.

The EU part of the slide lists constraints, saying that short-term dependence on US security guarantees limits strategic autonomy and that EU companies want to maintain access to the Chinese market. It adds that the EU lacks the capacity to coordinate national capitals and empower the European Commission. Farrell and Newman make a related point, saying that China and the United States can usually bet that 'Europe Always Chickens Out' in geoeconomic confrontations because Europe lacks the information, institutional clout and internal agreement to do much else. They also say other countries are building technological stacks that may be more appealing than the United States', and that American enthusiasm for stablecoins is pushing China and Europe to accelerate work on alternative payment systems. A 2026 Foreign Affairs essay offers a different emphasis, advising that instead of accepting dependence on American technology or betting the bank on autonomous tech stacks countries should use the leverage they already have, and saying that Europe has more means to develop self-reliance than it gives itself credit for.
questions: Short-term dependence on US security guarantees, companies wanting access to the Chinese market and weak coordination between national capitals limit Europe's strategic autonomy, a slide says, as it cites the _____ project.
While one 2026 essay warns against betting the bank on autonomous tech stacks, a lecture slide urges Europe to build an independent stack, citing the _____ project.

cards.question: European officials talk incessantly about their doomsday device, the _____, but adversaries feel sure it will never be deployed, which encourages them to coerce European companies and countries at their leisure.
cards.abstract:
The authors present the anti-coercion instrument as the exact opposite of the 'Doomsday Machine' in the film Dr Strangelove, the classic Cold War satire. They say that machine was a disaster because it automatically launched nuclear missiles in response to an attack but was kept a closely guarded secret until an attack was launched. In contrast, they write, European officials talk incessantly about their doomsday device, but Europe's adversaries feel sure that it will never be deployed. That certainty, they say, encourages those adversaries to coerce European companies and countries at their leisure. The article adds that, as with earlier European efforts to block sanctions, China and the United States can usually bet on the EACO principle that 'Europe Always Chickens Out' in geoeconomic confrontations.

It says Europe lacks the information, institutional clout and internal agreement to do much else. A Lecture 4 slide on the EU's institutional adaptation lists short-term dependence on US security guarantees, which it says limits strategic autonomy, the wish of EU companies to maintain access to the Chinese market, and a lack of capacity to coordinate national capitals and empower the European Commission. The same slide says Europe is to build its own comprehensive suite of institutions and an independent stack of technologies, and points to the EuroStack project. A 2026 Foreign Affairs essay takes a different view, saying that Europe and its allies have more means to develop self-reliance and to work out arrangements with other powers than they give themselves credit for. Its examples are that Europe could leverage its Airbus sales by withholding software updates for China's Airbus fleet, which would ground more than half the country's commercial planes, and could cut off market access for American social media companies to retaliate against US tariffs.

cards.question: A federal hiring freeze left key positions unfilled and budget proposals anticipate cuts even as sanctions-related programmes rise, a pattern a slide calls _____ and also sees at the National Security Council.
cards.abstract:
Institutional decay at OFAC is the condition a Lecture 4 slide says OFAC, the Office of Foreign Assets Control, and the National Security Council face because of Trump's overhaul of key positions, leaving many apparatuses understaffed. The slide says that under Biden OFAC developed maps of global finance and a detailed understanding of semiconductor supply chains, whereas the article gives the semiconductor understanding to key officials on Biden's National Security Council. The article says the second Trump administration imposed a hiring freeze across the federal government, hitting the Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, which oversees OFAC, and leaving key positions unfilled and departments understaffed. It adds that initial budget proposals anticipate an overall reduction in funding for the office, even as the number of sanctions-related programmes has continued to rise. It says the Bureau of Industry and Security, chiefly responsible for export controls, lost over a dozen employees in force reductions, despite support from Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

The article concedes that OFAC and the Bureau were never as all-seeing as their reputations suggested and sometimes made mistakes, but says they gave Washington an extraordinary edge, since other countries had no equivalent to OFAC's maps of global finance. It calls such institutional decay the inevitable consequence of Trumpism, arguing that in Trump's eyes all institutional restraints on his power are illegitimate. It says the National Security Council has cut its staff by more than half, the State Department has been decimated by job cuts, and the traditional interagency process has virtually disappeared. It argues that policy is now centred on Trump himself, so that personalism replaces bureaucratic decision-making and short-term profit trumps long-term national interest, as the slide also says. The closing section argues that strategy in an age of weaponised interdependence requires building up these institutions to make them more flexible and more capable of the deep expertise needed in a world where Washington's adversaries now hold many of the cards.

cards.question: After the go-go 1990s and 2000s the pace of economic integration stalled in the 2010s, a condition that The Economist labelled _____ when it described the fragile state of international trade.
cards.abstract:
Slowbalisation is the term that The Economist says, in a leader of 16 June 2022, it used three years earlier to describe the fragile state of international trade and commerce. The leader says that after the go-go 1990s and 2000s the pace of economic integration stalled in the 2010s, and that the flow of goods and capital stagnated. It adds that firms were grappling with the aftershocks of a financial crisis, a populist revolt against open borders and President Donald Trump's trade war. Many bosses, it says, postponed big decisions on investing abroad, so that just-in-time gave way to wait-and-see, and no one knew if globalisation faced a blip or extinction. A Foreign Affairs article of July and August 2019 also said that globalisation was in trouble, that a populist backlash was in full swing and that a simmering trade war between China and the United States could easily boil over.

The leader's next paragraph says the waiting is over, because the pandemic and the war in Ukraine have triggered a once-in-a-generation reimagining of global capitalism in boardrooms and governments. In its account the new kind of globalisation is about security, not efficiency, and prioritises doing business with people you can rely on, in countries your government is friendly with. The leader warns that it could descend into protectionism, big government and worsening inflation, but says that with restraint from firms and politicians it could keep the benefits of openness while improving resilience. Lecture 1 says the post Cold War dominance of globalisation and liberal-Western-style values and institutions is being challenged, and a Lecture 3 slide pairs national sovereignty and democracy with limits on globalisation, giving 'America First' as its example. A 2026 essay adds that economic nationalism and protectionism are on the rise, while a Lecture 4 slide says the world is more economically interconnected than ever, with record trade, yet geopolitically more fragmented.

cards.question: After 1989 firms put production where costs were lowest, but when lean chains break the bill can be crippling, so the leader weighs _____ and ends by seeking a new balance.
cards.abstract:
Efficiency against resilience is the choice behind a leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022, which says that after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 the lodestar of globalisation was efficiency. Companies, it says, located production where costs were lowest, investors deployed capital where returns were highest, and governments aspired to treat firms equally and to strike trade deals with democracies and autocracies alike. The leader says this gave rise to value chains that account for half of all trade, kept prices low for consumers and helped lift 1 billion people out of extreme poverty. A 2019 article in Foreign Affairs says that the centre-right and centre-left disagreed over how to accommodate national economies to the new world economy, but both agreed that economies needed to be refashioned in the name of global competitiveness. The leader concedes that hyper-efficient globalisation also had problems, because volatile capital flows destabilised financial markets and many blue-collar workers in rich countries lost out.

Its first recent worry is that some lean supply chains are not as good value as they appear, since mostly they keep costs low but, when they break, the bill can be crippling. Today's bottlenecks, it adds, have reduced global GDP by at least 1 per cent, and as chip shortages have stalled car production carmakers' cashflows have dropped by 80 per cent year on year. The standfirst reads 'Why too much resilience is dangerous', and the text says one indication that companies are shifting from efficiency to resilience is a vast build-up in precautionary inventories. Indiscriminately replicating supply chains, the leader warns, would bring enormous long-run inefficiency, and duplicating a quarter of all multinational activity could add annual costs above 2 per cent of world GDP. Its conclusion is that resilience comes from diversification, not concentration at home, and that a new balance between efficiency and security is a reasonable goal, while a Lecture 4 slide names a balance between dependence and autarky on issues like semiconductors.

cards.question: The hope that economic integration would lead autocracies to reform, which the Germans call _____, has been dashed, a leader argues, noting that autocracies account for a third of world GDP.
cards.abstract:
Change through trade is, in a leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022, what the Germans call the hope that economic integration would lead to reform. The leader says that such hopes have been dashed, and notes that autocracies account for a third of world GDP. It says the single-minded pursuit of cost advantage has led to a dependency on autocracies that abuse human rights and use trade as a means of coercion. Earlier it says that, after the Berlin Wall fell, governments aspired to strike trade deals with democracies and autocracies alike. The course materials also use a German phrase, 'Wandel durch Annäherung', which a Lecture 3 slide places beside the words Interdependence and Peace and a Lecture 5 slide on Nord Stream 2 sets against business interests.

The leader says that Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine has painfully exposed Europe's reliance on Russian energy, and that McDonald's in Moscow, which opened in 1990, has restarted under local control with Big Macs no longer on the menu. It adds that Xi Jinping's China has a trade footprint seven times as big as Russia's and that the world relies on it for goods from active pharmaceutical ingredients to the processed lithium used in batteries. The Lecture 5 slide sets business interests against interdependence as conflict avoider or conflict enhancer, and a Lecture 4 conclusion says interdependence is increasingly seen not only as a stabilising factor but also as an element of insecurity and vulnerability. A 2025 article in Foreign Affairs says economic and technological integration have turned from a promise to a threat, and a 2026 essay says architects see globalisation as a means to transform others while artisans worry about the vulnerabilities that interconnectedness creates. The leader adds that a citizen of the world should hope globalisation's next phase involves the maximum possible degree of openness, and it argues that the choke-points autocracies control amount to only about a tenth of global trade.

cards.question: At the biggest 3,000 firms globally, _____ rose from 6 per cent to 9 per cent of world GDP after 2016, which a leader calls one indication of a shift towards resilience.
cards.abstract:
Precautionary inventories are the stocks whose vast build-up a leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022 calls one indication that companies are shifting from efficiency to resilience. Its figure is that for the biggest 3,000 firms globally they have risen from 6 per cent to 9 per cent of world GDP since 2016. Its second paragraph speaks of 9 trillion dollars in inventories, stockpiled as insurance against shortages and inflation, among the ways supply chains are being transformed. That paragraph also mentions the fight for workers as global firms shift from China into Vietnam, and says the pandemic and the war in Ukraine triggered a once-in-a-generation reimagining of global capitalism. The leader's first paragraph describes the earlier mood, in which many bosses postponed big decisions on investing abroad and just-in-time gave way to wait-and-see.

The leader says lean supply chains mostly keep costs low, but when they break the bill can be crippling, with today's bottlenecks reducing global GDP by at least 1 per cent. Its examples are that carmakers' cashflows have dropped by 80 per cent year on year as chip shortages have stalled car production, and that Tim Cook, who runs Apple, reckons such snafus could reduce sales by up to 8 billion dollars, or 10 per cent, in the quarter. It adds that wars, extreme weather or another virus could easily disrupt supply chains in the next decade. The leader also warns that duplicating a quarter of all multinational activity could add annual costs above 2 per cent of world GDP, and says resilience comes from diversification, not concentration at home. A 2026 analysis of a fertiliser shock cites World Bank assessments showing that, as of March, grain inventories remained stronger than during the 2022 food crisis, among global factors that may moderate the shock, though that concerns grain stocks and not the stockpiles of firms.

cards.question: Governments from Europe to India are keen on _____, a leader says, encouraging pressured industries to reinvent their business models, from vertical integration to cutting assets in China.
cards.abstract:
Strategic autonomy is the aim that, according to a leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022, governments from Europe to India are keen on, and those governments are encouraging the industries under most pressure to reinvent their business models. The leader offers no definition, but the paragraph goes on to describe car makers moving towards vertical integration, Taiwan's electronics assemblers cutting their share of assets in China from 50 per cent to 35 per cent since 2017, and the West seeking long-term supply deals from allies and cosying up to gas-rich Qatar. Elsewhere it says the new kind of globalisation is about security, not efficiency, and prioritises doing business with people you can rely on. It warns that a reasonable pursuit of security could morph into rampant protectionism, jobs schemes and hundreds of billions of dollars of industrial subsidies, with more volatility and fragmentation that would push prices yet higher. Lecture 1 lists China-US strategic autonomy versus interdependence among the uncertain and unexpected themes that the course will explore.

A Lecture 4 slide on institutional adaptation says that for the EU short-term dependence on US security guarantees limits strategic autonomy. The same slide says Europe aims to build its own comprehensive suite of institutions and an independent stack of technologies, citing the EuroStack project, and that EU companies want to maintain access to the Chinese market. A 2026 essay in Foreign Affairs says that countries should not accept dependence on American technology or bet the bank on building autonomous tech stacks, and should instead use the leverage they already have. A 2025 article in the same journal notes that the US Secretary of State emphasised self-reliance as a solution, but says the administration's rush to make a deal with China demonstrates the limits of going it alone. A closing Lecture 4 slide names a balance between dependence and autarky on issues like semiconductors, and says the interconnection of economic, technological and security dimensions co-determines foreign economic policy.
