cards.question: Many firms are adopting _____ and longer-term contracts, a leader says, as one of the signs, alongside a build-up of precautionary inventories, that companies are moving from efficiency to resilience.
cards.abstract:
Dual sourcing is a practice that, according to a leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022, many firms are adopting, together with longer-term contracts. The leader does not define it, so this background reports where the leader places the practice and sets beside it what other course texts say about concentration and diversification. It mentions the practice directly after the build-up in precautionary inventories, which it calls one indication that companies are shifting from efficiency to resilience. Its second paragraph mentions the fight for workers as global firms shift from China into Vietnam. It also says that Taiwan's electronics assemblers have cut their share of assets in China from 50 per cent to 35 per cent since 2017 as clients such as Apple demand diversification.

Among the leader's worries is that the single-minded pursuit of cost advantage has led to a dependency on autocracies, with the world relying on China for goods from active pharmaceutical ingredients to processed lithium. A Lecture 4 slide on the technological stack lists concentrations of this kind, saying China controls 90 per cent of global refining capacity of resources used in high-tech industry and that Taiwan's TSMC produces more than 90 per cent of the most advanced chips. In the leader's closing section, the answer where autocracies control choke-points is to require firms to diversify their suppliers and let the market adapt, and it adds that resilience comes from diversification, not concentration at home. It cautions, however, that the long-run inefficiency from indiscriminately replicating supply chains would be enormous, since duplicating a quarter of all multinational activity could add annual costs above 2 per cent of world GDP. The leader pairs dual sourcing with longer-term contracts, and a 2026 analysis says Morocco's fertiliser exports are increasingly tied to long-term commercial relationships and forward supply agreements, limiting its ability to redirect supply quickly to higher-risk markets without coordinated intervention.

cards.question: The car industry is copying Tesla by moving towards _____, a leader says, in which a firm controls everything from nickel mining to chip design.
cards.abstract:
Vertical integration is, in a leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022, a strategy in which a company controls everything from nickel mining to chip design. The leader says the car industry is moving towards it by copying Elon Musk's Tesla. It presents this as one way in which the industries under most pressure are reinventing their business models, encouraged by governments that from Europe to India are keen on strategic autonomy. Its wider argument is that some lean supply chains are not as good value as they appear, because when they break the bill can be crippling. As evidence it says that chip shortages have stalled car production and that carmakers' cashflows have dropped by 80 per cent year on year.

It also says the world relies on China for the processed lithium used in batteries, a point it makes in discussing the dependency on autocracies that the single-minded pursuit of cost advantage has produced. A 2025 article in Foreign Affairs says administration officials acknowledge that they made concessions on semiconductor export controls in return for China easing restrictions on rare-earth minerals that were crippling the US auto industry, and Lecture 1 repeats the point. A Lecture 4 slide says that in a world of weaponised interdependence power comes from controlling technological stacks, systems of interconnected layers running from foundational technologies to advanced applications. Its example layers run from rare earths through manufacturing equipment and high-precision manufacturing to chip design and AI, a span that can be set beside the leader's range from nickel mining to chip design, though neither text draws the comparison. A 2026 essay adds that China could further restrict the rare earths used in US and European weapons systems and high-end technologies, or leverage its control over the global electric vehicle, solar and wind industries.

cards.question: A leader says that 69 per cent of multinational investment now takes the form of _____ by subsidiaries, a pattern that echoes the 1930s response to nationalism.
cards.abstract:
Local reinvestment is the pattern in which multinational investment comes from local subsidiaries reinvesting locally, rather than from parent firms sending capital across borders. A leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022 says the pattern of multinational investment has been inverted, with 69 per cent now from local subsidiaries reinvesting locally. It places this directly after the build-up in precautionary inventories, which it calls one indication that companies are shifting from efficiency to resilience. The leader says this echoes the 1930s, when global firms responded to nationalism by making subsidiaries abroad more self-sufficient. An earlier paragraph on the years after the Berlin Wall fell says that companies located production where costs were lowest and investors deployed capital where returns were highest.

In the 2010s, it adds, many bosses postponed big decisions on investing abroad, as just-in-time gave way to wait-and-see. Other changes in its account include Taiwan's electronics assemblers cutting their share of assets in China from 50 per cent to 35 per cent since 2017, and global firms shifting from China into Vietnam. The leader warns that the pursuit of security could morph into rampant protectionism and industrial subsidies, and that duplicating a quarter of all multinational activity could add annual costs above 2 per cent of world GDP. A Lecture 1 slide notes that the arenas where power is exercised are used not only by nation states but also by multinational corporations. A 2025 article in Foreign Affairs warns that, without clear and enforceable limits on US coercion, the most dominant US-based multinational firms, such as Google, will find themselves trapped in the no man's land of a new war zone.

cards.question: In a leader's count, _____ in goods with leading market shares over 10 per cent and few substitutes amount to only about a tenth of global trade, so it urges targeted diversification.
cards.abstract:
Autocracies' chokepoints are, in a leader in The Economist of 16 June 2022, exports of goods in which autocracies have a leading market share of over 10 per cent and for which substitutes are hard to find. The leader says that the choke-points autocracies control amount to only about a tenth of global trade. It reaches this figure in its closing section, headed 'The trouble with safe spaces', after arguing that governments and firms must remember that resilience comes from diversification, not concentration at home. Its earlier worry is that the single-minded pursuit of cost advantage has led to a dependency on autocracies that abuse human rights and use trade as a means of coercion. It says autocracies account for a third of world GDP, and that China has a trade footprint seven times as big as Russia's, with the world relying on it for goods from active pharmaceutical ingredients to the processed lithium used in batteries.

The leader's answer is to require firms to diversify their suppliers in these areas and to let the market adapt. It fears that a reasonable pursuit of security will morph into rampant protectionism, jobs schemes and hundreds of billions of dollars of industrial subsidies, and it calls living in a subsidised bunker an unreasonable goal. Lecture 1 says control over strategic chokeholds is, with the ability to weaponise global interdependence, as vital a marker of national power as GDP or the size of the military. A Lecture 3 slide lists geographic chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Taiwan Strait, and notes limits to interdependence but also limits to the use of chokepoints, naming alternatives and pipelines. A 2026 essay says that potential bottlenecks are innumerable, existing not only in physical waterways but also in the supply chains for weapons, food, health care and basic technology, whereas the leader's count covers only goods that autocracies lead in and that are hard to substitute.

cards.question: An article on global development argues that, oil exporters aside, _____ is the rule, since about 95 per cent of economies reaching high-income status passed through a period of heavy manufacturing.
cards.abstract:
The article by Oks and Williams rests on the premise of no development without industrialisation, meaning that it knows of no widely replicable strategy to turn a country from poor to rich that does not involve an economy becoming highly industrialised. It says that despite attempts to find alternative models, the growth of manufacturing in recent decades has been overwhelmingly concentrated in East Asia, particularly in China. Across Latin America, South Asia, the Middle East and sub-Saharan Africa, it says, economies have meanwhile experienced simultaneous deagrarianisation and deindustrialisation, especially in the years after 1980. The article notes that the move from agrarian stasis to industrial growth is central to many radically different theories of development, among them Marx's account of social progress, Rostow's modernisation theory and the national developmentalism of Kaldor and Prebisch. It adds that very few economies have gone from poor to rich without a large manufacturing share of both employment and GDP, and that about 95 per cent of those reaching high-income status passed through such a period.

It quotes Justin Yifu Lin, the World Bank's former chief economist, who gives the verdict that except for a few oil-exporting countries no country has ever got rich without industrialising first. The authors call the oil exporters, such as Norway, Saudi Arabia and other Persian Gulf autocracies, quite exceptional, and say that the resource path offers far more failures, among them Iraq, Mozambique and the Congo, than triumphs like Norway's or even middling successes like Gabon and Botswana. They conclude that for most of the world there is no real path to development that does not run through manufacturing. In their view most emerging markets have grown over recent decades, but dependence on services and commodity exports has not made them rich. The article ends by calling industrialisation at once necessary and impossible in the poor world, particularly in Africa, and says that Western elites do not have an answer.

The article treats oil exporters like Norway and Saudi Arabia as exceptions to the rule of _____, since the resource path offers far more failures, such as Iraq and the Congo.

cards.question: Unlike agriculture or services, formal manufacturing firms are said to show increasing returns to labour and _____ in productivity between rich and poor nations, a catching-up that holds whatever other conditions apply.
cards.abstract:
The article lists unconditional convergence among the qualities that make manufacturing special, saying that formal manufacturing firms show an 'unconditional' convergence in labour productivity between rich and poor nations. It introduces the idea by asking what is so special about manufacturing, and answers that Kaldor, and later Dani Rodrik, offered sets of stylised facts about the sector's growth-pulling qualities. Of these facts three are of particular note, and the first is that manufacturing has productivity dynamics that other sectors do not. Unlike agriculture or services, the article says, formal manufacturing firms show increasing returns on each marginal unit of labour as well as this unconditional convergence. A note to that passage points to a 2013 article by Rodrik, titled 'Unconditional Convergence in Manufacturing', in the Quarterly Journal of Economics.

The second quality is that manufactured goods are tradable, so manufacturing growth has no automatic limits, unlike services, which are self-limiting, or primary commodities, which face ecological restraints. The third is that manufacturing can absorb large amounts of labour, including relatively unskilled labour, into high-productivity work, which the article says services, agriculture, finance and mining have never been able to do. The article applies the idea to Bangladesh, whose garment success sits alongside manufacturing dominated by small informal firms, where it says unconditional productivity convergence usually does not apply. It adds that this was not the case in China or South Korea, and that diversification into higher-value-added goods has proven elusive, since in 2019 just 2 per cent of Bangladesh's manufactured exports were classed as medium- or high-tech. Elsewhere it argues that commodities could never take the place of manufacturing in absorbing large numbers of low- and high-skilled workers at decent wages, and that most service work offers none of manufacturing's growth-pulling features.

cards.question: An American-sponsored modernisation theory made the industrial moment known as _____ the make-or-break step in a multistage account of development, ironically in a book subtitled A Non-Communist Manifesto.
cards.abstract:
Rostow's take-off is the industrial 'takeoff' that the article says the American-sponsored modernisation theory of Walt Rostow treated as the make-or-break moment within a multistage account of economic development. The article says he laid out the theory in his book Stages of Economic Growth, and it calls the case ironic because the book was subtitled A Non-Communist Manifesto. It sets the theory beside others in which the move from agrarian stasis to industrial growth is central, among them Marxian schemata of societal progress that saw manufacturing as a precondition for an industrial proletariat. Kaldor and Prebisch, whose work the article says enjoyed great popularity in developing countries in the middle decades of the last century, also emphasised industrially oriented national developmentalism. The authors present all of this as the background to their own judgment about the fundamental role that manufacturing plays in economic development.

The article ties the theory to the golden age, saying that the strong performances of those years allowed Rostow to predict to John F. Kennedy in 1961 that several nations would 'attain self-sustaining growth by 1970'. His list had Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, India, the Philippines, Taiwan, Turkey and Greece, with Egypt, Iran, Iraq and Pakistan added as 'possibly'. With growth so evident, the article says, everything seemed to be going according to plan, and almost anything seemed possible. It describes the years from about 1950 to 1980 as a boom of an intensity and duration never seen before or after, whose optimism is now hard to recall. Later it says premature deindustrialisation was contrary to what the economists of the golden age had predicted, and not just the more hubristic ones like Rostow, as though fruit was rotting before it even ripened.

cards.question: A study of countries that grew rich found that reaching a _____ of 18–20 per cent has been almost sufficient and absolutely necessary for high-income status, according to an article on global development.
cards.abstract:
Manufacturing employment share is one of two percentages, alongside the manufacturing share of GDP, that the article uses to show that very few economies have gone from poor to rich without a large manufacturing sector. It says about 95 per cent of economies that have reached high-income status passed through a period of high manufacturing concentration. To back this it quotes one study of the historical trajectories of high-income countries, which found that a manufacturing employment share of 18–20 per cent has been 'almost sufficient and absolutely necessary' for achieving high-income status. A note to that passage cites a 2014 Asian Development Bank working paper whose title says that manufacturing matters, but it is the jobs that count. The article's third reason for manufacturing's special place is that it can absorb large amounts of labour, including relatively unskilled labour, into high-productivity work.

Because manufacturing employment is typically a more useful measure of industrialisation than output, the article uses it to date peaks, which came in Brazil in 1986, India in 2002, Colombia in 1970, Mexico in 1980, Peru in 1971, Indonesia in 2001, Ghana in 1978 and Nigeria in 1982. It says all these peaks came at rates of manufacturing employment and per capita GDP significantly below those of Western nations in their peak years of manufacturing. Latin American countries, it says, were hit most severely, with nearly no floor for industrial decline, while in many Asian countries the situation was more akin to a long plateau. Many African countries lost their manufacturing bases at such a low level of industrialisation, it adds, that they can hardly be said to have industrialised at all. The authors call this premature deindustrialisation, and say that in places like Brazil or India it coexisted with a still overwhelming degree of backwardness and poverty, leaving industrialisation's historical task undone.

cards.question: Measured at $2.15 a day, _____ is about 45 per cent of the fall in extreme poverty since 1981, but at $10 a day it reaches 70 per cent, the article says.
cards.abstract:
China's share of poverty reduction is the proportion of the global fall in poverty since 1981 that the article attributes to gains inside one country. The article says China's gains have contributed about 45 per cent of the total reduction in the extreme-poverty metric since 1981. At $5 a day, it says, China is responsible for nearly 60 per cent of total gains, and at $10 a day for a full 70 per cent of global poverty reduction since 1981. It stresses that $10 a day is several dollars above the poverty threshold for upper-middle-income countries, yet translates to an annual income of just $3,650. The authors argue that at higher levels of income, more representative of a durable entrance into middle-income status, China's contribution is even stronger.

They call it striking, given the optimism about global poverty reduction in the 21st century, how much of the progress has come from a single powerhouse, the People's Republic of China, and say that since 1980 the lion's share of actual development and poverty reduction has occurred there and in smaller East Asian economies such as South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong. Behind the shares they report that Chinese per capita GDP grew sixfold between 1981 and 2018, and that the proportion earning under $2.15 a day fell from 92 per cent to just 0.14 per cent over four decades. Median incomes show the gap, they say: China's rural median rose ninefold between 1981 and 2019, India's rural median doubled between 1983 and 2019, and in some countries, such as Kenya, Argentina and the Ivory Coast, median income has declined since World Bank measurement began. The authors conclude that Asian success has obscured a bleaker picture in the rest of the world. An Economist article in the course readings says that the efficiency-driven globalisation after 1989 helped lift 1 billion people out of extreme poverty as the emerging world, including China, industrialised.

cards.question: Gains in industrialisation and income across East Asia have statistically offset stagnation almost everywhere else, a _____ that the article says is partly due to East Asia displacing other countries' manufacturing bases.
cards.abstract:
Statistical compensation is the article's name for the way in which industrialisation, development and massive income growth in East Asia have statistically 'compensated' for stagnation almost everywhere else. It adds that East Asian industrialisation was partly responsible for the loss of other countries' manufacturing bases. Incomes did rise in most of the poor world, the article says, mainly on account of the 2000–15 commodity supercycle, driven in part by explosive growth in demand from the Chinese market. It calls it ironic that this demand helped lock emerging markets into low-tech, undiversified export profiles, and it concludes that Asian success has obscured a bleaker picture in the rest of the world. Most emerging markets, it adds, have not found an engine of durable growth comparable to manufacturing, and most developing countries are in a worse structural position than a few decades ago.

The authors say they aim to show that the prognosis for the poor world is much worse than the standard picture, which they describe as preoccupied with a purely quantitative account. They point out that China alone accounts for about 45 per cent of the fall in the extreme-poverty metric since 1981, and 70 per cent of the fall at $10 a day. Income growth in the poor world outside China, they say, looks weaker still once one considers how much came from the 2000–15 commodities boom, and thus indirectly from Chinese growth. A reading on fragile states notes that when the Millennium Development Goals ended in 2015, poverty was increasingly concentrated in the most fragile countries. Looking ahead, the article says that as East Asian populations decline the compensation effect in poverty statistics will no longer hold, and because there has been so little real economic progress in sub-Saharan Africa, rapid population growth there will spell a grim several decades for poverty reduction.

cards.question: Critics call the _____, the World Bank's 'extreme poverty' threshold at 2017 purchasing-power-adjusted prices, far too low to provide for sustenance or normal human health outcomes.
cards.abstract:
The $2.15-a-day line is the 'extreme poverty' metric that the article says was promoted by the World Bank. The article says that in the first two decades of the 21st century, a period of tremendous optimism about the poor world, poverty on this measure was in speedy decline. It records that the Bank announced in October 2022 that progress in reducing extreme poverty had ground to a halt, with the prognosis for the next few years uncertain. The authors say that even in its heyday the triumphal narrative around global development had an uncertain relationship with reality. They trace some flaws to statistical issues, such as troubled calculations around inflation and purchasing power parity, especially urban-rural price differentials, which they say significantly undercount the global poor.

Other problems are more subjective, the article says, since many have criticised the threshold, set at 2017 purchasing-power-adjusted prices, as far too low to provide for sustenance or normal human health outcomes. Such a low line, the critics argue, cannot measure anything meaningful about real graduation from poverty, because it was designed to reflect who would be poorest in countries like Mali or Afghanistan and not in slightly richer ones like Angola or Pakistan. The authors nonetheless use the line themselves, noting that in China the share of people earning under $2.15 a day fell from 92 per cent to just 0.14 per cent over four decades. They add that China's gains account for about 45 per cent of the fall in extreme poverty since 1981, but 70 per cent at $10 a day, an annual income of just $3,650. A reading on fragile states says the Millennium Development Goals aimed to end extreme poverty and that, when they concluded in 2015, poverty was increasingly concentrated in the most fragile countries.

cards.question: Driven in part by explosive growth in Chinese demand, the _____ of 2000–15 raised incomes across much of the poor world while ironically locking emerging markets into low-tech, undiversified export profiles.
cards.abstract:
The commodity supercycle of 2000–15 is the long boom in commodity markets that the article says was driven in part by explosive growth in demand from the Chinese market. The article says that incomes rose in most of the poor world mainly on account of it, yet ironically it helped lock emerging markets into low-tech, undiversified export profiles. It says hot commodities markets in those years allowed Latin American, Southeast Asian and some African nations to increase incomes and reduce poverty. Those gains depended on the knock-on effects of Chinese growth and masked a structural weakening of development potential, so the type of takeoff seen in China is more out of reach than a few decades ago. The article uses the same term for an earlier boom, saying that the rapid industrial expansion of the golden age was underwritten by an upswing in the commodities supercycle.

In boom periods like 2000–15 the extractive model could prove hugely lucrative, the article says, with exporters such as Ecuador, Bolivia and Brazil able to support 'Pink Tide' governments that married resource extraction to redistribution. In less functional regimes, such as Nigeria or Angola, revenue from resource exports was absorbed almost entirely by corrupt rentier elites and siphoned out of the country. The cycle turned in 2014–15, with Chinese growth slowing and oil prices tumbling as American fracking surged, and the extractive model then proved its fragility. The Pink Tide era ended chaotically, budget crises crimped governments in Iraq and Nigeria in their battles with Islamist insurgents, and Brazil's poverty rate was higher in 2019 than in 2014. Looking ahead, the authors say that with ageing populations in the United States and Europe and a Chinese economy apparently entering a low-growth equilibrium, another global commodities boom to rescue poor economies seems distant.

cards.question: Though measures of poverty and hunger were far higher than today, the years from about 1950 to 1980 stand in retrospect as the _____, a boom of unmatched intensity and duration.
cards.abstract:
The golden age of development is the article's name for the period lasting roughly from 1950 to 1980. The article finds it ironic, because measures of poverty, hunger and all varieties of misery were far higher then than they are today. It says the global economy underwent a boom of an intensity and duration never seen before or after, while the capitalist West had its trente glorieuses and the Soviet bloc enjoyed relative peace and consumer surplus. For poor countries this meant three decades of vigorous growth, with rapid industrial expansion underwritten by an upswing in the commodities supercycle. An international financial regime built on the Bretton Woods model limited capital mobility and allowed a degree of financial stability, which helped emerging markets pursue aggressive development strategies without the boom-bust dynamics that later became common.

Citing Dani Rodrik, the article says that in countries including Brazil, Mexico, Iran and Kenya average growth exceeded 2.5 per cent per capita per year in 1945–75, doubling incomes roughly every three decades. An optimistic, state-centred national developmentalism was in vogue, represented by Sukarno, Nasser, Nkrumah and Nehru, who sought not just to match the West but in many ways to exceed it. Growth in the richer economies of the poor world was so strong that, had Brazil kept its 1970–75 rate for 25 more years, it would have been richer than France and the United Kingdom by 2000. Even poorer nations were ambitious, the article says, and the Ivory Coast, growing 9 per cent a year in the 1960s, was a poster child, with Lyndon Johnson telling doubters in 1967 to look at it. The article then says the system supporting this growth was under serious strain by the 1970s, since Bretton Woods effectively died in 1971–72 and energy crises struck in 1973 and 1979.

cards.question: Interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve in 1979–81, the _____, brought rich countries lower inflation and severe recession and sent the prices of lumber, copper, coffee and sugar tumbling.
cards.abstract:
The Volcker shock is the name the article gives to the Federal Reserve's interest-rate hikes of 1979–81. The article places it at the end of a series of strains on the system that had supported the golden age: the effective death of Bretton Woods in 1971–72, the energy crises of 1973 and 1979 and the long economic doldrums in the West. It says the energy crises contributed to the Great Inflation of the 1970s, although their effects in poor countries were uneven and petroleum exporters were certainly not badly hurt. In the rich world, the article says, the post-Volcker moment meant lower inflation, severe recession and a jump in unemployment, with a concomitant decline in commodity prices. Between 1979 and 1982 the average price of lumber fell by 40 per cent, copper by 25 per cent, coffee by more than 20 per cent and sugar by about 10 per cent.

The pain in the poor world was arguably much greater, it says, because the booming commodity cycle met its chaotic death and dozens of economies screeched to a halt. Expansionary fiscal programmes built on the assumption of strong growth fell into crisis, and higher borrowing rates significantly increased the cost of servicing dollar-denominated debts. Brazil is called paradigmatic, since its real per capita GDP rose by more than 140 per cent from 1960 to 1980 but by less than 20 per cent from 1980 to 2000. Guatemala's per capita GDP in 2018 was only 20 per cent above its 1978 level and the Ivory Coast's only 16 per cent above, while in several countries, including Haiti and Niger, output was significantly lower than 40 years earlier. The article sums up the 20 years that the shock inaugurated as two lost decades for development, with incessant crisis replacing stable growth.

cards.question: Prolonged stagnation in Mexico, Brazil and Argentina during the Latin American _____ is listed beside the Shining Path insurgency in Peru and civil wars in Nicaragua, Guatemala and El Salvador.
cards.abstract:
The década perdida is the Latin American 'lost decade' that the article lists among the events of the two lost decades inaugurated by the Volcker shock. The article says the 20 years that the shock inaugurated can be summarised as two lost decades for development, with incessant crisis replacing stable growth. Across the poor world, it says, deep recessions led to fiscal insolvency, social and political collapse and massive bloodletting. In the Western Hemisphere the década perdida ushered in prolonged stagnation in Mexico, Brazil and Argentina. The same list has severe economic crisis in Peru, which contributed to the rise of the Shining Path insurgency, civil wars in Nicaragua, Guatemala and El Salvador, and escalating conflict in Colombia between drug cartels, leftist insurgents and the state.

The article gives Brazil as the paradigm, with real per capita GDP up by more than 140 per cent from 1960 to 1980 but by less than 20 per cent from 1980 to 2000. Beyond Latin America the list includes the traumatic 'shock therapy' applied to postcommunist Russia, the economic 'primitivization' of Mongolia, where industrial workers returned to herding, the genocide in Rwanda, the collapse of Mobutu's state in the Congo, and wars in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Africa was hit worst, it says, with a death toll stretching well into the millions, and Giovanni Arrighi dubbed it the African Tragedy. Most poor states emerged from the two decades severely weakened, and the bold national developmentalism of earlier decades had been discredited by economic contraction and declining living standards. The article adds that the central structural transformation of the 1980–2000 period was of a deeper and more damaging nature than these crises, namely the unexpected arrival of deindustrialisation in the poor world.

cards.question: Required by the IMF for debt relief and championed independently by enthusiastic liberalisers, _____ programmes further diminished state capacity through privatisations, deregulation and government layoffs in poor countries.
cards.abstract:
Structural adjustment programmes, in the article's account, were the measures that the IMF required for debt relief in the poor world. The article adds that enthusiastic liberalisers such as Hernando de Soto advocated such programmes independently. It says they further diminished state capacity through privatisations, deregulation and government layoffs. Its word 'further' marks them as an addition to the withdrawal of expansionary fiscal regimes and to internal conflicts that moved the focus of government activity elsewhere. A separate section lists the withdrawal of state agricultural subsidies and tariffs during the crises of 1980–2000 among the strains on small farmers, though it does not link that step to the programmes by name.

In desperation, the article says, many poor-world governments also liberalised their capital accounts to spur foreign investment, which increased volatility and culminated in financial crises in Mexico in 1994, various Asian economies in 1997 and Russia in 1998. A reading on globalisation describes a similar opening of finance in terms of outside pressure, saying that, pushed by the United States and bodies such as the IMF and the OECD, countries freed up vast quantities of short-term finance to cross borders. A Lecture 4 slide gives the Washington consensus policies as an example of the corner of Rodrik's trilemma that pairs national sovereignty with globalisation and limits democracy, a phrase the article does not use. The article says all these reforms, despite the support of Western economists and acolytes like de Soto or Anatoly Chubais, did little to improve growth fundamentals and instead gave the poor world hollowed-out states for the new century. Among its proposals is a new Bretton Woods-style framework for regulating international monetary flows, meant to prevent the boom-bust cycles that have scarred many emerging markets and to return some measure of autonomy over economic policy to poor-world policymakers.

cards.question: In the worst-hit poor countries, such as Somalia after its 1990s collapse, what little remained of government was described as _____, with core functions handed to the international humanitarian complex.
cards.answer: Government by means of the aid industry
cards.abstract:
Government by means of the aid industry is a phrase the article borrows from the Nigerien historian Rahmane Idrissa for a state that has surrendered core governmental functions to the international humanitarian complex. The article places it after two lost decades that followed the Volcker shock, which left most poor states severely weakened and discredited the bold national developmentalism of earlier years. It says the structural adjustment programmes that the IMF required for debt relief diminished state capacity through privatisations, deregulation and layoffs, and that liberalised capital accounts then ended in crises in Mexico in 1994, Asia in 1997 and Russia in 1998. The authors argue that these reforms did little to improve growth fundamentals and instead gave the poor world hollowed-out states, many with public sectors too desiccated to manage their societies. In the worst-hit places, such as Somalia, where state collapse in the 1990s led to the return of customary law, the article says what little remained of government can be described in this way.

It says the Congo, Somalia and the Central African Republic, however brutal the regimes of Mobutu, Siad Barre and Bokassa, were politically sovereign a few decades ago and governed by semi-functional regimes. Today, it says, they are wards of external institutions, from African Union forces holding Mogadishu against al-Shabaab and French troops in the Sahel to unaccountable if well-intentioned Western humanitarian bodies. It adds that Western development experts, in Idrissa's words, ask not how to strengthen the state but how to further debilitate it, and focus on small-scale interventions such as randomised controlled trials run by non-governmental organisations and research teams. Its own agenda for poor countries includes conscious attempts to rebuild state capacity and to reduce the outsourcing of governance to foreign institutions. A set reading on humanitarian diplomacy says the public image of humanitarian action is of universal principles regardless of political interests, yet neutrality has always been questioned because of hidden political interests.
cards.answerText: Government by means of the aid industry

cards.question: Brazil's manufacturing employment peaked in 1986 and India's in 2002, at incomes far below Western nations at their peaks, a pattern an economist named _____, as though fruit rotted before ripening.
cards.abstract:
Premature deindustrialisation is the name the economist Dani Rodrik gives to the loss of manufacturing in poor countries at levels of employment and income well below those Western nations reached at their peaks. The article calls the arrival of deindustrialisation in the poor world the central structural transformation of the years from 1980 to 2000, and says it was unexpected. Its opening adds that across Latin America, South Asia, the Middle East and sub-Saharan Africa, economies saw simultaneous deagrarianisation and deindustrialisation, especially in the years after 1980. After 1980, it says, poor countries suffered a relative deindustrialisation as intense as that of advanced economies, and often more so, owing to the same primary cause, the emergence of the Chinese industrial behemoth. Manufacturing employment peaked in Brazil in 1986, India in 2002, Mexico in 1980 and Nigeria in 1982, among other cases, all at incomes below those of Western nations at their peaks.

It treats manufacturing employment as typically a more useful measure than output, and says Latin America was hit most severely, while many African countries lost their manufacturing bases at so low a level that they can hardly be said to have industrialised. It adds that Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, knocked off course by the 1997 Asian financial crisis, have experienced premature deindustrialisation of varying degrees of intensity. Its occurrence was contrary to what the economists of the golden age of development had predicted, it says, as though fruit was rotting before it even ripened. In the West, it argues, deindustrialisation could be fitted into a story of evolution into affluence, but no such story could be told for Brazil or India, where it coexisted with overwhelming backwardness and poverty. A set reading says that trade with China and other low-wage countries accelerated the decline of manufacturing employment in the developed world, and a Lecture 4 slide lists the difficulty of industrialising among reasons for WTO reform.

cards.question: From the 1970s, costly fertiliser inputs, cash-crop specialisation and withdrawn state subsidies pushed small farmers into debt and into cities, an accelerating process the article calls _____ after 1980.
cards.abstract:
Deagrarianisation is the decline of farming and of the rural share of a population, a process the article says accelerated across the poor world after 1980. The rural share of populations had been falling everywhere since the Second World War, it says, largely because agrarian reforms raised farm productivity, through land reform in some countries and Green Revolution techniques in others. Even so, farming remained the occupation of most of the world's population until late in the 20th century, and in 1970 80 per cent of Indians and 83 per cent of Indonesians lived in rural areas. From the 1970s, it says, post-Green Revolution farming demanded inputs such as artificial fertiliser that many could not afford, and national agricultures were pushed toward cash crops chosen for comparative advantage. The withdrawal of state agricultural subsidies and tariffs during the crises of 1980 to 2000, and desertification and soil degradation in places such as Southeast Africa and Haiti, added further strain.

Many small farmers were forced into insurmountable debt, the article says, leading to an epidemic of suicide among Indian farmers, while others took seasonal city jobs to supplement their farm incomes. The result was mass migration into urban centres, with the article giving urban population increases between 1980 and 2010 of 24 per cent in East Asia and the Pacific and 14 per cent in sub-Saharan Africa. China was the single biggest contributor to global deagrarianisation, it adds, but about 75 per cent of global urbanisation in those years took place elsewhere, and Lagos grew from 1.4 million people in 1970 to 13.9 million in 2022. Simultaneous deagrarianisation and deindustrialisation, amid massive population growth, produced in its words a plethora of unoccupied labourers in slum cities such as Karachi, Lima, Jakarta, Lagos and Cairo. It expects droughts, floods and crop failures to intensify deagrarianisation, and a 2026 reading on the Sahel says that when input prices rise or credit tightens, fertiliser use declines, especially in cash-constrained systems.

cards.question: Brazil was ranked 26th most economically complex nation in 2000, near Poland and Mexico, but 60th twenty years later, below Kyrgyzstan, a speedy slide the article calls _____ of its economy.
cards.abstract:
Decomplexification is the article's word for an economy becoming less economically complex as higher-end products give way to raw commodities, which it argues happened in Brazil. Its opening says that most developing countries are in a worse structural position than a few decades ago, less economically complex and more socially unstable. As Brazil deindustrialised, vehicle parts, machinery and electronics took diminished roles in its exports and were gradually replaced by a surging trade in iron and oil. In 1995 iron ore made up 3.8 per cent of Brazilian exports and crude petroleum 0.1 per cent, but by 2020 they made up 10.8 per cent and 8.1 per cent, while industrial machinery fell from 7.1 per cent to 3 per cent. Oil rents rose from 0.1 per cent of Brazil's GDP in 1970 to 2.4 per cent by 2008, and mineral rents from 0.5 per cent to 1.9 per cent.

This, the article says, resulted in a speedy decomplexification of the Brazilian economy, with extractive rentierism becoming increasingly central. In 2000 Brazil was assessed as the 26th most economically complex nation in the world, near Poland and Mexico, but 20 years later it had fallen to 60th, lower than Kyrgyzstan and North Macedonia. The same process of decomplexification and export reprimarisation occurred, it says, in other prematurely deindustrialising economies such as Ukraine, Ecuador, Argentina, Mongolia and Kazakhstan. For economies that never escaped middle-income status, such as Mexico, Brazil, Egypt and Russia, it describes stagnation at a middling income with a decomplexifying economy dependent on commodities. The article's notes cite the Harvard Atlas of Economic Complexity for what Brazil exported and for its ranking, and a Lecture 1 slide on trading partners names the Atlas of Economic Complexity as the source of its figure, which is based on United Nations trade data.

cards.question: With industry and agriculture both in relative decline, many postindustrial economies reverted to raw commodity exports, which the article calls _____, especially after global demand revived in the mid-1990s with China's takeoff.
cards.abstract:
Reprimarisation is the article's term for the export profile of an economy that, with industry and agriculture both in relative decline, reverts to raw commodity exports. It says many postindustrial economies took this path, especially after global commodity demand began to pick up again in the mid-1990s with the Chinese takeoff. Its opening argues that the 2000 to 2015 commodity supercycle, driven in part by Chinese demand, ironically helped lock emerging markets into low-tech, undiversified export profiles. Brazil is the main example, with higher-end products giving way to iron and oil, and the article says the same decomplexification and export reprimarisation occurred in Ukraine, Ecuador, Argentina, Mongolia and Kazakhstan. A Lecture 1 figure shows that between 1995 and 2022 Asia displaced Europe as the main trading partner for most countries in the Global South, in both imports and exports.

In boom years the extractive model could prove lucrative, and resource exporters such as Ecuador, Bolivia and Brazil supported 'Pink Tide' governments that combined extraction with redistribution and significantly reduced poverty. In less functional regimes such as Nigeria or Angola, it says, resource revenue was absorbed almost entirely by corrupt rentier elites and siphoned out of the country. When the cycle turned in 2014 and 2015, with Chinese growth slowing and oil prices tumbling, the extractive model proved fragile and a wave of global political instability followed. Companies such as Petrobras, Gazprom and NNPC, it adds, could never absorb a significant share of their countries' labour forces, so commodities could not take the place of manufacturing in employing large numbers at decent wages. The article says the resource path offers far more failures, such as Iraq, Mozambique and the Congo, than Norwegian-style triumphs, and sees a new global commodities boom to rescue poor economies as a distant prospect.

cards.question: In Arabic, the listless unemployed youth of poor-world cities are called _____, 'the men who lean against walls', and the article sees them as ideal destabilisers of Third World societies.
cards.abstract:
Hayateen is the Arabic word for the listless youth of poor-world cities, whom the article glosses as 'the men who lean against walls'. It places them within what it calls mass underemployment, saying informal, casual and irregular work is no cure for unemployment because the line between a casually employed jobber and an unemployed person is very thin. An abundance of cheap labour, with too many workers and far too few good jobs, leads to unproductive uses of it, it says, such as middle-class Pakistani families routinely affording several domestic servants. Competition for formal jobs is fierce, and in 2015 the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh put out a notice for 368 clerical jobs and received 2.3 million applications. The article blames simultaneous deindustrialisation and deagrarianisation, amid massive population growth, for a plethora of unoccupied labourers in slum cities such as Karachi, Lima, Jakarta, Lagos and Cairo.

Unoccupied and discontented, it says, hayateen are the ideal destabilisers of Third World societies, and the link between youth bulges, high youth unemployment and unrest has been studied for decades. At the extreme, such youths became foot soldiers for criminal or insurgent groups, among them MS-13, the narco groups of Mexico and Colombia, gangs in Haiti, Boko Haram and the Islamic State. More mundanely, they supply manpower for criminal violence and urban rioting, as in the sozaboy subcultures of northern Nigeria or South Africa's 'Zuma riots'. The article warns that, at its worst, the growing number of hayateen will add to the appeal of violent groups such as Boko Haram and al-Shabaab, though it adds that large youth populations are not bad in themselves. A Lecture 3 slide of potential answers on the Sahel says economic pressures can erode public trust in government and raise opportunities for recruitment by armed groups, and a reading on fragile states says connectivity is exploited by groups such as Al Qaeda to recruit foreign fighters.

cards.question: Money sent home by emigrants rose from about 0.5 per cent of El Salvador's GDP in 1976 to 24.1 per cent in 2020, an example of _____ that the article pairs with Kerala.
cards.abstract:
Remittances as lifelines describes how, in the article's words, the money that expatriate workers send home became a lifeline for entire economies in the age of migration after 1980. The article calls migration the main 'release valve' for the worsening economic situations of poor countries, often internal and seasonal, as with rural Indians who periodically work in urban construction. As national prospects dimmed, it says, migration increasingly became international: between 1980 and 2000 the number of international migrants swelled by 83 per cent, to 172 million, against 30 per cent between 1960 and 1980. By 2015 the total had reached nearly 250 million, much of it moving to countries well-off only relative to dysfunctional neighbours, such as Haitians in the Dominican Republic or Afghans in Iran. In 1976 El Salvador received about 0.5 per cent of its GDP from remittances, and by 2020 the figure was 24.1 per cent, overwhelmingly from the large Salvadoran diaspora in the United States.

The article says the same happened in Kerala, India's most advanced state by most measures of health and wellness, whose economic model it says now depends largely on exporting young men to indentured servitude in the Persian Gulf. It adds that this population transfer leaves Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar with the most heavily male populations in the world, while Kerala is the only large Indian state with more women than men. Remittances also form large and growing shares of the economies of the Philippines, Nepal, Uzbekistan, Guatemala, Jamaica and Kosovo, with the note citing World Bank data. Looking ahead, the article says emigration, even when risky, is a logical calculation for a young person in Ibadan or Luanda with no real opportunity, and that demand for migration will not fall without real global development. It expects wealthier governments to keep trying to reduce the supply of migration opportunities, and a Lecture 4 slide lists tariffs to stop Mexican migration among its examples of economic diplomacy.

cards.question: The classic model in which manufacturing spreads to any labour-abundant economy that can make goods more cheaply, forming an international queue, is called the _____ model, which the article doubts still holds.
cards.abstract:
The flying geese model, the article says, is the classic picture of industrialisation in which manufacturing spreads to any labour-abundant economy where goods can be made more cheaply. It implies an international queue for industrialisation, but the article argues that the model may no longer hold. As the economist Dani Rodrik and others have pointed out, it says, each wave of industrialisation has been weaker than the last, and its note cites a May 2022 report he wrote for the Brookings Institution. The first possible factor it names is heightened global competition, with countries today having less control over their home markets than America in the 19th century, Japan in the 1950s or China in the 1990s. The second is a shift in demand, linked to a decline in global growth, wealth inequality and demographic change in rich countries, which leaves a smaller consumer demand impulse.

The third, perhaps the most important, is the decline of manufacturing labour intensity due to labour-saving automation, which may accelerate if entrepreneurs succeed in building 'sewbots' and other machines. The article adds that China's own rise cut into others' factories, since the Chinese industrial behemoth displaced Mexican and Iranian workers as fiercely as American or French ones. It argues that poor societies today differ from earlier late industrialisers such as South Korea in 1960 or China in 1980, which were largely agrarian and combined high state capacity at low incomes with coherent developmental elites. On rules, it says WTO agreements from TRIPS to TRIMS ban or limit strategies used by successful industrialisers, and a Lecture 4 slide gives the difficulty of industrialising for both emerging and advanced economies as a reason for WTO reform. A Lecture 1 slide comparing GDP per capita with that of the Netherlands in 1990 and 2023 says some parts of the Global South, particularly in Asia, are catching up with western countries, while countries in the Middle East and Africa are falling further behind.

The article contrasts today's poor societies with South Korea in 1960 and China in 1980, largely agrarian, with high state capacity and coherent elites, when it doubts the _____ model still holds.

cards.question: Once-thriving economies such as Argentina or Turkey, and now perhaps Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia after 1997, risk relative stagnation at a middling level of income, the _____ the article describes.
cards.abstract:
The middle-income trap, in the article's usage, is relative stagnation at a middling level of income, a fate it associates with once-thriving economies like Argentina or Turkey. It says the challenge for relative success stories such as Bangladesh is not necessarily impoverishment but this trap. Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable, it says, because the 1997 Asian financial crisis knocked them off a path roughly on par with Chinese growth and they have since seen premature deindustrialisation of varying intensity. Escaping would require a change like that of Korean elites in the 1980s and 1990s, who shifted from low-skill sweatshop to high-tech manufacturing while guiding national champions such as Hyundai and Samsung to world-leading status. Because that pivot demands more skilled workforces and challenges the original developmental coalitions that lifted countries into the middle-income stratum, the article calls it a difficult transition that most countries do not make.

For economies that never escaped middle-income status, such as Mexico, Brazil, Egypt and Russia, it calls the situation darker, since long sojourns have entrenched large firms and elites oriented around unproductive rent-seeking. Their trajectories converge, it says, on what Alex Hochuli has called 'Brazilianisation', a stagnation with rising informality, rentierism and inequality, a decomplexifying economy dependent on commodities and an elite sequestered from its people. Brazil shows the contrast: its golden-age growth put it on a path of rapid convergence with Europe and the United States, with real GDP per capita up more than 140 per cent from 1960 to 1980, but it grew by under 20 per cent from 1980 to 2000. India, with its decentralisation and powerful local and national rentiers, faces a similar trajectory, the article says, with higher growth but a much lower income. By contrast, the article presents Vietnam as a successful transition to middle-income status with a sophisticated manufacturing base, and says China's GDP per capita grew sixfold between 1981 and 2018, solidly into middle-income status.

cards.question: Nomadic pastoralists and farmers competing over ever-scarcer land and water in Nigeria and the Sahel caused _____, which the article says killed six times as many Nigerians as Boko Haram in 2018.
cards.abstract:
Farmer–herder conflict is the article's name for fighting in Nigeria and the Sahel between nomadic pastoralists and settled agriculturalists over ever-scarcer land and water. The article places it among the effects of ecological disruption on the poor world, which it says will accelerate existing violence in some places. It says drought and land erosion have already exacerbated ethnic conflicts in Sudan and East Africa. In Nigeria and the Sahel, it says, farmer–herder conflicts are often ignored in the West because of their unclear political dimensions, yet they have grown increasingly lethal. It states that in 2018 these conflicts killed six times as many Nigerians as did the Boko Haram insurgency, and the article cites no source for that comparison.

The article sets this within its wider argument that increasingly common droughts, floods and crop failures will imperil national agricultural systems, intensifying deagrarianisation and further fuelling social instability. Its example of such a shock is the Horn of Africa, where a locust crisis was followed by a severe regional drought and famine alerts, with humanitarian organisations claiming that more than fifteen million were at risk. It also says that in poorer commodity exporters such as Nigeria, severe budget crises after the commodity cycle turned crimped governments' abilities to battle destructive Islamist insurgencies. A 2026 reading on the Sahel, which does not use the term, says that as of February 2026 local conflicts in the Lake Chad Basin and Liptako-Gourma region had constrained access to farmland and disrupted markets, and that millions remain displaced. A Lecture 3 slide of potential answers on the Sahel says economic pressures can erode public trust in government and raise opportunities for recruitment by armed groups, and a reading on fragile states lists Northeastern Nigeria among places teetering on the edge of famine in late 2017.

cards.question: If the problem of the 20th century was the colour line, the article argues, the problem of the 21st is the _____, as migration grows and rich countries try to restrict it.
cards.abstract:
The problem of the border line is the article's reversal of a saying it attributes to Du Bois: if the problem of the 20th century was the problem of the colour line, the problem of the 21st is the border line. The article expects mass migration to grow, saying that the immigration crises of the 2010s and the political backlashes to them only presage what is to come. It says new technologies have made movement easier and more attractive, and that social and economic changes have unleashed people from the bonds of traditional communities. For a young person in a city like Ibadan or Luanda with no real opportunity, it says, emigration, even when risky, is a logical calculation, though much migration by the poorest is likely to stay internal. A reading on fragile states describes the pressure from Europe's side, saying that, driven out of their homes by violent conflict and poverty, historic levels of refugees and migrants have reached its shores.

Climate harms will sharpen the calculation, the article says, and it calls the line between 'climate refugee' and 'economic migrant' thin and ultimately subjective. It expects wealthier governments, in Europe and in richer African nations such as South Africa, to keep trying to reduce the supply of migration opportunities, a future of barbed wire, border fences and migrant detention facilities. Western regimes, it adds, will increasingly outsource these programmes to less scrupulous partners, as the European Union has done with Morocco and Niger, and its note cites reporting on both partnerships. A set reading on globalisation notes that countries across Europe are shutting their borders to immigrants, and a Lecture 4 slide lists tariffs to stop Mexican migration among uses of economic diplomacy. The article insists there is no way to reduce the demand for migration without real global development, and that even successful population transfers will only partially compensate for the failure to develop the poorest parts of the world.

cards.question: Skills left unused during a civil war atrophy through neglect, a process the authors of a Sierra Leone firm study call _____, which slows the pace of recovery once peace returns.
cards.abstract:
Forgetting by not doing is the authors' term for the way a civil war lets skills atrophy through neglect, which they say slows the pace of recovery once peace returns. The working paper reasons that wartime effects on cost and demand look readily reversible, so the lasting channel in a low income country such as Sierra Leone is human capital, lost through the atrophy of skills. It builds on the theory of learning by doing, adding that doing is more evidently essential to the retention of task-specific knowledge. Directly, technical regress means reverting to practices that would be inefficient in normal times, as when workers without electricity switch to manual operations and forget techniques that peace will make feasible again. Indirectly, a contraction of output shrinks the labour force, and the decline in employment deskills those who lose work, in a process analogous to the deskilling of workers who remain unemployed for long periods.

The atrophy matters only once peace is restored, the paper says, when firms find themselves in a favourable disequilibrium, with demand rising and scope to abandon the reversionary technologies. As firms expand they meet a shortage of skilled labour, so firms in conflict-affected areas must make do with lower quality workers and have lower productivity. In its formal model knowledge grows with output as usual, but when output falls, which the paper calls characteristic of conflict, knowledge declines and a forgetting by not doing effect replaces the learning effect. The 2013 conclusion restates the theory as a significant loss in human capital stock, broadly analogous to learning by doing, with civil war inducing a reversion to more subsistence activities and less sophisticated techniques. Both versions add that firms stuck with lower quality workers lose productivity and are slower to acquire new techniques of production, so the growth process is likely to be slowed.
questions: The paper borrows the idea of learning by doing but reverses it: when output falls in wartime, knowledge declines and _____ replaces the usual learning effect in its formal model.
When peace returns, firms in conflict-affected areas expand but meet a shortage of skilled labour and make do with lower quality workers, a legacy the paper blames on _____ during the war.

cards.question: A study says the flight of workers, unreliable transport and fear of looting raise the unit cost of formal sector output, an effect on production that it labels _____, separate from falling demand.
cards.abstract:
Technical regress is the term the paper uses for how violence affects production during a civil war, while violence affects demand through a reduction in income. The paper judges that the most important effects of violence on firms are likely to have been disruption through the flight of employees, unreliable transport and the fear of looting, not physical destruction. It reasons that physical destruction may be relatively minor in low income countries, because there is little capital at risk and replacements can swiftly be imported after the conflict. It cites a study of the bombing of Vietnam, which it calls probably the most destructive civil war in any developing country, as finding no discernible long term economic effects. Unreliable transport would normally push firms to carry larger inventories, the paper adds, but the fear of looting warrants the opposite, and it calls such costs of disruption technical regress, which raises the unit cost of output.

The regress is also a reversion to production practices that would be inefficient in normal times, as when a lack of electricity forces workers to switch to manual operations. The 2013 conclusion calls the change a reversion to more subsistence activities and less sophisticated techniques, and the working paper says the service sector had shrunk to a quarter of its 1980 size by the end of the conflict. Demand falls too, the paper says, through a decline in cash incomes as people move liquid assets abroad for safety and shift into subsistence activities, combined with the higher unit cost of output. Firms in chiefdoms with more intense fighting are now significantly smaller, the paper finds, and it suggests a shortage of labour as workers moved into the armed forces or were displaced. Even so, the paper treats these wartime effects as readily reversible, so that with a secure peace productivity and demand would be restored, and it looks to the atrophy of skills for more persistent damage.

cards.question: Beginning in 1991 at the border with Liberia, the _____ spread across the whole country, reached Freetown on 6 January 1999, and ended in 2002 when British troops intervened to bring peace.
cards.answerDate: Fought1991 – 2002Freetown reached6 January 1999
cards.abstract:
Sierra Leone's civil war ravaged the country between 1991 and 2002, in the working paper's words an extremely violent conflict that led to over 50,000 deaths and the displacement of 500,000 civilians. The paper adds that it caused a wholesale destruction of the national economy, and that by its end Sierra Leone had sunk to the bottom of the UNDP's Human Development Index. On its account the war erupted in 1991 at the border with neighbouring Liberia, later spread over the entire country and reached Freetown on 6 January 1999. Its list of war techniques includes the systematic targeting of civilians as a terror tactic, cutting of limbs, abduction of child soldiers and intensive looting of diamonds, and a 2013 note says child soldiers were used in the different fighting factions. The decade of fighting was rhythmed by rebel advances towards Freetown and defeats against the government army, it says, and later by ECOWAS peacekeepers pushing the rebels back towards their stronghold in the East.

Peace came in 2002 through the intervention of British troops, the paper says, and the insurgent Revolutionary United Front rapidly collapsed, with a continued British military presence aiding security since. It stresses that the conflict, though intense and prolonged, was concentrated in particular locations, a spatial variation it later uses to estimate the impact of violence on firms. The fighting, it says, was not dictated by the destruction of particular economic sectors apart from mining, because the primary incentive was to control Freetown and whatever lay in the rebels' way was destroyed. GDP per capita fell during the 1980s, eventually leading to the war, and between 1980 and 2000 it halved from $300 to $150, while in 2008 the country still lay at the bottom of the Human Development Index. A reading by Oks and Williams places the wars in Liberia and Sierra Leone in a simultaneous crisis in West Africa during what it calls two lost decades for development.

cards.question: After British troops intervened in 2002, the insurgent _____ rapidly collapsed, and a continued British military presence has since aided security in Sierra Leone.
cards.abstract:
The Revolutionary United Front is introduced in the working paper as the insurgent group that rapidly collapsed in 2002, when British troops intervened and peace was achieved in Sierra Leone. The paper gives the group no fuller description, but it calls Kailahun district, in the East at the border with Liberia, the group's stronghold. Its account of the war speaks of rebels without naming the group each time, saying the fighting was rhythmed by their advances towards Freetown and defeats against the government army. It adds that ECOWAS peacekeepers later pushed them back towards their stronghold in the East, and that the war itself had erupted in 1991 at the border with neighbouring Liberia. A note in the 2013 article on how the districts of the 2006 employers survey were chosen says that for the eastern region Kailahun was chosen to include a poorer district.

A note in the 2013 article says it is now widely believed that the war was, to a great extent, orchestrated by neighbouring Liberia, with parts of the rebel factions at its start in 1991 appearing to be Liberian soldiers. The working paper's version of that note says the rebel parts appeared to be Liberian citizens, not soldiers, so the two texts differ on this detail. Both notes add that diamonds mined in Sierra Leone were smuggled by the rebels through the border, probably in exchange for arms and ammunition. The 2013 note adds that none of these facts has been proved so far and says the trial of former President Charles Taylor, begun in 2006, should answer some questions about the group's Liberian linkages. Liberia also matters to the paper's method, which assumes that the closer a chiefdom lies to Liberia the more intense the conflict there and so uses distance to Monrovia to instrument intensity.

cards.question: The World Bank's _____, undertaken in 2006 and carried out in five districts for budget reasons, had enumerators interview the owner, the top manager and ten employees at each sampled business.
cards.abstract:
The Sierra Leone Employers Survey was undertaken by the World Bank in 2006 and, the working paper says, constitutes the core of its database. A note in the 2013 article says data collection started in May 2006, with enumerators interviewing the owner, the top manager and ten employees at each sampled business. The note adds that national coverage was not possible because of budget constraints, so the survey was carried out in five districts. The districts were chosen to reflect differences in location, to include one from each of the four regions, eastern, southern, northern and western, and, outside the east, to take the district with the most businesses. The working paper counts four districts out of eleven, listing the Western urban and rural areas, Bo, Bombali and Kailahun, while another 2013 note treats the entire Western Area as one district though it is really two.

The working paper relied only on the urban area data, which surveyed 419 formal and 248 informal businesses, and says all 30 large and 136 medium-sized firms were surveyed along with 502 small ones. It warns of a possible selection bias, because only survivor firms were surveyed, and says it is impossible to assess why they survived and the data are insufficient to enable correction. Employers were asked about income only in ranges, the working paper says, listed in a note from fewer than a million Le to over 25 million Le, with the exchange rate against the US dollar varying around 1/3,000. Employers were also asked whether they would be willing to pay for the training of their employees, and a note defines unskilled workers as those doing a job that any person taken off the street could do within a day. The working paper cites a 2007 World Bank study for the finding that labour availability is not in itself a constraint for firms, though the availability of skilled workers remains a major problem for the largest.

cards.question: Because the war was intense but concentrated in particular places, the study compares firms in chiefdoms that suffered more violence with others, exploiting _____ to estimate the effect of war on firm growth.
cards.abstract:
The geographic variation in conflict intensity is what the study uses to estimate the impact of violence on the growth of firms, because the war was intense but concentrated in particular locations. The paper says the fighting was not dictated by the destruction of particular economic sectors apart from mining, so the variation was not systematically related to the structure of the economy. Its measure comes from household data, which a 2013 note says were collected in 2005 and are nationally representative, covering 6,341 households in 635 enumeration areas. For each chiefdom the paper averages household answers to four questions on deaths and injuries from the war, and defines intensity as the mean of the four variables, which range from 0 to 1. It notes that almost 80 per cent of the households surveyed moved to their community before 2002, so it expects the measure to represent the reality, not population movements.

A 2013 note says the earlier researchers based their indicator on whether household members were made refugees, not on information about the community, and the working paper uses that slightly different measure to check robustness. A problem of endogeneity may arise, the paper says, because higher intensity areas might have had intrinsic characteristics making them more likely to be affected by hostilities, which could bias its estimators. To avoid this it instruments intensity with the distance to Monrovia, assuming that the closer a chiefdom lies to Liberia the more intense the conflict there, while distance itself should not affect the outcomes studied. It defends the instrument by noting that roads between the two countries are in bad condition and the main border bridge was closed from 1990 until June 2007, after the data were collected. First stage regressions confirm distance to Monrovia as a strong predictor, significant at the one per cent level, and Table 4 of the 2013 article reports first stage coefficients of −0.125 and −0.141, each marked significant at that level.

Distance to Monrovia serves as an instrument on the assumption that fighting was more intense nearer Liberia, answering the worry that _____ reflects intrinsic characteristics of places more likely to be attacked.

cards.question: Because firms in areas not directly affected still operated in a country at civil war, the paper treats its estimates of the impact of violence as a _____ on the war's full effects.
cards.abstract:
A lower bound is what the working paper says its approach gives, because the approach is likely to underestimate the full effects of civil war. Its reason is that even firms in areas not directly affected by violence were nevertheless operating in a country at civil war, which is likely to have affected their performance. The paper adds that during wartime government policies deteriorate, trade with conflict-affected areas is reduced, and firms may fear that violence will spread to their own area. Its chiefdom-level results find no significant relationship between war intensity and the existence of firms in 2006, which the paper reads as either uniform destruction of the economy or rapid re-establishment of firms. A second reason concerns physical capital: if physical and human capital are complementary, the paper says its analysis would constitute a lower bound, because violence would have destroyed more physical capital where fighting was intense and so decreased the need for training.

It cannot realistically conclude whether the two are substitutes or complements in Sierra Leone, although it thinks labour-skill complementarity might be more likely. Selection is a third reason, as the sample holds only firms that survived the war or were born after it, so survivors should be bigger where conflict was more intense, potentially underestimating the interaction coefficient. For income the paper reasons that smaller firms were destroyed and only the most productive large ones survived, so the intensity coefficient should be upward biased and the effect on income might have been even lower. The bias does not always run one way, since for its training results the paper says the effect of selection is unknown and it is not clear how it affects, if at all, the war intensity coefficients. The paper also acknowledges that the poor quality of the dataset calls for further investigation, and a 2013 note says its calculations do not control for the initial size of firms for lack of data.

Because only survivor firms were surveyed, and smaller ones were destroyed, the estimated effect of conflict on firm income may understate the damage, making the figures a _____ rather than the full cost.

cards.question: Reading a higher _____ among employers in the worst-hit chiefdoms as a sign of a more acute shortage of qualified labour is how the study tests its theory that war leaves skills scarce.
cards.abstract:
Willingness to pay for training is the study's survey measure of a skills shortage, based on asking employers whether they would be willing to pay for the training of their employees. The underlying assumption, the working paper says, is that the more employers feel a need to train their employees the more severe their shortage of qualified labour must be. The paper concedes that the variable might not be the ideal proxy for human capital and could capture unobserved characteristics such as wealth effects, credit constraints or the costs of physical capital. To guard against this it controls for financing constraints on growth and for physical assets acquired in the two years before the interview. A 2013 note defines unskilled workers as those doing a job that any person taken directly off the street could do within a day, and skilled workers by previous experience and training, among other things.

The working paper finds a positive effect of conflict intensity on this willingness, significant only without district effects, so conflict appears to cause a scarcity of skills where the war was more intense. In Table 4 of the 2013 article the probit intensity coefficients are 0.208 and 0.825, not significant, while the instrumented ones are 2.739 for training in general and 1.779 for skilled workers only, both significant. The physical capital coefficient is positive but never significant, which the working paper takes to suggest complements, since substitutes would lead firms not investing in assets to compensate by training staff. The interaction of financial constraint and conflict intensity is negative and significant, so the working paper says intensity lowers the constraint's effect, which the 2013 text calls partially offset in high intensity areas. Both conclusions read the pattern as a more acute shortage of skilled labour in the most affected areas, and the working paper adds that post-conflict governments should prioritise training in sectors that produce non-tradable goods.

cards.question: After a civil war, with too few competent teachers and trainers, the study offers _____ as one solution, encouraging expatriates to return and pass on the knowledge they acquired abroad.
cards.abstract:
Diaspora knowledge transfer is the remedy the working paper's conclusion proposes for a shortage of competent teachers and trainers, namely encouraging the diaspora to return and pass on the knowledge they acquired abroad during wartime. The 2013 conclusion likewise calls training a necessity and offers as one solution encouraging the diaspora, with knowledge acquired abroad. The problem it answers is that civil war not only deskills the existing labour force but also brings huge disturbances in schooling, so that the education system often collapses completely and children miss important years. In Sierra Leone, the working paper says, many children were prevented from going to school during the conflict, and 35 per cent of 15 to 24 year olds and 63 per cent of 25 to 35 year olds never attended. Once peace is settled, it says, there is a clear necessity to reconstruct the education system but no competences in the economy to achieve it, and if this is not addressed generations will continue to be lost.

Earlier in its conclusion the working paper says that post-conflict governments should prioritise training in sectors that produce non-tradable goods, especially the capital non-tradable goods. It adds that if the lack of skills in post-conflict economies is tackled early, recovery would likely be much faster. The 2013 version also mentions psychological support for youngsters who grew up amid violence, in connection with training programmes meant to help them integrate into society. The proposal comes at the end of a conclusion that sums up the paper's results on firm size, recovery and training, and none of the working paper's results concerns the diaspora. Where the Oks and Williams reading mentions a diaspora, it is as a source of remittances, which it says became lifelines for entire economies, as with the large Salvadoran diaspora in the United States.
