cards.question: Signalled in trade by the creation of the WTO in 1995 and in finance by a shift toward liberalisation, the _____ of the 1990s put economies in the service of the world economy.
cards.abstract:
Hyperglobalisation is the article's name for the path on which, it says, policymakers set the world in the 1990s, putting domestic economies in the service of the world economy instead of the other way around. In trade, it says, the change was signalled by the creation of the World Trade Organization in 1995, which made it harder for countries to shield themselves from international competition. In finance, it says, the change was a fundamental shift in governments' attitudes away from managing capital flows and toward liberalisation, so that vast quantities of short-term finance moved across borders in search of higher returns. At the time, the article adds, these changes seemed to rest on sound economics, since openness to trade would put resources where they were most productive and freer finance would fuel growth. Lecture 3 sets hyper-globalisation beside national sovereignty and democracy in what it calls Rodrik's trilemma, of which governments can only choose two.

The article argues that these arrangements carried risks which the hyperglobalists did not foresee, though economic theory could have predicted the downside as well as the upside. It lists a decline in manufacturing employment in the developed world that increased trade with China and other low-wage countries accelerated, the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression, and, after the crash, austerity policies promoted by international institutions. It adds that the new hyperglobalisation was closer in spirit to the historically more distant and more intrusive gold standard, one of two earlier models alongside Bretton Woods, and calls that the source of many of today's problems. Even so, it insists, nothing was inevitable about the path the world followed from the 1990s, because hyperglobalisation was more a state of mind than a genuine, immutable constraint on domestic policy. A climate slide in Lecture 3 shows the trade-off, saying that if states insist on full sovereignty while global markets are deeply integrated, governments fear capital flight if they impose stricter rules.

Nothing about the _____ of the 1990s was inevitable, the article argues, since it was more a state of mind than a genuine, immutable constraint on domestic policy.

cards.question: For roughly 50 years before World War I, plus a brief revival between the wars, the _____ set the rules of economic management, according to a Foreign Affairs reading.
cards.abstract:
The gold standard is, in the article's account, one of two very different models of globalisation that countries experimented with before the hyperglobalisation of the 1990s. The article names the other as the Bretton Woods system, and it calls the gold standard historically more distant and more intrusive and the principles of Bretton Woods more flexible. It says that for roughly 50 years before World War I, plus a brief revival during the interwar period, the gold standard set the rules of economic management. The section that carries this sentence is headed 'The Golden Straitjacket', a phrase that the pages supplied do not explain. The pages supplied end in the middle of the next sentence, which opens with the words 'A government', so they do not say what the rules of the standard required.

What the article does say is that the new hyperglobalisation was closer in spirit to the gold standard, and that this is the source of many of today's problems. Its opening page describes the hyperglobalist path of the 1990s as requiring domestic economies to be put in the service of the world economy instead of the other way around. It also argues that there was nothing inevitable about that path, because hyperglobalisation was more a state of mind than a genuine, immutable constraint on domestic policy. Its recommendation in the pages supplied is that policymakers look to the more flexible principles of Bretton Woods in order to craft a fairer and more sustainable global economy. Lecture 3's trilemma slides do not mention the gold standard, but they say that pairing national sovereignty with globalisation means limits on democracy, with the Washington consensus policies as an example.

cards.question: Before the 1990s, countries had experimented with two very different models of globalisation, the gold standard and the _____ system, whose more flexible principles one article urges policymakers to revisit.
cards.answerDate: Golden agec. 1950 – 1980Effective end1971 – 1972
cards.abstract:
The Bretton Woods system is, in the article's account, one of two very different models of globalisation that countries experimented with before the hyperglobalisation of the 1990s, the other being the gold standard. The article calls the principles of Bretton Woods more flexible and says that today's policymakers should look to them if they are to craft a fairer and more sustainable global economy. The pages supplied name the system but do not describe how it worked, so the course material has no account of it from the article. A reading on global development says an international financial regime built on the Bretton Woods model placed limits on capital mobility. It says this allowed a degree of financial stability that helped emerging markets pursue aggressive development strategies without the boom-bust dynamics that would later become so common.

It places a golden age for development in roughly 1950 to 1980, and says that period relied on a system of managing global economic flows which by the 1970s was under serious strain, the effective death of Bretton Woods in 1971–72 coming first. Near its end the reading calls for a new and credible Bretton Woods–style framework for regulating international monetary flows, to prevent boom-bust cycles and to return some autonomy over economic policy to poor-world policymakers. A Dædalus article on fragile states uses the name for institutions, saying that nearly 70 years ago, from the ashes of conflict, the world united to establish the Bretton Woods institutions, which it lists as the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. It cites that history to argue that the United States and the international community have long proven their ability to do hard things. Lecture 3 says an effective multilateral response to a disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could integrate emergency financial assistance from the IMF and the World Bank, two of the institutions that article names.

cards.question: Created in 1995, the WTO reached into agriculture, services, intellectual property, industrial policy and health regulation, taking trade rules _____ and into areas they had not previously touched.
cards.answerDate: WTO created1995GATT1947
cards.abstract:
Beyond tariffs is a label that none of the course texts uses, for the article's point that the World Trade Organization, created in 1995, reached into policy areas that international trade rules had not previously touched. The article lists those areas as agriculture, services, intellectual property, industrial policy, and health and sanitary regulations. It says the WTO also made it harder for countries to shield themselves from international competition, and that even more ambitious regional trade deals, such as the North American Free Trade Agreement, took off around the same time. It presents this as part of the hyperglobalist path of the 1990s, which required domestic economies to be put in the service of the world economy instead of the other way around. A slide in Lecture 3 says the WTO was founded in 1995 as successor to the GATT of 1947, and lists among its functions a forum for negotiations, with tariff reductions as an example, and administering agreements on goods, services and intellectual property.

A Lecture 4 slide lists reasons why the WTO needs reform, among them that it does not deliver sufficient benefits for the most vulnerable and that it is difficult to industrialise for both emerging and advanced economies. A reading on development argues that WTO agreements from TRIPS to TRIMS, which ban or limit strategies used by successful industrialisers of the past, have limited the scope of national industrial policies, and says they will need to be adjusted. Lecture 3's trilemma slide likewise cites the 'policy space' of African countries, with the EPA Agreements as the example, as a difference of opinion that economic diplomacy does not exclude. Lecture 4's version of the WTO slide lists criticisms that include rigid negotiation progress, with the Doha Round deadlock as an example, and a perceived bias favouring developed nations. An essay of 2026 says the WTO carries on adjudicating trade disputes despite a surge in protectionism, and later calls its appeals mechanism deadlocked.

cards.question: Pushed by the United States, the IMF and the OECD, countries moved from managing capital flows to _____, letting vast quantities of short-term finance slosh across borders in search of higher returns.
cards.answerDate: Mexico crisis1994Asian crisis1997Russia crisis1998
cards.abstract:
Liberalised capital flows names what, the article says, happened in finance in the 1990s, when governments shifted fundamentally away from managing capital flows and toward liberalisation. It says that, pushed by the United States and by global organisations such as the International Monetary Fund and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, countries freed up vast quantities of short-term finance to slosh across borders in search of higher returns. At the time, the article says, this seemed to be based on sound economics, because capital would flow from the countries where it was plentiful to the countries where it was needed. It adds that more trade and freer finance were expected to unleash private investment and fuel global economic growth. A reading on development describes the contrasting earlier arrangement, an international financial regime built on the Bretton Woods model that placed limits on capital mobility and allowed a degree of financial stability.

The article argues that the new arrangements came with risks that the hyperglobalists did not foresee, although economic theory could have predicted the downside just as well as it did the upside. Among those risks it lists the financialisation of the global economy, which it says produced the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression. The development reading says that many poor-world governments liberalised their capital accounts in order to spur foreign investment, which increased volatility and culminated in a series of financial crises, in Mexico in 1994, in various Asian economies in 1997 and in Russia in 1998. It adds that all these 'reforms' did little to improve growth fundamentals, and its closing proposals include a new and credible Bretton Woods–style framework for regulating international monetary flows. A climate slide in Lecture 3 gives the political version of the problem, saying that where states insist on full sovereignty while global markets are deeply integrated, governments fear capital flight if they impose stricter rules.

cards.question: A US president called globalisation the economic equivalent of a _____, like wind or water, while a British prime minister said you might as well debate whether autumn should follow summer.
cards.abstract:
Force of nature is the phrase with which, the article reports, US President Bill Clinton described globalisation, exclaiming that it is the economic equivalent of a force of nature, like wind or water. British Prime Minister Tony Blair, it says, mocked those who wanted to debate globalisation, saying that you might as well debate whether autumn should follow summer. The article cites both remarks in a passage on politicians and policymakers who downplayed the problems of the new global economy, denying that its terms entailed sacrificing sovereignty. Yet it says they seemed immobilised by these same forces, and that the centre-right and the centre-left disagreed not over the rules of the new world economy but over how to accommodate their national economies to them. The right wanted to cut taxes and slash regulations, it says, while the left asked for more spending on education and public infrastructure, and both sides agreed that economies needed to be refashioned in the name of global competitiveness.

The article rejects the premise, saying that there was nothing inevitable about the path the world followed beginning in the 1990s. It argues that international institutions played their part, but that hyperglobalisation was more a state of mind than a genuine, immutable constraint on domestic policy. It also says that more and more of what happened to ordinary people seemed the result of anonymous market forces or of distant decision-makers in foreign countries. It describes a populist backlash, personified by US President Donald Trump, as being in full swing when it was written, and Lecture 1 likewise says that populism is making ground across the world. Lecture 3's second trilemma slide says populism thrives on this di- or trilemma, and poses as its key question how to combine the need to reinforce the domestic social contract with international economic traffic rules and policy space.

Politicians who spoke of globalisation as a _____ denied that its terms entailed sacrificing sovereignty, the article says, yet seemed immobilised by the same forces.

cards.question: By 2030 the World Bank expects around 80 per cent of the global extreme poor to live in _____, where basic services are minimal and security and rule of law are absent.
cards.abstract:
Fragile and conflict-affected states, shortened to FCS, are described on an FMO web page as not only the world's toughest markets but also the most challenging places to live and thrive. It says they are countries where access to basic services such as education, health and infrastructure is minimal, worsened by the absence of security and rule of law. It adds that these dynamics affect lives and livelihoods and generations to come, and that the World Bank expects around 80 per cent of the global extreme poor to be living in such states by 2030. The page concedes that no definition of fragility is widely agreed and says that actors in the international community generally treat it as a continuum rather than a binary concept. It quotes a definition as the degree to which state power is unable, unwilling or both to deliver security, protection of property, basic public services and essential infrastructure to most of its people.

Despite that concept, it warns against treating fragile states as one homogenous whole and says that no one-size-fits-all approach exists for situations affected by fragility, violence or risk. A Dædalus essay in the course readings says many policy-makers agree that nearly all outbreaks of violent intrastate conflict trace back to the absence or breakdown of the social contract between people and government, a condition often called fragility. The essay says fragility can stem from a lack of legitimacy in citizens' eyes, a lack of effectiveness, or both, and that high fragility creates conditions for armed conflict and political instability. Quoting the national security strategy of the Obama administration, the essay writes that fragile and conflict-affected states incubate and spawn infectious disease, illicit weapons and drug smugglers, and destabilising refugee flows. It adds that the fifty most fragile states on earth are home to 43 per cent of the world's most impoverished people, while internationalised internal conflicts now account for one-third of all global conflicts.

cards.sub: Reading 10 · Investing in Fragile and Conflict-Affected States (FMO)

cards.question: An FMO web page says that fragile states are increasingly in the spotlight of _____, which it urges to stop competing for the same deals and to work together based on comparative advantages.
cards.abstract:
Development financial institutions, shortened to DFIs, are the investors that an FMO web page has in view when it says that fragile and conflict-affected states are increasingly in their spotlight as needing attention. The page puts that attention down to the role fragility plays in inequality between countries, and it reports that FMO commissioned NIRAS and TrustWorks Global to study the conditions for successful investing in such states. The study relied largely on external sources of knowledge, namely a literature review and interviews with experts and investors experienced in fragile contexts, and it also included case studies of six customers funded through the Dutch government fund MASSIF. The page says the report's recommendations are applicable also to all DFIs, and the first is that a DFI should ensure a clear strategic position, having clarified the rationale and narrative of being active in these countries. Lending, the page says, still represents the most common instrument that DFIs use in these states, though the report finds that other instruments, such as development impact bonds or equity, could prove even more effective.

Depending on its strategic profile, a DFI may also deliver technical assistance at the sector or country level, besides the customer level. Partnerships, the page says, are essential in fragile states, and there is room for improvement through stronger cooperation between DFIs and with other key strategic actors across the humanitarian–development–peace nexus. The page says DFIs should not compete for the same deals but should work together based on their comparative advantages. Strategies formulated on comparative advantage would not only help maximise development impacts but also help share risk, especially if well coordinated with the broad range of national humanitarian, development and peace partners. It also says that collecting granular data on fragility should include collaboration with other DFIs for monitoring and data-driven insights, and that the report has been shared with other DFIs and interested parties.

cards.question: Investing in fragile and conflict-affected states is one of the core strategic pillars of _____, the Dutch government fund managed by FMO to support MSMEs in low income countries.
cards.abstract:
MASSIF is described on an FMO web page as the Dutch government fund, managed by FMO, that supports MSMEs, a term the page does not spell out, in low income countries and in fragile and conflict-affected states. The page calls investing in fragile and conflict-affected states one of the core strategic pillars of the fund, in a passage noting that these states are increasingly in the spotlight of development financial institutions. FMO commissioned NIRAS and TrustWorks Global to study the conditions for successful investing in such states, and the study included case studies of six customers funded through MASSIF. Those case studies were meant to show where FMO currently stands in its approach in fragile contexts. The report acknowledges, the page says, that the 2017 MASSIF strategy has set FMO on the right path for its engagement in these states, enabling a clear focus on the Base of Pyramid.

The report adds that FMO is well positioned to be much more strategic in fragile states, ensuring a more transformative development impact with the scarce resources available. It suggests, for example, achieving this through in-depth country analyses and sector diagnostics, which would enable FMO to better identify the sectors most likely to have transformative impacts. A review of the six case studies suggests that FMO is making increased efforts to tailor its approach, capturing many factors of fragility and gathering the information needed to manage the risks that an investment poses to FMO. The page says the approach could be broadened to account for the risks an investment poses to the context itself, or for the ways in which it can have a positive impact on the dynamics of peace and security. The page closes by saying that the report and its framework are taken onboard as FMO explores how to shape its activities in these states, where both the potential for positive development impact and the levels of risk are high.

cards.question: A study for FMO says that, whichever strategic profile is chosen, investments in fragile states should be approached through a lens of _____, looking beyond formal, state-centric actors.
cards.abstract:
Conflict sensitivity is the lens through which, according to an FMO web page, a study recommends as essential approaching all investments in fragile and conflict-affected states, whichever strategic profile an investor chooses. The page says that assessments of a country's context by development financial institutions tend to focus on state-centric, formal rather than informal actors and dynamics. The study states that this is likely to be insufficient in fragile contexts, because such assessments overlook the fact that these states are characterised not by a lack of governance but by competing sources of governance. It adds that state-centric analyses often overlook the unpredictable nature of these states, and that the informal aspects of operating there must not be underestimated. Without combining country-level analysis with a customer's specifics, the page says, it is difficult to assess what kind of impact an investment will have on drivers of conflict.

The page therefore calls it crucial to elaborate a country-based screening process that accounts for informal aspects of operating there and to combine it with rigorous due diligence built on a sustainable peace perspective. A review of six case studies suggests that FMO captures many factors of fragility, but the page says its approach could be broadened to account for the risks an investment poses to the context itself. A more strategic approach also requires a variety of staff skills, the page says, and it lists conflict sensitivity beside political economy analysis and risk management. The Dædalus essay in the course readings does not use the term, but it says that traditional development efforts long steered clear of politics, while the United States Agency for International Development later included conflict analysis in its development agenda. The same essay, drawing on a study of coalition efforts in Afghanistan, says that the methods employed by the intelligence and military actors served to exacerbate corruption and undermine people's trust in their state, undercutting the investments made to rebuild it.

cards.question: At one end of the range of approaches to conflict open to an investor in fragile states is a minimal _____ approach, and at the other is positively impacting fragility and conflict.
cards.abstract:
Do no harm appears on an FMO web page as the minimal end of one of two dimensions along which a development financial institution can choose its strategic direction in fragile states. That dimension is the approach to conflict, which the page says can range from a minimal 'do no harm' approach to one of positively impacting fragility and conflict. The other dimension is the approach to development, which can range from seeking narrow development impact to seeking transformative development impact. The page uses the phrase only once, setting it against positively impacting fragility and conflict, and it does not define the phrase any further. It says that institutions may choose different strategic directions along these two dimensions, and that such an institution should ensure a clear strategic position, having clarified the rationale and narrative of being active in these countries.

Whichever strategic profile is chosen, the report recommends approaching investments through a lens of conflict sensitivity, noting that without combining country analysis with a customer's specifics it is difficult to assess an investment's impact on drivers of conflict. A review of six case studies suggests that FMO's approach captures the risks an investment poses to FMO but could be broadened to account for the risks it poses to the context itself. The same passage says the approach could also take in the ways an investment can have a positive impact on the dynamics of peace and security. The report also advises measuring the impacts of investments over time more comprehensively, so that FMO can track its positive contributions more clearly and avoid unintended negative consequences. The Dædalus essay in the course readings does not use the phrase, but it says that in Afghanistan the methods employed by intelligence and military actors served to exacerbate corruption and undermine people's trust in their state, undercutting investments in rebuilding it.

cards.question: A report for FMO says fragile and conflict-affected states are characterised not by a lack of governance but by _____, namely informal institutions or personalised 'rules of the game'.
cards.abstract:
Competing sources of governance is the phrase an FMO web page uses for what, in its view, characterises fragile and conflict-affected states, rather than a lack of governance. The page names these sources as informal institutions or personalised 'rules of the game'. It says that the informal aspects of operating in such states must not be underestimated, and that informal power relations influence all business decisions. Assessments by development financial institutions, it says, tend to focus on state-centric, formal actors and dynamics, which the study holds is likely to be insufficient in fragile contexts because such assessments overlook the competing sources of governance. The page therefore calls for a country-based screening process that accounts for informal aspects of operating in these states, combined with rigorous due diligence built on a sustainable peace perspective.

The page's recommendations name no country and give no further account of what the competing sources are. The Dædalus essay in the course readings does not use the phrase, but it says that fragile states often cannot extend the reach of government over their whole territory, so that illicit transnational forces such as terrorist and organised criminal groups often hold territory in them. A development essay in the course says that in the worst cases, like Haiti, governments have outright lost sovereignty to gangs, militias and warlords and are structurally incapable of political governance. The same essay describes Somalia, where state collapse in the 1990s led to the return of customary law, and says that what little remained of the state can be termed, in a historian's words, 'government by means of the aid industry'. It adds that the Congo, Somalia and the Central African Republic are now wards of external institutions, and says a new framework for development would need, at a minimum, to rebuild state capacity and reduce the outsourcing of governance to foreign institutions.

cards.question: An FMO web page urges development financial institutions to cooperate more strongly with other key strategic actors across the _____ rather than compete for the same deals in fragile states.
cards.abstract:
The humanitarian–development–peace nexus appears on an FMO web page, with no definition, in a call for stronger cooperation between development financial institutions and other key strategic actors across it. The page says that partnerships are essential in fragile states, and that these institutions should not compete for the same deals but should work together based on their comparative advantages. It adds that strategies formulated on comparative advantage would help maximise development impacts and share risk, especially if well coordinated with the broad range of national humanitarian–development–peace partners. The page does not define the nexus, and the Dædalus essay in the course readings uses the word only once, for the link between fragility and multiple challenges to security. The essay itself calls for joining up United States defence, diplomatic and development capabilities, moving away from deeply stovepiped bureaucracies to a 'shared consciousness', a phrase it attributes to General Stanley McChrystal.

It notes that the United States agencies concerned are organised geographically in inconsistent ways, which, with their different capabilities, can lead the three D's of diplomacy, development and defence to analyse fragile contexts within different frameworks. Its example is Afghanistan, where a study found three separate lines of effort, intelligence, military and development, each pursued with a different definition of the problem and with different timelines, frameworks and goals. The development community, it says, typically looks at longer-term change while defence and diplomatic efforts address more immediate problems, so that without more closely aligned goals short-term gains too often result in longer-term crises. On the humanitarian side, the essay reports that key agreements at the first Global Humanitarian Summit focused on breaking down the stovepipes between humanitarian and development activities, with more emphasis on understanding and addressing the drivers of violent conflict. A development essay in the course describes humanitarian institutions from the West as unaccountable if well-intentioned, forced each year to triage crises that states such as the Congo and Somalia are too weak to handle themselves.

cards.question: Along the development dimension of a study's framework for investing in fragile states, an investor can seek narrow impact or _____, which most experts say requires moving beyond one-off deals.
cards.abstract:
Transformative development impact is, on an FMO web page, one end of a range of approaches to development open to a development financial institution in fragile states, the other end being narrow development impact. The page says that most experts suggest that investing in fragile states in an impactful way requires shifting from a one-off deal approach towards a transformative one, so as to maximise the use of scarce resources. More strategic approaches, it says, focus on steering market development, improving working conditions and spurring economic growth, while addressing conflict fault-lines and societal divisions. Doing so comes with a need to understand and actively manage political, economic, societal and environmental dynamics when selecting countries, investees and partners. The report acknowledges that the 2017 MASSIF strategy has set FMO on the right path, and that FMO is well positioned to be much more strategic, ensuring a more transformative development impact with the scarce resources available.

It suggests, for example, reaching this through in-depth country analyses and sector diagnostics, which would let FMO better identify the sectors most likely to have transformative impacts. The page adds that the peculiarity of the context requires each investment to be approached case by case, which translates into tailored financing solutions and ad hoc structured instruments aligned with a customer's needs. It also says that measuring the impacts of investments over time more comprehensively, on development or fragility, would let FMO track its positive contributions more clearly. The Dædalus essay in the course readings does not use the phrase, but it describes development as arguably undergoing a paradigm shift, from narrowly focused investments and isolated sector-based programming to a more systemic approach of managing risk and building resilience. A development essay in the course complains that a consensus among Western experts focuses inordinately on small-scale interventions such as randomised controlled trials rather than on questions of elite coordination and political economy, and it calls for a new framework for development.

cards.question: A May 2026 analysis projects acute food insecurity in the Sahel rising above 50 million people during the June to August 2026 _____, up from more than 40 million.
cards.abstract:
The lean season is the June to August 2026 period for which a May 2026 analysis projects rising hunger in the Sahel, though the article's opening uses the term without defining it. The article says more than 40 million people in the Sahel are already experiencing acute food insecurity, with projections rising to above 50 million during that lean season. In parts of northeastern Nigeria, it adds, localised populations are already at risk of catastrophic hunger, a potential precursor to famine if conditions worsen. It opens by saying that war-time disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is spreading through the fertiliser market and affecting supply chains encompassing regions that have no margins to absorb the impact. A lecture slide poses an assignment question, asking how a maritime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz transmits a severe socio-economic and political shock to the Sahel and what multilateral interventions could mitigate it.

The article says the stress predates the current conflict, and that as of February 2026 local conflicts in the Lake Chad Basin and across the Liptako-Gourma region had constrained access to farmland and disrupted market activity. In Niger and Chad, it adds, high dependence on imported food and agricultural inputs had left households exposed to higher food prices, while millions of people remained displaced and more reliant on markets and assistance. Even before February 2026, the article says, farmers were selling livestock early on unfavourable terms, and humanitarian agencies facing funding constraints had been cutting rations or narrowing coverage. In other words, it says, people in the Sahel were already getting less food before the onset of the war in the Gulf, so any further rise in input costs or delay in delivery was bound to have disproportionate effects. A lecture slide of potential answers names oil prices as a channel, saying they raise the costs of transportation, agriculture and food and disproportionately affect populations already facing poverty and food insecurity.

cards.question: Between February and March 2026, benchmark prices for a nitrogen fertiliser rose roughly 46 per cent month-on-month, according to the World Bank, a _____ that a May 2026 analysis links to the conflict.
cards.abstract:
The urea price spike is the rise in benchmark urea prices between February and March 2026, which the article puts at roughly 46 per cent month-on-month, according to the World Bank. The article says the rise reflects the tightening of fertiliser flows linked to the conflict, and it introduces the figure as a sign that the pressure is already visible in market indicators. Its opening sentence says that war-time disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is spreading through the fertiliser market and affecting supply chains encompassing regions that have no margins to absorb the impact. The article names urea, together with ammonia, among the nitrogen-based fertilisers that Algeria is well positioned to produce and already exports. It adds that Egypt, a significant fertiliser producer, is a source of 8 per cent of global urea manufacture.

Several Sahelian importers, already facing currency weakness and tighter access to trade finance, are meeting higher financing costs and delayed procurement at precisely the point in the agricultural calendar when fertiliser purchases are normally finalised. Governments across the region, already under fiscal strain, face increasing difficulty sustaining subsidy programmes or extending seasonal credit to smallholders. The article says that in many areas farmers depend on seasonal credit or state-supported input programmes, and that when input prices rise or access to credit tightens, fertiliser use declines, especially in cash-constrained farming systems. It concedes that some global factors may moderate the shock, since as of March grain inventories remained stronger than during the 2022 food crisis and fertiliser output outside the Gulf offers alternative sources of supply. Even so, it argues, redirecting fertiliser cargoes, securing trade finance and moving inputs inland through fragile logistics networks takes time that the region does not have.

cards.question: Typically beginning in May in the south and moving north through June and July, the seasonal rains open the _____, by which Sahelian farmers must have fertiliser in hand.
cards.abstract:
The rain-fed planting window is the narrow window into which, the article says, the Sahel's agricultural cycle is compressed, tied to the onset of seasonal rains. Those rains typically begin in May in southern zones and move northward through June and July, so the starting point differs between the south and the north. Because production is overwhelmingly rain-fed, the article says, planting decisions are closely tied to rainfall onset, and crops are grown over short seasonal cycles. Inputs such as fertiliser must therefore be available at the start of the season, and delays in access or financing directly affect application and yields. In many areas, it adds, farmers depend on seasonal credit or state-supported input programmes, so that fertiliser use declines when input prices rise or access to credit tightens, especially in cash-constrained farming systems.

Reduced application and delayed planting, the article says, lead to lower yields in rain-fed systems, as crop performance is highly sensitive to the time of rainfall and sowing. In the Sahel, it says, missing the optimal planting window shortens the growing season, which reduces yields. That leaves a narrow margin for action, which the article says is measured not in months but in weeks. In much of the Sahel, it says, the difference between mitigation and crisis will be determined over the next four to eight weeks, as planting decisions are made and input use is fixed. It argues that redirecting fertiliser cargoes, securing trade finance and moving inputs inland through fragile logistics networks takes time the region does not have, and that in systems where planting decisions are fixed within weeks, delays of even a few weeks can mean lower application and weaker harvests.

cards.question: Spanning Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, the _____ region is where, as of February 2026, local conflicts had constrained access to farmland and disrupted market activity.
cards.abstract:
Liptako-Gourma is a region that the article describes as spanning Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, and it names the region in a sentence on local conflict, alongside the Lake Chad Basin. The article says that as of February 2026 local conflicts in these areas had constrained access to farmland and disrupted market activity. It offers this as background to its account of the Sahel, which it says now faces a severe threat of widespread hunger, with more than 40 million people already experiencing acute food insecurity. Across the region as a whole, it adds, millions of people remain displaced, which increases reliance on markets and assistance at a time when both were already under pressure. In Niger and Chad, it says, high dependence on imported food and agricultural inputs had left households exposed to higher food prices before the disruption.

The article says this stress predates the current conflict, and that even before February 2026 farmers were selling their livestock early on unfavourable terms. Humanitarian agencies facing funding constraints, it adds, had been cutting rations or narrowing coverage, so that people in the Sahel were already getting less food before the onset of the war in the Gulf. A lecture slide on why peacekeeping is harder lists, among the features of present conflicts, that conflict is 'not national but regional' and that borders between rebellion and terrorists, and between the legal and illegal economy, are porous. The lecture slides never use the name Liptako-Gourma, but a slide on the current situation in Mali says that after violence increased in the centre and north the army and vice president orchestrated the third coup d'état in 10 years, on 24 May 2021, and a later slide says MINUSMA and France have fully withdrawn. A lecture slide on Mali's sovereignty adds that the military coup leader of Burkina Faso, Ibrahim Traoré, claims that no country has developed under democracy.

cards.question: Morocco holds about 70 per cent of known global phosphate reserves, and its state-backed fertiliser company, _____, has built distribution networks and agricultural partnerships across Africa.
cards.abstract:
OCP Group is the state-backed fertiliser company of Morocco, which the article says holds roughly 50 billion metric tons of phosphate reserves, or about 70 per cent of known global reserves, according to the United States Geological Survey. The article says the company has built distribution networks and agricultural partnerships across Africa, including soil-mapping, agronomy and fertiliser-access programmes in West Africa, giving Morocco an existing platform for targeted support. It describes the Maghreb as exposed to the same shock as the Sahel but as occupying a different position in the chain of energy, fertiliser and food flows that connect the Gulf to the Sahel. While the region is vulnerable to the disruption of commerce through the strait, the article says, it also has capabilities that could potentially offset it, particularly in Morocco and Algeria. It adds that these capacities are not readily deployable at scale or on short notice to meet Sahelian needs.

Morocco's production is not unconstrained, the article warns, because Moroccan fertiliser output depends in part on imported sulphur, some of it linked to Gulf supply chains. More fundamentally, it says, Moroccan fertiliser exports are globally integrated and increasingly tied to long-term commercial relationships and forward supply agreements, which limits the ability to redirect supply quickly to higher-risk markets without coordinated intervention. It also notes that fertiliser production outside the Gulf, including in parts of North Africa, provides alternative sources of supply, although this does not remove the immediate problem in the Sahel. None of the countries it surveys is insulated from the crisis, it says, and Morocco remains exposed to imported sulphur and global fertiliser pricing. Yet all of them retain greater industrial, financial and logistical capacity than the Sahelian states most exposed, and on current evidence, the article says, the Maghreb remains relatively more capable of absorbing and redirecting risk.

cards.question: Moroccan fertiliser output depends in part on _____, some of which a May 2026 analysis links to Gulf supply chains, so that disruption feeds back into Morocco's own cost structure.
cards.abstract:
Imported sulphur is an input on which, the article says, Moroccan fertiliser output depends in part, in a passage warning that Morocco's production is not unconstrained. The article says that some of that imported sulphur is linked to Gulf supply chains. It draws the consequence that disruption feeds back into Morocco's own cost structure. It makes the point in a passage that credits Morocco with roughly 50 billion metric tons of phosphate reserves, about 70 per cent of known global reserves, and with a state-backed fertiliser company, OCP Group, whose networks in Africa it says give Morocco an existing platform for targeted support. In its passage on Morocco, the article says only that some of the imported sulphur is linked to Gulf supply chains, and it gives no tonnage, no share and no origin for the rest.

The article's opening frames the wider crisis as war-time disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz spreading through the fertiliser market and affecting supply chains encompassing regions that have no margins to absorb the impact. It says the Maghreb is exposed to the same shock as the Sahel but occupies a different position in the chain of energy, fertiliser and food flows that connect the Gulf to the Sahel. Later it lists Morocco's exposure to imported sulphur and global fertiliser pricing beside Algeria's competing demands for natural gas and Egypt's foreign exchange pressure as reasons why none of these countries is insulated from the crisis. None of them, it says, can absorb a prolonged regional shock without cost, yet it judges that all of them retain greater industrial, financial and logistical capacity than the Sahelian states most exposed. It adds that the capacities of the Maghreb are not readily deployable at scale or on short notice to meet Sahelian needs.

cards.question: Because natural gas is both feedstock and energy source for nitrogen fertilisers, _____ leaves Algerian output tied to competing domestic and export demands for gas.
cards.abstract:
Algeria's gas-to-nitrogen link is the connection the article draws between the country's substantial natural gas reserves and its ability to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers. The article says Algeria is well positioned to produce such fertilisers, including ammonia and urea, both of which it already exports. Natural gas, it explains, is both a feedstock and an energy source for nitrogen fertilisers. The article names Algeria, with Morocco, as a country whose capabilities could potentially offset the disruption, while adding that these capacities are not readily deployable at scale or on short notice to meet Sahelian needs. It places Algeria in the Maghreb, which it says is exposed to the same shock as the Sahel but occupies a different position in the chain of energy, fertiliser and food flows connecting the Gulf to the Sahel.

Because natural gas serves as both feedstock and energy source for nitrogen fertilisers, the article says, Algerian production is closely tied to competing domestic and export demands for gas. Algeria's fertiliser exports are also structured around existing commercial contracts, which the article says constrains the scope for rapid reallocation. The article lists Algeria's competing domestic and export demands for natural gas among the exposures that mean none of the countries it surveys can absorb a prolonged regional shock without cost. A Foreign Affairs essay says Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz, bringing 20 per cent of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipping to a near halt, and that energy disruptions can become food-price crises within weeks. Even so, the article says, the countries it surveys retain greater industrial, financial and logistical capacity than the Sahelian states most exposed to the current disruption.

cards.question: With 8 per cent of global manufacture of one fertiliser yet 12.5 million tons of one grain imported each year, Egypt is summed up by _____ in a May 2026 analysis.
cards.abstract:
Egypt's urea and wheat are the two figures the article gives for Egypt, one for its place among fertiliser producers and one for its place among wheat importers. It says Egypt is a significant fertiliser producer and a source of 8 per cent of global urea manufacture. It also says Egypt is one of the world's largest wheat importers, at 12.5 million tons a year. Major port infrastructure links Mediterranean and Red Sea routes, the article says, and handles a large share of Egypt's external trade. The article treats Egypt in a section on the capacities of the Maghreb and Egypt, saying that capabilities that could offset the disruption lie particularly in Morocco and Algeria and, in other respects, in Egypt.

At the same time, the article says, Egypt faces significant domestic economic constraints, including foreign exchange pressures, high import dependence and elevated financing needs, which limit its ability to act as a stabilising force beyond its borders, particularly in periods of volatility. The article repeats the point in its summary, saying that Egypt continues to operate under foreign exchange pressure and high food-import dependence. None of the countries it surveys can absorb a prolonged regional shock without cost, it says, yet all retain greater industrial, financial and logistical capacity than the Sahelian states most exposed to the current disruption. Separately, it notes that as of March grain inventories remained stronger than during the 2022 food crisis, one of the global factors that it says may moderate the shock. A Foreign Affairs essay adds a wider warning that over 55 per cent of globally traded maize, wheat, rice and soybeans pass through at least one maritime chokepoint, and that energy disruptions can become food-price crises within weeks.

cards.question: Two AI titans endorsed a call on 12 September to _____, meaning to slow AI's progress, a slowdown that a left-wing senator and a right-wing populist are also said to favour.
cards.abstract:
Pace the frontier is the call that, the article says, Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, made and that Sam Altman and Elon Musk, two AI titans, endorsed on 12 September. The article glosses the phrase as meaning to slow AI's progress. It says that those in favour of a slowdown include Bernie Sanders, a left-wing senator, and Steve Bannon, a right-wing populist. The same paragraph says that, following the recent resignation of a researcher at Anthropic, public fear of AI doom has spread. In a post viewed more than 170m times, the article says, the researcher said that Anthropic and OpenAI were 'gambling with our lives'.

The article's opening says that two things should make readers consider what AI could mean for humanity, the first being that those working with the technology are warning that it could lead to catastrophe, human extinction even. It says that these two things, the second being how technological innovation is aggravating the destruction of Ukraine, offer conflicting lessons for whether AI's rapid progress can or should be slowed down. Its standfirst says that America will struggle to make the technology safe while staying ahead of China, and headings linked to the rest of the package say that real co-operation on AI is likely to elude China and America. A Lecture 4 slide says that since 2017, 70 per cent of foundational AI models have been developed in the United States and 15 per cent in China, and that the American company Nvidia dominates 84 per cent of the market for graphics processing units. The lecture's concluding slide says that geostrategic rivalries are superimposed by an effort to obtain 'key technologies' like AI and quantum computing, with a risk of a two-tier world.

cards.question: In the first of its warnings, the article says bots may outwit their creators before _____, bringing their goals and ethics into line with humanity's, has been achieved.
cards.abstract:
Alignment is the term behind the first of the article's warnings, that bots may become brainy enough to outwit their creators before they are 'aligned' with humanity's goals and ethics. The article puts the word in inverted commas and, in the paragraph supplied, explains it only through the phrase humanity's goals and ethics, without saying how such alignment would be achieved or tested. It says leading AI bosses have signalled for years that their technology could become lethal, and the paragraph names a second danger, that bad people could use AI to wreak havoc. Its opening says that those working with the technology are warning about it leading to a catastrophe, human extinction even. That opening frames the article's question, whether AI's rapid progress can or should be slowed down, on which it says the warnings and the destruction of Ukraine offer conflicting lessons.

The article says the warnings have become more credible as AI agents have escaped their sandboxes during testing, co-ordinated with one another and hacked organisations, including an AI lab itself. It reports that, following the recent resignation of a researcher at Anthropic, public fear of AI doom has spread, and that in a post viewed more than 170m times the researcher said that Anthropic and OpenAI were 'gambling with our lives'. Its standfirst says America will struggle to make the technology safe while staying ahead of China, and a linked heading says agreeing to make AI safer may be impossible. A Lecture 4 slide lists AI, with climate change, pandemics and conflict-driven displacement, among the threats that no state can manage alone. A Lecture 1 slide says that an important focus of a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, attended by the leaders of China, Russia, India and seven other nations, was AI governance.

cards.question: An AI model-maker says it has caught people using its models for malign ends, from Mali's intelligence services to Houthi rebels, examples of the _____ that the article warns of.
cards.abstract:
Misuse by malign actors is the second danger in the article's list of ways that AI could become lethal, namely that bad people could use AI to wreak havoc. The article says that Anthropic, one model-maker, has caught people using its models for malign ends. Its first example is Mali's intelligence services getting a mass-surveillance system built. Its second is Houthi rebels in Yemen, who are thought to be writing software for ballistic missiles. The article hedges the second example with the words 'thought to be', so it does not state as established fact that the software was written, and it gives no further detail on either case.

Lecture 2's slide on the current situation in Mali, which does not mention AI, records a military coup in August 2020 and a third coup in 10 years on 24 May 2021. The same slide says that Russia's Wagner Group arrived in Mali at the request of the junta, and that in 2025 approximately 2000 foreign Russian agents were present, operating for the Russian Defence Ministry and the Malian government. An essay of 2026 on the abandoned order says that smaller countries and nonstate actors are increasingly exploiting chokepoints, and that the Houthi militia in Yemen was using cheap drones and missiles to block transit through the Red Sea even before Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz. Lecture 2 cites David Kilcullen's list of features of the current state of conflict, which includes nonstate actors acting like states and states acting like nonstate actors, both taking advantage of low-tech capabilities. Lecture 3's list of risks of regional conflagrations as middle players compete for regional hegemony names Yemen among the places concerned, alongside Palestine, Lebanon, Qatar and Syria.

cards.question: Warnings of AI catastrophe from those working with it and the technological aggravation of Ukraine's destruction offer _____ for whether AI's rapid progress can or should be slowed, the article's opening says.
cards.abstract:
Conflicting lessons is the article's phrase for what two things, set out in its opening paragraph, offer to the question of whether AI's rapid progress can or should be slowed down. The first of the two things, it says, is that those working with the technology are warning about it leading to a catastrophe, human extinction even. The second is how technological innovation is aggravating the destruction of Ukraine. The paragraph supplied does not say which technologies it means in Ukraine or what lesson the war teaches, and it does not spell out how the two lessons conflict. It begins by saying that these two things should make readers consider what artificial intelligence could mean for humanity.

On the side of the warnings, the article says that leading AI bosses have signalled for years that their technology could become lethal, and that agents escaping their sandboxes during testing have made the warnings more credible. It adds that a call to 'pace the frontier', meaning to slow AI's progress, was endorsed on 12 September by Sam Altman and Elon Musk, and that those in favour of a slowdown include Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon. The standfirst frames the difficulty differently, saying that America will struggle to make the technology safe while staying ahead of China. Lecture 2 describes technology changing war, citing iPad firing tables using consumer electronics in the Ukraine war as an example of an explosion of connectivity, and listing drones among emerging technologies, with a slide titled 'Drone Warfare: Ukraine-Russia'. Lecture 5 adds that both Moscow and Kyiv believe another year will yield a better bargaining position amid shifting global dynamics that include technology, political shifts in the United States and the European Union, and European rearmament.

cards.question: In a theory of security partnerships, the _____ of an international organisation's secretariat is defined as 'the capacity to act intentionally', and outside funding can either diminish or increase it.
cards.abstract:
Recipient agency is the quantity that, the article says, outside funding can either diminish or increase, and the article builds it on a definition of agency as 'the capacity to act intentionally'. For the secretariat of an international organisation, the article says, 'intention' is the secretariat's agenda and 'capacity' is its administrative capacity. It therefore defines secretariat agency as the administrative capacity to use resources meaningfully and efficiently to control and act on a policy agenda that guides resource mobilisation and institutional operation. The first element, capacity, is the ability to use administrative and political expertise to mobilise and transform resources, and it is required for financial management, project management, project design and implementation. The second element, the policy agenda, describes the presence of policy goals, which may result from delegation by member states or may deviate from or add to those principals' agendas.

The article treats this agency as the dependent variable and the design of financing agreements as the independent variable, since such contracts set the type of resource, the financial management provisions and the purposes of the contract. The article captures the variation with two interaction modes, a cooperative one in which the partnership enhances the recipient's agency and a coercive one in which a partner imposes a change against the recipient's will. Its recipient organisation is the African Union Commission, whose agency it calls a central dimension of African agency and which, it argues, exercises considerable organisational agency. That agency, the article argues, relegates the EU, despite being a large payer, to the role of a small player, particularly when it comes to directly influencing the AU. The article adds that African agency, as the general capacity to act intentionally, does not necessarily prevent the pursuit of policies that resemble postcolonial arrangements.

'Intention' is a secretariat's policy agenda and 'capacity' its administrative ability to use resources meaningfully and efficiently, and together they make up its _____, which the article says funding can raise or lower.

cards.sub: Reading 13 · EU–AU security partnership (Staeger)

cards.question: A funder can raise or lower a recipient organisation's agency depending on which of the two _____ governs their relationship, one enhancing agency and the other imposing change against the recipient's will.
cards.abstract:
Cooperative and coercive interaction modes are the two ideal-typical ways, in the article's theory, that an outside partner and an international organisation's secretariat can relate to each other. In the cooperative mode the partnership enhances the recipient's agency, while in the coercive mode a partner imposes a change against the recipient's will and so lowers its agency. In a cooperative relationship, the article says, the principal may support the agent's intentions or simply allow the agent to act intentionally by not imposing conditionality. Principals and secretariats in that mode may be driven by the joint attainment of a goal, and resources may be provided with fewer strings attached, becoming more likely to arrive without conditionality when the funder aligns with the secretariat's preferences. Coercive relationships, by contrast, lower agency by restricting the secretariat's capacity to act intentionally, which happens when the principal's purpose is implemented against the secretariat's intentions.

Funders may apply sanctions or conditionality to achieve particular policy agendas or changes in secretariat capacity, and even a recipient that invited the relationship must accept the decrease in agency to continue it. The article says this type of relationship has been described extensively in the Europeanisation and conditionality literature, where the EU offers cash payments or promises of progress in accession for policy reforms. Its analysis finds the EU's security partnership with the African Union dominated by cooperative agenda-setting and capacity-building, which enhances the overall agency of the AU Commission, alongside rare but important instances of EU coercion. It established the modes through a multi-source content analysis, focused on the inter-organisational realm of direct power, whose first and main method was to examine discursive evidence in the language of EU and AU documents and interview transcripts. The conclusion adds that direct inter-organisational relations are far more cooperative than much literature and popular critique would suggest, though cooperative relations do not preclude coercive patterns in the indirect realm of coloniality.
questions: The two _____ are contrasted in that one offers money with fewer strings when the funder aligns with the secretariat, while the other attaches sanctions or conditionality to secure a policy agenda.
A study of the EU's security partnership with the African Union finds the two _____ unevenly spread, with cooperation dominant and coercion appearing only in rare but important instances.

cards.question: The two mechanisms of agency change, _____, differ in that one concerns the purpose of a financing agreement while the other concerns its financial management provisions.
cards.abstract:
Agenda-setting and capacity-building are the two causal mechanisms through which, in the article's theory, an outside partner can change the agency of an international organisation's secretariat. The article says agenda-setting captures how the purpose of a financing agreement shapes the secretariat's agenda, while capacity-building describes how financial management provisions in an agreement shape the secretariat's capacity. Both mechanisms relate to the content and design of specific financing agreements, in which principals state the resources to be provided along with precise terms for their transfer. Cooperative agenda-setting can increase agency, for example when an agreement docks onto the secretariat's existing policy agenda or stipulates purposes that the organisation actively requests during negotiations. Coercive agenda-setting is agency-decreasing mandating, which occurs through conditionality or policy goals the secretariat has not previously espoused, and earmarking funds is a particularly common form of it.

The capacity-building mechanism describes how a funding relationship can shape the secretariat's capacity, by changing its ability to mobilise administrative and political expertise. Cooperative capacity-building occurs when agreements specify financial management purposes that match the secretariat's requests, or when a funder supplies resources to enhance the secretariat's capacity. Coercive capacity-building occurs when agreements impose capacity-related purposes on the secretariat in return for continued or future resources, which reduces its ability to run its bureaucracy as it intended. The article reports that the African Union succeeds more easily at politicising and criticising coercion in agenda-setting than in capacity-building, where the politics of financial management are buried in bureaucracy. It concludes that resource mobilisation should be understood through these separate mechanisms, which pertain to the recipient's agenda and capacity, and that this disaggregated view helps assess the seldom unidirectional effects of diversified funding.
questions: Earmarking funds counts as coercive mandating under one of the _____, while an agreement that supplies resources to enhance a secretariat's capacity is cooperative under the other.
Of the two _____, the African Union can politicise and criticise EU coercion more easily in the one about purposes than in the one about financial management, which is buried in bureaucracy.

cards.question: Because the EU claims a post-postcolonial status while any involvement in African integration can be framed as colonial continuity, the partnership is structured by the _____, which makes direct coercion costly.
cards.abstract:
The postcolonial paradox is the article's name for the tension that structures relations between the EU and the African Union, which occur within a context of complex and persisting coloniality. On the one hand, the article says, the EU operates on the disproven assumption that it is a post-postcolonial entity whose normative power entitles it to a leadership role in Africa's pan-African integration process. On the other hand, any EU involvement in African integration can be framed as a continuity of practices from colonial times. This creates an imperative for both the EU and the AU to avoid forms of interaction that appear neo-colonial, and the article says any EU coercion has high costs in how the relationship is perceived. The EU addresses this by eschewing most direct uses of coercive power, since such direct power is likely to be criticised as neo-colonial.

In the broader ideational and normative space of Africa-EU relations the EU still imparts strong indirect influence, through standard-setting, ideational leadership and blueprints for regional integration, and the diffuse nature of this power makes it harder to pinpoint and criticise. In the direct relationship, the article says, the postcolonial imperative to avoid coercion means the EU tends to shift its focus away from coercion over the Commission's agenda and capacity and towards cooperative engagement where interests coincide. When the EU capped troop reimbursements for the African Union's mission in Somalia, the article says, the directive nature of the imposition cost it dearly in perceptions, as it had acted against the paradox's push for cooperation. The article adds that the Commission's pursuit of African agency results in an overarching interest in working closely with the EU while locking it out of actual decision-making processes. Its conclusion says the EU and AU have invested considerable resources in a highly capitalised partnership that accommodates the paradox's contradictory imperatives: African-led governance of security as well as the appetite for readily available European funds.
questions: The EU's avoidance of direct coercion towards the African Union Commission, with influence kept in indirect forms such as standard-setting, follows from the _____ and the wish not to look neo-colonial.
The directive way the EU capped troop reimbursements for the African Union's mission in Somalia cost it dearly in perceptions, since it acted against the _____'s push for cooperation.

cards.question: Operating outside the EU budget, with €2.7 billion allocated between 2004 and 2017, the _____ paid for almost all African Union peace and security operations yet gave Brussels little say.
cards.abstract:
The African Peace Facility is the main vehicle through which the EU, which has supported African security initiatives since 2004, provides resources to the African Union for peace and security, particularly for non-lethal military materials and services. It operates outside the EU budget and had a substantial €2.7 billion allocated between 2004 and 2017, and as a result the AU's peace and security operations were funded almost exclusively by it. The article's section heading calls it 'a purse without power', and says that despite the EU's leading role as a funder the African Union Commission does not allow the EU many opportunities to impose policy purposes on its agenda. The Commission achieves this by front-loading political decisions and separating agenda-setting from resource mobilisation, and the EU's cooperative role rests on its alignment with the agenda of the Commission's Peace and Security Department whenever possible. The EU tends to respond positively to all requests for support, and the article reports no known instance of it refusing an African Peace Facility request altogether.

In planning an operation, finding political agreement among member states and resource mobilisation are 'two different vectors' of decision-making, and mobilisation is usually an informal process that follows agreement on the mandate. The department also holds conferences at which pre-approved mission budgets are presented to partners, and in either situation facility support comes in after it has made critical decisions independently of the EU. The EU has a latent possibility for agenda-setting at the level of mission planning, but because the department's planning processes lack institutionalisation, its agenda-setting capacity remains marginal. Few of the draft planning documents are officially endorsed, which leaves EU counterparts 'a bit lost', and the article says this bureaucratic dysfunctionality, though perhaps not entirely intentional, is an effective barrier to conditionality-based EU agenda-setting. Contributions through the African Peace Facility required a formal role for the African Union Commission, the article notes, whereas the new European Peace Facility enables EU forum-shopping in African security.
questions: Because the African Union Commission decides on missions before seeking money, support from the _____ arrives after critical decisions are taken, and no outright EU refusal of a request is known.
The EU's newer European Peace Facility lets it forum-shop in African security, whereas contributions through the earlier _____ required a formal role for the African Union Commission.

cards.question: The EU's partnership with the African Union is summed up as _____: it pays by far the most, yet its direct influence over the African Union Commission is slight.
cards.abstract:
Big payer, small player sums up the contradiction at the centre of the EU's partnership with the African Union, in which, the article says, large contributions suggest considerable EU influence yet there is a perception of little influence in EU circles. The article reports that the EU argues it must 'stop being a payer and start being a player', a phrase it attributes to an interview with a European External Action Service official. The EU is by far the biggest funder of peace and security initiatives at the AU, and it accounts for up to 80 per cent of external contributions to the AU's peace and security budget. Yet at the AU, the article says, the EU's importance is concealed by showcasing less resource-rich partnerships with other actors. African media and citizens, it adds, regularly accuse Europe of neocolonial influence in the continent's regional institutions.

The abstract argues that the AU Commission exercises considerable organisational agency, which relegates the EU, despite being a large payer, to the role of a small player. The conclusion says that the adage 'he who pays the piper calls the tune' fails to capture the dynamics between money and power in this partnership. It adds that the Commission holds a surprising amount of power over its funders and has built its resource mobilisation so that the EU is a marginal player in its decision-making processes. Member states funded only 48 per cent of the programme budget of the Commission's Peace and Security Department in 2020, and the EU and other partners fill the gaps left by arrears and the financial inability of member states. Even so, the conclusion says, the Commission's over-reliance on the EU hinders its agency, despite its diversified partner base.
questions: Funding up to 80 per cent of the external money in the African Union's peace and security budget, the EU is nonetheless a _____, marginal in the Commission's decision-making.
The article rejects the adage 'he who pays the piper calls the tune' for the EU and the African Union, whose position as _____ means large payments buy little direct influence.

cards.question: In 2016 the EU capped payments at €738 without consultation, a decision over _____ that the African Union had little choice but to accept despite significant resistance.
cards.answerDate: EU first pays2007Matches UN rates2009EU cap2016
cards.abstract:
AMISOM troop reimbursements are payments for the African Union Mission in Somalia that cover the costs of deploying personnel abroad, including personal equipment, direct deployment allowances and often small troop salaries. Troop reimbursements are the largest expense in the AU's peace and security operation budget, and AMISOM, its largest operation, had more than 20,000 soldiers at times while AU member states financed only about 4 per cent of its cost. The arrangement with the EU stems from 2009, when the EU agreed to match UN rates, after first agreeing in 2007 to pay US$500 per soldier per month. By 2016 AMISOM's troop size had grown almost fifteen-fold to 22,000, while the UN aimed to raise its rate from US$1,028 to US$1,410 per soldier per month by 2017, which the AU expected the EU to follow. The EU opposed the increase and capped troop reimbursements at €738 in 2016, which an EU representative said was done to avoid inflating AMISOM's budget from US$20 million to US$33 million.

The EU asked the AU to choose other AMISOM budget lines on which to spend an unchanged total of EU funds, and implemented this without consultation as a 'fait accompli'. Despite significant resistance the AU had little choice but to accept this conditionality, though its Military Operations Coordination Committee made a rare public criticism, regretting a 20 per cent cut in the troop allowance. The article treats the cap as coercive agenda-setting that curtailed the African Union Commission's agency, and focuses on AMISOM because close to all interviewees brought it up as a leading example of EU coercion. It says the case clearly affected AMISOM's course and eventual drawdown, and six months after the ceiling took effect the Peace and Security Council endorsed a concept of operations referencing an exit strategy. The conclusion adds that the AU is considerably better at marginalising the EU in agenda-setting and capitalised on this highly publicised incident, while the directive imposition cost the EU dearly in perceptions.

cards.question: Failing the EU's _____ in 2014, in accounting, procurement and sub-delegation, led Brussels to interrupt disbursements to the African Union Commission for several months and caused a cash flow crisis.
cards.answerDate: First assessed2014PassedDecember 2019
cards.abstract:
The Pillar Assessment is an ex-ante assessment of the financial management systems of the EU's funding recipients, and through it the EU imposes conditionality regarding financial management. The EU establishes whether a recipient precisely matches the 'principles, standards, and methods' of EU financial management, and the assessment covers the recipient's internal control, accounting and independent external audit systems. If the recipient does match, the EU can use its financial management systems through 'indirect management', which promises considerable efficiency gains and effectively makes the recipient an agent implementing EU external action programmes. The article says the assessment effectively imposes a wealth of financial management conditionalities on the African Union Commission by linking them to the promise of future disbursements that are easier to handle. Although it is based on positive incentives and cushioned with additional support, the article says, it remains coercive.

The Commission was first assessed in 2014 by the consultancy firm EY but failed in the accounting, procurement and sub-delegation areas, and the EU then interrupted disbursements for several months, leading to a cash flow crisis. In line with what the article calls the postcolonial paradox, the Commission does not communicate publicly about the assessment, and the AU prefers to keep its acquiescence to EU coercion in capacity-building below the radar of public scrutiny. Because the conditions demanded significant bureaucratic resources, the article says, the assessment decreased the agency of the Commission's Peace and Security Department in the short term. The EU cushioned its conditionality with short-term fixes, including paying for consultants, funding activities towards a second attempt, contracting EY to accompany the follow-up and financing the valuation of all the Commission's assets for audit purposes. These measures helped the AU pass in December 2019, since when the department has accessed EU resources more easily, which raises the question whether short-term coercion with potential long-term positive effects on agency is more palatable than other forms of coercion.

The African Union eventually passed the EU's _____ in December 2019, after Brussels paid for consultants and an asset valuation to cushion conditions that had decreased the department's agency.
