cards.question: When partners' capacity-building takes up so much room that the Peace and Security Department cannot develop its own, the result is _____, which the article says creates structural conditions for continued dependence.
cards.abstract:
Capacity substitution is what the article says EU-led capacity-building often amounts to, as partners' efforts take too much space for the Peace and Security Department of the AU Commission to develop its own capacity. The article says the department faces considerable capacity challenges as the secretariat of the AU's peace and security operations, and that external partners have laudable intentions to fix them. Funders can increase a secretariat's capacity through financial management and resources, it says, and such capacity-building increases agency if it is devoid of conditionality and aligns with the secretariat's funding requests. The agency outcomes are mitigated, because EU-led capacity-building solves some short-term problems, such as salary payments and the lack of technical expertise, but often amounts to substitution. This ultimately creates, the article says, the structural conditions for continued dependence on partners.

On salaries, the EU directly supports the department's pay but has no say in hiring and firing at the Commission, which has about 40 regular and 130 short-term staff. The Joint Financing Agreement for salaries is devoid of conditionality, so the article counts it as cooperative capacity-building that enhances agency, although partners lament not having enough of a say in return for their contributions. The department also set up a Project Management Team of about twelve staff chiefly to deal with EU funding, with other staff hired to focus exclusively on large contracts. While helpful for eventual compliance with the EU's Pillar Assessment, the article says, this form of capacity-building arguably substitutes secretariat capacity rather than building it up sustainably. The conclusion adds that over-reliance on the EU hinders the Commission's agency despite its diversified partner base, and that handling more than 60 partners, most making small contributions, comes at considerable administrative cost.
questions: Although EU-led capacity-building solves short-term problems such as salary payments, it often amounts to _____, in which a project management team built chiefly to handle EU funding arguably replaces rather than builds capacity.
Even where salary support carries no conditionality, the article warns of _____, whereby partners' efforts take too much space for the department to develop its own capacity sustainably.

cards.question: By using the European Peace Facility to negotiate funding with sub-regional organisations, member states and ad hoc coalitions, the EU can practise _____ and circumvent the African Union in African security.
cards.abstract:
Forum-shopping is the label the article gives to what the new European Peace Facility enables in African security, namely the EU's ability to circumvent the African Union in future contributions to other security actors. The article says the postcolonial paradox limits how far the EU can shape policy processes at the Commission coercively, which makes alternative organisational fora around the African Peace and Security Architecture an attractive option. Its account of the paradox already says the EU may shift direct forms of power outside the inter-organisational relationship, and it notes that the EU shifts potential coercion onto other actors in the African Peace and Security Architecture. Contributions through the earlier African Peace Facility required a formal role for the African Union Commission, whereas the new European Peace Facility enables EU forum-shopping in African security. The article cites ample institutional design evidence of forum-shopping, while saying that the impact of the European Peace Facility on EU-Africa security partnerships remains to be seen.

As one piece of that evidence, the EU has entered into a 'General Programme' with the AU, which excludes the provision of lethal military assets that is otherwise possible through the European Peace Facility. The article reads the General Programme as arguably a commitment to a normative, cooperative EU, and says the AU will likely be the only EU partner to receive one. It lets the Commission request EU funds through a simplified procedure with fewer veto points for EU member states, and it carries over many activities previously funded under the African Peace Facility. New European Peace Facility assistance measures with other African security actors show, the article says, that the EU is ready to balance the AU's primary role with negotiating funding with less subsidiary actors such as sub-regional organisations, member states and ad hoc coalitions. It adds that time will tell what impact the interaction mode and volume of non-AU support will have on the agency of the Commission.

Because the postcolonial paradox limits how coercively the EU can shape policy inside the African Union Commission, alternative organisational fora around the continent's security architecture make _____ an attractive option.

cards.question: The extension of parts of the acquis communautaire to non-member states, short of formal membership, is what the article calls _____, an approach taking systems of rules, not countries, as its starting point.
cards.abstract:
External governance is a concept that seeks to capture the expanding scope of EU rules beyond the borders of the Union. The article gives it a basic definition, saying that it takes place when parts of the acquis communautaire are extended to non-member states. It sees the Union's rules in fields such as environmental, competition or immigration policy developing an external dimension, which consists in an attempt to transfer them to third countries and international organisations. Enlargement is called the most prominent case of external action based on projecting the acquis, whereas external governance also covers forms of integration into the European system of rules that remain below the threshold of membership. It varies across countries, regions and policy fields, from the European Economic Area and the European neighbourhood policy to bilateral agreements with Switzerland and looser frameworks with the African, Caribbean and Pacific countries.

The approach rejects the unitary state actor model that traditional foreign policy analysis projects on to the Union, and adopts a more institutionalist view instead. A foreign policy perspective, the article says, concentrates on countries or regions as units of analysis, whereas the governance perspective takes systems of rules as its point of departure. When third countries take part in defining the relevant EU policies, the authors speak of extended governance. The summary finds external governance particularly intensive with the close neighbours in the West who have committed to adopting significant parts of the acquis, and also intensifying with the countries of the neighbourhood policy. It concludes that the Union has shown it can establish institutional order in its neighbourhood without expanding its membership, but that this order is more sectorally fragmented and differentiated, and less Europeanised, than the one projected through enlargement.

cards.question: Transferring the Union's rules and policies to third countries usually rests on the _____, a term the article never defines, and in accession talks the Union can demand it be transposed in full.
cards.abstract:
The article never stops to define the acquis communautaire, but it treats it as the basis of EU external action, the rules and policies that the Union tries to transfer to third countries. It adds that the deepening of integration in fields such as environmental, competition or immigration policy is giving that action an external dimension. Its basic definition is that external governance takes place when parts of the acquis are extended to non-member states. Enlargement is the most prominent case of external action based on projecting the acquis, and the article reports the Commission calling it the Union's most successful foreign policy. A further reason for interest in external governance, it says, lies in certain qualities of the acquis itself and the externalities it produces.

EU norms and rules may gain prescriptive qualities towards third countries or their citizens by default, without purposeful policy transfer on the part of the Union. The most spectacular case is competition policy, which applies not only to mergers, acquisitions and cartels within the EU but also to firms like Boeing or Microsoft based outside Europe. Where the acquis is strongly integrated, in the sense of precise and enforceable supranational law, the article associates it with the hierarchical mode of governance. In accession talks, the power-based explanation says, candidates are much more dependent on the Union than it is on them, which puts the Union in a position to demand the full transposition of the acquis. Beyond membership, the summary says external governance is less fixated on exporting the precise acquis in its entirety than on promoting approximation to EU norms and practices, at least with the neighbourhood policy countries.

cards.question: Marked by domination and subordination, binding rules and sanctions, _____ comes closest in the European Economic Area, though non-members formally retain full sovereignty vis-à-vis the Union.
cards.abstract:
Hierarchical governance is one of three basic institutional forms of external governance that the article distinguishes, the other two being networks and markets. It takes place in a formalised relationship of domination and subordination and rests on binding prescriptions and proscriptions, which the modern state exerts through legislation that defines enforceable rules whose violation may be sanctioned. Influence is exerted in an asymmetric manner, and at the sectoral level it means steering by formal and precise rules that are non-negotiable, legally binding and enforceable. In the EU it is associated with the Community method, based on supranational law that the European Court of Justice can enforce and sanction, and on decision-making by qualified majority. The article's summary table sets the actor constellation as vertical, with domination and subordination, the institutionalisation as tight and formal, and the mechanism of rule expansion as harmonisation.

In external relations the term must be qualified, since formally non-members retain full sovereignty vis-à-vis the Union. Informally, certain types of external governance come close to a hierarchical system, and the clearest example of such a quasi-hierarchical system is the European Economic Area. The external modes reach from hierarchical settings, in which third countries adapt to a predetermined and legally constraining acquis, often through conditionality, to more horizontal forms of network governance. The institutionalist explanation expects hierarchy to be the most effective mode because rules are normally more legalised in it and strong monitoring and sanctioning promote adoption and application, while the power-based explanation agrees but credits superior EU power. A study of 32 European states between 1980 and 2006 found that EU environmental norms have repeatedly been adopted in third countries and that hierarchy has been the most effective mode of external governance to date.

cards.question: Among formal equals, where no party can bind another without its consent, _____ spreads rules by co-ordination, as through the Joint Committee of the European Economic Area.
cards.abstract:
Network governance is the second of three basic modes of external governance, one in which, in contrast to hierarchy, the actors are formally equal. This does not preclude power asymmetries, but it means that actors have equal rights and that no party can bind the other to a measure without its consent. Networks usually produce less constraining instruments based on mutual agreement, often prescribing procedures rather than final policy solutions. The literature sometimes calls them negotiation systems, in which conflicts of interest are solved through negotiation and voluntary agreement and not through law and jurisdiction. The article's summary table describes the mode as horizontal, with formal equality of partners, medium-tight institutionalisation both formal and informal, and co-ordination as the mechanism of rule expansion.

Inside the EU, network governance has come to challenge the Community method where a lack of permissive consensus precludes transferring legislative power to supranational organs, and it works through agencies, committees and policy networks. Applied to external relations, regulatory expansion occurs through the co-ordination of national rules, and the article finds elements of this in the Joint Committee of the European Economic Area, decentral co-ordination within the sectoral agreements with Switzerland, and the joint Action Plans and Association Councils of the neighbourhood policy. Its voluntary basis and process orientation favour influence through socialisation, social learning and communication, and it leaves negotiating parties more room for manoeuvre, including to use other shared rules such as international rules or new jointly negotiated rules. The power-based explanation expects it where power relations are symmetric and interdependence is medium, because its co-ordination mechanisms compensate for the absence of a dominant power and of an integrated market. When third countries take part in defining relevant EU policies, the article speaks of extended governance, and its summary finds a tendency to rely more on networked forms than on the hierarchical forms of policy export practised in enlargement.

cards.question: Outcomes produced by competition between formally autonomous actors, with the principle of mutual recognition as its typical EU form, are what the article calls _____, the third basic mode of external governance.
cards.abstract:
Market governance is the third basic mode of external governance, in which outcomes result from competition between formally autonomous actors rather than from hierarchical harmonisation or networked co-ordination. The political science literature usually does not regard markets as governance because they lack an overarching system of rule, but newer governance approaches sometimes include competition as an institutionalised form of political market interaction. The article's summary table sets the actor constellation as horizontal with formal equality of partners, the institutionalisation as loose and informal, and the mechanism of rule expansion as competition. In the EU the typical form of institutionalised market governance is the principle of mutual recognition, at least in its application in the Single Market. Avoiding the definition of common rules, mutual recognition unleashes a regulatory dynamic in which, owing to consumers' demand, the most competitive products and services prevail.

This may lead to a voluntary de facto approximation of legislation, and regulatory adaptation may also occur without institutionalised mutual recognition, as a consequence of competitive pressure. Externally, mutual recognition has been extended to the European Economic Area through the full transfer of Single Market legislation, whereas the agreements with Switzerland allow only very limited application of it in the economic sphere. Even without such rules, EU rules can lead to third-country adaptation indirectly, because the Union's impact results from its 'presence' and from third countries' interdependence with its Single Market. The institutionalist explanation expects external governance to take a market mode if the internal policy domain does, while the power-based explanation says it presupposes significant market integration but no dominant, centralised provider, and expects it where interdependence is high and symmetric. The domestic structure explanation adds that market governance does not work without a high degree of economic liberalisation.

cards.question: Three levels of effectiveness, running from international negotiations through domestic legislation to practice in administration and politics, are named _____ in the article's framework for measuring whether EU rules are transferred.
cards.abstract:
Rule selection, adoption and application are the three levels at which, the article says, the effectiveness of EU external governance can be measured. Effectiveness is defined as the extent to which EU rules are effectively transferred to third countries, and joint rules that embed EU rules in international norms are counted alongside them. Rule selection concerns international negotiations and agreements, and asks whether EU rules, or joint rules, form the normative reference point of relations between the Union and a third country. The alternatives are rules set by other international organisations, rules of other states such as the United States or Russia, or purely domestic rules. The article calls selection a relevant first step because, unlike in the study of enlargement, it cannot be taken for granted that EU rules will dominate negotiations.

Rule adoption asks whether the selected rules are then transposed into domestic legislation, which is shown by ratifying agreements with the EU or adopting laws that incorporate EU and joint rules. Rule application asks whether the rules are also acted upon in political and administrative practice, and the article calls it the deepest impact of external governance, while noting that the sequence may be interrupted at any level, so the three levels are studied separately. A note says the authors prefer these terms to transposition and enforcement, which refer to compliance with EU law and so imply a hierarchical mode, since selection, adoption and application are open enough to fit the network and market modes. One contribution examined rule selection in foreign and security policy with Morocco, Ukraine, Georgia and Russia, and found the Union promoting convergence mostly on international and mutually negotiated rules rather than on the acquis alone. The closing pages say the Union may be quite successful at getting third countries to adopt its rules in domestic legislation, yet its impact is much less visible at the level of rule application.

cards.question: Early studies of enlargement stressed _____, in which the geographic expansion of EU rules was mainly driven by the conditional promise of membership, a mode now said to be losing predominance.
cards.abstract:
Governance by conditionality is the label that early studies of enlargement used, the article says, for the expansion of EU rules driven mainly by the conditional promise of EU membership. Other models of Europeanisation, such as social learning or lesson-drawing, were found to be only marginally relevant in the accession process. On the power-based explanation, accession negotiations are the prototypical case of high EU bargaining power, since the Union offers an extremely strong incentive. Candidate countries are usually much more dependent on the Union and eager to join than the reverse, which puts it in a position to demand the full transposition of the acquis, and accession negotiations show an extremely fast and massive adoption of EU rules. Another course reading, on the EU's partnership with the African Union, notes that the Europeanisation and conditionality literature describes how the Union offers cash payments or promises of progress in accession in return for policy reforms.

The article lists precise rules, formal procedures, monitoring and sanctioning, features associated with hierarchy, as necessary prerequisites for the effective exercise of conditionality as a top-down mode of policy transfer based on external incentives. In the more hierarchical settings of external governance, third countries adapt to a predetermined and legally constraining acquis, and the article says this is often done by the use of conditionality. The article expects enlargement to lose momentum and recede into the background, and says accession conditionality is losing its predominance now that accession is becoming less of an option, so other mechanisms need renewed attention. One contribution found that, without hierarchy or accession conditionality, the Union can still induce neighbouring countries to adopt policy-specific democratic governance provisions, particularly when the EU rules are strongly legalised and linked to international norms. The summary adds that even hierarchical democracy promotion through political conditionality is likely to be effective only in countries that are at least partly democratised.

cards.question: Firms like Boeing and Microsoft, based outside Europe, fall under EU competition policy, the most spectacular case of _____, where rules reach outsiders by default and not through purposeful transfer.
cards.abstract:
Governance by externalisation is the article's name for the way EU rules produce negative and positive externalities for outsiders who adopt and comply with them, because ignoring or violating them would create costs. The article says it is most obviously produced by the internal market and competition policies of the Union, since firms interested in participating in the EU market need to follow its rules. It counts the external effects of integration as such as a third and less purposeful trigger for the expansion of external governance, after enlargement and the need to address interdependence with neighbours. It notes that the 'externalities of European integration' persist and that interdependence with the surrounding world creates a need for further external engagement. EU norms and rules may even gain prescriptive qualities towards third countries or their citizens by default, that is, without purposeful policy transfer on the part of the Union.

The most spectacular case is EU competition policy, which applies not only to mergers, acquisitions and cartels inside the Union but also to firms like Boeing or Microsoft based outside Europe. More generally and less visibly, it affects all countries and firms with an interest in exporting to the EU market. The article sees this as in line with a competition mode of governance, which may affect societal actors such as firms and business associations as well as governments induced to change their own rules in line with the EU's. Even where no mutual recognition rules or other direct institutional settings for rule transfer exist, EU rules can lead to adaptation indirectly, through the Union's 'presence' and third countries' interdependence with its Single Market. The Union may also serve as a model that other regions, states and societal actors come to see as an appropriate solution to their own problems, an indirect impact termed lesson-drawing, deliberate emulation or enabling impact.

cards.question: Without high _____ in its favour, the power-based explanation says, the Union cannot impose hierarchical governance, as it could on candidate countries during Eastern enlargement.
cards.abstract:
Asymmetric interdependence is the condition under which, the power-based explanation says, the Union can impose hierarchical governance, namely high interdependence that works in the Union's favour. That explanation attributes the modes and effects of EU external governance to EU resources towards third countries, to interdependence with them, and to alternative poles of influence, namely the United States and Russia. In this view the modes of external governance correspond not to the Union's internal institutional structures but to external structures of power and interdependence. The hierarchical mode requires third countries to be strongly dependent on the EU and more strongly dependent on it than on alternative governance providers, as was the case in Eastern enlargement. The article starts from the assumption that low interdependence will not generate any demand for governance.

Its first power-based hypothesis says that high and asymmetrical interdependence in favour of the governance provider tends to produce hierarchy, high and symmetrical interdependence is conducive to market governance, and medium interdependence to network governance. A second hypothesis says that effectiveness increases with the bargaining power of the governance provider, and on this view accession negotiations are the prototypical case of high EU bargaining power. Outside enlargement, the article says, EU bargaining power is weaker and varies more strongly across countries and policies. A study of Ukraine looked at the limits set by Russia's influence and the Commonwealth of Independent States, and found the effectiveness of EU rule export varying with patterns of interdependence, stronger in trade and weaker in energy and foreign policy. The summary says that constellations of interdependence and bargaining power were identified as central conditions of effectiveness in EU relations with Ukraine, yet none of the hypotheses can safely be discarded.
questions: A study of EU rule export to Ukraine found its effectiveness varied with patterns of _____ with Russia and the Commonwealth of Independent States, stronger in trade than in energy and foreign policy.

cards.question: Lacking the legal formalisation of association relations with the western neighbours, the _____ nevertheless shows network elements such as jointly elaborated Action Plans and joint evaluation of progress in Association Councils.
cards.abstract:
The European Neighbourhood Policy, or ENP, appears in the article as an overarching foreign policy initiative of which external governance is sometimes part, alongside the European Economic Area. The article names the ENP with the European Economic Area and negotiated bilateralism with Switzerland as overarching institutional structures of relations between the Union and third countries. It says the ENP lacks the legal formalisation of association relations with the western neighbours, although a sectoral view shows a more varied picture. Elements of networking in its macro-institutional structure include the joint elaboration of Action Plans, the joint evaluation of progress in Association Councils, and stable communication between sectoral experts in subcommittees. The special issue examines the Union's relations with its western, eastern and southern neighbours across fields from foreign and security policy to trade, energy and democracy promotion.

A comparison of the European Economic Area, Swiss bilateralism and the ENP found that overarching macro-institutional structures have little impact on the modes of governance in individual sectors, which follow largely sectoral dynamics. Another contribution found a hierarchical mode only in the Balkans, while the network mode prevails with Ukraine and the Mediterranean ENP countries, and democracy promotion was moderately effective in the Balkans and Ukraine but weak in the Middle East and northern Africa. The summary finds external governance intensifying with the countries of the ENP and differing significantly from the way the Union exports norms to candidates in the context of enlargement. With the ENP countries it is less fixated on exporting the precise acquis in its entirety than on approximation, and with the eastern and southern neighbours it is an open issue whether EU rules alone provide the normative foundation, since approximation often draws on international or jointly negotiated rules. The article concludes that the Union has established institutional order in its neighbourhood without expanding its membership, but that this order is more sectorally fragmented and differentiated, and less Europeanised, than the order projected through enlargement.
